News.title: Zack Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss
News.content:
Asked whether he agreed with the motion that Zionism is racism, Polanski, who is Jewish, said: "I grew up in a Zionist household and I grew up with the idea that that region was a land without a people and a people without a land and as I've educated myself, learned, discovered, I don't believe that's true.

"And what we're seeing is an ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people. I believe that's clearly racist."

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is currently hearing a case brought by South Africa that accuses Israeli forces of genocide, but it could take years to reach a conclusion. Israel has called the case "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

Pressed again over whether he agreed that "Zionism is racism", Polanski said: "The displacement of the Palestinian people, the genocide, is totally racist."

Asked if he would apologise to Jewish people upset by the vote on the motion, Polanski said: "It's my job to reassure people and to make sure that we bring our party together.

"Nobody will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion."

He denied he had lost control of his party, adding: "I've got a party that was 55,000, 60,000 members when I was running for leader, [which] is now 220,000.

"Any member is entitled to their opinion - we're a democratic grassroots party."

Those who were supportive of the motion want Polanski to come out and explicitly declare it was now party policy.

However, those against it want him to distance himself from the motion and make it clear that he does not support it.

Lucas's comments came shortly after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, but before the result was declared.

Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."

She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told the BBC's Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.

"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.

"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."

The motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's by-election campaign, where the Greens had been hoping to overturn a substantial Labour majority in the seat vacated by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Although Polanski lost out to Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, the party saw its majority reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.

The motion has sparked days of controversy and exposed divisions between the Green Party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Four of the five Green MPs opposed the motion, while the party's co-deputy leaders were split over whether they supported it.

The vote also led to the resignation of the Green deputy leader in Wales and condemnation from the European Green Party, as well as the Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews.

News.title: Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
News.content:
But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election â and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.

Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.

The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And â until today at least â he has been repeatedly declining to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.

"He has created a monster he either can't or won't control," was how one Green figure put it to me - this person one among many left furious at what has happened.

Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.

Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.

And â significantly â the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.

Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".

He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people".

"I believe that is clearly racist," he added.

Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

And asked if he believed in a two-state solution â an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other â he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".

He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together".

"No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.

But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.

The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

News.title: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review
News.content:
There is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism, an official review in England has found.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

The review called for tougher regulation of private firms offering assessments for the NHS, saying they had concerns about quality and consistency, and a ban on advertising.

It concluded economic uncertainty combined with social media was driving an increase in mental health problems among young people and said there needed to be better support in place for all conditions.

The review - led by leading doctors in the field - was ordered 10 months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It looked at people of all ages, but particularly focused on young people and children who have the highest rates of diagnoses.

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

News.title: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.

Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.

His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table.

"Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."

There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"

Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"

But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.

News.title: As freezing winter approaches, Kyiv residents look for shelter elsewhere
News.content:
As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.

"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.

With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.

"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."

Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.

"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.

"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."

News.title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
News.content:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".

In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation".

"Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.

The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.

Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers".

"I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."

Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting.

The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".

He was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS statement.

It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.

News.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
News.content:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.

"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.

For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.

That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.

And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

News.title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
News.content:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.

But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.

The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.

The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.

Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.

Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.

"Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam," he said.

News.title: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says
News.content:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.

Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.

The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.

News.title: Two men arrested on suspicion of trespass at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
News.content:
Two Latvian men were arrested after a fence was breached at an RAF base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, counter-terrorism police have said.

The alert was raised when a Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrol at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday.

Searches revealed a small breach of the fence at the site in Cambridgeshire, and a few hours later, police said the pair were arrested inside the perimeter.

The two men are aged 36 and 32 and live in the UK, the Met Police said.

The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating and commander Helen Flanagan said officers were not currently linking it to the high-profile incident in Gloucestershire.

"We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week," said Flanagan.

However, she stressed the inquiry was in its "very early stages".

They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station.

The pair were later arrested on suspicion of an offence under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, external â namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

RAF Molesworth is home to the US's intelligence operations centres for Europe and Africa, as well as a Nato intelligence hub.

It is not used as a flying station.

News.title: Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds
News.content:
Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said.

On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim.

Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters".

He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link.

In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart".

He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child.

"To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined."

He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added.

If you are experiencing emotional stress, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line here.

The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton.

"It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known."

News.title: Harry says he 'slipped into depression' after leaving UK
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" after relocating to Canada in 2019 ahead of his move to the US.

Prince Harry, who recently returned to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, said he had originally left the country to "get some space."

The duke also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales, because he felt "disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her".

He opened up about his mental health with a neuroscientist in a session for a video learning platform.

He and his brother, the Prince of Wales, have previously been candid about their mental health struggles, including over their mother's death, and both are involved in mental health charities.

Prince Harry, who stepped back from royal duties to move to California with Meghan, made the latest comments as part of a paid-for online masterclass on dealing with grief.

"Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," he recalled.

"It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house.

"I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks and I felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline."

News.title: Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia
News.content:
A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court.

Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligence, allegedly retained UK defence and intelligence material that he had access to and made preparations to disclose sensitive information, a court was told.

The 24-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday after being charged under the National Security Act.

The BBC understands that the allegations against Young include translating a message into Russian and looking for a web portal that invited people to submit information to Russia.

Wearing a police-issue grey sweatshirt, Young spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and his address in Clapham, near Bedford.

He is formally charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for disclosing protected information, and obtaining, copying, recording or retaining protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.

The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025.

"The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service told the court in a written summary of the allegations.

Police said the alleged offences were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident that resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base.

In total, seven men have been arrested and later released on bail in connection with the incident, which is being investigated by counter-terror police.

Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday.

He is the first member of the armed forces to be charged under the new National Security Act 2023.

Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces.

"We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."

A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."

Judge Annabel Pilling remanded Young in custody. He will next appear at the Old Bailey on 16 October.

News.title: Death prompts call for allergy management ratings
News.content:
Assistant coroner Briony Ballard listened to evidence at London Inner South Coroner's Court before publishing a narrative conclusion on Mia's death.

In a statement read after the conclusion of the inquest, Mia's parents Adrian St Hilaire and Chanel Spence said families with food allergies should not be "at risk" when eating out.

"We hope that lessons will be learned from Mia's death and that changes will be made to prevent other families enduring the devastation that we now have to live with," they said.

"Consumers rely on food hygiene ratings when deciding where it is safe to eat, but they do not tell us anything about the way a food business runs allergy management systems.

"There should be a separate, clearly displayed rating dedicated to the allergy management, like the food hygiene rating.

"This would mean that people with allergies could make more informed choices about where they eat."

Natasha's Foundation founder Tanya Ednan-Laperouse, whose daughter died aged 15 from an allergy to sesame in a Pret A Manger baguette, said allergies were "a serious, unpredictable medical condition".

"The inquest into Mia's death illustrates just how far we still have to go to improve awareness, understanding and regulation of food allergies," she said.

"Natasha's Foundation is working hard with business, schools, communities and the government to increase awareness and understanding of food allergies to try to prevent other families from having to go through the terrible loss that Mia's family endure."

Rebecca Sudworth, director of food policy at the Food Standards Agency, said her "deepest sympathies" were with Mia's family.

"Food businesses must take allergen risks seriously, every time," she said. "People have the right to know exactly what is in their food and drink, and it is a business's legal duty to provide accurate allergen information.

"We recently produced new guidance for businesses to make sure they understand their responsibilities to inform consumers about allergens, including the risk of cross-contact, and we are keeping this policy under review. We also have free allergy training and practical tools that businesses can use."

News.title: Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women
News.content:
Police Scotland has said 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

Chief constable Jo Farrell said she expected more would face sanctions over their behaviour following a spate of former officers being convicted for sexual offences.

Farrell said a review into the handling of the case surrounding officer Alan Greer â who was exposed as a serial rapist after taking his own life â was under way.

She added about 8,000 members of staff were still to be "re-vetted" for their roles after a change in regulations earlier this year.

First minister John Swinney said he had "full confidence" in Police Scotland and the renewed vetting process.

In an interview with BBC Scotland News, Farrell described the scale of violence against women and girls in Scotland as an "epidemic", and that police forces were not immune to the problem.

She said: "We've got in the order of between currently 40 and 50 people currently suspended, so not at work, who are being investigated for offences that relate to violence against women and girls.

"Those investigations are at various stages."

News.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
News.content:
Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.

One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.

The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know.

"What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.

With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

News.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Zelensky slams US and says Kyiv needs Starlink after Putin’s ‘horrifying’ bus attack
News.content:

News.title: A relationship expert explains why time apart is a good thing. Just ask Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When couples get married, they vow to stick together for better or worse, in sickness and in health. But what happens if they can’t work through a rocky patch together and need to work on themselves instead?

Michael Douglas has shed light on his several months-long split from his wife, Catherine Zeta-Jones, in his new memoir One Helluva Ride. The pair had been married for 13 years when they separated briefly in 2013 — around the time he told a newspaper his cancer had been caused by HPV he’d contracted through oral sex. Zeta-Jones was reportedly upset by his admission at the time, and he later said he regretted causing her embarrassment.

The Welsh actress had said in a statement the couple was “taking some time apart to evaluate and work on their marriage,” and they reunited a few months later. Asked how he rekindled the flame in a recent interview with The Sunday Times, Douglas replied: “What, I won her back? It was a mutual… You know, we had our problems, but I love her dearly and, 25 years, you know.” It seems to have worked out: they will celebrate their 26th wedding anniversary this November.

They are not the only Hollywood couple to take time apart to figure things out before coming back to one another. Ben Stiller and his wife Christine Taylor split in 2017 after 17 years of marriage but rekindled their relationship during the pandemic; Sylvester Stallone and Jennifer Flavin went back on their 2022 divorce announcement and said they were “extremely happy”; Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard came back from a breakup when they first started dating; Justin Timberlake and Jessica Biel split in 2011 but wed a year later.

There are others to add to that list: Gabrielle Union and Dwayne Wade; Pink and Carey Hart; Richard Burton and Elizabeth Taylor famously married twice.

open image in gallery Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones had been married for 13 years when they separated briefly in 2013. They rekindled their relationship months later ( Getty Images for The Hollywood R )

Taking a break in any type of relationship can be extremely beneficial, says Dr. Eli Kraiem, couples and relationship expert and adjunct professor at Ferkauf Graduate School in New York City. A split could be for a multitude of reasons — a break of trust due to infidelity, financial problems, poor communication or a lack of intimacy — but Kraiem says a brief separation could be an opportunity for both partners to step away and ask themselves a simple question: Do I really want to be with this person?

“A brief split could be really helpful because it gives each partner the space to reflect on the negative patterns that they got stuck in,” says Kraiem. “A break can help us kind of rediscover who we are, what we want, what our values are, what our true feelings are. It’s also an opportunity to make an intentional decision about choosing your partner again.” Kraiem adds that deciding to pick a partner again can be extremely powerful and romantic.

“It creates a lot of hope to see your partner show up differently, or see yourself show up like that. It might be, ‘Wow, I didn’t know we were capable of this,’” he continues. But the relationship can’t go on as it previously was, of course. “The couple must choose to be different people, for the relationship to be different and to work on things that weren’t right in the past,” he says.

The therapist says he doesn’t prescribe rules to his clients when they take time apart, but he says the less contact, the better. “It’s so that you don't get engulfed by the relationship, even if you're physically apart, because you need to have the emotional space to process without feeling stuck in the relationship,” he says.

open image in gallery Ben Stiller and his wife Christine Taylor split in 2017 after 17 years of marriage but salvaged their marriage during the pandemic ( AFP via Getty Images )

Anna Elton, a Florida-based couples therapist and author of The Formula of Desire, does offer some loose rules for her clients who take relationship breaks. She says that 30 days could be the magic number for taking time apart and advises on minimum contact. “It gives you a chance to calm your nervous system down so you are not impulsive, and that you’re able to think clearly,” she says. “It’s an opportunity to step back and analyze the whole situation, the relationship and your thinking.”

Elton says she asks couples three things: “Why did you like the person? Why did you commit to the person? And why are you still trying to make it work?”

She says that couples need to figure out what needs to change before they rekindle, so that they have a clear roadmap. “If nothing changes, you’ll just reenter the same scenario.”

“That honeymoon period of missing each other will be over very quickly,” she says. “After two weeks max, you will be back in the same cycle again.”

Elton’s 30-day break advice has no scientific research to back it up, but many of her clients try it. What Elton says matters more is how much work is actually done during the separation.

open image in gallery Sylvester Stallone and Jennifer Flavin went back on their 2022 divorce announcement and stayed together. They have been married for 29 years ( Getty Images )

“Are both people reflecting on why the relationship stopped working?” she says. “Are they changing the patterns that led to the split? And when they reconnect, are they coming back because something has actually changed, or simply because they miss one another?”

There are, of course, times when a relationship should not be salvaged. If microcheating, infidelity and more serious issues, like domestic abuse, have occurred, then there may be a point of no return (each relationship is different and would be judged by a therapist on a case-by-case basis). Couples who repeatedly break up and reconcile without resolving underlying issues may not reap the benefits of a fresh slate. A break can only work if both parties are intentional.

During an interview with The McBride Rewind podcast, Christine Taylor reflected on reconciling with Ben Stiller during the lockdown after four years apart, saying that the changes and pressures that came in adult life made them grow apart. “I met Ben when I was 28 years old … you have different chapters and stages in your life, and I feel that’s also true for adults and particularly women,” she said. “You get married, become a mom, for those who become mothers … career, put your career on hold, all those different chapters, and I think at that moment in time for us, we were just not on the same page with a lot of things.”

It was a similar story for Gabrielle Union and Dwyane Wade, who broke up in 2013 after dating for four years, got back together and were married one year later. “We kind of took a step back. We supported each other, but we took a step back for a little while,” Wade said on The Tonight Show. “At the end of the day, we came back together and said, ‘Listen, we want to continue this. We want to try to continue to get better each day,’” he said.

As for Douglas and Zeta-Jones, who have a 25-year age gap, the Basic Instinct actor seems to think the reconciliation paid off.

“I never gave up hope that we would reconcile,” he wrote in his new memoir.

He told The Sunday Times: “We’re in good shape. It’s all I can say.”

News.title: Kim Kardashian reveals number of nannies she has for her and Kanye West’s four kids
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Kardashian-West kids are outnumbered by their nannies.

Kim Kardashian shares her four children — North, 13, Saint, 10, Chicago, eight, and Psalm, seven — with her ex-husband Kanye West.

In a new interview, the reality star told The Sunday Times Style magazine she has five nannies who work on rotation to help look after her children.

The billionaire Skims founder explained that although one nanny is always on duty, Kardashian is the one who drops her kids off and picks them up from school each day — and that they all have dinner together every night.

“I think I am an intermediate-strict parent,” Kardashian, 45, told the magazine. “I’m extremely patient and loving. I still have a kid sleep in my bed when they want. I read books with the kids every night.”

open image in gallery Kim Kardashian said she always has dinner with her four children ( Reuters )

The reality TV star said that she takes it upon herself to discuss wealth and privilege with her children.

“It’s something I talk to my kids about constantly, about hard work, never taking things for granted, always having gratitude,” she said. “I lead by example. I’m really open with them about my work, all of the hard work that I put into my law studies, and they’re proud. I think that you can have a big life and still have that spirit in you. But it is more challenging.”

Kardashian spoke briefly in the interview about how she co-parents with 49-year-old West, to whom she was married from 2014 to 2022, when it comes to North’s solo music career.

“That is something that her dad and I have better communication about,” Kardashian said. “We make sure we’re aligned and that she’s in projects that we both approve.”

open image in gallery Kardashian said she communicates well with Kanye West about North West’s music career ( Getty )

open image in gallery Kim Kardashian and Kanye West were married from 2014 to 2022 ( AFP/Getty )

Kardashian and West have had a publicly turbulent co-parenting relationship since the businesswoman filed for divorce in 2021.

In October 2025, Kardashian said during her interview on Call Her Daddy that sharing custody with the famous rapper has been “a lot of work.”

“It’s not easy, but I raise the kids full time,” she said on the podcast. “They live with me. I welcome a great, healthy relationship with my kids and their dad. He knows that. I push for it all the time. But I also protect them when it's time for that... it’s a lot of work.”

She added: “The one thing that gets me is that there’s this narrative that I keep the kids...away from him. I never once [have] done that.”

News.title: Joe Manganiello blames mystery autoimmune illness for Sofía Vergara divorce
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Joe Manganiello has opened up about the seven-year illness that left him fearing he was going to die.

Manganiello, 49, wrote about his struggles in his forthcoming memoir, Bloodlines, and how the autoimmune illness led to “major organ amputation.” He also shared the impact of the illness on his marriage to Sofía Vergara. The two married in 2015 and filed for divorce in 2023.

Speaking to People about the ordeal, the True Blood star said: “I can’t believe I’m alive. I feel like I was reborn.

“For seven years I thought I was going to be dead the next week. The world has opened back up to me.”

Manganiello began feeling ill shortly after his 2015 wedding to Vergara, suffering from abdominal pain, fevers, rashes, fatigue and headaches. Between then and 2022, he lost 60 pounds and had multiple surgeries, all due to autoimmune disease.

open image in gallery Joe Manganiello and Sofia Vergara were married from 2015 to 2023 ( AFP/Getty )

He was prescribed medications to manage nerve pain and treat Crohn’s and colitis, but “none of them worked on me,” he said. To ease the pain, he relied on hydrocodone pills, fentanyl patches and marijuana. But that led to him grappling with his 13 years of sobriety.

“I didn’t feel like I deserved to say that I was sober,” he said, “[but] I had to put the pain and the condition first.”

Manganiello’s condition caused a rift in his marriage, which he said in the memoir had “become devoid of any emotionality whatsoever.” In the book, he claimed Vergara refused to hug him, People reported.

The marriage hit another speed bump, he said, over having kids. Failed IVF attempts had the couple considering an egg donor. But Manganiello said he didn’t want to die and leave the Modern Family star with a child “who wasn’t biologically hers.”

The Modern Family alum, meanwhile, told Spanish newspaper El País at the time of their breakup that their split had stemmed from the Magic Mike actor wanting a child, while she did not. Manganiello later disputed that claim in a July 2024 interview with Men’s Journal.

open image in gallery Manganiello shared new details of his harrowing health journey ( Getty )

“There were things said and printed about me that were false,” he told People.

The Independent has contacted a representative for Vergara for comment.

Ultimately, Manganiello sought help beyond traditional medicine. He believes his healing came from a shaman in Santa Monica who said the illness was connected to Manganiello’s generational trauma.

“Whatever chains there were to the past suffering of my ancestors, they were completely broken. There’s not an ounce of fear in me about moving forward with my life,” he said.

Manganiello told People he is now symptom-free and off medications. He’s engaged to Winning Time: The Rise of the Lakers Dynasty actor Caitlin O’Connor and the two recently left Los Angeles in favor of their native Pennsylvania.

News.title: The government wants UK households to stock up on nine items. Here’s what to buy
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

UK households should keep small supplies of cash, bottled water and tinned food at home in case of emergency or war, the Defence Secretary has warned.

Wes Streeting said Britain faces a growing threat of being disrupted by fires, floods, and enemy attacks, including cyber warfare.

He called for a "whole society approach" to strengthen national resilience, though he insisted people should remain "alert not alarmed" regarding potential risks.

Speaking to The Sun ahead of the Labour Party conference, he said: "It’s just a simple ask of people.

"Do they have what they need indoors, should they lose access to their online banking for a period? Should they have a power cut?”

open image in gallery British households are being advised to stock up on tinned food. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

It comes as the government releases a list of supplies for an emergency kit they say everyone should keep at home.

Here we look at the key items you should stock up on in case disaster strikes.

What should people stockpile?

Wes Streeting has advised the British public there are certain items they should store for emergencies.

He said: "These are basic things, and of course, you know, a lot of people just have that in their cupboard naturally.

"It’s having some cash at home, having a supply of bottled water indoors, having some tinned goods that you can access if your electric goes and you’re not able to cook on the hob or in the microwave.”

Nutritionists and “preppers” on social media also say people should consider intake of carbohydrates and protein, and so suggest items such as oats, rice and pasta be included in any stockpile.

Kidney beans, peanut butter and tinned fish provide high levels of protein.

What should I keep in my emergency kit?

The government says people should put together an emergency kit that includes key provisions you and your household would need during a short-term incident lasting several days, such as a power failure or a disruption to your water supply.

Recommended emergency kit supplies include:

A battery or wind-up torch – torches are safer than candles.

– torches are safer than candles. A portable power bank for charging your mobile phone.

for charging your mobile phone. A battery or wind-up radio to get updates during a power cut – a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside.

– a car radio can be used, however in severe weather it might be safer to stay inside. Spare batteries for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on.

for torches and radio and a backup battery for any medical equipment you rely on. A first aid kit (or some first aid items) including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers.

including items such as waterproof plasters, bandages, a thermometer, antiseptic, eyewash solution, sterile dressings and gloves, medical tape for dressings, and tweezers. Hand sanitiser and wet wipes for hygiene purposes when the water is off.

for hygiene purposes when the water is off. Bottled water – there is no standard figure for this as emergencies can vary in duration and people use different amounts. A minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day is recommended by the World Health Organisation for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets.

A minimum of 2.5-3 litres of drinking water per person per day is recommended by the World Health Organisation for survival. 10 litres per person per day will make you more comfortable by also providing for basic cooking and hygiene needs. Additional water might be needed to make up baby formula, for medical devices and for pets. Non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets.

that doesn’t need cooking, such as ready-to-eat tinned meat, fruit or vegetables (and a tin opener). As with water, how much you need will vary based on your own circumstances. Don’t forget food for pets. Baby supplies such as nappies and baby formula – ready made or ‘ready-to-feed’ formula is best as you may not be able to boil water or sterilise bottles.

open image in gallery Keep some batteries, a radio, a torch and tinned food in your emergency kit at home. ( Getty Images )

Rather than buying all the items at once, you could just add to your emergency kit when you are able and build it up over time. You should try to store these items together in a single location in your home, ideally in a spot that remains simple to locate if the lights are off.

Maintaining a supply of prescription medication to cover several days is also essential. For those who depend on any medical devices or equipment, ensure that printed physical copies of all operating instructions are kept on hand. Furthermore, any available back-up batteries ought to be kept fully charged at all times.

What threats is the government worried about?

Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia.

The government is also concerned following the record-breaking heatwaves the UK has experienced this summer, plunging the country into drought and causing numerous wildfires.

According to the FT, the government is accelerating work on its “war book” – a manual for the defence of the nation against external threats – as well as a social media campaign with advice to help people to deal with the impacts of extreme weather.

It also recently updated its national risk register, with the risk of interference in the UK’s democratic process added to it.

open image in gallery Vladimir Putin’s government warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia. ( AFP/Getty )

The national risk register is the government’s assessment of the most significant risks facing the UK.

It is a planning tool designed to help professionals prepare for risks and is not intended to be a prediction of future events.

Vladimir Putin’s government recently warned that British facilities in Ukraine will be considered “legitimate targets” if they are used to support long-range strikes against Russia.

The Independent also reported that rogue drones are targeting Britain’s military bases almost daily, leaving the UK vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran.

Some 340 security incidents involving drones were reported at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026, data obtained under freedom of information laws show. In 2025, there were a total of 250 incidents recorded – double the 126 recorded the year before.

open image in gallery The Government also plans to advise people on how to deal with the impacts of extreme weather ( Getty )

Why are the heatwaves a concern?

Analysts have warned extreme heat and ongoing droughts are putting Britain at risk of its “worst food security crisis in decades”.

The knock-on impact of five back-to-back heatwaves and prolonged dry conditions could destroy farmers’ harvests, leading to food shortages later this year and increasing reliance on foreign imports, according to analysts from the investment bank Shore Capital.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) warned the situation is “increasingly concerning” and that dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing.

News.title: Jenna Dewan’s fiancé responds to fans saying she’s been ‘touchy’ with DWTS partner
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Jenna Dewan’s fiancé has spoken out about her chemistry with Dancing With the Stars partner Val Chmerkovskiy after fans called out her behavior on this week’s episode.

Dewan and Kazee have been together since 2018 and engaged since 2020. They share two children, a son and a daughter. Chmerkovskiy, meanwhile, has been married to fellow DWTS pro Jenna Johnson since 2019, and they share a son.

On this week’s Mariah Carey-themed episode of the ABC reality competition series, Dewan and Chmerkovskiy danced a rumba to the singer’s “My All,” earning the duo a 24 out of 30 from the judges.

Afterwards, a blogger shared a clip from the episode on Instagram, suggesting Dewan had been “a bit too touchy” with Chmerkovskiy in their post-dance interview.

“They don’t have chemistry. They have too much chemistry. They have chemistry in the wrong place. Make up your minds,” Kazee commented on the post.

open image in gallery Jenna and Val’s chemistry was noted by fans, but her fiancé Steve Kazee brushed it off ( Disney/Getty )

“Y’all really got too much time on your hands. The spouses are unbothered. Stay hatin.”

Kazee then commented again, cementing his support of his spouse: “Also put some respect on my queens name and at least pronounce her name correctly when you try to slander her.”

The video gained enough traction that DWTS judge Carrie Ann Inaba also weighed in, writing: “Dancers are physical beings. This is like the way we say hello. Don’t try to turn it into something it is not. Have some respect for both Jenna and Val and their partners please.”

Inaba previously defended Dewan’s casting on season 35 of the long-running series after fans were critical of her experience as a professional dancer.

The judge told Entertainment Weekly that ballroom is very different from the celebrity’s past training.

“What’s difficult — and I don’t think people realize this — is when you go from being a jazz dancer or a hip-hop dancer or all the other forms of dancing [to ballroom], the weight placement is so different,” Inaba explained.

open image in gallery Kazee and Dewan have been together since 2018 ( Getty )

“It’s weird because your body has memory, so it remembers how to dance, and it thinks it already knows how to do these moves, but it doesn’t. It takes a lot of time to un-train the body to put your weight on the front more over your toes instead of back and down and grounded.”

“It’s not as easy as people think,” Inaba added.

Dewan, 45, started her career as a backup dancer on Janet Jackson's 2001 “All for You Tour” before landing featured roles in music videos for Christina Aguilera, Pink, Missy Elliott and NSYNC, among others. She famously performed alongside Channing Tatum — to whom she was married from 2009 until their divorce was finalized in 2024 — in the 2006 dance movie Step Up.

She went on to host Jennifer Lopez’s dance competition show World of Dance and also served as a judge on the 2022 CBS series Come Dance With Me.

Dewan and Chmerkovskiy were sent through to the next round and will return for DWTS week five, airing Tuesday night.

News.title: Ben Affleck reveals the former co-star he’s still afraid of
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ben Affleck has named the co-star whose performance has continued to haunt him more than a decade after acting together.

The Good Will Hunting star portrayed Nick Dunne, a suspect linked to the mysterious disappearance of his wife, Amy Dunne, in the 2014 David Fincher-directed thriller Gone Girl.

Affleck has admitted that he’s “still afraid” of his co-star and on-screen wife Rosamund Pike in an interview with Variety, while looking back on some of the conversations they had after they shot the movie.

“I’m like, ‘Hey Rosamund. How are you?'” Affleck, 54, said in the recorded video interview, pretending to be skittish.

“She still has that, sort of, look. You know what I mean?” he continued, as he then attempted to mimic Pike’s cold performance in the movie, as well as her British accent.

open image in gallery Ben Affleck and Rosamund Pike acted as a husband and wife in the thriller ‘Gone Girl’ ( 20th Century Studios )

open image in gallery Ben Affleck has admitted that he’s ‘still afraid’ of Rosamund Pike’s haunting performance in the 2014 movie ‘Gone Girl’ ( 20th Century Studios )

“Hello Ben, it’s nice to talk to you,” Affleck said in a mysterious tone, in character as Pike.

“I’m like, ‘Oh, f***,'” Affleck joked. “She still has that quality. It was a great performance. She was great in the movie.”

Adapted from the Gillian Flynn novel of the same name, Gone Girl follows Nick and Amy, a couple with a seemingly perfect marriage. Their love story takes a turn when Amy unexpectedly goes missing on their wedding anniversary, and Nick becomes a prime suspect. It emerges that she staged her own disappearance to frame her husband.

Pike earned an Oscar nomination for Best Actress in 2015, but the award ultimately went to Julianne Moore for her role in Still Alice.

Affleck and Pike were not the first choices to play the couple at the center of the storyline. Jon Hamm was originally considered for the role, but he was unable to film it due to his commitments to the TV series Mad Men, which was in its sixth season.

open image in gallery ‘Gone Girl’ was a huge hit and grossed $369 million at the global office ( Getty Images )

“It was meant to be me, but we had to film the continuing adventures of Mr. Draper,” he said during an appearance on Watch What Happens Live in 2023.

Pike’s role almost went to Reese Witherspoon until Fincher decided she wasn’t right for the role.

“[Fincher] sat me down — and this is not on David, but David’s like, ‘You’re totally wrong for this part, and I’m not putting you in it,’” Witherspoon told the Las Culturistas podcast.

Though she missed out on the role, she said in retrospect that “he was totally right.”

“Fincher just killed it, and Rosamund Pike is so diabolical and Ben Affleck is sort of the rube on the other side of it.”

Gone Girl was a huge hit, grossing $369.3 million at the global box office.

News.title: Costco’s new dessert is convincing people to sign up for memberships: ‘You got me’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Costco is breaking out sweet treats that fans are willing to pay a yearly membership for.

The warehouse chain is known to sell classic bakery items like croissants and sheet cakes, but is now trying out new pastry recipes that have left shoppers raving online.

After the beloved Blueberry Caramelized Cheesecake Croissants became popular last year, the wholesale store has now released its latest endeavor: the Kirkland Signature Lemon Cream Caramelized Croissant.

The lemon dessert is exactly what its name describes: flaky dough and a lemon filling baked into a crispy pastry. But these treats are baked in a round paper liner and get their name, in part, due to sugar at the bottom of the liner that caramelizes while in the oven.

Influencer Laura Jayne Lamb, who has amassed more than three million Instagram followers for her Costco-related content, said it is “one of the best things the Costco bakery has ever done,” adding, “The outside is crisp, buttery, and caramelized, and the middle has this soft tangy lemon cream that balances it out perfectly.”

In the comments of Lamb’s video reviewing the new treat, which costs $12.99 for half a dozen, fans were eager to get their hands on the croissant. “Do I have a membership? No, am I gonna buy one JUST FOR THIS? Maybe,” one person wrote, referencing the store’s $65 annual fee.

“Ok Costco…you got me..I’m gonna get a membership. Idc anymore that I have to drive over an hr to get there and over an hr back,” another person commented. A third added, “Say less I’ll be there tomorrow.”

Other Costco shoppers were excited to see a variation of the fan-favorite blueberry pastries. “The blueberry ones were so good I can only imagine how delicious this will be. Must try!” one person wrote on TikTok.

“The blueberry ones were delish and lemon is one of my favorite flavors…problem is I’ll eat them all myself,” another customer admitted.

Costco is putting out a new pastry ( Getty )

The croissants are rolling out to Costco locations across the U.S., and shoppers can call their local store to see when they will hit shelves.

Costco has not released any information about how long the pastries will remain available, and did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment.

It comes months after Costco began selling buttermilk biscuits in its bakery section. A 10-count box costs around $6.99, depending on location, and is still available for purchase in many stores.

However, the lemon croissants have been met with more excitement than the butter biscuits, which shoppers criticized online as being dry to the taste.

News.title: What is the XFG Covid strain? Symptoms and what to know as the variant hits the UK
News.content:
Cases of Covid-19 have risen sharply across the UK this month, driven largely by a variant of the virus known as ‘XFG’.

Sometimes referred to as ‘Stratus’ and the ‘American strain’, owing to the fact that it is now the most common strain in North America, it was first identified in January 2025 and has since spread worldwide.

Between August and September, Covid cases in Britain jumped 230 per cent, from 1,374 to 4,589 new infections, half of which were caused by the XFG strain.

Hospitalisation rates have also increased by 15 per cent in the same period, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The true number of cases is likely to be much higher, as most people who contract Covid-19 experience a milder illness and will not visit hospital or receive an official diagnosis via their GP.

What are the symptoms, and how is it different from other variants?

Symptoms of XFG are similar to other variants of Covid-19 like Delta and Omicron, and typically begin with a sore throat, before developing into a cough and fever.

However, experts have noted that patients diagnosed with XFG tend to present with a characteristic hoarse, croaky voice, which is distinctive from older strains.

More than 30 other symptoms have been known to be associated with XFG and other Covid strains, including diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of taste and smell, shortness of breath, headache, and muscle aches.

Why are cases rising?

Current data does not suggest that XFG leads to more severe illness than any other variant in circulation, according to the UKHSA.

As the UK moves into winter, colder and wetter weather naturally influences the rise in respiratory illnesses like Covid-19 and the flu, given people spend more time indoors and in closer proximity to each other, where viruses can more easily transmit between them.

It has also been roughly a year since the last significant wave of Covid-19 cases, meaning that the population-wide immunity has somewhat waned, making people more susceptible to the disease, the UKHSA said.

Can you be vaccinated against XFG?

The current Covid-19 vaccine is designed to protect against XFG and related strains specifically, after modelling suggested it would become the dominant variant this season.

Those eligible for a Covid-19 autumn booster include adults over the age of 75, residents in care homes, and anyone over six months old with a weakened immune system, due to a health condition or treatment.

Covid vaccines are also available to buy privately for those who are not eligible for a free jab, and typically cost around £98 per dose.

What should you do if you suspect you have XFG?

The NHS no longer advises that people with symptoms of Covid-19 take a test, unless they want to do so.

If you feel unwell or have a high temperature, health authorities advise you to try and stay home and avoid contact with people until you feel better.

They also recommend avoiding contact with vulnerable people, like those undergoing chemotherapy or the elderly, for at least 10 days.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Harry’s Invictus Games challenge in Kenya is helping veterans battle physical and mental scars
News.content:
Wounded veterans from 10 countries have gathered in Kenya’s Great Rift Valley for a week of endurance challenges, organised by the charity behind Prince Harry’s Invictus Games.

Twenty-five serving and former personnel, among them a Ukrainian who survived a direct bomb hit in Donetsk and a Danish combat engineer who cleared roadside bombs in Afghanistan, will run, hike or cycle up to 120km across the area on Saturday October 10, World Mental Health Day.

The Invictus Games Foundation, the charity the Duke of Sussex founded in 2014 for wounded, injured and sick service personnel, has organised the event.

For Vasyl, a Ukrainian soldier, it will be his first time in Africa and his first long-distance challenge.

After three weeks of military training in the UK, the 34-year-old joined a brigade in Donetsk as a reconnaissance squad commander, spending more than 19 months on the front line. He was wounded when a drone dropped a grenade three metres from him, and the shrapnel still causes frequent pain in his leg which can sometimes make walking difficult.

But he said the physical injury was easier to bear than the loss of the friends he made in the trenches.

“There is a level of kindness between comrades in a trench that you will never find in civilian life,” he said. “If someone made a mistake or said something wrong, we immediately forgave them and thought nothing more of it.

“For me, the pain of loss is the hardest thing the war has left behind.”

News.title: From Yale to the Congo: The mathematician who became one of Africa’s most intrepid reporters
News.content:
Sundaram has a lot of experience with the Rwandan methods of control. After spending 17 months in DRC, he moved to Kigali and he is eloquent about the convoluted effects of dictatorship. “Living in Rwanda taught me so much about how dictatorships function internally and how counter-intuitive they can be. A friend of mine who was working in public health told me ‘When we ask people in India to wash their hands we get a 30 per cent success rate from a campaign, but when we need people in Rwanda to wash their hands, we just need to slip a line in one of Kagame’s speeches and we get a 90 per cent success rate. That’s fantastic isn’t it?’

“And I said, ‘well is it? It’s great for short term health outcomes but what does that say about society? Isn’t democracy about people choosing freely? What if the government tells them to do something bad – like what happened in the genocide when people were told to kill all the Tutsis?’

“Kagame and his army stopped the genocide, and he has restored peace, but he governs using the same system that was used to perpetrate the genocide.”

In Bad News: Last Journalists in a Dictatorship, the book Sundaram went on to write about his time in Rwanda teaching journalists, he describes a more extreme version of this phenomenon, recalling how Kagame once commented that thatched roofs on huts were primitive. “And the local authorities took that as a sign that he didn’t like thatched roofs, and that they should get rid of them. And without replacements being built, people climbed up and dismantled their own thatched roofs. And I saw these villages with houses which just had mud walls without roofs, and the families were sitting outside with their children and their goats, the thatch strewn on the ground. In the rain, quite often. The children would get sick, and it was like a war zone.

“At the end of my time in Congo, I was at a UN base and they were digging latrines, when they found some human bones. They stopped digging and alerted the press, and I happened to be in Goma nearby.” He subsequently found out that it was one of a series of mass graves containing the bodies of Congolese killed by forces controlled by Kagame. “And so when I arrived I had a sense of what Rwanda had done in Congo, but I didn’t fully appreciate the extent to which it was totalitarian. I’d heard that the country was a shining example of progress – aid programs were successful, and poverty reduction programs. The streets were clean, public services functioned. I was living in a nice house with a big garden provided by the journalism programme I was working in.”

Many European governments, including Britain, are enamoured with Rwanda, because, says Sundaram, “dictatorships can be very efficient”. But it is a “mirage of a country”, he says.

The teaching programme he was running was briefed not to challenge the government on any level, and an embassy official told him that if any of the journalists mentioned repression they would be expelled.

“Layer by layer, as I began to talk to the journalists I was training, the true story unravelled. The first instance was when one of them left the programme, and I heard him on the radio one day praising the president, but with a degree of flattery that was completely exaggerated, and I didn’t understand why. The rest of the class were reluctant to talk about it but eventually I learned that another student had been beaten to a coma on the day he criticised the president.

“I started to realise that my class contained some of the most courageous journalists in the country.” As a foreigner, if he transgressed, Sundaram could have his visa cancelled or get kicked out, or even locked up for a couple of days, but for the Rwandan journalists, everything was at stake. They could be killed or their families threatened.

“But still they persisted, and they took me around the country and showed me all the things the government didn’t want anyone to see – things they couldn’t report on because it was too dangerous, so they wanted to show me because they wanted somebody to speak up. It’s really a book about them – they’ve been my greatest teachers in journalism.”

News.title: I tried Amazon’s new iPad rival – and there’s one standout feature
News.content:
Amazon says that this tablet has three times the computing power and nine times the graphics power of any previous Amazon tablet, so this is a significant boost in performance to previous models.

That will make light tasks, such as crunching through emails, browser-based activity like online shopping and document work. With a keyboard factored in, it could work as a laptop alternative for some. The same could be said of the iPad Air, although with recent price increases from Apple and the matte screen, for my money, this is a better proposition.

The premium makeover that comes with the Alexa Tablet Pro includes a slim aluminium design, with flattened edges, so it looks like an iPad or Samsung tablet, only 6.5mm thick. The Pro version only comes in the Graphite colour seen here. All models in the new line-up feel more grown-up and less like kid’s tablets than the Fire range. Plus the switch to proper Android over Fire OS is welcome and will result in better app compatibility (although I noticed that these tablets were running Android 16, which is now an old version).

It has a battery that’s good for 16 hours of video playback and supports 27W charging. There are cameras front and rear although like any tablet, these won’t be as good as your phone, while there’s support for Dolby Atmos from the speakers, so your movies will sound decent.

The AI capabilities are a step up

As the name suggests, Amazon is keen to promote the AI element here. It has customised the interface slightly with access to Alexa+ meaning you can utilise Amazon’s AI at any time to ask about what’s on the screen, to control smart home devices or search for content. If you are a keen Alexa user, then that will be a plus, but for me it’s not the headline news.

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.
