Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.

Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.

Sports.title: Christian Horner's ex-colleagues turn on him as £67m Red Bull pay-out to Geri Halliwell's husband is revealed, calling out 'lying' and how behaviour caused 'constant spicy tension'
Sports.content:
Christian Horner's ex-colleagues turn on him as £67m Red Bull pay-out to Geri Halliwell's husband is revealed, calling out 'lying' and how behaviour caused 'constant spicy tension'

Christian Horner's former Red Bull colleagues have called him out for 'lying' and 'causing spicy tension'.

Earlier on Thursday, it was uncovered that Horner, 52, was paid a staggering £67million in severance after being sacked by Red Bull following a texting scandal.

The Daily Mail's Richard Eden revealed that documents filed this week at Companies House from Red Bull Racing disclose that Horner, 52, banked £33.5m. The husband of former Spice Girl Geri Halliwell was then paid an extra £33.5m from other Red Bull accounts.

The team's superstar driver Max Verstappen has opened up about what life was like in the team under ex-team principal Horner, while the cloud of scandal was hanging over them.

He said: 'To be honest, I like to see that people get on. It is not nice when you constantly have tension between people.

'Of course, from the outside, people like it, but honestly between the teams, it is better when you have just a friendly relationship.

Max Verstappen said their was 'tension' in Red Bull when Christian Horner was in charge

The team principal was axed after a texting scandal, though two investigations cleared him of impropriety

'It is not as spicy, but I obviously quite like how things are going at the moment, with everyone’s behaviour, let’s put it like that.

'It is less stressful. We are all leading a stressful life and, when you can take a bit of stress out of it at times, it is good.'

There were more scathing comments from Helmut Marko, who was a colleague in his role as Red Bull adviser. Horner, in his upcoming autobiography 'Drive', claims Marko did not want Verstappen in the team.

Marko, 83, rubbished that allegation by referring to former F1 driver Ralf Schumacher assessment that Horner's version of events was an 'absolute lie'.

'I'm ignoring it as much as possible. Ralf Schumacher handled it very well,' Marko told Austrian outlet OE24.

On an episode of the Backstage Boxengasse podcast, Schumacher said: 'Marko approached Max when he was just 11-and-a-half years old. At the time, Jos said it was still too early for him. 'The doctor, as you know him, was a bit miffed and said: "Okay, if you don't want to, then so be it."'

And Marko added: 'I brought Max into Formula 1 and had to stand my ground against Horner at his first race for Red Bull in Barcelona. He thought Max was too young, too inexperienced.'

Horner had been the longest reigning team principal in the sport, steering Red Bull for 20 years and winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' titles, but was sacked in July 2025, a year after the scandal that engulfed him over texts he apparently sent to a female employee.

Horner claims Helmut Marko (right) did not want Max Verstappen at Red Bull, which the Austrian vehemently denies

The settlement payment is disclosed in the small print of Red Bull Racing's latest accounts for last year and is reported as 'compensation for loss of office' in the directors' remuneration section.

Horner has always denied the claims and was twice cleared of any impropriety in internal investigations at Red Bull, despite a tranche of supposedly intimate text exchanges between the pair being made public in an explosive email sent to F1 figures before the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

His wife Geri stood by him throughout the scandal. They live together in a £9.2m mansion near the Oxfordshire border with Northamptonshire.

Last month, it was revealed that the woman who accused him of coercive behaviour had been mysteriously released from her latest role in motor racing.

A source told Daily Mail Sport that she was informed her services were no longer required moments before her scheduled flight to Budapest, a race won by McLaren's British world champion Lando Norris.

Her then employers, who can also not be named, said: 'We do not comment on personnel matters.'

It is understood her latest position was terminated after her new boss, with whom she worked closely, lost confidence in her 'for a lack of discretion'.

The saga that unfolded surrounding Horner's supposedly coercive behaviour was one of the biggest to hit F1 in recent years.

Seventy-nine screenshots of WhatsApp chats between Horner and the female then colleague were leaked in an explosive email sent to F1 figures ahead of the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

The file allegedly containing texts and images was leaked to almost 200 people involved in the sport, including owners Liberty Media, team principals and the media.

Horner had been at the top of Red Bull since its inception in 2005, and led them in two phases to world championship success through Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

There have been growing rumours of the 52-year-old potentially returning to the grid. He recently told The Times that Ferrari are his 'dream' team to join and the only one he would consider signing up for without an equity stake.

'Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1,' he said.

'I've been a hired hand. I did 21 years sitting on the pit wall. I don't need to go back to that.

'At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership [Ferrari].'

A week ago Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time world champion, backed his beleaguered team principal Fred Vasseur as the ‘right guy’ to lead Ferrari amid speculation that Horner might take over.

Hamilton did not elaborate on what changes he wanted to see but his comments were hardly an overwhelming vote of confidence in the organisation he joined last season in search of his eighth world title.

But Horner's hopes of a return took a blow when Ferrari publicly backed current team principal Fred Vasseur.

Ferrari’s chief communications officer Maria Conti led the conversation, saying to a group of some 15 reporters: ‘Ferrari want to end speculation over the leadership of the team.

Horner oversaw eight drivers' titles at Red Bull, including four in a row with Max Verstappen

‘I am officially saying that Ferrari has made its choices and has full confidence in Fred Vasseur and his team. Nothing has changed. So that’s it.’

It remains the case that Vasseur has failed to deliver the results chairman John Elkann would have wished for, never getting close to a world championship despite paying Lewis Hamilton £80million-a-year to race for them.

Vasseur is also widely condemned within the organisation for failing to learn more than a few words of Italian, instead speaking in English, or his native French, since taking over as Scuderia boss in 2023.

As Daily Mail Sport revealed in September, the 58-year-old is also believed to have health problems – relating to his heart and the stress of the job. Furthermore, his elevation to such a senior status in the sport remains scarcely believable given his limp years as Alfa Romeo boss, where he won exactly nothing. They were at the back of the field year after year.

Sports.title: Stats boffins reveal the Premier League side with the TOUGHEST fixtures before the next international break as Man United face tricky tests and City have mixed run after guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Stats boffins reveal the Premier League side with the TOUGHEST fixtures before the next international break as Man United face tricky tests and City have mixed run after guilty verdict

Fans of the Premier League will be filled to the brim with excitement as the top flight returns to our screens following the three-week extended international break this weekend.

However, Liverpool supporters may not share quite the same level of enthusiasm.

That is because Andoni Iraola's Reds have not been blessed with a kind fixture list over the next month. They are deemed to have the trickiest upcoming five league games before the November break arrives, according to Opta.

The sports data wizards have rated the difficulty of every Premier League team's matches over the next four weeks. Fulham are believed to have been handed the easiest run, while a quick glance at the teams Liverpool will face suggests they may be in for a Nemesis Inferno-level rollercoaster ride.

Their rough run begins on Sunday as they take on Manchester City at Anfield in what is set to be a monumental affair. The club's rivalry that has grown over the past decade will come to the fore after City were found guilty of breaking financial rules. Anfield is going to be a cauldron of hostility.

However, despite the noise that is inevitably going to greet Enzo Maresca's side, and could well cause them to crack under the pressure, they still – at this moment in time – have a team filled with quality and sit top of the Premier League with a 100 per cent record.

Liverpool's next five Premier League games have been dubbed the most difficult in the division

The Reds resume their rivalry with Man City on Sunday in their first clash since City were found guilty of breaking financial rules

Iraola's side then face two of the 'Bermuda Triangle' – where social media says points are lost and never seen again – in back-to-back games. Having already faced one of the third team in the dynamic trio, Bournemouth, they will take on Brentford away from home and then host Brighton.

Both sit above Liverpool in the table, with the Seagulls, who beat champions Arsenal in their last game, placed third and the Bees just below them in fourth after electric starts to the campaign.

The 20-time champions then host the side who took their title from them last season, the Gunners, before finishing off their nightmare spell of games away at Crystal Palace, where they were beaten by a dramatic stoppage-time winner last season. Opta has given their five fixtures a difficulty rating of 95.4.

That is one difficulty rating higher than the second-placed team in this graph, Nottingham Forest.

Forest have had a mixed start to the season, earning an impressive draw at Anfield and a win away at Aston Villa, before slipping up at home to Midlands rivals and promoted side Coventry City.

It was not the result Oliver Glasner wanted heading into a three-week break, and things may get worse before they get better with the run of games they have coming up. Forest take on Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park, host Arsenal, travel to Ipswich and Brentford and play City at home in their next five games.

Brighton and Villa are also set for a tricky run of fixtures. In addition to taking on Liverpool, Fabian Hurzeler's side travel to the Etihad and also host one of the first 'Bermuda Triangle' derbies as they face Brentford.

Meanwhile, once their ears have stopped ringing after being subject to raw emotion at Anfield, City players are in for a calmer ride over the next month.

A trip to Anfield is champions Arsenal's trickiest fixture over the course of the next month

Maresca's men will host Ipswich in their first game back at the Etihad following the guilty verdict, before games against Villa, Brighton and Forest.

However, for their rivals across the city, Manchester United, things are not set to get any easier after a difficult start to the season, in which they have only picked up five points from a possible 15.

The Red Devils will be looking for only their second win of the season when they face basement boys Tottenham at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. That blockbuster clash is followed up by a meeting with bitter rivals Leeds United at Elland Road.

A date with bogey team Bournemouth, who United haven't beaten since 2023, follows at the Theatre of Dreams, before a trip to Xabi Alonso's Chelsea. They finish off their run of games by hosting Aston Villa.

Elsewhere, after hosting the Cherries, Alonso's side have a trip to Everton and a derby with Tottenham to contend, in addition to clashes with United and Sunderland.

Champions Arsenal are judged to have a more difficult run than the Blues, but a more reasonable than Liverpool and the two Manchester clubs.

They will look to bounce back from defeat at the Amex before the break as they host Leeds this weekend, before travelling to the City Ground to face Forest. Then, sandwiched either side of the grand clash at Anfield, are dates with Everton and Hull.

The side deemed to have the easiest run is Fulham, with a difficulty rating of 91.1. That is because they face all three promoted sides – Hull, Ipswich and Coventry – in their next three matches.

Alvaro Arbeloa's team then finishes off their run with games against Villa and Newcastle.

Sports.title: Arsenal were the biggest losers from the three-week international break as team with the most average minutes is revealed - but how did it affect YOUR club?
Sports.content:
Arsenal will return to Premier League action with a much-depleted squad after they were hit hardest by injuries during the dreaded international break. There are several reasons why most football fans dislike international breaks – especially when they last three weeks – but chief among them is the fact they regularly leave their club's best players injured. It is usually the league's top teams that are most affected because they have so many high-quality players at international level. And it is no different this time. Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and the Gunners all ranked in the top four of the Premier League for the most players involved in international fixtures, including at Under-21, Under-20, Under-19, Under-18 and Under-17 level. Meanwhile, Tottenham averaged the highest minutes played per player across all levels during the break. Their 12 players averaged 254.1 minutes of game time across a combined total of 38 matches played. Arsenal left the Amex following a humbling 3-0 defeat last month with just one casualty, with Declan Rice pulling out of the England squad due to 'load management'. Now potentially six of his team-mates are in need of the treatment table. Piero Hincapie was the first to drop, missing the entire break, before Kai Havertz had to leave Jurgen Klopp's first Germany camp after picking up a hamstring problem against the Netherlands. Kai Havertz (pictured) was one of six Arsenal players to get injured during international break Max Dowman, Ezri Konsa, Christos Tzolis and Martin Odegaard also sustained minor issues, but the latter of the trio returned to the pitch with Norway by the end of the break. Liverpool were similarly unfortunate, with four of their big guns picking up knocks during their combined 51 matches played by their top-ranked 17 stars in action. Alexander Isak was forced to take an early leave from Sweden duty after suffering a 'minor injury' during a 2-1 win over Romania, a game in which he scored. But there is hope he will return for the Reds' monster clash with Manchester City on Sunday. Jeremy Jacquet impressed on his full France debut against Italy, with new Les Bleus boss Zinedine Zidane so impressed that he stated the defender was 'very good' four times in a matter of moments. However, a 'hamstring strain' kept him out of their 4-1 win over Belgium this week, which is cause for concern for Andoni Iraola. Fellow starters Cody Gakpo and Milos Kerkez are also doubts for the Anfield affair with City, after leaving their respective international teams early due to injury. City themselves have plenty of scares with three of their stars picking up various problems during the break. The biggest concern for Enzo Maresca is that main man Erling Haaland appeared to hobble off during Norway's defeat to Portugal. Nico O'Reilly missed three of England's four games due to a knock, while Rayan Ait-Nouri withdrew from the Algeria squad after their first game. Neighbours Manchester United also have plenty to attend to, with their treatment tables starting to overflow. Tottenham players averaged the most minutes played for their international teams during the three-week period

Your browser does not support iframes.

Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Benjamin Sesko and Karl Darlow pulled out of international duty due to existing injury issues, and two players, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui, have joined them on the list. Bruno Fernandes also picked up a niggle with Portugal but eventually returned to action. Another among the biggest losers were Sunderland, who could do without injuries due to their first foray into Europe in 53 years, adding extra load onto their already thin squad. Their biggest concern will be the fitness of star striker Brian Brobbey, who bagged a hat-trick away at Manchester City before the break, as he pulled up with a hamstring problem while on duty for the Netherlands. Dan Ballard suffered the same fate while playing for Northern Ireland and could be sidelined until the next international break. Rock bottom Spurs, despite seeing their players feature the most, were one of the big winners during the break. They only lost one additional big star to injury, with Jan Paul van Hecke withdrawing from Netherlands duty after hurting his foot in a Nations League clash with Serbia. However, starting right-back Pedro Porro was already on the injury list and withdrew from meeting up with his fellow Spanish world champion team-mates. He is a major doubt for their upcoming clash with United. Meanwhile, Chelsea lost two further players, Mike Penders and Jamie Gittens, to knocks, while Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro will be hopeful for a return to action after missing international duty despite being called upon. The real winners of the break are Fulham, Nottingham Forest and Ipswich, who lost no further players to injury. That is despite all three being ranked in the top ten for averaging the highest minutes played per player across all levels.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho aims playful dig at Man City over bombshell guilty verdict - and insists he 'would rather have a laugh' about club's cheating scandal
Sports.content:
Jose Mourinho says he 'would rather have a laugh' about Man City's cheating verdict than be drawn into a serious discussion of the financial cheating scandal.

The former Man United boss, currently in charge of Real Madrid, was asked for his view of City being judged to have broken competition rules over a nine-year period by illegally pumping in more than £900million.

Speaking to Italian newspaper Corriere dello Sport, the 63-year-old said: 'Manchester City? I’d rather have a bit of a laugh about it.

'I think that we will reach a conclusion but, being in my sixties, I will have to be lucky enough still to be here when the final verdict arrives. Now a ruling will come, then an appeal… I’ll be 80.'

Mourinho has previously said that he may still receive a winners' medal if City are stripped of the prize. The Portuguese led United to second behind City in the 2017-18 season.

If City's appeal fails, debate will continue to swirl over whether the club will be stripped of their titles as severe punishments are decided.

Jose Mourinho joked that he will be in his 80s by the time Man City's case has concluded

City lodged their appeal against the verdict, which found that the club had artificially inflated commercial revenues by over £830million between 2009 and 2018, last Thursday evening.

The independent commission came to their decision over three years after the Premier League first brought charges against the club, with its ten-week hearing taking place in late 2024.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters claimed in a statement released alongside the bombshell core decision that the club 'systemically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade' with their use of 'sham' contracts.

In an interview with club media on a day when chief executive Ferran Soriano is understood to have addressed players returning from the international break, manager Enzo Maresca sounded a defiant note.

'Personally, I'm very calm to be honest,' he said. 'The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.'

Maresca added that his squad's concentration remained on the pitch, where they will face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

'The players are just focused on that (football),' he said. 'They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise.'

Police on Merseyside have a plan in place while some fans are planning to provide a 'welcoming party' to the visitors as they arrive for the 4.30pm kick-off.

Meanwhile, Haaland has urged fans to keep the faith and 'enjoy the ride' despite the ruling, which found them guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's rules.

Enzo Maresca (pictured arriving to training on Thursday morning) insists he is 'very calm' about Manchester City's situation with the Premier League despite being found guilty

The Norwegian told Sky Sports that he believes fans will 'have a good time' at Anfield. 'We have to stick together,' he added.

'We have to stay with each other and we have to stay positive no matter what happens in life - we always have to have a smile. We have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and then try to enjoy the situation and win the game.'

The prolific striker also called for unity within the club. 'We have to stick together and we have to spread the love to each other,' he said. 'Stick together and enjoy the ride and smile.'

Next Wednesday, City will play their first game at the Etihad since they were found guilty and Pep Guardiola will be in attendance in a show of solidarity.

The former manager, who left the club at the end of last season, previously shared a message of support for his ex-employers, telling fans: 'We will get through this together. I love you all.'

Guardiola will be joined at the Etihad Stadium by the City board, including chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, for the club's first home European match since his summer departure.

Sports.title: Stephen Ireland opens up on 'life-changing' double-leg break while playing for ex-Premier League all-stars, why there's a target on their backs - and the 'f***ing mental' mistake by a Man United cult hero!
Sports.content:
Stephen Ireland cries out in pain as the paramedics try to stabilise the fractured tibia and fibula bones in his right leg.

'It's completely broken,' says the former Manchester City and Aston Villa midfielder as the camera zooms in on the gruesome injury and team-mates gather around him. A sickening snap was audible in the footage.

As Ireland's recovery continues five months on, he is fully focused on managing Wythenshawe FC Veterans, the Sunday League team in South Manchester made up of a growing number of ex-Premier League stars like him.

Last season, Wythenshawe won the Cheshire Veterans League Premier Division title with a goal difference of plus 85 from 14 games.

This season, the squad includes Emile Heskey, Antonio Valencia, Joleon Lescott, Papiss Cisse, Danny Drinkwater, Nedum Onuoha, Marc Albrighton, Tom Huddlestone, Maynor Figueroa, Jefferson Montero, George Boyd and Oumar Niasse.

You have to fear for Greenalls Padgate St Oswalds in the President's Cup this weekend.

Former Manchester City star Stephen Ireland has opened up on his double leg break suffered playing for Wythenshawe Vets and their 12-month recovery he faces as a result

Last season, Wythenshawe won the Cheshire Veterans League Premier Division title with a goal difference of plus 85 from 14 games with the XI including several ex-Premier League stars

Ireland's injury in the Premier Division Cup final against South Liverpool in May does raise the question of whether it's safe for professionals to put themselves at risk at this level. Heskey has admitted that he almost quit following Ireland's double leg break.

'We don't go out there to be disrespectful but there are players and opposition teams that will want to hurt you if they get the opportunity - there is a target on your back, for sure,' says Ireland.

'The realisation straightaway of, "this is me for 12 months" and what's ahead of you is tough. I was worried when I broke my leg that the guys would be like, "that's enough, I don't want any more".

'If anybody in the squad was going to get that injury, I'm happy that it was me. I wouldn't want it on my conscience or the responsibility if it happened to somebody else.'

Ireland's graphic injury and rehab is one of the storylines in Every Given Sunday, the new docuseries following Wythenshawe Vets which began airing on YouTube last weekend.

His wife Jessica describes her shock at what happened to the 40-year-old. 'I never thought he would end up having this life-changing injury from playing what was supposed to be fun Sunday football,' she says, before admitting that Ireland is actually busier now as Wythenshawe's manager than he was playing full-time in the Premier League where he made nearly 250 appearances for City, Villa and Stoke.

The documentary opens with Ireland berating Valencia over the phone after the former Manchester United captain missed a flight back from Honduras before a game.

'This is really bad,' says Ireland. 'How do you miss your flight? You're a grown man. It's f***ing mental.'

Ireland's wife Jessica has called his injury was shocked about the 'life-changing' injury he got

Ireland is now manager of the side as he recovers from his broken leg and finds himself busy

Ex-Newcastle United striker Papiss Cisse (right) is one player who Ireland now manages

He has to call Cisse to make sure he is out of bed and moans about having to sort out parking for Lescott and his kids. Niasse calls to say he will be 20 minutes late because he is lost in the car park at Ikea.

But, really, Ireland is loving the matchday routine of a manager as he works his way back to playing again. One of his post-match duties involves shaving the head of a player who has lost a bet by failing to score.

For Ireland and the other ex-Premier League stars like him, it fills the void left by retirement which can lead to loneliness and even mental health issues.

Asked if he ever considered hanging up his boots after the injury, he replies: 'No, not at all. I'm like a dog with a bone. I'm going to get back stronger and faster, and I will surprise everybody.

'I miss football every single day. This Wythenshawe Veterans team just makes me feel alive again.

'I've been asking myself a lot recently why the hell I'm doing this. This is why I'm doing it. Football is all we've ever known, and one day that is just whipped away from you.

'I'm very mindful of people being lonely or lost, climbing the walls not knowing what to do with themselves anymore. The guys are planning their lives around these games now. It's become something that's really important to them.

'I think we are the best Sunday league team in the country - I'd be very surprised if we're not.'

Sports.title: 'He's not a p***y President': Mike Tyson launches wild defense of Trump and says president has overcome problems only 'black' people face
Sports.content:
'He's not a p***y President': Mike Tyson launches wild defense of Trump and says president has overcome problems only 'black' people face

Donald Trump is 'not a p***y President,' according to his longtime friend and boxing legend Mike Tyson.

Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Tyson discussed his history with Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s as the future President was making a name for himself in New York and Atlantic City real estate.

'I voted for him,' the 60-year-old Tyson told Morgan. 'I ran the streets for him. You know, me getting votes… I'm very proud of him. He's somebody that everybody should be proud of.'

Tyson doesn't have many remaining personal ties to his early days in the ring. The boxing legend's famed trainer, Cus D'Amato, died in 1985, his turbulent marriage to actress Robin Givens ended four years later and Tyson's fragile business relationship with promoter Don King finally ruptured in the late 1990s.

But for all of the turnover surrounding Tyson, Trump has been a constant for the former heavyweight champion. Not only did Tyson fight at Trump's hotels and casinos, later adding the real estate mogul to his unofficial entourage, but the two remained friends throughout the ups and downs of their later lives.

And it's those obstacles that make Trump an admirable figure in the eyes of Tyson: 'Listen, if you didn't know who Donald Trump was and you didn't know his name, you would think he's Black.'

Speaking on the latest episode of Piers Morgan Uncensored, Mike Tyson discussed his history with President Trump, whom he first met as a young heavyweight in the 1980s

Trump and Tyson attend the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) 287 in April of 2023

Donald Trump and Mike Tyson attend March of Dimes Gourmet Gala Benefit in 1989

According to Tyson, it's Trump's perseverance in the face of multiple bankruptcies and sexual misconduct allegations that have made him a formidable figure.

'When he went for President, he was bankrupt... He owed taxes, he owed so much money,' Tyson said, somewhat erroneously.

While Trump's businesses did declare bankruptcy six times, the last filing came in 2009, well before his successful 2016 White House run.

But it's not just the financial problems that give Trump credibility in Tyson's eyes. Tyson was also impressed with the way Trump survived multiple waves of sexual misconduct claims.

'All this sex abuse and all that stuff that he went through,' Tyson continued. 'People don't normally go that well. They normally have a nervous breakdown. He handled it. And that's why everyone has to respect him. Just from the way he handled his court procedures… I don't care if you hate his guts… you have to respect that. Just off the bat.'

Trump has never been convicted of any sexual misconduct, although in May of 2023, a federal jury found him liable in a civil trial for sexually abusing and defaming writer E. Jean Carroll. A later trial resulted in a federal jury ordering Trump to pay an additional $83.3 million on top of the initial $5 million penalty he was ordered to pay Carroll.

Previously, Trump supported Tyson in the face of sexual misconduct claims. When Tyson was convicted of rape in Indiana in 1992, the future President told NBC the boxer was 'railroaded in the case' and questioned the victim's story.

While heavyweight champ Mike Tyson steals a kiss from his wife Robin Givens (R), real estate developer Donald Trump and Givens' mother Ruth Roper (L), talk to the media in 1988

Tyson chats with an attorney during a court hearing aimed at ending his contract with manager Bill Cayton. Sitting with Tyson's wife Robin Givens and her mother Ruth is Donald Trump

Donald Trump, Mike Tyson and Fred Trump attend a press conference at the Plaza Hotel

Donald Trump, Mike Tyson and Don King attend Gourmet Gala Benefit for March of Dimes on November 21, 1989 at the Plaza Hotel. King and Tyson later broke their business ties

Trump went so far as to publicly suggest Tyson should be allowed to dodge prison by giving 'millions and millions' of dollars to the victim.

'What has happened to him, the conviction, is already punitive,' Trump told the New York Post in 1992. 'The victim has had the satisfaction of humbling him and being vindicated.'

Speaking with Morgan, Tyson did not address the support he received from Trump in 1992.

He did, however, discuss the assassination attempt Trump survived in Pennsylvania on the campaign trail in 2024 by explaining he is 'not a p**** President.'

As for his immediate future, Tyson's planned exhibition with Floyd Mayweather Jr. is currently on hold after the former heavyweight broke his hand in May. Another complicating factor is a lawsuit against Mayweather by the promoter, CSI Sports.

In his previous return to the ring in 2024, Tyson was easily defeated by cruiserweight Jake Paul, who scored a unanimous decision victory that was watched by an estimated 60 million households on Netflix.

Sports.title: Where it's all gone wrong for Arsenal Women: A coach in trouble, terrible finishing, letting tenacious duo leave, predictable substitutions and the Alessia Russo and Steph Catley dilemmas
Sports.content:
On October 4, 2025, Renee Slegers’ Arsenal team fell to a 3-2 defeat to eventual champions Manchester City after a frustrating start to their season.

After the game, the Dutch coach told the media: ‘We’re very disappointed. I think it is two top teams going against each other, so you have to be prepared that momentum will shift. When we have momentum, capitalise, be ruthless and protect yourself really well for when the momentum shifts again.’

Exactly a year later, to the day, Arsenal once again fell to a 4-2 defeat to Manchester City following another painful start to the season. Slegers said: ‘We all said it afterwards: we have to be better in the critical moments in the game. And we were there, we had it, and then we didn’t have it.’

Same story. Same message. For the Arsenal fans looking to stop the tape on this freaky feedback loop, it seems that a thorough audit is on the agenda for this international break, but the burning question remains: will it solve anything?

Arsenal have continued to look average. Mediocre. Underwhelming. Though even that feels flattering because they can’t claim to be mid-table.

Sitting 10th, defeat at Manchester City last weekend has left the 2025 Champions League winners a mere three points off the drop zone. With London City Lionesses putting six past Tottenham at the weekend, it looks as though Michele Kang’s big-money spenders may just be in for a three-way title scrap with Chelsea and City.

Arsenal Women coach Renee Slegers appears to be struggling to get her message across to her team who are repeating the same mistakes from a year ago

Alessia Russo (left) and Leah Williamson discuss where Arsenal are going wrong

As for Arsenal, Slegers admitted at the weekend that they’re not ‘in the conversation’ for the title ‘at the moment’.

This was a generous way of putting it, one that is most likely intended to ensure the players do not down tools in October rather than reflecting any real belief that a title push could still be salvaged.

It’s also one that lacks any precedent, given that no team has ever won the WSL with as few as five points after their opening five games. In fact, only one team has ever won it with fewer than 10: Liverpool in 2014 with six.

You’d think that after signing world-class calibre in the summer, with Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle trading the continent for north London alongside exciting youngster Lisa Baum and one of Switzerland’s brightest midfield talents, Geraldine Reuteler, many of those problems posed last season would have been solved.

Instead, the same story is unfolding again. Despite creating opportunities, Arsenal are continuing to underperform in front of goal, with their shot conversion rate of 4.3 per cent the lowest in the top flight. Reuteler, meanwhile, has only played eight minutes.

Statistics say one thing, the vibe from the stands says another, and the tension emanating from the crowd over their team’s passive, ponderous play is no doubt being felt by those on the pitch.

Against Chelsea, boos directed towards their former lieutenant Katie McCabe diminished in gusto as the game trudged towards defeat. Replacing them were frustrated whistles and groans when yet another chance fell by the wayside.

How Arsenal could have done with someone like McCabe, or even Beth Mead, against City at the weekend, or in their painful 0-0 draw against Manchester United. Experienced players willing to take the game by the scruff of the neck. Both were let go in the summer amid the club’s aims of bringing the average age of the squad down.

Arsenal brought in world-class midfielder Georgia Stanway in the summer but have not seen the marked improvement they would have hoped for

Spanish full back Ona Batlle (left) joined in the summer too, coming in from Barcelona

Whether Slegers feels the right players were kept and moved on will, for now, remain unanswered by the diplomatic and uncontroversial head coach, yet losing McCabe looks like a big mistake.

McCabe was a demanding voice in the dressing room, and it is baffling that, a year after their head coach was complaining about a lack of ruthlessness, the club opted to let one of the most hardened, edgy players in the WSL sign for their biggest rivals for free.

There have been rare positives, including Kyra Cooney-Cross’ increased game time and Stanway’s commanding return to England. Youngster Baum has also looked promising.

Yet for the most part, and in the areas they arguably need it most, many of the players have looked devoid of confidence. Amid a rare goalscoring drought for Alessia Russo at the start of the season before her first goal against City, only the 19-year-olds Baum and Smilla Holmberg have found the back of the net.

Where historically that load has been more evenly shared among the squad, including from the likes of Chloe Kelly and Caitlin Foord, Russo’s struggles in front of goal were inevitably more keenly felt.

Meanwhile, Slegers’ predictability with her substitutions has clearly made it easier for opponents to snuff out danger. Like clockwork, Kelly and Foord are brought on at the hour mark. In some instances, as was the case against Manchester United with Baum, the best player on the pitch was taken off.

At other times, it has seemed as though Slegers has been trying too hard to get her best players on the pitch, yet the square pegs have only been finding round holes. She has consistently dropped Russo into the No 10 role, only to move her back to No 9 when Stina Blackstenius is substituted.

Steph Catley, a natural left-back, continues to be played as a centre-back. A natural right-back, Batlle has looked less potent on the left.

Arsenal are missing the tenaciousness of their former midfielder Katie McCabe (left) who moved to Chelsea in the summer

Like clockwork, Chloe Kelly is brought on at the hour mark by Slegers

At 37, Slegers remains fairly green, with the Arsenal job her first in the WSL. As an Arsenal academy graduate, there is no doubt that the Dutch coach cares deeply about both the job and her players.

Her withdrawal from speaking to the media after her side conceded a late equaliser to Paris FC in the Champions League because she was ‘too angry’ last week spoke to both.

There’s no doubt that the fairytale of Lisbon, which ended Arsenal’s 18-year wait for European glory, still gives her a good deal of credit in the bank, and all the signs appear to indicate that Slegers deserves, and will be given, more time to arrest this slide.

Yet she will be aware more than anyone how thin the ice is becoming. The success of this audit could make or break both her and Arsenal’s season. If this campaign is to be rescued, this feedback loop must, at last, be broken.

Sports.title: Defiant Enzo Maresca insists players and staff 'completely trust' Man City despite guilty verdict and insists there are NO concerns in dressing room after Erling Haaland became first star to speak out
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca says he is 'very calm' despite Manchester City's seismic guilty verdict and has claimed the club's players 'don't care too much about the noise'.

The Premier League giants have appealed a devastating independent panel verdict that they broke competition rules over a nine-year period by illegally pumping in more than £900m, and are currently awaiting a sanction that could see them relegated, with trophies stripped.

Speculation has been rife that City's stars may soon be forced to seek an exit from the Etihad Stadium over what could be a potentially-crippling few months.

But Maresca, whose side return to action for the first time since the verdict was made public at what is sure to be a hostile Anfield on Sunday, believes City will prevail and has attempted to play down concerns.

In an interview with club media on a day when chief executive Ferran Soriano is understood to have addressed players returning from the international break, he sounded a defiant note.

'Personally, I'm very calm to be honest,' he said. 'The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.'

Enzo Maresca (pictured arriving to training on Thursday morning) insists he is 'very calm' about Manchester City's situation with the Premier League despite being found guilty

The City boss says he 'trusts' the club completely as they await their appeal against sanctions

Some have wondered what the impact of the verdict, which raises huge questions over a glittering period in City's history from 2009 to 2018, will have on the likes of Erling Haaland and Eliot Anderson.

However, the former Chelsea manager attempted to downplay any fears over the atmosphere within his dressing room. 'The feeling is fantastic, to be honest,' he said.

'The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league.'

Maresca added that his squad's concentration remained on the pitch, despite all of the noise around the club.

'The players are just focused on that (football),' he said. 'They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise.'

City are in for a noisy afternoon in Liverpool, with previously reporting how police on Merseyside have a plan in place while some fans are planning to provide a 'welcoming party' to the visitors as they arrive for the 4.30pm kick-off.

But Maresca, who will face the media on Friday, is hoping for a repeat of last year's victory.

'They (the players) are just focused in this moment on how we can bear Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield.'

Marc Guehi kept a low profile as he drove into Man City's training ground for the first time since September

Josko Gvardiol returned to Manchester after facing off with England for Croatia at Wembley

Summer signing Elliot Anderson arrived around lunchtime after returning from England duty

Antoine Semenyo and Ayyoub Bouaddi were also on parade as they returned to their club

When asked by if he had a message for City fans, he asked for their support.

NOTTINGHAM FOREST BOSS OLIVER GLASNER ON MANCHESTER CITY Oliver Glasner has urged football chiefs to wrap up the Manchester City case quickly or risk fans turning their backs on the Premier League. City were found guilty of all but one of their charges of breaking financial rules in a bombshell verdict that has rocked English football. The club have appealed against the findings that they artificially inflated commercial revenues by £830million through 'sham' contracts with a range of Abu Dhabi-based companies. City were charged with 115 financial breaches in February 2023 and three-and-a-half years passed until the verdict. Nottingham Forest boss Glasner is hoping for much swifter timeline now. Glasner said: 'Let's wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick. When I was at Crystal Palace, we didn't know until 10 days before the European competitions started whether we would be playing in the Conference League or the Europa League. 'And that's why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It's a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can't trust it, they won't watch it anymore.' Glasner was in charge of Palace when they beat Manchester City in the 2025 FA Cup Final. He takes his new club to Selhurst Park to take on the Eagles on Sunday. By Tom Collomosse

'Anfield away, we're going to bring our [patience], we're going to bring our gameplan. But for sure we need their voice, their [patience]. In the last two days I watched last year's game at Anfield and the celebration at the end was fantastic.

'We need to be all together. I said many times the reason why this organisation in the last 15 years was top was because from the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, the manager, players, fans, they are all on the same page. And this is fantastic.'

The Italian was also quizzed by the in-house team on whether the motto on the club's former crest 'Superbia in Prelio (Pride in Battle)' was particularly significant during these deeply troubling times.

'Yes, Superbia in proelio - Latin, Italian, we are quite close on that,' he said. 'It's what we need. We know that the next two games are going to both be battle, especially Anfield away.

'We're going to bring all our [patient] feeling there. But at the same moment we need our fans with us. We need their patience and their voice and hopefully at the end of the game we can all be happy.'

Meanwhile, Haaland has urged fans to keep the faith and 'enjoy the ride' despite the ruling, which found them guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's rules.

The Norwegian told Sky Sports that he believes fans will 'have a good time' at Anfield. 'We have to stick together,' he added.

'We have to stay with each other and we have to stay positive no matter what happens in life - we always have to have a smile. We have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and then try to enjoy the situation and win the game.'

The prolific striker also called for unity within the club. 'We have to stick together and we have to spread the love to each other,' he said. 'Stick together and enjoy the ride and smile.'

Erling Haaland has urged Manchester City to 'enjoy the ride' following their guilty verdict

Elsewhere, Real Madrid boss and fierce City critic Jose Mourinho does not expect a conclusion or sanctions around the case any time soon.

'I'd rather laugh a little bit because I think that we are yet to have a final decision,' he told Corriere dello Sport. 'There will be a final decision, but I'm in my 60s and will be lucky to be here when that final sentence comes.'

The majority of Maresca's squad spent time on international duty during the break, with the manager himself only returning to the Etihad Stadium on Monday ahead of meeting up with his group for the first time.

COVENTRY CITY BOSS FRANK LAMPARD ON MANCHESTER CITY Frank Lampard believes Manchester City players will always feel like champions even if their titles are scrubbed from the records. City were found guilty of all but one of their charges of breaking financial rules in a bombshell verdict that has rocked English football. The club have appealed against the findings that they artificially inflated commercial revenues by £830million through 'sham' contracts with a range of Abu Dhabi-based companies. Coventry boss Lampard played for City in the 2014-15 campaign and was also with New York City FC, who are part of the City Football Group. He won 13 trophies in his playing career and says City stars will forever cherish their achievements, no matter what the future holds. 'I have titles and I don't have my titles hanging on my wall at home, I have them in my head,' Lampard said. 'Most players who have played [know] you are competing against the best in the Premier League. 'A lot of things that are out of your control but you are competing against the best and they're very hard to win. 'So I think it would be very hard to take someone's title away as an individual player. I think they should be in your head as opposed to in a beautiful glass cabinet.' Reflecting on his time in the City orbit, Lampard added: 'I was offered the opportunity to go to New York at the age of 36, which was an amazing life experience. When Manchester City came along, it was a quick decision. I was probably flattered to go to the champions at the time and play. 'I was really well looked after so I can't come away from that. We played Man City a month ago and I saw lots of friendly faces, and they were as warm as they were to me when I was there. 'When you're playing and competing you don't think about external things. You think about winning things. We did it at Chelsea and City have done it. Now all these conversations [about City] will happen but I don't want to be part of them. Being with the City Group was a very interesting time.' By Tom Collomosse

Man City lodged their appeal against the charges, which found that the club had artificially inflated commercial revenues by over £830million between 2009 and 2018, last Thursday evening.

The independent commission came to their decision over three years after the Premier League first brought charges against the club, with its 10-week hearing taking place in late 2024.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters claimed in a statement released alongside the bombshell core decision that the club 'systemically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade' with their use of 'sham' contracts.

The club also repeatedly breached duties of 'co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League' by failing to help with the investigation. In the core decision, the independent commission deemed evidence given by a number of Man City's witnesses called on behalf of the club to have been 'untrue' and 'dishonest'.

If Man City fail in their appeal, they will face severe sanctions which could include expulsion from the Premier League, future points deductions, stripping of titles and transfer bans.

But goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma's agent Enzo Raiola revealed the Italian - and likely his team-mates - was been given assurances by the club, who still insist on their innocence in the wake of the damning verdict by the independent commission.

He told Radio Napoli Centrale, per Calciomercato: 'Can the Manchester City chaos change anything? No, it won't change anything for us or for Gigio. News comes out periodically.

'The club has spoken to Gigio, and everyone is calm. Now there are important matches against Liverpool and PSG, and then sporting justice will take its course. But Gigio has received reassurances from Manchester City.'

Ahead of Sunday's return to Premier League action, Daily Mail Sport reported on Wednesday that Merseyside Police are braced for fan trouble with some Liverpool fans preparing a hostile 'welcome' for Man City's team bus.

One social media post is advertising a 'Bus Greeting' around two hours before the 4.30pm kick-off on Anfield Road.

Fans are asked to bring 'flags, banners, pyros, flares, kopparbergs'. A wink emoji is placed after Kopparberg, which is a popular cider served in a bottle.

Police are aware of the poster and have said that they will have 'an appropriate policing plan in place'.

Next Wednesday, City will play their first game at the Etihad since they were found guilty and Pep Guardiola will be in attendance in a show of solidarity.

The former manager, who left the club at the end of last season, previously shared a message of support for his ex-employers, telling fans: 'We will get through this together. I love you all.'

Guardiola will be joined at the Etihad Stadium by the City board, including chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, for the club's first home European match since his summer departure.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions.
