The great grandson of Oba Ovonramwen, the current Oba of Benin, Oba Eheneden Erediauwa, Ewuare II, was crowned on 20 October, 2016. King Charles Douglas MacPepple Jaja, Jeki VI of Opobo has just begun an expected long reign. May their era be peaceful and progressive.

Eric Teniola, a former director at The Presidency, wrote from Lagos.

World.title: Abiodun approves J4-Gao Road, sets November for Deep Sea port ground breaking
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, has approved the construction of the J4-Gao Road in Ogun Waterside Local Government Area as part of measures to open up the axis and provide critical infrastructure to support the emerging investments in the area.

Abiodun disclosed this on Wednesday at an All Progressives Congress (APC) stakeholders’ engagement meeting held in Ibiade, headquarters of Ogun Waterside Local Government Area.

The Governor, who lamented the prolonged neglect of the area by successive administrations, said the decision to construct the J4-Gao Road was informed by the strategic importance of Ogun Waterside to the State’s emerging economic and industrial landscape.

He also disclosed that the Federal Government had approved the construction of a four-kilometre bridge that would connect the local government to the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, describing the development as a major infrastructure intervention that would facilitate access to the area and support the take-off of major investments planned for the axis.

According to him, the proposed infrastructure would complement the development of the Gateway Deep Sea Port and the Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) project, both of which are expected to significantly alter the economic profile of Ogun Waterside and strengthen the State’s position in the maritime, energy and logistics sectors.

Abiodun expressed appreciation to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for supporting the development of the Deep Sea Port and other strategic projects in the area, saying the projects would position Ogun State as a major energy, maritime and international trade hub.

He announced that the groundbreaking ceremony for the Deep Sea Port had been scheduled for November, with construction expected to commence before the end of the year and be completed by 2030.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Abiodun said the development of the port was the culmination of sustained efforts by his administration to create an enabling environment for large-scale investments, stressing that the administration had consistently pursued infrastructure and policy interventions designed to make Ogun more attractive to investors.

He noted that the Deep Sea Port and associated investments would create significant employment and business opportunities, particularly for young people and residents of Ogun Waterside.

The Governor therefore urged youths in the area to acquire the skills and competencies required to take advantage of the opportunities that would emerge from the projects.

“These projects will change the economic fortunes of Ogun Waterside. Our young people must begin to prepare themselves now to take advantage of the opportunities that will come with these investments,” he said.

Abiodun noted that the strategic investments in the area were expected to generate more than 50,000 direct employment opportunities, while also creating extensive opportunities across logistics, transportation, construction, hospitality, services, manufacturing and other sectors.

The Governor said the development of the Deep Sea Port would also complement Ogun’s growing industrial base and strategic location within the Lagos-Ogun economic corridor, further strengthening the State’s reputation as Nigeria’s industrial capital.

He described Ogun Waterside as strategically important to the State, noting that the local government has 126 polling units and about 62,000 registered voters.

Abiodun urged residents and APC members in the area to remain united and sustain their support for the party, saying continued political stability and support would help consolidate the gains recorded by the APC-led administrations at the State and Federal levels.

He called on party members to intensify mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections and urged voters to support APC candidates across the ballot, from the presidential election to the State House of Assembly.

The Governor assured the people that continued support for the party would strengthen the prospects for sustained development and effective representation.

Speaking at the event, the APC Presidential and Governorship Campaign Director-General, Senator Lekan Mustapha, urged residents to protect the development gains recorded in the area under the APC-led government.

Mustapha cautioned against taking political decisions that could jeopardise the ongoing transformation, urging the people to remain committed to the party and its candidates in the 2027 elections.

Also speaking, a former Commissioner for Education, Science and Technology, Prof. Segun Awonusi, commended Abiodun for what he described as his role in driving the development taking place in Ogun Waterside.

Awonusi expressed confidence that the people of the area would reciprocate the administration’s interventions with massive support for the APC in the 2027 elections.

World.title: Lagos’ War on Beggars: 911 arrested, but streets keep calling
World.content:
File photo of street beggars in Ebute Metta, Lagos.

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

At Ikeja Under-Bridge, opposite the Lagos State Teaching Hospital, a young mother clutches a sleeping toddler to her chest and stretches a plastic bowl towards motorists trapped in traffic. A few metres away, an elderly man chants prayers for loose change. Children dart between moving vehicles, dodging horns and exhaust fumes in a desperate search for alms.

Read Also: How we paid millions for release of NYSC members — Parents; We’re not aware – Imo govt

The scene is repeated thousands of times across Lagos. From Oshodi and Agege to CMS, Oyingbo, Pen Cinema and the Lekki-Epe corridor, begging has become woven into the daily life of Africa’s largest megacity. But Lagos is no longer treating it simply as a humanitarian problem. The government now sees street begging as a threat to public order, environmental safety and, increasingly, security. And it is fighting back.

This information is for general knowledge, should not be taken as medical advice, and you should consult with a healthcare provider if you have medical concerns.

Enforcement in Lagos

In June and July 2026, more than 900 beggars were arrested during enforcement operations across Lagos. Officials said the Lagos State Environmental Sanitation Corps, LAGESC, popularly known as KAI, and other enforcement agencies apprehended 515 persons in June across Oshodi, Agege, CMS, Lagos Island, Ikorodu, Ikeja, Mushin, Alimosho and Falomo. Another 396 were arrested in July.

The figures have added urgency to the government’s push for a tougher legal framework. But behind the statistics are people who say they have nowhere else to go.

From Pity to Panic

For many Lagos residents, the issue has moved beyond sympathy. Motorists have complained of aggressive begging, particularly at night, with allegations of people banging on windscreens, surrounding vehicles and using dangerous objects to intimidate those who refuse to give money.

At some locations, residents say beggars cling to moving vehicles or run between lanes, creating dangerous situations for motorists and themselves. “What we see now is not just begging. It is coercion,” a motorist, Gerald Okoh, said, describing incidents in Oshodi where people allegedly surround vehicles and threaten drivers.

The government says street begging is already prohibited under Lagos environmental laws and has urged residents to channel donations through registered charities and religious organisations rather than handouts on highways.

Bill Raises the Stakes

Now, lawmakers want to give the crackdown greater legal teeth. At a public hearing on September 16, the Lagos State House of Assembly considered the Street Begging and Street Urchins (Prohibition, Prevention and Rehabilitation) Bill, 2026.

The proposed law would prohibit street begging and related activities, including soliciting, loitering or sleeping in public places for the purpose of begging. It would also target anyone who procures, aids or encourages begging.

The proposed sanctions would escalate with repeated offences. A first offender could receive a warning and be referred to a rehabilitation centre. A subsequent offence could attract a fine of up to ₦200,000, a non-custodial sentence or imprisonment of up to three months. Serial offenders could face up to two years’ imprisonment upon conviction. Parents and guardians who use children for begging or hawking could also face prosecution.

Children Caught in the Middle

But the debate has exposed a difficult question: where does enforcement end and the criminalisation of poverty begin?

The Nigeria Bar Association backed the bill but urged lawmakers to treat children found begging as children in need of care and protection, rather than criminals. NBA Lagos Branch Chairman, Uchenna Akingbade, warned that the law must target exploitation and harmful conduct, not poverty, homelessness or disability.

Other stakeholders called for clearer definitions and safeguards, particularly for people with mental health challenges and vulnerable children. Representing the Oba of Lagos, Chief Gbolahan Oki argued that repeated arrests had failed to deter offenders and advocated tougher sanctions combined with community service. Policy analyst Otunba Muhammed, however, stressed the need to ensure children were not exploited as instruments of economic survival or cultural practice.

The Faces Behind the Figures

The statistics tell only part of the story.

Suleiman, 42, from Kano State, said he lost a leg in a motorcycle accident and could no longer farm. He came to Lagos after his brother told him people gave money on the streets. “I have four children at home,” he said, explaining that some days he made about ₦3,000 and on other days nothing.

Fati, 28, said she started begging after her husband abandoned her while her child was ill. She had previously hawked sachet water but could not raise enough money for medical treatment.

Chidi, 19, travelled from Ebonyi State looking for work as a conductor. When work dried up, he joined friends begging around traffic.

Their stories differ, but their conclusion is similar: they want alternatives.

Beyond the Arrests

The Lagos Government insists its approach is not simply punitive. The proposed legislation provides for rehabilitation and welfare centres where rescued persons could receive accommodation, medical attention, counselling, literacy education and vocational training.

Government figures show that 1,315 vulnerable persons were rescued during the review period. They included 587 beggars, 560 people with mental health challenges, 143 destitute persons and 25 street children.

The Ministry of Youth and Social Development also said 459 beggars were prosecuted through the Mobile Court and sentenced to community service, with an option of fine. Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Mobolaji Ogunlende, said 1,295 rehabilitees were accommodated at the Rehabilitation Training Centre, while 1,072 people were admitted during the reporting period.

Of these, 998 were reunited with their families after rehabilitation and placed under follow-up monitoring. Others received vocational training in tailoring, horticulture, barbing and phone repairs.

The Bigger Question

Yet concerns remain. Human-rights advocates and legal experts have questioned provisions granting enforcement officers broad powers, including warrantless arrests and seizure of property connected to alleged offences.

The bill prohibits torture, degrading treatment and unlawful detention and provides for profiling before suspects are transferred to the police or appropriate security authorities. Deputy Speaker Mojisola Meranda said public submissions would be considered before the bill proceeds to third reading and, if passed, is sent to the governor for assent.

For Lagos, the stakes are high. The government wants safer, cleaner and more orderly streets. Residents want an end to harassment and dangerous encounters in traffic.

But beneath the crackdown lies a harder reality: poverty, disability, homelessness, migration and unemployment continue to push vulnerable people towards the streets. The arrests may clear an intersection for a day. The bigger question is whether they can empty the streets for good—without leaving the people who depend on them with nowhere else to go.

World.title: UNGA, SDGs: Beyond the jamboree, where are results?
World.content:
By Morenike Taire, Woman Editor

UNGA has come and gone. The flags have been lowered, the motorcades have disappeared, the bilateral meetings are over and the Nigerian delegation has returned home. But the questions that followed Nigeria to New York remain. What, after decades of attending global development summits, has Nigeria actually achieved? And, more pointedly, as the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) draws closer, are these annual pilgrimages producing results at home or merely another jamboree on the international calendar?

Read Also: FG offers petrol at N1,350 for next 30 days

For Nigeria, the uncomfortable answer is difficult to escape. The United Nations General Assembly, UNGA, may be about diplomacy, global partnerships and international advocacy. But in the context of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and now the SDGs, it should also be about accountability. Nigeria has participated, presented reports, made commitments and signed up to targets. Yet, on many of the indicators that matter to ordinary Nigerians, progress remains painfully slow.

From MDGs to SDGs

The MDGs, adopted at the UN Millennium Summit, ran from 2000 to 2015. They later gave way to the 17 SDGs under the 2030 Agenda, with a broader emphasis on universal development, country ownership and Voluntary National Reviews. The MDGs recorded important global gains, including a reduction in extreme poverty and increased access to primary education. But progress was uneven, and Nigeria struggled to translate the goals into sustained national outcomes.

Professor and former Health Minister, Adenike Grange, told Vanguard that the problem was never simply a shortage of policies. “We must have the right political structure, commitment, and we must also be able to retain our trained human resource,” she said, arguing that without meritocracy and coordination, no number of development goals could deliver the desired outcomes.

The same structural weaknesses now haunt the SDGs.

SDGs: Exposing the Gaps

Nigeria’s record remains sobering. The 2026 Sustainable Development Report places Nigeria 143rd out of 169 countries, with an SDG Index score of 55.7. India ranks 94th, Kenya 106th and South Africa 109th.

Nigeria’s life expectancy is about 55 years, compared with 66 in South Africa and 64 in Kenya. At the $3-a-day poverty line, the comparable figure for Nigeria is 41.8%, against 17.4% for South Africa and 45.5% for Kenya.

More troubling is the pace of progress. Since 2015, Nigeria’s SDG score has risen by only about 2.3 percentage points, compared with 9.6 points for India.

The gaps are visible across virtually every major development indicator. Multidimensional poverty reached 62.9% in 2021. About 45.4 million Nigerians were undernourished in 2023, while 33.8% of children under five were stunted in 2024.

Even where access has improved, the quality of that access remains a concern. In 2024, 82.2% of Nigerians had access to basic drinking water, but only 29.9% had safely managed drinking water. Electricity access stood at 61.2% in 2023, while only 26.2% primarily used clean cooking fuels and technologies.

Government spending on essential education services also fell dramatically, from 8.5% of total government expenditure in 2012 to just 3% in 2024.

These are not merely statistics. They are evidence of the distance between Nigeria’s international commitments and the lived reality of its citizens.

The Government Perspective: Goal Mainstreaming

The Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on SDGs, OSSAP-SDGs, insists that Nigeria has built a comprehensive architecture for implementation.

According to the office, the SDGs have been integrated into national and sectoral development plans, supported by the Nigeria SDGs Implementation Plan 2020–2030, national indicators, monitoring frameworks, financing mechanisms and three Voluntary National Reviews. State SDG offices have also been established, while six regional SDG Innovation Hubs are being developed to strengthen implementation.

There have, undoubtedly, been interventions and measurable gains in some areas. The problem is that they are difficult to reconcile with the scale of Nigeria’s development deficit. As OSSAP-SDGs itself acknowledges, Nigeria has also been battered by the “Triple C” crises of climate change, conflict and COVID-19. But crises do not explain everything.

Fiscal Constraints, Insecurity to Blame

Country Director of the International Rescue Committee, Babatunde Ojei, puts the problem more bluntly: Nigeria’s challenge is less about policy intent than execution, financing and data quality. Fiscal constraints, insecurity, weak service delivery and inadequate data continue to undermine implementation.

Nigeria also faces a huge financing gap. UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed has estimated that the country needs about $10 billion annually to achieve the SDGs by 2030. That cannot come from government alone. But attracting private capital requires trust, transparency, credible institutions and an environment in which investors believe projects will survive beyond political cycles.

UNGA: Jamboree or Opportunity?

This is where the annual UNGA spectacle becomes difficult to ignore. For years, Nigeria’s participation has attracted criticism over large delegations, foreign trips, estacode, shopping excursions and the perception that international meetings are opportunities for personal travel rather than national development.

The criticism is not new. During the Jonathan administration, then Foreign Affairs Minister Ambassador Bashir Wali reportedly sought to limit Nigeria’s delegation after an estimated 600 Nigerians attended the 2013 General Assembly. The Buhari administration later reduced the official delegation dramatically, with only 17 government delegates attending one UN gathering.

After the controversy surrounding Nigeria’s 1,411-strong delegation to COP28 in Dubai, the Tinubu administration again moved to restrict official travel. The government has since required conditional clearance for delegates to major international meetings. The message is clear: Nigerians expect value for money.

They Are Not Jamborees — But…

OSSAP-SDGs argues that UNGA, the High-Level Political Forum and similar meetings are not inherently jamborees. They provide opportunities to report progress, negotiate priorities, attract investment, build partnerships and advocate reforms to the global financial system. That is true.

But the real test is not whether UNGA has diplomatic value. It is whether Nigeria converts that value into development outcomes. A country cannot continue presenting impressive plans abroad while its citizens struggle with poverty, insecurity, poor schools, unreliable electricity, inadequate healthcare and unsafe water at home.

Beyond UNGA

Perhaps the most promising development from the latest UNGA was the effort by seven northern governors to present the Northwest as an investment destination rather than merely a region defined by banditry and insecurity. UNDP Resident Representative Elsie Attafuah described the initiative as “exciting”, noting that the governors had developed a Peace, Security and Development framework and were attempting to make the region investable.

That is the kind of diplomacy Nigeria needs: diplomacy that comes home with investors, partnerships, technology, financing and measurable projects. As Attafuah rightly observed, having a framework is one thing; making it investable is another. And therein lies Nigeria’s larger UNGA challenge.

The jamboree is not the meetings, the receptions or even the shopping. The jamboree is what happens when the ceremony becomes an end in itself and the commitments never make it home.

The MDGs came and went. The SDGs have less than four years to run. Nigeria does not need another declaration of intent. It needs results.

As UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned, unless the world acts, the 2030 Agenda could become “an epitaph for a world that might have been.” For Nigeria, the question is whether, after all the UNGA speeches and handshakes, 2030 will be remembered as a missed opportunity—or the point at which the country finally moved beyond the jamboree.

Vanguard News

World.title: Trading children as commodities in Benue
World.content:
•Some rescued victims and the alleged trafficker (in handcuffs).

By Peter Duru

A young girl is told there is a job waiting for her in Lagos, another city or even another country. She is promised good pay, accommodation and a chance to help her family escape poverty. Sometimes, the person making the offer is a relative, a trusted acquaintance or someone introduced by a family member.

Read Also: How we paid millions for release of NYSC members —Parents; We’re not aware – Imo govt

But somewhere along the journey, the promise changes. Her phone may be taken away. She may be moved through unfamiliar routes, transferred from one vehicle to another and eventually taken to a destination she never agreed to visit. For many, they never have the luck of returning home alive to their siblings. Those who are fortunate to reunite with their kinsmen have unsavoury tales to tell. For many vulnerable young Nigerians, that is the beginning of a nightmare of sexual exploitation, forced labour and modern-day slavery.

In Benue, the problem has assumed an especially troubling dimension amid worsening insecurity, displacement and economic hardship. Thousands of residents have been forced from their ancestral communities by violence, leaving families and children struggling for survival in unfamiliar environments. It is in this vulnerability that traffickers are finding opportunities. At 36, anti-trafficking campaigner Sughnen Yaaya has found himself confronting a trade he describes as increasingly organised and difficult to contain. Since March 2026, Yaaya says he has intercepted 573 Benue girls within Nigeria and facilitated the return of 103 others from Ghana, Mali, Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina Faso and other countries. He also claims that about 32 Benue girls have died abroad in circumstances linked to trafficking. “From March till now, I have intercepted 573 girls,” he said. “By interception, I mean that we stop them before they are taken out of the country. We could intercept them at a motor park or somewhere along the route.”

‘Why I do it’

For Yaaya, the decision to take on the campaign was not driven by money or political ambition but by the growing number of vulnerable young people he encountered. He said that while he could not solve the insecurity and kidnapping challenges confronting the state, he believed he could contribute by exposing trafficking networks and warning families about the dangers. His intervention, however, has come at a personal cost. According to him, some alleged traffickers and their families have attempted to intimidate him, while financial constraints have severely limited his operations. “I am very scared. I count my days every day,” he admitted, explaining that he has no personal security and depends largely on God and assistance from individuals who support his work.

His experience provides a glimpse into a much larger problem that has attracted the attention of government agencies, civil society organisations and Nigerians in the diaspora. The Nigerians in Diaspora Organisation Africa, NIDO Africa, has visited Benue twice this year as part of its campaign against human trafficking and drug abuse. During a June sensitisation programme at Government Model Secondary School, Makurdi, its Continental Chairman, Prof. Jude Osakwe, called for legislation imposing stiff penalties on parents and guardians who aid or permit the trafficking of their children.

Osakwe said some families had become accomplices by allowing their children and wards to be taken away under the guise of employment or other opportunities.

“Most of the time, traffickers promise them jobs in restaurants and several other places, but in the end, they are used as sex slaves, prostitutes and for forced labour,” he said.

NIDO

NIDO Africa, according to Osakwe, has rescued many trafficked children in the last two years and established task forces in countries including Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to strengthen the arrest and prosecution of traffickers.

He said the organisation was also planning vocational and skills acquisition centres for rescued victims because many of them remained vulnerable to re-trafficking when they returned without means of livelihood. “Prevention is better than rescue,” Osakwe said, explaining the decision to take the campaign to secondary schools and other grassroots communities. That emphasis on prevention has become particularly important in Benue, where insecurity has removed thousands of people from their communities and disrupted the lives of children.

The Director of Public Prosecution in the Benue State Ministry of Justice and Secretary of the State Task Force on Human Trafficking, Dooshima Ortsega, described the campaign as timely, noting that many displaced and out-of-school children had become easy targets for traffickers. For children who have lost their homes, schools and familiar surroundings, an offer to travel may sound less like danger and more like an opportunity. The scale of the vulnerability became particularly evident following the attack on Yelewata in June 2025, when hundreds of children were reportedly separated from their communities. The Makurdi Zonal Commander of the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), Hembadoon Kuma, said more than 400 children were taken away from Yelewata, with the agency subsequently rescuing 100. According to her, 97 of those rescued children had been reunited with their families, while three remained at the NAPTIP shelter as efforts continued to locate their parents. Some of the children had been taken to Abia, Rivers, Imo and Enugu Astates.

For Kuma, the Yelewata experience demonstrates why trafficking cannot be treated as a problem that belongs only to one agency. “Human trafficking cannot be fought by NAPTIP alone. We need stakeholders,” she said, welcoming the collaboration with NIDO Africa and other government and community institutions. That collaboration is already extending to an unlikely frontline: the motor park. Benue Links, the state-owned transport company, has intercepted and transported about 250 trafficked persons or intending victims back to their communities as at August 2026, according to its General Manager, Comrade Alexander Fanafa. At the company’s terminals, monitoring officers have been trained to look closely at adults travelling with children or girls who do not bear the same surname. Where circumstances appear suspicious, the adults and children are separated and questioned to establish their relationship, destination and purpose of the journey.

Suspected cases are subsequently handed over to NAPTIP, the police, the DSS or other relevant agencies. Fanafa said the company had also been directed to transport legitimate trafficking victims found anywhere in the country back to Benue free of charge and facilitate their reintegration with their families.

The intervention has come at a cost to the company. Fanafa said Benue Links had virtually lost the profit from its Lagos route because rescued victims were transported without payment. But beyond the financial cost is a deeper human cost. A rescued girl returning home may have lost months or years of her life. She may return without the money she was promised, carrying the psychological scars of exploitation and uncertainty about what comes next. Without support, she may once again become vulnerable to the same people or another trafficking network.

This is why the intervention of the wife of the Tor Tiv, Prof. Felicia Ayati, has focused not only on receiving rescued victims but also on helping them rebuild their lives. Fanafa said she had taken an interest in victims brought to the Tor Tiv’s palace, speaking with them, supporting them and encouraging them to acquire skills before they are reunited with their families.

Speaking on the Benue situation, the Secretary of the Campaign for Equal Rights and Opportunities for all Nigerians (CERON), Francis Odiir, identified poverty and insecurity as two major factors fueling the illicit trade in the state. “Benue has become the epicentre of human trafficking in the country, if we go by the recent figures we are seeing all over the place. Sadly, the majority of the victims are in their teens because they are mostly used for sexual exploitation, and the trade is being fuelled by worsening poverty and insecurity in the state. The state government owes the people a duty to step in and do so decisively, and quickly too,” he said.

For Benue, the growing trafficking crisis therefore presents a challenge that goes beyond arrests and rescues. It is a battle over the future of children whose vulnerability has been intensified by insecurity, displacement, poverty and the absence of opportunities. As traffickers continue to exploit desperation, the real test for Benue will be whether the state and its partners can close the gaps that make vulnerable people easy targets, before another child is persuaded to board a vehicle in search of a future that turns into a nightmare.

World.title: Insurers pay N347bn claims despite N10.9bn premium decline
World.content:
By Rosemary Iwunze

Claims paid by insurance companies rose by 0.1 per cent, year-on-year, YoY to N346.87 billion in the first half of 2026, H1’26, from N346.59 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The rise in claims payment was in spite of a 1.8 per cent YoY decline in Gross Premium Written, GPW, raising concerns over pressure on underwriting margins in the industry.

Analysis of the H1’26 financial statements of 18 insurance companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Limited, NGX, showed that aggregate GPW fell to N579.25 billion, from N590.2 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The companies are AIICO Insurance, Axa Mansard, Consolidated Hallmark Insurance, Cornerstone Insurance, Coronation Insurance, Custodian Investment, Guinea Insurance, International Energy Insurance, Lasaco Assurance, Linkage Assurance, Mutual Benefits, Nem Insurance, Prestige Insurance, Regency Assurance, Sovereign Trust Insurance, SUNU Assurances, Universal, as well as Veritas Kapital Assurance.

Experts are of the opinion that the figures indicate that while insurers generated less premium income during the period under review, their claims obligations continued to rise, albeit marginally.

Speaking on the development, Managing Director of Boof Insurance Brokers, Mr. Olumide Fatogun stated that the figures also suggest that a larger proportion of premium income was absorbed by claims during the period. Although the increase in the claims-to-premium ratio appears marginal, it could become significant for insurers if claims continue to grow while premium income remains subdued.

He said: “There is a need for insurers to sustain premium growth while maintaining disciplined underwriting and claims management. This becomes particularly important as the industry moves into the post-recapitalisation era, with stronger capital requirements expected to translate into greater capacity to underwrite risks and improve policyholders’ confidence in insurance.”

According to NAICOM, about N1.079 trillion has been mobilised through the recapitalisation exercise, comprising fresh capital and existing funds that strengthened the financial position of operators.

But as the industry enters the post-recapitalisation era, questions are increasingly being raised about whether the new capital will translate into better underwriting capacity, faster claims settlement, greater domestic retention of risks and, ultimately, wider insurance coverage.

World.title: Labour gives FG two-week ultimatum to revert petrol price to 2024 level
World.content:
File image

— Says basic necessities now unaffordable for Nigerian workers

— Demands commencement of new minimum wage negotiations before end of October

By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA — Organised Labour has given the Federal Government a two-week ultimatum to revert the price of Premium Motor Spirit, PMS, popularly known as petrol, to its level before the signing of the current national minimum wage in 2024.

It said the measure would cushion the impact of the energy crisis on workers and the masses, as is being done in other countries.

Labour also demanded that the Federal Government commence the process of renegotiating a new national minimum wage before the end of October.

The demands were contained in a communiqué issued at the end of a joint meeting of the National Executive Council, NEC, and the Central Working Committee, CWC, of the Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC. The communiqué was signed by the NLC President, Comrade Joe Ajaero.

According to the communiqué: “The joint meeting issues a two-week ultimatum to the Federal Government, beginning from Friday, October 9, 2026, within which it is expected to, among other things:

“Take measures to reduce the price of petrol across the nation to what it was at the signing of the current national minimum wage in 2024, to cushion the impact of the energy crisis on workers and the masses, as is being done in other countries;

“Commence the process of renegotiating a new national minimum wage;

“Implement the dictates of the Terms of Settlement reached with the Joint Health Sector Unions and Assembly of Healthcare Professionals, JOHESU, on February 5, 2026, and address other demands that have arisen since then;

“Implement the demands of the Joint Public Sector Negotiating Council, JPSNC.

“Failure to do so will compel the NLC to take remedial steps as may be directed by the relevant organs.”

The communiqué explained that the joint meeting deliberated on the state of the nation, the existential threats facing Nigerian workers and the downtrodden masses, and the urgent tasks confronting the trade union movement in Nigeria.

After extensive discussions on the grave economic and political crises, as well as the survival challenges confronting workers and the nation at large, the NEC-in-session, in conjunction with the CWC, arrived at the following resolutions.

On the state of the nation and the existential crises confronting Nigerian workers and the masses, it said: “The joint meeting-in-session notes with profound alarm the deepening misery inflicted on the Nigerian working class and the broader masses by the neo-liberal policies of the Federal Government and its state institutions.

“Inflation continues to soar unabated, the naira remains traumatised, wages have been rendered worthless, and the cost of living has become unbearable.

“The ruling elite, acting as enforcers of global monopoly capital, have demonstrated a worrying indifference to the suffering of the people, choosing instead to transfer the burden of their fiscal negligence onto the already impoverished working masses, thereby abandoning the people to the dictates of comprador fat cats.

“NEC-in-session declares that no society can sustainably develop under a regime of corporate plunder and neo-liberal enslavement.

“The Nigerian working people must, therefore, remain resolute, organised and uncompromising in the collective struggle for a fair and equitable Nigeria.”

On the urgent need to commence the renegotiation of the national minimum wage, the communiqué stated: “The joint meeting observes with grave concern that the current national minimum wage has been rendered worthless by the relentless depreciation of the naira and the astronomical rise in the cost of living.

“Nigerian workers can no longer afford the basic necessities of life — food, shelter, healthcare, transportation and education — on their current wages.

“Consequently, NEC-in-session demands that the Federal Government commences the renegotiation of the national minimum wage before the end of this month.

“The Congress demands a living wage that reflects the true cost of living and the dignity of the Nigerian worker. Any further delay by the Federal Government remains unacceptable.”

The communiqué further stated that the meeting deliberated on the urgent need to reduce the price of petrol.

It said: “The joint meeting reiterates its call on the Federal Government to work with relevant agencies to immediately reduce the price of Premium Motor Spirit, PMS, commonly known as petrol.

“The exorbitant pump price of petrol has had a cascading effect on the cost of transportation, food and other essential goods, further deepening the hardship faced by workers and the masses.

“The government must abandon its insensitive policies that have allowed indiscriminate hikes in the prices of petroleum products, which have only served to enrich a handful of oil marketers while pauperising the masses.”

On tax relief and wage awards for workers, the joint meeting demanded that the Federal Government grant tax relief to workers as agreed and immediately provide wage awards to cushion the impact of the rising cost of living.

“These measures are the bare minimum required to alleviate the suffering of Nigerian workers and restore a measure of dignity to their lives.

“The government cannot continue to demand sacrifice from workers without offering any relief to the suffering masses and workers,” it stated.

The NEC-in-session reaffirmed the historical responsibility of the NLC to resist all forms of exploitation and oppression. It called on all affiliates and progressive allies to remain on high alert and fully prepared to engage in decisive action against all anti-people policies.

“The Congress reiterates that Nigerian working people must remain resolute, organised and uncompromising in the collective struggle for a fair and equitable Nigeria,” it concluded.

World.title: How we paid millions for release of NYSC members — Parents; We’re not aware – Imo govt
World.content:
The rescued.

By Adeola Badru

THE parents of the 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members abducted in Imo State have revealed that they paid millions of naira in ransom before their loved ones were freed. While some relatives paid N3 million, other families raised up to N6 million to secure their children’s safety.

Read Also: Rescued 20 prospective NYSC members arrive Ibadan

These revelations directly contradict statements from the Nigeria Police Force, which claimed security agencies rescued the victims on Wednesday, October 7, 2026. The abduction occurred six days earlier while the youth were travelling from Ibadan, Oyo State, to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states.

I could raise only N3 million — Mother

One of the mothers shared her grueling experience of scrambling for funds while fearing for her child’s life:

“I paid as much as ₦3 million as ransom while I was hoping that nothing happened to my child. I ran helter-skelter to raise the money. I eventually got the money and sent someone to deliver the ransom directly to them.”

Family converged in Ibadan to raise N6 million

The father of another captive explained that his family had to form an emergency alliance to raise N6 million:

“We had to converge somewhere in Ibadan, Oyo State, to put the money together. Some of us even changed the money to dollars and sent it to Imo State to meet whoever was coming to pick it. I am excited that my son is coming back. However, how do I repay the N6 million I borrowed? I’m just a farmer.”

Another mother detailed her negotiations during an interview with News Central Television. She revealed that the kidnappers initially demanded an astronomical N50 million per head.

“Initially, they asked us to pay N50 million per head. We asked whether the amount was for all of them, but they insisted that no, it was for each person. Later, we started begging them to take N500,000. But they said no and started scaring us,” she said in Yoruba.

“Three days ago, they called and said we should pay N15 million. We kept begging them that all we had was ₦5.5 million. They said no and insisted on N6 million. So, it’s that N6 million we paid.”

The abductors instructed the parents to send representatives to Ibadan to organize the logistics:

“They called all the parents of all the victims. Twenty of them are in the bush. They then asked us to send three persons each to meet with them in Ibadan. My husband and my son’s elder brother went. When they got to the meeting place, they asked them to send the money to an account, and that when they got to Imo State, they should change the money into dollars. This is not a rumour. They have all been released and sent to us. His brother is among the people who went to meet with the abductors three days ago. They left with the ransom.”

The ordeal took a severe physical and psychological toll on her

“Since he was kidnapped, I have been stooling. I couldn’t sleep either. But I was relieved when I heard they had been released. It was as though the chains all over me were loosened.”

The ambush at Ogbaku

The 20 prospective corps members were ambushed on Thursday, October 1, 2026, while travelling in two buses. The incident took place at Ogbaku in the Mbaitoli Local Government Area of Imo State, along the busy Owerri-Onitsha Expressway. They were en route to the NYSC camps in Bende, Abia State, and Uyo, Akwa Ibom State.

The official police narrative

The Nigeria Police Force presented a completely different account, maintaining that a joint security operation rescued the youth. Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Ani Iniedu, stated that the victims were recovered at Amakohia Ubi Village in Imo State following sustained search-and-rescue operations.

The official police statement read: “The Nigeria Police Force, in collaboration with sister security agencies, has rescued the 20 prospective NYSC corps members abducted in Imo State on 1st October 2026. The victims were rescued on 7th October 2026 at Amakohia Ubi Village, Imo State, following sustained search-and-rescue operations. They have since been taken for medical assessment and necessary care.”

The police added that coordinated operations are ongoing to track down and prosecute the masterminds of the abduction, thanking the public for their cooperation and support during the rescue operation.

Ransom paid in U.S. Dollars, parents tell BBC

In a separate interview with BBC News Yoruba, another parent speaking on the condition of anonymity reiterated that the kidnappers collected the ransom strictly in U.S. dollars. This parent forcefully denied that security agencies were responsible for the release.

“Not a single person was responsible for securing the release of our children. The parents, alongside friends and support from people online, contributed money so that each parent could pay the amount demanded by the kidnappers.”

The parent claimed that the Department of State Services (DSS) was involved in the investigation and was fully aware of the ransom payment process:

“The DSS was involved in rescue efforts and had invited parents to assist with investigations. The DSS was fully aware that we had converted money into U.S. dollars through a local currency exchanger (aboki) before delivering it to the kidnappers. It was a huge amount of money. The money was substantial.”

Relocation demands and palace confirmation

Following the trauma, one mother declared that her child would pull out of the NYSC scheme entirely if forced to remain in her original posting. She stated she would only allow her child to continue the service year if redeployed to safer regions like Oyo State or Ogun State.

Meanwhile, the palace of the Olubadan of Ibadan—the traditional ruler of the city where the youth began their journey — released an official statement confirming that the victims had safely regained their freedom.

Imo Police deny knowledge of ransom

When confronted with the parents’ claims, the Imo State Police Command firmly denied any knowledge of financial exchanges. Speaking with Channels Television, the Commissioner of Police for Imo State, Audu Bosso, insisted the command was completely unaware of any ransom paid for the 20 corps members and another independent victim who was freed.

Commissioner Bosso maintained that the criminal gang fractured under immense pressure from security forces:

“The kidnappers eventually succumbed to pressure from security agencies, which combed the forest in a sustained rescue operation.”

The commissioner emphasized that tactical teams forced the abductors to abandon their victims and flee the area, concluding that official pressure, not cash, secured their liberty

Rescued 20 prospective NYSC corps members arrive Ibadan, taken to DSS

Meanwhile, the rescued 20 prospective corps members arrived in Ibadan, the Oyo State capital, yesterday, where they were taken to the Department of State Services, DSS, headquarters for debriefing.

The prospective corps members arrived at the DSS office in the Aleshinloye area of Ibadan South-West Local Government Area of the state, following their release from captivity.

At press trime, only representatives of the victims’ parents were allowed access to the DSS premises, while other relatives and sympathisers remained outside the facility.

World.title: Mental health: Nigeria’s action gap comes under scrutiny
World.content:
File image

By Sola Ogundipe

Nigeria’s response to the mental health challenges facing its young people comes under fresh scrutiny today as policymakers, psychiatrists, health professionals, security and correctional authorities, regulators, media and other stakeholders converge on Lagos for the 4th Vanguard Mental Health Summit holding at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos.

The summit, organised by Vanguard Media Limited, comes against growing concerns over depression, suicide, substance abuse, anxiety, trauma, social isolation and the mounting psychological pressures confronting young Nigerians online and offline.

With the theme, “Advancing Youth Mental Health in Nigeria through Access, Action and Advocacy,” and sub-theme, “Mental Health in a Digital Age: Navigating Social Media, Technology and Wellbeing,” the gathering is expected to move the conversation beyond awareness and confront the more difficult issues of access to care, early intervention, treatment, rehabilitation and accountability.

At the centre of the discussion is the question of what happens when a young Nigerian needs mental healthcare but cannot find, afford or access it. Beyond the expert presentations, the summit is expected to confront the gap between Nigeria’s mental health policies and the experience of young people who actually need care.

Chief Host of the summit is Lagos State Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, while the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Pate, and Chairman of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, Brig. Gen. Buba Marwa (retd) are special guest of honour.

The forum will be chaired by Corps Marshal Shehu Mohammed of the Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC. The Director-General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, and the Controller of Corrections, Lagos State Command, Nigerian Correctional Service, Mr. Daramola George are special guests.

Other stakeholders that will feature are President of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Dr. Veronica Nyamali; Prof. Taiwo Sheikh, Professor of Psychiatry and Psychopharmacology at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria; Prof. Mashudat Bello-Mojeed, Professor of Psychiatry and Public Health, as well as senior officials of the Lagos State Ministry of Health, mental health practitioners, academics, development partners, civil society organisations, youth representatives and educators.

Nyamali will deliver the keynote address, while Sheikh will speak on “Mental Health as Our Social Capital.” The President of the Nigerian Medical Association will speak on “Making Youth Mental Health Everyone’s Business: From Policy to Practice,” bringing the perspective of the nation’s umbrella body for medical practitioners to discussions on how mental health policies can translate into practical support and services for young Nigerians.

A major panel session, “Who Takes Responsibility for Young People’s Mental Health?”, will examine the roles of government, families, schools, healthcare providers, communities, civil society and technology platforms in preventing young people from reaching crisis points.

The summit will also examine substance abuse and its intersection with the justice system and other attendant effects. Technology’s growing role in mental healthcare will also come under scrutiny, including the use of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in treating common mental health conditions among young people who do not respond adequately to conventional treatment.

As the stakeholders gather, health commentators note that the question is no longer whether Nigeria has a youth mental health problem, rather, the question is whether its institutions are ready to take responsibility for tackling it. Their participation underscores how deeply mental health now cuts across substance abuse, public safety, the justice system, correctional services and drug regulation.

Vanguard News

World.title: FG offers petrol at N1,350 for next 30 days; opposition kicks
World.content:
File image

*Only at NNPC filling stations; Plans forward crude oil sale to domestic refiners; To invest in National Strategic Fuel Reserve; Says FG didn’t devalue Naira; NNPC discount measure for petrol has Tinubu’s backing — Presidency; What happens on Day 31? — Atiku attacks Tinubu’s 30-day relief; It’s packaged deceit — NDC; It’s desperate attempt to bribe Nigerians ahead elections — ADC campaign

By Emma Ujah, Henry Umoru, Johnbosco Agbakwuru & Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA — The Federal Government, yesterday, said it would offer a discount on petrol dispensed at the filling stations of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company, NNPC, Limited for the next 30 days.

Read Also: NLC draws battle line with FG, gives 14-day ultimatum on petrol, wages

It said the designated NNPC stations will sell petrol at N1,350, a price that would be reviewed every month.

Meanwhile, the Presidency, yesterday explained that the measure taken by the NNPCL to forgo its petrol retail profit margin and sell to Nigerians at cost to cushion the impact of global crude oil price shocks and volatility on vulnerable households has the approval of President Bola Tinubu.

This came as the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar and the national leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, condemned the move.

Atiku rejected the FG’s proposed 30-day fuel discount at NNPC stations, describing it as a temporary political fix that cannot ease the hardship caused by high fuel prices.

NDC on its part described the measure as “tokenism” and an attempt to deceive Nigerians.

On its part, the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, ADC-PCC, dismissed it as a desperate attempt to bribe Nigerians ahead of the 2027 elections.

Minister of Finance, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, who made this disclosure, when he addressed newsmen in Abuja, warned that the proposed reintroduction of fuel subsidy by some presidential candidates could hike the price of Petroleum Motor Spirit (PMS) to N2,000 per litre.

He also warned that such a move would destroy the nation’s economy, with foreign exchange crashing to as low as N3,000/$1.

He said: “We are offering a discount on petrol dispensed by NNPC Limited for the next 30 days in the first instance with priority for public transporters nationwide,” he said.

The minister said transporters will be given first priority, adding that the measure is not a subsidy but an arrangement for government to sell petrol at a ceiling cost.

On measures to alleviate the economic pressures households experience, the minister said the government plans forward sale of crude oil to domestic refiners at a yet-to-be determined period and price.

“That preserves your budget, provides certainty to the refiners and price stability to consumers.

“Pump prices do not have to follow every swing in global crude prices or the exchange rate. Government is negotiating a ceiling prices of N1,350 a litre on the ex-gantry or the landing cost of petrol to keep fuel prices stable.”

Oyedele said the price will be reviewed monthly.

Ealier, he warned that the proposed reintroduction of fuel subsidy by some presidential candidates could hike the price of Petroleum Motor Spirit (PMS) to N2,000 per litre.

He also warned that such a move would destroy the nation’s economy, with foreign exchange crashing to as low as N3,000/$1.

His words: “Return subsidy and the sequence is familiar. Weaker revenue invites a sovereign credit downgrade, as the rating agencies have already signalled.

“That would put at risk the upgrades we have recently earned, including our first from S&P in 14 years. Borrowing becomes costlier. Capital leaves. Reserves fall. The naira weakens.

“The progress on inflation, which has allowed the Central Bank to begin lowering interest rates, would be put at risk. Our estimate is that the exchange rate could approach N3,000 to the dollar within months, and so-called subsidised petrol would cost at least N2,000 a litre. That is well above what Nigerians pay today.”

Oyedele said removal of fuel subsidy did not mean that government is doing nothing to alleviate pains the policy has brought on ordinary Nigerians.

“Removing the subsidy has never meant doing nothing. Over the past three years, government has acted to moderate prices in ways that are sustainable.”

He said deregulation made domestic refining viable, which was why supply has held while other countries scramble for scarce cargoes and that Dangote refinery would not have been able to operate under a regime of fuel subsidy.

Oyedele added that efforts to source cheaper transport alternatives such as through the Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) and electric vehicles are part of steps by the Federal Government to reduce the cost of transportation.

“More than 120,000 vehicles now run on CNG, served by over 400 conversion centres, 96 refueling stations and 18 Liquefied-to-Compressed Natural gas (L-CNG) stations.

“Over 550 CNG buses have been deployed so far. Where they run, fares have fallen by 30 to 50 percent. We have also removed taxes on electric vehicles and solar equipment, and cut import duties on all vehicles. Customs data show that imports of CNG-powered vehicles including tricycles, electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment have more than doubled since May 2023, with duty waivers of over N100 billion. Some states plan to introduce CNG buses and electric tricycles at scale,” he said.

FG didn’t devalue Naira

The minister clarified that the current administration did not devalue the Naira, rather, according to him, the Naira depreciated because the nation ran out of reserves.

His words: “Naira was not devalued, rather Naira depreciated because we ran out of reserves to defend the artificial exchange rate which was only accessible by the highly connected while manufacturers and average Nigerians pay a huge premium for FX in the parallel market.

“Today, the gap between the official and parallel rates has narrowed from over 60 per cent to under five per cent. Reserves stand at about $55billion, the highest level in eighteen years. This is the single biggest lever on pump prices, and one we cannot afford to lose.”

National Strategic Fuel Reserve

Oyedele also disclosed that to protect households and businesses from future energy shocks, the Federal Government is investing in a National Strategic Fuel Reserve.

He said: “Refined products will be released into the market under clear, published rules whenever a global disruption or hoarding threatens supply and price stability. This is not a subsidy and it does not fix prices, rather it secures supply and reduces price volatility. It will prevent artificial scarcity, deter market manipulation and anchor long-term energy security.”

NNPC discount measure for petrol has Tinubu’s backing — Presidency

The Presidency explained that the measure should not be interpreted to mean that the government was out to reverse a necessary reform designed to set the country on the path towards sustained prosperity.

A statement by the Special Adviser to President Tinubu on Information and Strategy, Mr. Bayo Onanuga, said: “To be clear, none of these measures restores a blanket subsidy. Doing so would create longer-term harm for a short-term cure. Each measure is designed to reach the people who need help, without putting the wider economy at risk.

“Removing the fuel subsidy came at a price. But the alternative has been tried. Nigeria has already lived through that cycle: scarcity, smuggling, a collapsing currency and a fiscal crisis. We cannot afford to live through it again, least of all in response to a temporary disruption, and at the very moment the results of reform are gathering pace.

“Government is not out to reverse a necessary reform designed to set our country on the path towards sustained prosperity. It is to ensure its gains reach more Nigerians, faster and in more tangible ways. That is our work, and we are committed to doing it.

“The Federal Government is also working on a comprehensive package of fiscal measures to bring inflation down to single digits sustainably in the near term.

“NNPC Retail, which already sells petrol at the lowest price in the market, will offer this new deal within the next 30 days. This means if NNPC’s landing cost is N1300, it will sell fuel to Nigerians, especially commercial vehicles, at the same price,” it stated.

What happens on Day 31? — Atiku attacks Tinubu’s 30-day relief

In his reaction, former Vice-President, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar said Nigerians who had endured years of soaring transport fares and food prices could not be expected to regard a one-month discount as a solution to a crisis that would remain after the offer expires.

In a statement by Phrank Shaibu, his Director of Strategic Communication, “Atiku totally rejects this calendar-scheduled, election-laced subsidy package. Nigerians are not fools to be offered a month of discounted fuel after years of punishing prices and then expected to forget the hardship when the discount expires. This is shameless and heartless.

“What happens on Day 31? Nigerians wake up to the same brutal prices, the same punishing transport fares and the same rising cost of food. The government cannot manufacture relief for one month and expect Nigerians to applaud while the hardship remains,” he said.

Atiku also faulted the restriction of the discount to NNPC stations, saying the government had yet to disclose how much motorists would save per litre or guarantee that transport operators would pass any savings on to passengers through lower fares.

He said the government’s sudden shift towards a subsidy-style intervention exposed what he described as the failure of its earlier argument that meaningful relief was impossible.

“This volte-face proves that the production-support proposal I have advanced is workable, achievable and not complicated. The Tinubu government and its spin doctors have tried to make it sound impossible, yet they are now reaching for a temporary subsidy-style intervention because the pain has become impossible to ignore,” Atiku said.

Atiku reiterated his proposal for capped and budgeted production support tied to fuel refined in Nigeria, with safeguards to ensure consumers benefit while supporting local refining.

“Nigerians need lasting relief, not a countdown to the return of hardship. Tinubu’s government cannot spend years telling Nigerians to endure, then offer 30 days of relief and call it a solution,” he said.

He restated his commitment to making life more affordable, saying: “Tinubu made life expensive. I will make life affordable again.”

It is packaged deceit — NDC

NDC in a statement, yesterday, by its National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, said the temporary discount announced by FG is inadequate to address the economic hardship allegedly caused by the removal of petrol subsidy.

NDC described the initiative as a “Greek gift” from the administration of President Bola Tinubu, arguing that subsidy removal was implemented without adequate consultation or measures to cushion its impact on Nigerians.

It said: “The NDC has noted the breaking news by the Federal Government announcing a 30-day discount on petrol through NNPC stations.

“According to the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, “We are offering a discount on petrol dispensed by NNPC Limited for the next 30 days in the first instance, with priority for public transporters nationwide. So, it’s not a subsidy. The government is just saying we sell to you at cost.”

“This is nothing but tokenism and a Greek gift from a government that whimsically removed fuel subsidy without proper consideration, consultation, or cushions for Nigerians.

“Nigerians cannot be deceived.

“What happens to the millions of Nigerians who lost their jobs and whose businesses collapsed as a result of the callous and poorly planned removal of subsidy? What about those who lost their lives in poorly equipped government hospitals that have now become mortuaries?

“It is clear that President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress, APC, government are desperate, and Nigerians must not be deceived. Emilokanomics has failed woefully.

“The attempt to reintroduce petrol subsidy through the back door is not only mischievous but a sign of a government in free fall, ready to clutch at anything to survive.

“Even the bogus promise to dispense discounted fuel at designated NNPC retail outlets is not pragmatic. How many such outlets exist in Nigeria to serve over 200 million Nigerians?

“Is this not the recipe for another stampede that could have many more Nigerians trampled to death at the filling stations?

“Several questions beg for answers, but the only answer staring Nigerians in the face is that the economy is in a tailspin and at a tipping point. The APC has shown itself glaringly incapable of rescuing the country from imminent collapse.

“But hope is on the way. Peter Obi, under the NDC, will put Nigeria back on the right track. A New Nigeria is POssible with Obi.

“In a few months, specifically on January 16, 2027, Nigerians should come out en masse and vote for Peter Obi and all other NDC candidates to vote out the most clueless and rudderless government in the history of Nigeria.”

It’s desperate attempt to bribe Nigerians ahead elections – ADC campaign

ADC-PCC in a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, said: “After over three years of subjecting Nigerians to excruciating pain through the reckless removal of fuel subsidy, the collapse of the naira and suffocating economic policies, the Tinubu administration now thinks it can bribe Nigerians with 30 days of cheaper fuel.

“Nigerians will reject your one-month bribe.

“What happens after 30 days? Will Nigerians return to buying petrol at over N1,400 per litre?

“This is not governance; this is deceit. It is a negotiated bribe designed to be reviewed monthly to suit the government’s political calendar.

“Atiku was right all along. This half-hearted 30-day gimmick is proof that the government has finally acknowledged the truth, although it has done so too late and in a deceitful manner.

“If the government can reduce the burden of fuel costs for 30 days, with priority given to public transport operators, why did it allow Nigerians to suffer for more than 800 days?

“This proves that the government has always had the capacity to make life easier for Nigerians but chose not to do so and only remembers the suffering masses when elections are around the corner.

“No one-month palliative can buy the conscience of Nigerians.

“Nigerians are not for sale. You cannot buy their future with 30 days of cheaper fuel.

“They have seen through this fraud. They know the difference between genuine governance and a one-month electoral bribe. They have resolved to vote out hardship and hunger in 2027,” he said.

Nigerians speak

Meanwhile, some Nigerians spoke to Vanguard on what presidential candidates in the 2027 elections should campaign with:

The 2027 presidential campaign must move past rhetoric to tackle Nigeria’s biting cost of living, insecurity, unemployment, and collapsing purchasing power. Candidates must offer clear policy directions, demonstrate honest communication, and unite the nation. Discussions should also prioritize judicial independence, INEC’s autonomy, and abolishing state governors’ security votes to establish a new standard of leadership. — Uche Ruth Ogbonnaya, Journalist

As the 2027 election campaign begins, presidential candidates must focus on issues impacting daily Nigerian lives: economic growth, security, cost of living, electricity, healthcare, and education. Beyond making promises, aspirants need to clearly explain their implementation strategies, funding sources, and measurement metrics. Nigerians deserve issue-based campaigns, transparency, and realistic solutions for long-term development. — Romoke Olisa, Entrepreneur

The core challenge is Nigeria’s comatose oil industry; it uniquely imports petroleum, as even the Dangote refinery remains expensive. Fixing the unworkable state refineries to lower fuel prices is vital for the economy. Additionally, candidates must formalize the massive informal economy—which employs 93% of workers—by providing credit, social protection, and infrastructure to drive sustainable national development. — Gbenga Komolafe, Entrepreneur

As the 2027 election approaches, candidates must focus heavily on the cost of living and insecurity. They need to provide practical solutions for lowering the costs of food and energy, including fuel and electricity. Additionally, they must tackle the widespread insecurity that directly threatens Nigeria’s food security and employment. These critical issues must lead every campaign. — Endurance Ibhadore, Entrepreneur

As the presidential campaigns begin, the two most pressing issues are ending insecurity and easing economic hardship for Nigerians. Any candidate who lacks a clear template or a proposed plan of action to address these two critical areas needs to recalibrate their strategy and quickly rethink their approach to governance. — Francisca Ogar, Journalist

The 2027 presidential campaign must move beyond regular rhetoric to confront Nigeria’s most pressing challenges: insecurity, economic hardship, high unemployment, and collapsed purchasing power. Citizens demand a clear policy direction and tangible results. The next president must demonstrate the capacity to communicate honestly, take full responsibility, and unite a deeply divided nation, establishing a higher standard of leadership. — Oputa David, Communications expert

Vanguard News

World.title: INEC Insists on Supreme Court Verdict, Says Erring Parties Won’t Field Candidates
World.content:
• Insists those not in party registers at the close of regulatory time will be affected

•Seeks stakeholders’ support as voters’ register display begins Oct 9 in Sokoto

Chuks Okocha, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto





The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), has warned that political parties fielding candidates whose names were not in the registers submitted to the commission at the close of regulatory time will not be allowed to participate in the 2027 elections.

The Supreme Court had in a September 24, 2026 judgement affirmed the constitutionality of Sections 77(5), 77(6) and 77(7) of the Electoral Act 2026 and upheld INEC’s revised timetable and schedule of activities for the 2027 general election.

Those whose nominations might have attracted attention included Rivers State governorship candidate of All Progressives Congress (APC), Kingsley Chinda; Delta Central senatorial candidate of Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Ovie Omo-Agege; former Cross River State Governor and Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) presidential candidate, Donald Duke; and a former Delta State House of Assembly Speaker, Victor Ochei.

INEC National Commissioner for Information and Voter Education, Mohammed Haruna, explained the implications of the judgement while speaking on Trust TV’s Daily Politics programme, yesterday.

Haruna said the affected parties would also not be allowed to substitute such candidates, stating that parties should not benefit from violations of the law.

He said the commission was expected to make a definite pronouncement on the implications of the Supreme Court judgement by next Tuesday.

Haruna stated, “It’s like you committed an offence. And then, you come and benefit from it. You remember cases that we had of some in Zamfara, you remember Plateau? The same thing happened.

“The parties, because they did the wrong thing, they thought they could now steal through the candidates.

“And the law was very clear. Once you do that kind of thing, you cannot benefit from it. You are benefiting from it, if you are able to substitute a candidate.”

According to him, depending on when the commission concludes its review, some political parties may be unable to field candidates for some other elective positions.

Haruna stated, “All the candidates, all the way to the Houses of Assembly, we interviewed them. If their names are not on the party register, they were not members of the party at the time that they contested for those tickets.”

He explained that the delay in INEC’s final position was due to the need to obtain legal advice after receiving the Certified True Copy of the Supreme Court judgement.

Haruna said the commission had to exercise caution because forged copies of court judgements had been presented in the past.

He said, “You can’t be too careful with these things because even when you see copies and they tell you it’s a CTC, it may be forged. We’ve seen instances where people have even gone, have the audacity to forge a Supreme Court judgement.

“So, we have to be very careful to make sure that we take the right decision .”

Amupitan: Unverified Electoral Fraud Claims Could Damage Public Confidence

In another development, the Chairman of the Electoral Commission (INEC), Professor Joash Amupitan, warned yesterday that unverified allegations of electoral fraud could inflict lasting damage on confidence in the electoral process, even when subsequently corrected.

Amupitan gave the warning in Lagos while speaking at the 10th Annual Conference of the Guild of Corporate Online Publishers (GOCOP), with the theme, “2027 Elections: Trust, Transparency and Shared Responsibilities.”

The INEC chairman was represented by Resident Electoral Commissioner, Lagos, Professor Ayobami Salami.

Amupitan, in a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Adedayo Oketola, urged online publishers to place accuracy above the pressure to break stories ahead of competitors, warning against the use of clickbait headlines and unverified information in election reporting.

He said, “While INEC carries the legal mandate to conduct elections, the wider democratic health of Nigeria and, indeed, West Africa depends on the information infrastructure maintained by the media, particularly online publishers. This is where the core concept of Shared Responsibility becomes operational.

“We live in an era where the velocity of digital information frequently outpaces the verification of truth.”

Amupitan stated, “Across our sub-region, election windows are increasingly targeted by coordinated information warfare, political violence narratives, synthetic media, and AI-generated deepfakes designed to inflame ethnic divides or passion and undermine institutional legitimacy.

“Fake news, unverified leaks, and sensationalised reports directly destroy public trust, incite civil unrest, and induce voter apathy.

“When an unverified claim regarding electoral fraud is published, the damage to public confidence is immediate and enduring; subsequent retractions or fact-checks rarely repair the injury.”

Amupitan said the media had a critical responsibility in shaping public perception of the electoral process, stressing that inaccurate reports could have consequences beyond the immediate news cycle.

He urged publishers to provide proper context when reporting operational challenges during elections, rather than presenting isolated incidents as evidence of systemic failure.

The INEC chief said responsible journalism would require media organisations to verify claims with the commission and other credible sources, particularly when reporting polling-unit results, electoral irregularities and allegations of manipulation.

Responding to the issue of result declaration, Salami explained that the 1999 Constitution specifically vested the authority to return an election result to the Returning Officer.

Salami clarified that being an INEC official did not automatically confer the constitutional authority to return election results.

He stated that even as a Resident Electoral Commissioner, he did not have the constitutional power to announce or return an election result.

He explained that Returning Officers were appointed by the commission and the officials constitutionally empowered to return the results of the elections assigned to them.

In his opening remarks, Conference Chairman, Dr. Olisa Agbakoba, SAN, underscored the people’s constitutional right to vote, urging INEC to ensure that the 2027 elections are free, fair, and credible.

Agbakoba raised key issues expected to shape political discourse ahead of the elections, particularly the future of fuel subsidy.

He challenged presidential candidates to explain their positions on the subsidy regime and what they would do differently if elected.

INEC Seeks Stakeholders’ Support as Voters Register Display Begins October 9

INEC in Sokoto State is billed to commence the display of the Preliminary Register of Voters for claims and objections, alongside the distribution of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), from October 9 to 15. Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC) in the state, Hon. Umar Garba, disclosed this during a press briefing at the commission’s headquarters in Sokoto, yesterday.

Garba said the seven-day exercise would take place at the Registration Area (RA) level across the state, particularly in areas without security concerns, to enable voters verify their details ahead of the general election.

He said the commission had already taken delivery of newly produced PVCs for the exercise, and had put in place necessary logistics for a hitch-free conduct of the display and distribution.

According to the REC, the PVCs currently available for collection are exclusively for newly registered voters captured during the first phase of the last Continuous Voter Registration (CVR) exercise.

He, however, clarified that PVCs for requests relating to lost or damaged cards, updates, transfers, as well as those who registered during the second and third phases of the CVR, were not yet ready for collection.

Garba assured the people that the commission would issue further information once the outstanding categories of PVCs were received and ready for distribution to their owners.

He added that at the conclusion of the RA-level exercise on October 15, the distribution of PVCs would continue at INEC Local Government Area (LGA) offices across the 23 LGAs of the state for those who could not collect at the RA centres.

He encouraged all registered voters in the state to visit their designated display locations within their respective Registration Areas between October 9 and 15 to cross-check their names, photographs, and other details, and report any errors or omissions through the prescribed channels.

World.title: Fuel Price: FG Offers 30-day Discount at NNPC Stations
World.content:
•NLC gives two-week ultimatum to return to 2024 price

•Atiku: Tinubu’s new measure is panic move, publicity stunt

•ADC accuses government of attempting to bribe Nigerians

•Makinde Campaign: Fuel discount announcement deceitful

Ndubuisi Francis, Chuks Okocha and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja





The federal government yesterday unveiled a 10-point intervention to cushion the impact of rising petrol prices and the wider energy crisis, offering a 30-day discount at Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) filling stations nationwide, with public transporters to receive priority.

The measures, announced by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, also included a negotiated N1,350 per litre ceiling on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol, forward sales of crude to domestic refineries as well as removal of illegal levies.

Besides, the government said it was hastening the deployment of Compressed Natural Gas (CNG), increasing support for vulnerable Nigerians and the introducing a National Strategic Fuel Reserve.

Oyedele, who announced the measures at a press conference in Abuja, said the intervention was neither a return to fuel subsidy nor an attempt to impose price controls, but rather a mechanism to moderate the effect of global energy shocks on Nigerian consumers and businesses.

He said the federal government had taken several steps since the removal of fuel and foreign exchange subsidies to cushion the resulting hardship, but was compelled to introduce the new measures following the sharp increase in global energy prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East.

“We are offering a discount on petrol dispensed by NNPC Limited for the next 30 days, with priority for public transporters nationwide. As production rises and previously committed crude is freed up, this would shield pump prices from volatility in the global market,” Oyedele stressed.

On the proposed N1,350 ceiling, the minister said the arrangement would prevent domestic petrol prices from responding immediately to every movement in international crude prices and the exchange rate.

“Pump prices should not have to follow every swing in global crude or the exchange rate. The government is negotiating a ceiling of N1,350 a litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol, to keep pump prices stable.

“Where costs rise above the ceiling, refiners and importers will carry the shortfall and recover it later, when crude prices or the exchange rate allow, without breaching the ceiling,” he said.

Similarly, Oyedele said the ceiling would be reviewed monthly and the figures published to ensure transparency.

FG: Move Not Subsidy, Price Control
