World.title: Liberia: In Buchanan, Saya Doe Sio Honors Her Late Mother Annie T. Doe with a Memorial Bust—and A Living Legacy of Education, Faith and Service
World.content:
BUCHANAN, Grand Bassa County — For Saya Doe Sio, returning to the place where she was born and raised is always deeply personal. But on Monday, October 5, 2026, the return carried an even greater emotional weight.

Standing on the grounds of the Annie T. Doe Memorial Academy in Sugar Cane Farm, Lower Buchanan, Sio joined her husband and co-founder of the Annie T. Doe Memorial Foundation, Francis Sio, members of the family, friends from the United States, grandchildren and great-grandchildren to unveil a bust honoring the woman whose life and values continue to shape the institution.

That woman was her mother, the late Annie T. Doe.



The unveiling brought together generations of the Doe family and members of the wider foundation family, including supporters whose contributions have helped sustain the academy and its mission.

For the students, the occasion was not simply a ceremony. It was an opportunity to welcome the people behind an institution that has become part of their lives.

Melvina Saydee, a Grade 8 student, delivered a warm welcome on behalf of the students, administrators and staff.

“On behalf of our staff, students [and] administrators of this noble and prestigious institution, we wholeheartedly want to welcome you to our school, Annie T. Doe Memorial Academy,” Saydee said.

She told the visiting family and guests that she hoped their presence, conversations and interactions with the students would inspire them.

The students also presented roses as a symbol of “peace and love.”

Sio responded with gratitude, telling the students that whenever she returns to Buchanan, she comes with “good tidings and great joy.”

But the heart of the day belonged to the woman whose name the academy carries.

Remembering a Mother, Reclaiming a Dream

In an emotional reflection before the unveiling, Saya Sio pointed toward the family home where she was born and raised and recalled the humble beginnings that shaped her life.

“This is the house that I was born and raised in,” she said. “Just like Jenneh Peters, Eric Peters, we grew up in this house running around barefooted like all of you as you see today.”

Sio recalled that her mother raised nine children and instilled in them two principles that would ultimately become central to her daughter’s life’s work: faith and education.

“My mother was a missionary,” Sio said. “She believed in community. She believed that every child should have access to quality education.”

But Annie Doe had herself been denied the opportunity to receive a formal education.

According to her daughter, she survived through hard work, selling used clothes and doing whatever was necessary to provide for her family. Sio recalled accompanying her mother’s entrepreneurial efforts from an early age, even selling items after school to help put food on the family table.

Yet, amid hardship, Annie Doe continued to believe in education and the possibilities it could create.

“She believed in the power of education,” Sio recalled.

Then came a prediction that Sio said she did not fully understand at the time.

Her mother once sat on the porch of their home and told her: “I see you one day coming back to this community and rewriting the story for your friends.”

Decades later, that vision has become reality.

From Tragedy to Purpose



Sio’s recollection of her mother’s death was perhaps the most emotional moment of the ceremony.

She recalled that on September 20, 1989, Annie Doe traveled toward Monrovia to obtain used clothing for her business. Sio said she was supposed to accompany her mother but remained in Monrovia.

On her mother’s return journey to Buchanan, tragedy struck.

Sio said Annie Doe and two other people who were traveling with her died in a road crash.

“I came in the car right behind her and I met her lying in the pool of blood with the two individuals that me and my friend could have been in the car,” she recalled.

For the teenage daughter who lost her mother, the tragedy could have become the defining story of her life.

Instead, Sio says, it became the beginning of another story.

“But God always uses your pain to produce purpose,” she said.

That purpose, she explained, became the driving force behind the creation of the Annie T. Doe Memorial Foundation.

“And that’s the reason we are running with the vision for Annie Doe—to make sure what she dreamt of years ago, that every child should have access to quality education,” Sio said.

“That’s the reason the Annie T. Doe Memorial Foundation was formed—to give hope to all of you.”

A Memorial That Speaks to Generations

When the covering was removed from the bust, the inscription offered a concise tribute to the woman being honored:

“The late Annie T. Doe, mother and grandmother to many. A businesswoman, a woman of faith, passion, and dignity. Today we honor her legacy.”

Sio was joined at the unveiling by members of the next generations of the family, including grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

“My other siblings could not be here today,” she said, noting that she is the youngest of nine children. “But I will have her great-grand [children] and her grandchildren also join me to cut this.”

The moment transformed the memorial from a monument to the past into a gathering of generations connected by Annie Doe’s life.

Mrs. Saya Doe Sio and her husband and Co-founder of the Annie T. Doe Memorial Foundation sing Annie T. Doe Memorial Academy ode along with the students

Fifteen Years of Turning Vision Into Opportunity

Francis Sio, the foundation’s co-founder, used the occasion to reflect on the journey that brought the family back to the community.

“It’s been 15 years,” he told the students. “And it is only by the grace of God.”

He recalled seeing some of the students grow from kindergarten and first grade into young people now approaching graduation.

“When I look at the faces, some of you, you were just in the kindergarten or first grade. Now you guys are graduating. You guys have grown,” he said.

The foundation’s own account says the academy opened in 2014 with 75 students and has since expanded substantially. It now serves hundreds of students in Buchanan, with its educational mission centered on providing Christian-based education and opportunities for children whose economic circumstances could otherwise limit their futures.

The foundation has also expanded beyond education into women’s empowerment and basic healthcare, making Annie Doe’s legacy one that extends beyond the classroom.

The work has previously attracted attention in Liberia. FrontPage Africa has reported on the foundation’s efforts in Buchanan, including the construction of additional school facilities and its community outreach programs.

Remembering Those Who Made It Possible

The ceremony also recognized members of the foundation’s board and supporters who believed in the vision.

Sio described some of the supporters as “destiny helpers”—people who, despite not always being physically present in Liberia, invested in the lives and education of the students.

“These are people who also believe in Liberia, who have not even traveled to Liberia,” Sio said. “They are called destiny helpers.”

She recognized supporters who had contributed to the education of the academy’s students, noting that 44 people had contributed to one graduating class.

“Again, they are the ones who made it happen for our class,” she said. “And what a way to memorialize and honor the sacrifice.”

The foundation’s records similarly emphasize sponsorship as an important part of its model, describing supporters as “destiny helpers” who invest in students’ futures.

A Legacy Measured in Lives

The significance of Annie T. Doe’s memorial may ultimately be measured not in stone or bronze, but in the lives of the children walking through the gates of the academy.

Her daughter grew up in the same community, experienced the loss of her mother as a teenager, left Liberia for the United States and eventually returned with a vision shaped by the values her mother had instilled in her.

Today, children who might otherwise struggle to access quality education are studying on the very land where Annie Doe raised her family.

The symbolism is difficult to miss.

A woman who was denied formal education helped raise a daughter who returned years later to build an institution centered on education.

A mother who believed that children deserved opportunities now has her name carried by a school where hundreds of children are being prepared for their futures.

And a daughter who once mourned her mother’s death now stands before generations of students, family members and supporters, transforming that loss into a legacy of service.

As Saya Sio looked back on her mother’s life, she made clear that the memorial was never intended to be merely about remembering the past.

It is about continuing the work.

Annie T. Doe may be gone, but in Buchanan, her story is still being written—one child, one classroom and one opportunity at a time.

World.title: Liberia: Former NSA Official & Five Out of 19 Indicted In Major Drug, Money Laudering Case Taken to Monrovia Central Prison as Court Issues Writ
World.content:
Monrovia-Five of the 19 defendants indicted alongside former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor in a drug trafficking and money laundering case have been arrested, brought before Criminal Court “C” at the Temple of Justice and subsequently taken to the Monrovia Central Prison, where they are being held pending trial.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Among those arrested are Gerald Foley Smith, former Deputy Director for Administration of the National Security Agency, NSA, Jammel V. Jallah, Christian L. Nyantee, Cayce L. Nelson, Albenigo Janior and Sekou, according to information surrounding the court proceedings.



Mark Quiah, former Deputy Director for Operations of the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority was initially arrested late Wednesday night, October 7, and taken to the Monrovia Central Prison, making the number of arrest six, since the indictment.

The development followed a writ of arrest issued by Criminal Court “C” on October 7, 2026, ordering the Montserrado County Sheriff, Major Austine Seinavula, or his deputy, to arrest the defendants named in the indictment and bring them before the court to answer to the allegations.

The defendants have not been arraigned.

They were arrested and brought before the court pursuant to the writ and have since been taken to the Monrovia Central Prison pending further judicial proceedings.

11 Serious Criminal Charges

The indictment contains a range of allegations, including unlicensed possession of controlled drugs or substances; unlicensed importation of controlled drugs or substances; unlicensed exportation of controlled drugs or substances; unlicensed sale, trading, administration, dispensation, delivery, distribution, dispatch in transit and transportation of controlled drugs or substances; illicit trafficking; criminal conspiracy; criminal facilitation; criminal solicitation; money laundering; possession and sale of physical objects for lethal use; and possession of physical objects for lethal use.

The allegations represent some of the most serious criminal charges contained in the indictment, which has drawn former government officials and other individuals into the ongoing investigation and prosecution.

Court Orders Arrests

The writ of arrest, signed by J. Amos F. Gbowah, Clerk of Criminal Court “C,” commands the Montserrado County Sheriff to arrest the defendants and “forthwith” bring them before the court to answer to the charges contained in the indictment.

The writ states that the arrests are based on an indictment prepared by the Grand Jury of Montserrado County, which was duly selected, empaneled and sworn to inquire into the alleged offenses. The court further ordered the sheriff to make an official return showing the manner in which each writ was served. Former Security, Aviation Officials Caught in Case The inclusion of former senior officials from Liberia’s security and aviation sectors has added significance to the case. Smith previously served as Deputy Director for Administration at the National Security Agency, while Quiah served as Deputy Director for Operations at the LCAA. Their detention comes as the authorities move to enforce the court’s arrest orders against the individuals named in the indictment. The case also names former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor among the defendants, placing a former senior government official at the center of a prosecution involving allegations of drug offenses, illicit trafficking and money laundering. However, the indictment contains allegations only, and none of the defendants is guilty unless proven so by a court of competent jurisdiction. The defendants are entitled to due process, legal representation and a fair trial under the Liberian Constitution and applicable laws. The latest arrests are expected to be followed by further court proceedings to determine the next legal steps in the case.

World.title: Liberia: 1,500 Pupils, Too Few Chairs as Gbarnga Public School Struggles With Overcrowding
World.content:
GBARNGA, Bong County — The competition starts before the first lesson. Pupils arriving each morning at Chief Compound Public School look first for somewhere to sit: a chair, a gap on a broken bench, anything. Those who come after the seats are gone have one option. The floor.

By Selma Lomax| [email protected]

The school, which enrolls more than 1,500 pupils, is not in a remote village beyond the reach of government. It stands in Gbarnga, the administrative and political capital of Bong County, within easy reach of the government offices and education authorities charged with the welfare of the county’s children.



Inside some classrooms, children sit for hours on bare concrete, balancing exercise books on their knees as they try to follow lessons. Others crowd onto broken benches, squeeze onto whatever furniture is still usable, or bring chairs from home.

What they are asking for is modest. Not computers, air conditioners or science laboratories — just chairs and desks that would let them sit properly, write comfortably and concentrate.

Pupils at Chief Compound Public School in Gbarnga sit on the classroom floor during lessons. Those who arrive after the few usable seats are taken have nowhere else to sit. “We are in the city, not somewhere that people cannot reach,” one pupil said. “Our school is here in Gbarnga, and the people who are responsible for education are also in this city. We see government offices and other important people around us, so sometimes we ask ourselves why we have to sit on the floor to learn. We are children, and all we are asking for is a chair so that we can sit properly, write our lessons and concentrate. We want to believe that somebody will hear us.” FrontPageAfrica is not identifying the pupils interviewed for this story because they are minors. The distance between the school and the offices that could help it can be counted in streets. The distance between the problem and a solution, the pupils suggest, is far greater. For the children, the shortage is not a policy abstraction. It greets them every morning — and, they say, it may be keeping some of their classmates away altogether. Friends who stopped coming Pupils spoke of friends who no longer attend school, and they tied those absences to money: parents who could not afford to buy a chair.

FrontPageAfrica could not verify the claim against attendance records, and its scale is unknown. But it reflects a pressure familiar to many Liberian households. When income is thin, every expense competes with every other. A chair is not food. It is not medicine or transport fare. In the hard choices poor families are forced to make, a chair can lose.

The pupils spoke of their absent classmates less with anger than with a sense of loss, the way people talk about a friend who has moved away. What they want, they said, is for everyone to learn together.

Exercise books on their laps, pupils follow a lesson from the floor. The school is in Gbarnga, the administrative capital of Bong County. A desk in the doorway The staff room tells its own story. Its floor is pitted with holes, and a handful of chairs sit clustered in one corner. During a visit by FrontPageAfrica, a female teacher searched for somewhere to set down her lesson notes. She later carried pupils’ exercise books to the classroom doorway — the only place with enough light to read them. Teachers who improvise this way keep the school running, but the improvisation has a cost. A teacher straining to read a child’s handwriting in a doorway is more likely to rush her feedback, and it is the child who loses. An admission from the county Asked by FrontPageAfrica about conditions at the school, County Education Officer David Boakai said he had not been aware of them. His office, he said, would need to look into the situation, particularly the learning environment and the shortage of chairs and other basic facilities. His candor offers a clear starting point — and a commitment against which progress can be measured. But it also exposes a gap. Chief Compound is not hidden beyond a river crossing. It sits in the county seat and serves well over a thousand children. If its condition had not reached the county’s top education official, then somewhere between the classroom and his office, the system’s ability to notice has broken down.

A proper assessment would not be complicated: count the pupils and the usable seats; separate what can be repaired from what must be replaced; inspect classroom space and the condition of the buildings. Those figures would give parents something to hold on to — and officials something to answer for.

What a chair carry It is tempting to treat a shortage of chairs as a small matter beside Liberia’s larger struggles. But small things can carry large meanings. A chair holds up a child’s body so that the mind can do its work. It marks out a space that belongs, however briefly, to one pupil. It tells a child that the school expected her and made room. Take the chair away, and the message reverses. The child becomes someone to be accommodated by improvisation, someone whose comfort is optional. The pupils at Chief Compound have noticed. What they ask in return is neither grand nor unusual: equal treatment, a seat beside their friends, and an end to writing on their knees. Who will stand up? The pupils have done what they can. They have described their classrooms, named what they lack, and trusted a visiting reporter to carry their words further than they could. The responsibility now lies with others. The county has promised to look. Parents could organize. Donors, civic groups and local leaders could each take a share. However, the response takes shape, it will be judged by a simple test: whether, one morning soon, a child in Gbarnga walks into a classroom and finds a seat waiting. Until then, the children of Chief Compound will keep adapting, as children do. The question is how long the school system intends to rely on their patience.

World.title: Liberia: Errors, Contradictions Cloud Drug Case Against Ex-VP Taylor as she and several others Named in indictment
World.content:
MONROVIA – When officers raided a compound on Cement Road in the VOA Community on July 21, they found 3,971 “plates” of the drug, packed in 157 bags and valued at about US$317 million.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Two foreign men were arrested on the spot. Eleven weeks later, the State has gone much further. A 55-page indictment now names 20 people, among them senior security officers, an aviation official and the woman who was once a heartbeat from the presidency, former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor.



But a close reading of the document tells a messier story. Dates shift from page to page. Payments grow or appear out of nowhere. The indictment gets Taylor’s own term of office wrong, and the court that filed it is not the court that ordered the arrests.

Taylor’s lawyer, Cllr. Gbawou Kowou, says the case against his client rests on the word of one man, co-defendant Sheik Bashiru Kante.

“The entire indictment of Jewel is nothing more [than] the same ‘Sheikh say,'” Kowou told FrontPageAfrica, playing on the word “hearsay.” The government’s evidence, he said, “as referenced and narrated in Numbers 12, 29 through 31 of the indictment, clearly show[s] the same ‘Sheikh say’ reliance on which the case against Jewel is built.”

He also accused prosecutors of lumping strangers together. The State, he said, “placed everyone in one group, most of whom are not connected or known to each other.”

None of the allegations have been tested in court, and every defendant is presumed innocent.

An office she no longer held

The State’s theory is simple. In 2021, it says, Taylor agreed to use her power as Vice President to protect a cartel moving cocaine through Liberia to Europe. In return, money flowed to her and to her charity, the Jewel Starfish Foundation.

On that theory, she faces seven of the 11 counts: conspiracy, importation, transportation, trafficking, exportation, facilitation and money laundering.

The trouble starts with the calendar. The indictment says she served as Vice President until January 2023. In fact, the Weah–Taylor government left office on January 22, 2024. And nearly everything the cartel is accused of actually doing in Liberia happened after that date: the aircraft bought in August 2025, the beach scouting at Marshall that September, the land at Royesville, the May 2026 convoy and the July seizure.

Nowhere does the indictment say what protection a former Vice President could offer in 2025 or 2026. It does not describe a single phone call, order, or favor she gave the network at any time. “High-level political assurance and cover” is the phrase it uses, again and again, without saying what that cover was.

Even the story of how she was recruited changes. In one paragraph, two cartel men meet her at her Congo Town home in October 2021, and she flies to Dubai to meet their boss that November. In another, the introduction happens “in 2022,” and she is already called the “former” Vice President, though she was then in office. A third paragraph moves the Dubai meeting to November 2022.

The money moves too. A US$27,000 travel payment and a US$75,000 gift to her foundation appear early. A US$45,000 “shopping-gift bag” turns up only in the money-laundering count, 52 pages in. The 2021 payments are called “proceeds of the cocaine,” though no cocaine deal before them is described.

There is also a question of law. The 2021 conduct is charged under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act of 2023. Liberia’s Constitution, in Article 21(a), forbids punishing anyone under a law that did not exist when the act took place. Prosecutors may answer that a conspiracy is a continuing crime. That argument is much harder to make for the other counts.

One export charge even ties her to a cocoa shipment that left the Freeport of Monrovia on October 12, 2021, weeks before the Dubai meeting at which she was supposedly recruited. No cocaine was ever reported found in those containers.

Only the 2021 shipment and Dubai meeting fall inside her term. Everything else the indictment describes came after she left office.

The tapes, and the man in the middle

The newest evidence against Taylor is a set of WhatsApp voice notes she allegedly sent Kante on August 31, 2026. That is six weeks after the cocaine was seized and the first arrests made.

On the recordings, as quoted by prosecutors, she sounds like a politician short of cash. “You know things are really crazy on our end,” she says. “So please ask Nicholas if he could send me some help.” She thanks Kante for US$15,000, worries about a child’s school fees, and talks of party conventions and campaign vehicles across the 15 counties.

What she never mentions is drugs. The talk of “the 19 kilos” and “19 million or whatever that was” is put in Kante’s mouth, not hers. Her most suspicious-sounding line, “So maybe [they are] being hidden somewhere until a better time,” carries two words in brackets that the prosecution added.

The law asks more than whether she took money from Ivancic. For money laundering, the State must show she knew or suspected the money came from crime. The indictment says she knew who sent it. It does not say how she knew where it came from.

Nor does it explain how the recordings were obtained, or from whose phone. One of the files is even labeled an “Image,” though it is described as audio.

This is where Kowou’s “Sheikh say” argument bites. Read paragraphs 12 and 29 to 31, the ones he cites, and Kante is everywhere. He meets the cartel men in a Dubai nightclub. He promises them protection from top officials. He brings them to Taylor’s home, travels in her Dubai delegation, and receives her voice notes.

The indictment lists only three witnesses, all police officers, plus unnamed documents. It names no one outside the defendants who saw Taylor agree to anything. If the 2021 story rests on Kante, a man charged in the same case, his credibility will decide much of it.

Kante arranged or attended every meeting Taylor is accused of. The indictment never says she met, called, or paid anyone who ran the 2025–26 operation, which is the heart of Kowou’s complaint that strangers were lumped together.

A document at odds with itself

The problems are not confined to Taylor. The indictment itself was filed before Criminal Assizes “A” and Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie. The writ ordering the arrests came from a different court, Criminal Court “C” under Judge Ousman F. Feika, which describes the case as its own. The writ also misspells the former Vice President’s first name as “Jowel.”

The grand jury’s sign-off raises its own questions. There are 11 counts but only six “True Bill” endorsements, with no word on which counts they cover. The closing paragraph mentions only one crime, illicit trafficking. And on the copy FrontPageAfrica reviewed, the date beside the foreman’s signature appears to read 2025, a year before the seizure.

Perhaps the most striking gap is the cocaine itself. Drug charges in Liberia are graded by the type and amount of the drug, yet the indictment never gives a weight. It counts “plates” in one place and “bags” in another. It calls the substance lab-confirmed cocaine on one page and “suspected cocaine” on others.

The smaller details wobble too. One defendant is said to have “lived in” the Royesville house until his arrest, though he was arrested at a different address, on Cement Road. Former NSA official Gerald Folley Smith is paid “millions” in one paragraph and “more than US$80,000” in another. One co-defendant’s conduct is dated 2015, six years before the conspiracy began. Three NSA agents are described as knowingly escorting cocaine for cash, yet none of them is charged.

Each pair comes from the same 55-page document. May 30, 2026, was a Saturday.

What happens next

None of this means the cocaine was not real or that no crime took place. Two men were caught with the drugs, and the case against them looks direct. For the rest, prosecutors’ strongest ground is the conspiracy count, which needs only an agreement and a single act by any member.

The other charges against Taylor are harder to square with the text. They accuse her of importing, moving and exporting cocaine, but describe nothing she did beyond meetings in 2021 and money she received. Expect her lawyers to press on the dates, the 2023 law, and the two courts as soon as the case is called.

World.title: Liberia: Saudi Rice Trial Moves to Final Arguments As Evidence Phase Ends
World.content:
MONROVIA — The long-running trial involving the alleged misappropriation of Saudi-donated rice has entered its final stage, with the prosecution and defense scheduled to deliver closing arguments before the jury on Friday, October 9, 2026, at 8:00 a.m.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The development followed Wednesday’s sitting before Criminal Court “C,” where the prosecution presented its final rebuttal witnesses, bringing the evidentiary phase of the trial to a close.



With no further witnesses expected, the court ordered both sides to proceed to final arguments on Friday.

The court also directed the prosecution and defense to submit their respective post-trial memoranda to the Clerk of Court, outlining the legal authorities and citations they intend to rely upon in support of their positions.

Both parties and their legal counsel have been ordered to appear for Friday’s proceedings.

The transition to final arguments marks a critical juncture in a case centered on the handling and distribution of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to Liberia.

The prosecution has alleged that a substantial portion of the donation was unlawfully diverted, while the defense has challenged the State’s accounting of the rice, its movement among government institutions and the alleged criminal responsibility of the accused.

A Trial of Conflicting Accounts

Throughout the trial, prosecution witnesses sought to establish how the Saudi donation moved from its receipt into government storage and subsequently to various institutions and beneficiaries.

The State has maintained that 25,054 bags were at issue in the indictment after accounting for quantities it considers to have been legitimately supplied, placing the alleged value of the disputed rice at approximately US$425,918.

The defense, however, has questioned the State’s calculations and the evidentiary basis for some of the quantities presented during the proceedings.

A central issue has been the movement of the rice from the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) to warehouses operated by the General Services Agency (GSA).

Former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, who also chaired the NDMA Board, previously testified that the transfer was an institutional decision and rejected suggestions that former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah directed him to move the rice.

Former GSA Director Genera Mary T. Broh, who also testified during the trial, provided evidence concerning the involvement of various government agencies in the movement and distribution of the commodity.

Kemayah Maintains His Defense

Kemayah, one of the defendants, has consistently denied the allegations against him.

Testifying in his own defense, the former Foreign Minister said he did not steal any of the Saudi-donated rice and maintained that his involvement was connected to his role in facilitating the donation between Liberia and Saudi Arabia.

His testimony challenged the prosecution’s characterization of the movement of the rice, particularly the role of government institutions responsible for receiving, storing and distributing the commodity.

The defense has argued that administrative decisions involving the rice should not, by themselves, constitute evidence of criminal conduct.

Prosecution Gets Final Rebuttal

Wednesday’s sitting provided the prosecution its final opportunity to respond to the defense through rebuttal evidence before both sides rested their cases.

With the evidentiary phase now closed, neither side is expected to present additional witnesses when proceedings resume Friday.

Instead, the focus will shift from testimony and exhibits to legal and factual arguments, with each side expected to present its interpretation of the evidence before the jury.

The prosecution is expected to argue that the evidence presented during the trial establishes the offenses charged and links the defendants to the alleged wrongdoing.

Prosecution, Defense Set to Face Jury Friday in Case Over 29,412 Bags of Saudi-Donated Rice

The defense, meanwhile, is expected to challenge that conclusion, pointing to what it considers inconsistencies, evidentiary gaps and unanswered questions in the State’s case.

Court Seeks Post-Trial Legal Arguments

The court’s order requiring post-trial memoranda is expected to further narrow the legal issues arising from the evidence presented during the trial.

The memoranda will contain the legal authorities and citations on which the respective parties intend to rely as the court moves toward the next stage of the proceedings, including jury instructions.

For the jury, Friday’s final arguments will provide the prosecution and defense with their last opportunity to directly interpret the evidence and make their respective cases before jurors are instructed by the court and retire to deliberate.

The case has therefore moved beyond the competing accounts presented by witnesses on the stand.

The central question now is whether the evidence presented throughout the trial, measured against the applicable law and the State’s burden of proof, is sufficient to sustain the charges against the defendants.

Criminal Court “C” has ordered all parties and their respective legal counsel to be present at 8:00 a.m. Friday, October 9, for final arguments.

The defendants remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty according to law.

World.title: GTMS Liberia Disowns ‘General Manager’ and PR Executive, Says Appointments Came from Unknown ‘Director’ Linked to UK Firm in Liquidation
World.content:
GTMS Liberia Inc. has disowned Presley S. Tenwah and Elvis D. Johnson, who it says have been posing as its General Manager and Public Relations Executive. The company says the two were appointed by a self-styled “Director,” Sahr H. W. Ngegba, who has no position in its corporate structure. It insists it has no ties to GTMS-UK, a firm it says is in liquidation and under investigation in Britain, and has warned the public not to deal with the two men. It has also instructed its lawyers to pursue civil and criminal action.

Monrovia – Global Tracking & Maritime Solutions Liberia Inc. (GTMS Liberia Inc.) has publicly disowned two men who have been presenting themselves as senior officials of the company. The company says their appointments were made by a person who holds no position in its corporate structure.

In a press release issued Wednesday, October 7, GTMS Liberia said it had learned that Mr. Presley S. Tenwah and Mr. Elvis D. Johnson had been named General Manager-Liberia and Public Relations Executive & Operations Manager, respectively. The appointments were reportedly made by a Mr. Sahr H. W. Ngegba, who claims to be a Director of the company.



GTMS Liberia said it has no one by the name of Sahr H. W. Ngegba on its staff list or in its corporate structure, “let alone any position of Director held by such person.” The company described the appointments as “wishful thinking.”

Link to UK Firm Denied

At the center of the dispute is GTMS-UK, which GTMS Liberia says is currently in liquidation in the United Kingdom. The Liberian company said it is neither a partner nor a subsidiary of GTMS-UK.

In its release, GTMS Liberia alleged that the appointments were “a brazen attempt to mislead the public” and to conceal what it called administrative failings and financial fraud at the UK entity. The company claims British authorities are investigating GTMS-UK. It also accused the UK firm of trying to use the GTMS Liberia name “to shield itself from accountability.”

Lawyers Issue Formal Disclaimer

In a separate letter dated October 7, AFDASA Global Consultancy Inc., which says it has been retained by GTMS Liberia, wrote directly to Mr. Tenwah. The letter accuses him of “an escapade of misinformation” by “parading” himself as General Manager-Liberia. It says his appointment letter was dated September 10, 2026, and signed by Mr. Ngegba.

The letter, signed by AFDASA’s Corporate Administrative Manager, Joseph Papie Mulbah, says Mr. Tenwah’s appointment was structured under GTMS-UK, an entity with “no direct connection, affiliation, or partnership” with the Liberian company. It calls the appointment “a complete figment of the imagination of Mr. Ngegba,” with no force or effect on GTMS Liberia’s operations.

AFDASA advised Mr. Tenwah and “your benefactors” to stop immediately any actions suggesting he is an official, agent or representative of GTMS Liberia. The letter warned that the company “will not take kindly to any youthful exuberance for undue publicity.” It said Mr. Tenwah should act “to avert future embarrassment and to avoid both civil and criminal liability.”

The letter was copied to Ms. Aminata Bangura, Managing Director of GTMS Liberia Inc., and Cllr. Sayma Syrenius Cephus, Global Lead Counsel.

Public Warned; Legal Action Planned

GTMS Liberia warned customers and the public not to do business with Mr. Tenwah or Mr. Johnson in the company’s name “in any form, manner or shape.” The company said the two men “should be regarded as imposters.”

The company said it has instructed AFDASA Global’s Global Lead Counsel to begin civil and criminal proceedings against both men. It accused them of misleading the public and creating “a serious corporate crisis” that has disrupted its operations over the past few days.

World.title: Liberia: As Climate Change Gathers Pace, Monrovia Sees Another Destructive Rainy Season
World.content:
Flooding inundates school roads forcing students to walk in water to school, in Lofa Community. Photo: Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon.

Summary

Heavier and less predictable rainfall, intensified by climate change, is combining with clogged drains and construction in wetlands to worsen flooding across Monrovia’s low-lying communities.

Nearly 20,000 families have been affected, displaced, disrupted schooling, lost income, illness and with 7 deaths as floodwater surrounds their homes and remains for days in two counties.

Residents want blocked waterways reopened, while officials call for stronger forecasting, better drainage, wetland protection and increased disaster-response funding.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

LOFA COMMUNITY, Montserrado County – Paulina Manloh knows the water is coming before she sees it. She has lived in the Lofa community since 2019, long enough to recognize the pattern: rain falls, and within hours the ground around her home disappears beneath brown water.



When the rain is very heavy things get even worse.

“The water can get full until sometime entering the house,” she said, sitting near the swamp that has come to define six months a year of her family’s life. “So now we’re not able to get outside to go look for food or do other activities.”

Across Monrovia, seasonal flooding is becoming a persistent threat to thousands of families. An estimated 5,950 people in Lofa Community alone are affected by flooding, according to the community leader, while families face displacement, disrupted schooling, lost income, illness and death as floodwater surrounds their homes and remains for days. Scientists and government officials say climate change is bringing heavier and less predictable rainfall to a city already struggling with decades of unplanned growth, clogged drains and weak enforcement of environmental laws.

This year Kawi Badio, director for risk and early warning at the National Disaster Management Agency, the body responsible for coordinating disaster preparedness, emergency response and recovery efforts, said 19,986 people have already been affected by flooding across Montserrado, and Grand Cape Mount with seven deaths recorded.

Authorities warn that the crisis will worsen unless the government acts. Anthony Saah Tengbeh, chairperson of the Department of Environmental Studies and Climate Change at the University of Liberia, said flooding in Monrovia and its environs is not caused by climate change alone. He said heavier rainfall is colliding with inadequate drainage, blocked waterways, construction on wetlands and poorly planned urban development, leaving fewer places for floodwater to go.

Some families are displaced for a week at a time. Children cannot reach school, and parents cannot reach work. In June, Harris S. Quoiduo, a block leader in the Lofa community estimates that flooding affects about 85 percent of the roughly 7,000 people living across the community’s four blocks. A four-year-old girl drowned after she was swept from a flooded bridge while crossing to find her mother.

“It makes the community feel very, very sad,” he said. “Just imagine your child was not sick, you left the child home just to go and come back, and then you find out the child drowned.”

For Manloh, the consequences are immediate. She has five children, and when the water rises, their world shrinks to whatever dry ground remains. School stops. Errands stop. Sickness moves in. “It can really make me feel bad,” she said. “You struggle for money, pay your children’s school fees, but the water does not allow them to go to school.”

In Monrovia’s 13th Street community in Sinkor, Lansanah Mbawo, a 25-year-old teacher, described in July a newer version of the same problem. Water near his home no longer drains, he said, after a shop was built over what residents believe was the community’s drainage channel.

“We did not use to walk in water,” Mbawo said. “But now it is not really easy.” He said neighbors have fallen ill after wading through stagnant water to reach food, work or family.

Following repeated complaints to the Ministry of Public Works, the structure was eventually demolished.

A resident affected by flooding makes her way home through standing water on 13th Street, Sinkor, Monrovia last month.

A City Built on Water

Much of the damage can be traced to where and how Monrovia grew. “Monrovia was built not for the population that dwells in it today,” said Ansu V.S. Dulleh, the agency executive director. The drainage network installed decades ago was designed for a much smaller city.

As informal settlements expanded into wetlands and swamps, homes, shops and roads blocked the natural routes water once used to escape. “You know the water is very jealous,” Dulleh said. “Once the rain comes down, the water will try to find a way to its original inhabitants.” Until the city redesigns its drainage system and stops construction in wetlands, he said, flooding will continue.

A ClimSA/PUMA2025 system used to forecast weather at Roberts International Airport. Photo credit: Liberia Meteorological Service

Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo, executive director of the Environmental Protection Agency, put it more bluntly: “Monrovia is a sinkhole” – low-lying, where water naturally collects. The EPA can issue fines and enforce wetland protections, he said, but a land-starved population continues to push into swamps that flood every rainy season.

Enforcement is also constrained by limited resources.

Wetland destruction is part of the worsening flooding situation

Tengbeh said wetlands, (also known as mangroves because of the plants that grow there) act as natural storage areas for excess rainwater. But construction on top of them across the city is reducing their ability to absorb floodwater.

“When we build on the wetland, we build in the swamps, the swamp now will not play its role as a sponge.” Then the consequence: “And that excess water that should be absorbed by the swamp will now go to the dry land and now start to cause problem for us.”

But stopping construction in wetlands remains difficult. The EPA depends on police to carry out eviction orders, Yarkpawolo said, and officers can act only when they have sufficient manpower and logistics.

“Monrovia is overcrowded,” Yarkpawolo said. “The land space in Monrovia is not enough.”

Uncollected trash is also a major issue. With no money to hire heavy equipment, residents have tried to clear the clogged waterways themselves, sometimes with their bare hands and without gloves or boots. Quoiduo said the government should send two or three excavators to reopen the channel.

“That is the most important thing,” he said. “Giving an individual money will not help. They will give the money today, you use it, and the next day you experience the same thing.”

Flooding in Lofa Community left homes surrounded by water for days. Photo credit: Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon

Rainfall Is Becoming Harder to Predict

Residents’ sense that the weather is changing is supported by government forecasters. Albert Momolu Sherman, director of meteorological services at the Ministry of Transport, said Liberia’s historical data shows rainfall becoming more intense even as its timing grows less predictable.

“What we used to experience previously, we do not have now,” Sherman said. “It is like two to three days of rainfall falling in a few hours.” Liberia’s drainage systems were not engineered for that intensity, he said.

Tengbeh said researchers at the University of Liberia are studying whether Liberia’s traditional understanding of two seasons still accurately reflects changing weather patterns.

He holds the view that Liberia has more than three seasons, “all we need to do is to take into consideration the climatic condition over a number of years and have consistent data to determine what is happening in our country.”

The country also lacks the computing capacity to model storms independently. Forecasters instead rely largely on international satellite data supplied through the African Union and European Union. That gives them about two or three days’ warning before a major storm.

That is enough time to issue an alert, Sherman said, but not enough to constitute a complete national early-warning system. He said the deeper problem is institutional. Liberia does not have a fully resourced national service. Responsibility for weather-related work is scattered across several ministries.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives documented suspected corruption and a lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the US$10 million Climate Information System project, which was funded by international donors and intended to warn communities about hazardous weather.

The Boakai administration began the work to move the project forward, but it has faced obstacles. “That project also has its activities to make sure that the met service and the hydrological service go autonomous. We still have yet to see that project kicking off fully,” said Sherman.

Living With Standing Water

Still, the broader frustration remains: forecasts are issued, ministries meet and officials visit, but the same low-lying neighborhoods flood year after year. The disaster agency, created in 2016, coordinates the national response but relies on a small, mostly volunteer workforce.

Dulleh said only 30 to 40 volunteers serve nationwide, and the agency’s budget is too small for the scale of the problem. He is pressing the World Bank to help establish a national disaster trust fund.

Flooding is only one of the hazards the agency is tracking. This year, windstorms have also torn roofs from homes in Gbarpolu, Bomi, Bong and Nimba counties. When floodwater does not recede, Dulleh said, disease often follows, creating additional demands for health workers, food assistance and relocation support. “We cannot continue to go in a cycle,” he said. “Every time there is flooding, we move there.”

Residents Want Waterways Clear, Not Money

Residents living with the water say they are not asking first for relief packages or temporary compensation. They want blocked waterways reopened before the next storm.

“When they open the waterway, it will help us,” Manloh said. Residents repeatedly clear the channel near Lofa, she said, only to see it blocked again by new construction. “I want the government to help us open the waterway,” she said. “The main problem is the waterway.”

The worst may not be over. Dulleh said the seasonal forecast points to especially heavy rainfall through September, with Montserrado, Bomi and Lofa counties among the most exposed. Flash flooding has already affected West Point, Clara Town and Doe Community in Monrovia.

No deaths had been confirmed in those communities this season, he said, but families had been displaced and officials were preparing for disease outbreaks linked to standing water.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Zambia signs US$2.49bn US health pact after holding firm on data and minerals
World.content:
Zambia signs US$2.49bn US health pact after holding firm on data and minerals

Zambia and the United States yesterday signed a five-year health agreement worth about US$2.49 billion in Lusaka. The deal ends months of hard bargaining in which Zambian negotiators struck out a specimen-sharing clause, narrowed Washington’s demands for health data and kept the country’s copper and cobalt out of the deal. The memorandum of understanding will finance the recruitment of 40,000 health workers and secure an uninterrupted supply of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria medicines.

The United States will commit more than US$1.5 billion over the five years to priority health programmes. Zambia has pledged an extra US$975 million of its own money to the sector over the same period. The arrangement is therefore a co-investment, a clear break from the donor-and-recipient model that shaped American health support in Zambia for two decades.

The signing comes five months after the talks very nearly collapsed. In May, Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe halted negotiations. He described the American demand for sensitive health data as unconscionable and rejected any attempt to tie health support to a separate agreement on critical minerals.

Mr Haimbe returned to the table with a very different message. Speaking at the ceremony, he said Zambia had successfully “decoupled” critical minerals from the health agreement. That matter, he explained, is being handled in separate talks with the United States and has no place in the signed document.

The minister said the negotiations had removed several conditions and clauses that Lusaka found unacceptable. He added that the final text was shaped through wide consultation across Government.

“I am also pleased to note that the development of this Memorandum of Understanding has been undertaken through an extensive consultative process involving Government institutions,” Mr Haimbe said.

A workforce dividend

For Health Minister Roma Chilengi, the headline is the people the money will put on hospital wards and in villages. He called the agreement a monumental and landmark decision for Zambia’s health system, and set out how the 40,000 jobs would be shared.

“Forty thousand healthcare workers will be employed, 15,000 being front-liners like nurses, medical doctors, midwives, pharmacists, clinical officers and laboratory scientists. While 25,000 will be community health workers,” Professor Chilengi said.

He said the partnership would also protect the country’s medicines supply chain, particularly for drugs used against malaria, HIV and tuberculosis. Disease surveillance will be strengthened and electronic health systems expanded.

The funded programmes cover HIV and AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, maternal and child health, disease surveillance, and preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks. Together they make up the backbone of public health in a country where a single missed delivery of antiretrovirals can be felt in every district clinic.

The data fight, settled

The negotiations turned largely on information. Earlier drafts would have required Zambia to share health data for a period far longer than the five years of funding, along with requirements touching on personally identifiable information. Professor Chilengi said those provisions had been reviewed in the final agreement.

Zambia’s Ambassador to the United States, Chibamba Kanyama, went further. He said the requirement to share biological specimens had been removed entirely, and that data sharing was now restricted to monitoring and evaluating the programmes being funded.

Dr Kanyama said the public objections raised at home had shaped Zambia’s position at the table.

“In a true partnership, we cannot simply brush aside these public anxieties. They represent our cultural values, our sovereignty, and our right to protect our people’s data and resources,” he said.

Washington’s view

United States Embassy chargé d’affaires Mich Coker said American support to Zambia’s health sector since 2004 had exceeded US$5 billion, and that the new framework was designed to protect and build on those gains through Zambian institutions.

“This $2.49 billion MoU tells a powerful story of mutual commitment. Over the next five years, the United States, working with Congress, plans to provide more than $1.5 billion in Zambia’s priority health programmes,” Mr Coker said.

He said the agreement marked a shift towards a partnership based on Zambian leadership, ownership and shared accountability. The text, he added, carries clear protocols to protect personal health information, because data privacy is essential to keeping public trust. He repeated that critical minerals were not part of the deal.

Relief for the Treasury

Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane framed the agreement in fiscal terms. He said American support would ease the burden on a Government that would otherwise have to carry the full weight of the country’s health spending.

“The agreement that we have just signed provides relief in the sense that if we are to be 100 per cent responsible for our health expenditure, then life can be much harder,” Dr Musokotwane said.

World Bank data show that health spending reached 5.98 percent of gross domestic product in 2023, up from 5.21 percent the year before. That rising bill is the backdrop to the minister’s remarks.

A harder bargain than most

The agreement falls under the America First Global Health Strategy, which Washington launched in September 2025. It replaced traditional grants through USAID and the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief with five-year bilateral compacts.

Several African governments have struggled with the terms. Kenya’s agreement was stopped by its High Court amid challenges over patient data and pathogen information. Zimbabwe walked away from a deal worth about US$350 million, and Ghana turned down the American conditions over data sharing.

Zambia chose a third path: it stayed at the table, refused the clauses it could not accept and signed only once they had been rewritten. That outcome gives the Government a ready answer to those who warned that health aid would be traded for mineral concessions.

The recruitment drive and the Treasury’s US$975 million pledge now move from paper to practice over the next five years. The talks on critical minerals continue on their own, separate track.

World.title: Zambia, USA seal health deal
World.content:
Zambia and the United States of America have signed a Memorandum of Understanding and a Data Sharing Agreement to implement a five‑year Health Sector Cooperation Agreement.

Under the deal, the United States will provide more than US$1.5 billion over five years to Zambia’s priority health programmes, while Zambia will increase domestic health expenditure by US$975 million.

Minister of Finance and National Planning Situmbeko Musokotwane signed the MoU, while his Health counterpart, Roma Chilengi signed the Data Sharing Agreement, in collaboration with United States Chargé d’Affaires at the US Embassy in Lusaka, Mich Coker, who signed the agreements on behalf of his government.

Witnessing the signing ceremony, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe said the agreement renews and redefines the Zambia-US partnership that will continue to shape and transform the lives of many people positively.

Mr Haimbe expressed gratitude to the government and people of the United States for their unwavering support and friendship.

He reiterated the need to continue building a resilient, sustainable and people-centred health system that delivers better health outcomes for every Zambian.

“I wish to commend the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Finance and National Planning, the Ministry of Justice, Cabinet Office, and other government institutions for the hard work and dedication that culminated in today’s signing ceremony,” the Minister indicated.

He acknowledged the longstanding relations between the two countries as evidenced in various areas of cooperation, including democracy and governance, economic growth, health and education.

Mr Haimbe noted that the partnership with the United States has greatly assisted in stimulating the growth of various sectors in the country.

Professor Chilengi, noted that the signed MoU will serve as a catalyst for Zambia’s journey towards greater self-sustainability and enhanced domestic resource mobilisation.

Professor Chilengi revealed that the agreement will enable the recruitment of more health workers, strengthen medicine supply and enhance disease surveillance.

He also clarified that the only data that the Zambian government will be required to share with the United States during the agreement period is that which speaks directly to the operations of the program.

Meanwhile, Dr Musokotwane said the support comes at a time of financial pressures arising from global economic factors, including the anticipated severe drought next year.

He noted that the partnership will provide the much-needed relief to enable the Government channel additional resources towards other critical sectors of the economy, in line with the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

For the Chargé d’Affaires, Mr Coker described the MoU as a transformative partnership, shifting from a donor‑recipient model to a true partnership, grounded in Zambian Leadership, Zambian ownership and shared accountability

Mr Coker affirmed that the signed MoU is focused on improving health outcomes, strengthening health financing, and enhancing systems within Zambia’s health sector.

World.title: Parliament expansion preps advance
World.content:
The National Assembly of Zambia is undergoing major rehabilitation and expansion works to accommodate the increased number of Members of Parliament (MPs) and ensure that the members operate in a conducive environment.

Clerk of the National Assembly Loveness Mayaka says the works are part of preparations for the commencement of the First Session of the 14th National Assembly.

Ms Mayaka said this in Lusaka today during a media briefing on the preparedness of the National Assembly for the new parliament.

She said the reforms, provided for under the Constitution of Zambia Amendment Act No. 13 of 2025, have resulted in changes to the electoral system and increased representation of women, youth and persons with disabilities.

She explained that the National Assembly has undertaken extensive preparations in infrastructure, systems and processes to accommodate the increased membership and effectively support 280 MPs in discharging their constitutional mandate.

She said the preparations have focused on four key areas, namely infrastructure, physical accessibility, sensory and communication facilities, and administrative support and staff awareness.

She explained that the interventions are aimed not only at accommodating the increased number of MPs from 167 to 280, but also at strengthening parliament’s capacity to operate as a modern, inclusive, accessible and effective institution.

She said the Chamber has been expanded to provide an additional 113 seats, while Information and Communication Technology (ICT) equipment has also been installed and upgraded.

The Clerk stated that the National Assembly has also established facilities to support the 70 newly created constituencies, with most of the facilities already operational.

Ms Mayaka said the transition comes at an important time in the development of Zambia’s democracy, following constitutional and electoral reforms undertaken during the 13th National Assembly.

She said the Assembly has further installed and commissioned conference systems in the chamber and committee rooms to enhance the performance of parliamentary functions.

She said renovations are also underway at the Members’ Motel, including expansion of the restaurant and kitchen, renovation of the laundry and refurbishment of rooms to improve accessibility for members with disabilities.

Ms Mayaka further said additional offices have been constructed on the eastern side of the Chamber to address the shortage of office space, additionally new water tank has also been installed to strengthen water security at the institution to make them accessible to persons with disabilities.

She said the institution is further strengthening sensory and communication facilities to ensure that members with visual, hearing and speech impairments can participate fully in parliamentary proceedings.

Ms Mayaka said the National Assembly has strengthened the provision of sign language interpretation and introduced braille facilities and signage to improve access to information.

She said the procurement of a braille machine, which will facilitate the production of reading materials in Braille, is at an advanced stage.

And Ms Mayaka disclosed that plans are underway for the construction of a new parliament building in the near future to accommodate up to 500 parliamentarians.

Meanwhile, National Assembly Director Public and International Relations Anthony Mpolokoso led the media personnel touring some newly constructed works, disclosing that a local contractor was engaged to do the renovation and expansion works at the National Assembly of Zambia.

World.title: Govt. hands over fuel tankers to youth cooperatives
World.content:
Government has commenced the phased handover of 100 fuel tankers received from King Long Motors Zambia Limited to 100 youth cooperatives under the Fuel Tanker Empowerment Programme, with 12,000 youths expected to benefit.

Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts Permanent Secretary Kangwa Chileshe said the initiative is aimed at providing young people with productive assets to create businesses, employment and contribute to national economic growth.

Mr Chileshe said the handover demonstrates the government’s commitment to ensuring that young people are not merely beneficiaries of development, but become active participants, entrepreneurs and employers.

He said the Ministry settled outstanding balances owed to the supplier, King Long Motors Zambia Limited, resulting in the handover of the fuel tankers to the Ministry in August 2026.

Mr Chileshe said the handover will be conducted in phases, with the first batch comprising about 50 to 60 tankers, while the remaining tankers will be handed over once the necessary processes are completed.

Mr Chileshe has since urged beneficiary cooperatives to protect and properly maintain the tankers and ensure that they are used for their intended purpose.

He further called on the cooperatives to manage their businesses professionally, maintain proper financial records and comply with relevant laws and regulations.

Mr Chileshe said the government expects the tankers to generate income, create employment, support families and contribute to the country’s economic development agenda.

Speaking in an interview after the handover ceremony, beneficiaries of the Fuel Tanker Youth Cooperatives welcomed the development and commended the government for the initiative.

Deinopark Youth Enterprises Secretary General Innocent Sunkutu assured the government that the assets will be managed prudently and used to generate income.

World.title: Lavushimanda Council sets measures against El Niño
World.content:
Lavushimanda Town Council Secretary Jonas Mwendakawa has called for the 2027 annual budget to prioritise measures aimed at mitigating the anticipated effects of El Niño conditions in the country.

Mr Mwendakawa said the 2027 budget should take into account measures to mitigate the negative effects of the expected El Niño conditions.

He said this in a speech read on his behalf by Lavushimanda Town Council Director of Planning Daniel Mikandu during the 2026 budget performance stakeholders review meeting held at Mununga Pentecostal Assemblies of God Church.

He said climate-resilient projects should be integrated into the planning and budgeting processes to address the effects of climate change.

“Emphasis will be on inclusive growth, climate resilience, social equity and institutional strengthening,” Mr Mwendakawa said.

He said human capital development should also remain central to the budgeting process, with health, education and social protection being prioritised.

Mr Mwendakawa further called for adequate consideration of cross-cutting issues such as gender mainstreaming, disability support, food and nutrition, and the control of infectious diseases in the preparation of the 2027–2029 Medium-Term Budgeting Plan and the 2027 Annual Budget.

He said the budgeting process should also support the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda and its 10-10-5-3-3-1-1-1 production targets aimed at accelerating economic growth, increasing domestic production, expanding economic opportunities and creating jobs.

Mr Mwendakawa said the budget performance review provides stakeholders with an opportunity to receive feedback on what has been achieved, as well as the successes and challenges encountered in implementing the 2026 budget.

Meanwhile, Lavushimanda Town Council Socio-Economic Planner Mushimba Phiri has urged stakeholders to align the 2027 projects with the District Integrated Development Plan (IDP).

Mr Phiri said the district has an IDP which is running from 2022 to 2031.

“As we review our 2026 budget performance, we need to ensure that we align our 2027 projects with our IDP,” he said.

He explained that the document is not only meant to benefit the statutory environment but also the customary areas, noting that it is intended to benefit the whole district and not only the Central Business District.

World.title: Chipata seniors citizens call for youth history education
World.content:
Senior citizens in Chipata District of Eastern Province have called on stakeholders to proactively educate the youth on the country’s past struggles to preserve generational knowledge.

Joe Phiri, a senior citizen, says the celebration of Independence Day has mostly been left to learners in schools, while out-of-school youths completely shun the activities.

Mr Phiri said parents support children with all necessities as requested by schools during Independence celebrations, but youths who are not in school have no platform to learn from and participate in

“My fear is what will become of the youths who will be parents to some children, and do not have information on our past struggles, how Zambia has grown from the time of war to now, now that we have peace and can live freely,” Mr Phiri wondered.

He said the future still demands involvement of the youth as they are the future parents and leaders who need to understand the country’s liberation history.

Meanwhile, preparations for this year’s Independence Day commemoration in Chipata District have heightened, with various committees holding final meetings.

Chipata District Administrative Officer, Kapambwe Sikazwe, says the district is ready to host this year’s celebrations on 24th October at David Kaunda Stadium.

Mr Sikazwe said this year’s Independence Day will be commemorated under the theme “Zambia@62: Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future.”

Interpreting the theme, Mr Sikazwe said it reflects on Zambia’s painful journey to independence, the economic and social growth the country has recorded over 62 years, and the shared responsibility to secure a prosperous future for all Zambians.

“Our Journey reminds us of the sacrifice of our freedom fighters from the Cha Cha Cha days, Our Growth celebrates 62 years of peace, education and infrastructure development, and Our Future calls on every Zambian including the youth to guard this peace and work hard,” Mr Sikazwe said.

He said a number of activities have been lined up to mark the day, including a church service on 19th October, cleaning of public places and the heroes acre on 22nd October.

Mr Sikazwe disclosed that the main celebration on 24th October will start with a march past by security wings, schools, colleges, farmers, cooperatives, and various government departments.

He said other activities will include traditional dances from Ngoni, Chewa, Nsenga and Tumbuka cultural groups, poems and songs by school children, awarding of long-serving civil servants, and entertainment by the Zambia Army and Zambia Police brass bands.

The DAO further urged members of the public to turn out in large numbers and participate in the celebrations, adding that independence is for all Zambians regardless of age, political affiliation or social status.

He said gates at David Kaunda Stadium will be open by 07:00 hours and called on residents to be dressed in national colours.

World.title: Govt. commits to addressing illegal exploitation of natural resources
World.content:
Government has assured the Great Lakes member states of its commitment to ensure that the issue of illegal exploitation of natural resources is addressed.

Speaking during the 33rd meeting of the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region (ICGLR) Regional committee against the illegal exploitation of natural resources in Lusaka, Ministry of Mines and Minerals Permanent Secretary Hapenga Kabeta, urged member states to deepen regional cooperation as illegal exploitation and illicit minerals are regional in nature and require collaboration among member states.

Dr Kabeta said this in a statement made on his behalf by Ministry of Mines and Minerals Director Human Resource, Anthony Chilengi.

Dr Kabeta added that government remains committed to working with all ICGLR member states as well as the executive secretariat, United Nations, as well as cooperating partners to address exploitation issues.

“During this meeting, we will need to build on the progress made, take stock of the gaps that remain and agree on practical measures to strengthen implementation at both regional and national levels,” Dr Kabeta said.

He also highlighted that the government has put in measures to address exploitation of natural resources.

Dr Kabeta said some of the measures include the establishment of artisanal and small-scale mining, strengthening inspections and monitoring, as well as a mineral tracking system to curb smuggling in the region.

And Chairperson of the ICGLR Regional Committee, Balthazar Nyanduye, noted that ICGLR is rich in natural resources which represent job creation and industrial transformation for the betterment of the people.

Mr Nyanduye observed that for the natural resources to be sustained, there is a need for all member countries to work together.

“We need to fight the illegal exploitation of minerals and to strengthen cooperation between member states and organisations,” Mr Nyanduye said.

Meanwhile, ICGLR Executive Secretary, Mubita Lwabelwa, stated that collaboration between countries is important to fight illegal exploitation of natural resources.

Dr Lwabelwa further noted that the meeting is a great opportunity to turn shared knowledge into action and exchange of ideas, and best practices.

“Together we will strengthen partnerships and advance transparency and integrity across our sectors,” Dr Lwabelwa said.

World.title: Chipata Police nab 16 petrol smuggling suspects
World.content:
Police in Chipata District have apprehended sixteen suspects cumulatively in three days for illegal possession and suspected smuggling of petrol.

The apprehensions were made on 5th, 6th and 7th October, 2026 during separate operations by Chipata Central Police Station and Mwami Border Police Station.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba, has confirmed the development to the media in Chipata District.

Mr Mweemba said in the first incident, officers from Chipata Central Police Station apprehended 10 males on 5th and 6th October two males were apprehended at around 18:23 hours at Oasis Filling Station in Chipata District.

He identified the suspects as Moses Phiri aged 20 and Esau Joseph aged 28, both of Kaulembe area, Chief Chanje, Chipangali District.

Mr Mweemba said the two were found in possession of 3 by 20 litres containers of suspected petrol loaded in plastic containers after officers conducted a motorised patrol in the Chipata Central Business area.

He said the exhibits have been secured at Chipata Central Police Station and will be disposed of in line with Energy Regulation Board – ERB regulations.

In the third operation, Mr Mweemba said Mwami Border Police Station intercepted three unregistered motorbikes, two of them Gatoma make and one Toyota Corolla registration number ACT 7844 silver in colour at a security checkpoint along Mwami Mission Hospital road.

He said the interception occurred on 7th October, 2026 between 14:00 hours and 15:00 hours when officers were manning the checkpoint.

Mr Mweemba said upon inspection, officers discovered 35 by 20 litres containers of petrol and apprehended four suspects.

He identified the suspects as Lyford Banda 36, of Vubwi Center, Chimwendo Village, Chief Pembamoyo, Philemon Jere 27, of Benje Village, Chief Mpezeni, Frank Daka 36, of Indaba Village, Chief Mpezeni and Gabriel Miti 33, of Vubwi Center, Chief Pembamoyo.

Mr Mweemba said the suspects are detained at Mwami Border Police Station and the fuel has been kept as exhibits, while the motorbikes and motor vehicle have also been impounded.

“The suspects will appear in court soon for illegal possession and dealing in petroleum products without a licence contrary to the laws of Zambia,” Mr Mweemba said.

He warned members of the public to desist from illegal fuel vending and smuggling, saying the operation will continue across the province.
