World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

10 Quarantined After Kenya's First Ebola Case

Kenya is facing its first confirmed Ebola case after a man who travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo died in a Nairobi hospital. Health officials have quarantined ten people who came into contact with him, while tracing 57 others who may have been exposed. Concern is growing over screening measures after it emerged that the patient, who had reportedly been ill for about a month, travelled through several cities in DR Congo, crossed into Uganda and flew to Kenya without being detected. Kenyan authorities said that surveillance has been intensified at airports and border crossings, with more than 650,000 travellers screened and 267 samples tested so far. Health officials have also designated four hospitals to manage suspected Ebola cases, while the Africa CDC is working with countries in the region to strengthen their response.

Eritrean Troops Reportedly Move Into Ethiopia's Tigray Region



Eritrean soldiers are reportedly moving into northern Ethiopia's Tigray region as renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and Tigrayan forces raises fears of a wider conflict. Residents in Adigrat said that they had seen convoys of Eritrean military trucks travelling south towards areas where clashes have been reported. The developments come amid worsening relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea and accusations from Addis Ababa that Eritrea is supporting the Tigray People's Liberation Front, which Asmara has denied. The reported return of Eritrean troops has caused anxiety among Tigray residents, many of whom remember alleged atrocities committed during the 2020–2022 civil war.

UN Allocates $160m for Global Humanitarian Crises

The United Nations has allocated US$160 million from its Central Emergency Response Fund to provide life-saving assistance in 12 of the world's most underfunded humanitarian crises across Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. Of the funding, US$150 million will support emergency responses in countries including Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Cameroon and Afghanistan, as well as the occupied Palestinian territory, Cuba and Yemen. A further US$10 million will support people with disabilities and make humanitarian assistance more accessible and inclusive. The UN says the funding forms part of a wider effort to reach 87 million people facing severe humanitarian needs this year, while stressing that political action is also needed to secure humanitarian access to affected populations.

African Union Launches First Regional Credit Rating Agency in Mauritius

The African Union is launching the Africa Credit Rating Agency, the continent's first regional credit rating agency, in Mauritius, in an effort to provide an alternative perspective to the major global rating agencies. The agency will assess sovereign governments, financial institutions and private companies, with the AU saying it will draw on African data, expertise and economic realities to provide more context-specific assessments. African leaders have long criticised major international rating agencies over what they see as unfair assessments of African economies, although the agencies reject accusations of systemic bias. The AU says AfCRA could help improve investor confidence, market transparency and access to capital, particularly as African countries face rising debt-service costs and 23 economies currently lack ratings from the major global agencies.

Nigerian Authorities Launch Probe After Passenger Dies on Kenya Airways Flight

A passenger has died aboard a Kenya Airways flight from Nairobi to Lagos after becoming unresponsive about 20 minutes before the aircraft landed at Murtala Muhammed International Airport. The airline said its crew administered first aid and followed emergency procedures before medical personnel met the aircraft on arrival and confirmed the passenger had died. Nigerian aviation authorities said the passenger had reportedly been denied entry into Madagascar. He was being returned to Nigeria when complications arose during the flight. Authorities said the passenger had allegedly become aggressive, attempted to enter the cockpit and later tried to open a rear aircraft door before being restrained by crew members. Police have taken over the investigation, obtained statements from the crew and placed the body in a morgue in Ikeja. The passenger's identity and cause of death have not been disclosed.

Close 

Zambia Set to Sign $1.5bn U.S. Health Deal

Zambia is set to sign a U.S.$1.5 billion health funding agreement with the United States after resolving a dispute over the sharing of sensitive health data. The agreement will provide U.S.$1.5 billion in U.S. funding over five years. Zambia is expected to contribute U.S.$2.1 billion towards health programmes. Zambia had initially rejected the deal over concerns about requirements to share medical information and biological samples. However, officials said that the data-sharing provisions have now been narrowed to information needed to monitor and evaluate U.S.-funded programmes, with a clause allowing access to patient specimens removed. Meanwhile, Zimbabwe and Ghana have rejected similar U.S. funding terms over concerns about sovereignty and sensitive health data. Zimbabwe particularly warned against unrestricted access to epidemiological data and biological samples.

World.title: South Africa: Ten Cars Torched As Xenophobic Violence Erupts in Soweto
World.content:
Ten cars were set alight in Orlando West, Soweto, on Thursday following violence between community members and foreign shop owners.

It began as a peaceful demonstration in Orlando West, Soweto.

Residents had gathered on the streets on Thursday afternoon, upset by the recent Constitutional Court judgment on asylum seekers.

According to community leader Tshepo Mposule, residents were angered by the judgment and subsequent Home Affairs directive, which stated that foreign nationals should be allowed to apply for asylum regardless of whether they had entered the country legally.

"People are really angry because they came here peacefully to say that the issue of illegal migration needs urgent attention from our government," said Mposule. "On hearing about the court judgment, they came to voice out their dissatisfaction, and this was directed to the government of the day, so they went to Home Affairs."

The march to the Home Affairs offices went according to plan, Mposule said, with the community remaining peaceful.

Then things changed. Some members of the community began looking for foreign-owned shops with the intention of shutting them down.

Three shops had been closed when trouble broke out.

According to Mposule, the crowd had moved to a corner shop when a car carrying several armed foreign shop owners arrived.

The confrontation unfolded in the presence of the Johannesburg Metro...

World.title: Kenya: 77 Kenyans On Russia-Ukraine Frontlines As 84 Killed or Missing, Govt Says
World.content:
Nairobi — At least 84 Kenyans have been killed or remain missing in connection with the Russia-Ukraine war, while a total of 354 Kenyan nationals have been identified by the government as having become involved in the conflict.

The figures released by the Ministry of Foreign and Diaspora Affairs show the scale of Kenyan involvement in the war, with dozens still on the front lines, in military camps, hospitals or at unknown locations.

According to the government's latest records, 77 Kenyans are on the front lines, while another 38 are in camps.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

A further 52 Kenyans are listed at unknown locations or have yet to be classified, raising concerns over the whereabouts and welfare of dozens of nationals caught up in the conflict.

The government has recorded 34 Kenyans as hospitalised, while 62 have been repatriated to Kenya.

Five Kenyans are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, while one is in detention and another has completed their military contract.

Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign and Diaspora Affairs CS Musalia Mudavadi told Parliament that families often approach the government only after losing contact with relatives believed to be in Russia, making early reporting critical to tracing and verification efforts.

"It has been noted that families tend to engage with the State Department often after communication with their relatives in the Russian Federation has been disrupted or ceased. We encourage families to engage the Department as soon as possible," Mudavadi said.

The figures were contained in its response to a parliamentary petition concerning the recruitment of Kenyan nationals into the Russian military and the detention of Kenyans in Ukrainian prisons.

Five Kenyans held as POWs

The government said Ukrainian authorities confirmed on September 3 that five Kenyan nationals were being held as prisoners of war.

They are Kibet Evans, detained since May 2025; Macharia Willi Muniu, detained since November 2025; Haron Kibet Pachenge, detained since March 2026; Joseph, detained since April 2026; and Ndarua Ndungu Francis.

Kenya said its Honorary Consul in Ukraine had visited the Zakhid 1 prisoner-of-war camp and reported that the detainees were being held in humane conditions, with access to medical services and medical care.

The government is seeking to have the five Kenyans considered as potential victims of human trafficking, saying many reported being recruited under false promises of employment.

Close 

The proposed reclassification is intended to improve their access to assistance while Kenya pursues their repatriation.

62 Kenyans repatriated

The government said it had facilitated the return of 62 Kenyans who had been involved in Russia's military operation.

It is also pursuing the cases of those killed or missing, including efforts to establish the whereabouts of nationals whose remains may be in Ukrainian custody.

According to the government, Ukrainian authorities have reported that the remains of four Kenyan nationals are in Ukrainian custody.

Kenya has warned that more remains could be located in combat zones in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, where Ukrainian authorities say they cannot provide information on people in territories outside their control.

The government said Kenya had also secured a measure aimed at stopping further recruitment of its nationals into Russia's military operation.

During an official visit to Moscow in March, Kenya secured inclusion on Russia's "Stop List", which effectively prevents further enlistment of Kenyan nationals in the conflict.

The Kenyan Embassy in Moscow has since confirmed that no additional Kenyans have been enlisted following implementation of the measure.

The government said it continues to pursue the welfare and repatriation of Kenyans through diplomatic channels, while strengthening measures to protect citizens from deceptive recruitment and unsafe migration.

"Through the State Department for Diaspora Affairs, the Ministry continues to complement welfare interventions with preventive measures, including pre-departure orientation and coordination with the relevant regulatory agencies," Mudavadi said.

World.title: Ethiopia: Tigray Faces a Double Catastrophe - War and Worsening Hunger
World.content:
Mekelle, Ethiopia — "Many households experienced complete crop failure."

Nearly four years after a peace agreement was signed to end the devastating war in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, armed conflict has resumed. While the hostilities threaten to destabilise the broader Horn of Africa, they also obscure an equally catastrophic food crisis unfolding in the drought-hit region.

The fragile post-war period proved to be a textbook example of an unsustainable peace. In the diplomatic rush to celebrate the "silencing of the guns" in 2022, international mediators largely overlooked the unresolved structural collapse, persistent territorial occupation, and ongoing deprivation facing Tigray's civilian population.

Hundreds of thousands of people displaced from western Tigray remained unable to go home, leaving an estimated 44% of the region's prime cultivable land inaccessible. Farmers who managed to return to the northwestern, central, and eastern zones found their farms and communities devastated.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Rebuilding efforts proceeded with virtually no safety net, undermined by sweeping reductions in international food aid, persistent federal cash and fuel constraints, and acute shortages of essential agricultural inputs and medical supplies.

Drought and crop failure

Then came the climate shock. The early Azmera rains (April to the end of May) ceased nearly a month prematurely, disrupting seed germination and causing long-cycle cereal plantings to wither in the soil across multiple woredas (municipalities).

The still-active El Niño weather pattern has dealt a fatal blow to Tigray's fragile agricultural recovery. The Tsidia Spring harvest rains (September-November) arrived more than five weeks late this year across the eastern and southern zones, interrupted by dry spells lasting over a month in some areas.

According to regional multi-agency assessments, over 252,500 hectares of planted crops have been scorched, 140 districts are facing catastrophic conditions, and more than 3.5 million head of livestock face starvation and disease as seasonal pastures and water tables vanish.

With the September harvest failing and livestock-to-grain terms of trade collapsing, 3.9 million people - more than half of Tigray's population - required immediate emergency food assistance, according to a September humanitarian overview by the Tigray Disaster Risk Management Commission (DRMC), a copy of which was shared with The New Humanitarian.

"Many households experienced complete crop failure," the report warned. "Without continued rainfall, even minimal production cannot be expected." With people's ability to cope exhausted by the scorched earth tactics of the last war, and the lingering impact of the 2020-2023 drought, there is increasing nervousness over the potential for famine.

A renewed major conflict is the final blow. Media accounts attribute its beginning entirely to a ground offensive launched on 23 September by the newly formed anti-government coalition, the "Alliance for Survival", but that overlooks the sustained federal aerial campaign that was already underway.

Airstrikes hit targets across Tigray, including school grounds in the Degua Tembien-Samre corridor south of the regional capital Mekelle, internally displaced persons (IDP) hosting sites in Sheraro, and a food aid convoy in the northwestern zone.

Heavy government airstrikes also battered the Raya corridor around Alamata, 180 kilometres from Mekelle, on the eve of the coalition's ground push against government positions in the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.

Fighting blocks humanitarian access

One of the first casualties of the renewed combat has been basic access. Coalition forces seized control of Tigray's regional airports in Mekelle, Shire, and Axum. Simultaneously, regional telecommunications were severed.

While both sides traded blame over who switched off the connections, the operational consequence was total: Telecommunications and internet access across Mekelle and surrounding areas went dark.

Federal authorities also moved to freeze bank accounts linked to Tigray, although this measure was largely symbolic: An acute pre-existing physical currency deficit had already forced the local economy entirely onto mobile financial networks, which the telecoms outage instantly paralysed.

For 10 days, Mekelle was cut off from the outside world. Humanitarian operations across the region, largely coordinated from the regional capital, ground to a halt. Without telecommunications, fuel, or cash to pay people to load, unload, and drive trucks, the aid pipeline locked up.

After the drone strike that hit the food aid convoy in the northwest zone organised by Catholic Caritas Ethiopia - Adigrat, it was too risky to transport aid anyway. The federal government never acknowledged the attack, and offered no assurances that humanitarian assistance would be protected.

The dynamics shifted abruptly over the first weekend of October. As federal forces launched mechanised counter-offensives and advanced toward Mekelle, coalition forces vacated administrative buildings and police stations in the city.

For roughly 24 hours, an acute power vacuum gripped Mekelle. As night fell on 4 October, widespread lawlessness erupted. Armed groups - reportedly largely composed of inmates released amid the sudden abandonment of a nearby prison - looted government buildings, post offices, art galleries, and aid facilities.

The attacks targeted the infrastructure of the region's humanitarian response. Looters ransacked the offices and storage depots of the DRMC - the regional governmental agency tasked with coordinating lifesaving aid.

The headquarters of the Organisation for Social Services, Health and Development (OSSHD-Ethiopia) was likewise stripped of around 60 computers and tablets, some $1 million worth of non-food items, nearly all of their vehicles, and tens of thousands of dollars worth of medical equipment for their clinic in Mekelle.

According to an aid worker in the city, who asked not to be named to speak freely, the looting would not have happened if Tigray had law enforcement institutions that were beholden to the communities they served rather than the ruling TPLF party, which is now at war with the federal government.

The political affiliations of all police and security forces in Mekelle meant they were forced to flee with the TPLF leadership to avoid reprisals. The aid worker also criticised the religious clergy in Mekelle for failing to use their voices or influence to dissuade or condemn the looting and lawlessness.

Humanitarian pause needed

The OSSHD has been operating in Tigray for more than 30 years and provided a wide range of services to many of the roughly 900,000 displaced people in the 31 IDP camps across the region. Without vehicles and essential field equipment, they can no longer provide protection services - including for children - or monitor new arrivals fleeing the conflict.

Close 

They were also caring for around 7,000 children at their clinic in Mekelle who were either living with family members who were HIV+ or had contracted the virus themselves. The OSSHD is now no longer able to provide medical treatment, cash support, or psychosocial care to them.

Until the equipment and vehicles they lost are replaced, all OSSHD work has effectively been halted.

Unlike other aid organisations, REST-Tigray and World Vision's warehouses were spared - two of the three agencies responsible for food distribution in the region. The third major food provider, Catholic Caritas Ethiopia - Adigrat is safe for now, but the war is literally on its doorstep.

However, due to aid cuts by international donors, food distribution now targets only people who are displaced, and still misses a large portion of IDPs. This leaves around 3.2 million people in need without food assistance - trapped also without physical safety or essential medicines.

That dire situation could potentially improve if the 460-kilometre humanitarian corridor between Mekelle and Semera, in the neighbouring Afar region, remains open. It was the primary supply route for the aid response in the previous war, and, according to the humanitarian analysis hub ACAPS, was functional as of 4 October.

If the route remains safe, a surge in aid is possible and could make the difference between life and death for millions of civilians in Tigray who have absolutely nothing to do with this conflict.

To get aid to those who urgently need it, a humanitarian pause would have to happen immediately. Food, medicine, and fuel would also need to be able to freely flow into Tigray, along with cash.

Edited by Obi Anyadike.

Duke Burbridge, A board member at the health professionals network for Tigray

World.title: Africa: United States Accused of Exploiting Migrant Suffering With Africa Deportations
World.content:
U.S. Transferees arriving at the Robert International Airport in Monrovia (file photo).

The United States is violating international law by deporting migrants to African countries where they have no ties, NGO Human Rights Watch said on Thursday, accusing Washington of using deportation to remote destinations as a deterrent to immigration.

United States deportation policy has expanded sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, with his administration striking agreements with governments in Africa, Latin America and the Pacific to receive foreign nationals who cannot legally be returned to their own countries.

More than 500 people have since been deported from the US to African countries other than their own, according to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) data cited by Human Rights Watch.



A separate investigation published by the Forbidden Stories journalism consortium in September estimated that around 25,000 people had been deported to destinations worldwide under the third-country deportation programme.

Human Rights Watch said the policy "violates international human rights law and is designed to instrumentalise human suffering as a deterrent to migration".

Inside the US system deporting migrants through African countries

'The point is to scare people'

The organisation said it interviewed 24 people who had been deported from the US to six African countries - Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini and South Sudan.

Some described being kept in chains during flights of up to 18 hours and said they were not told where they were being taken.

The rights group also cited an unnamed US official who told a US Senate hearing that the choice of distant destinations was intended in part to frighten other migrants.

"With countries like Palau or Eswatini, the point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere," the official was quoted as saying. "The point is to scare people."

Human Rights Watch said Washington had also deported at least a dozen LGBTQI+ people to African countries where same-sex relations are criminalised or heavily repressed.

The group warned that transferring people to countries where they face persecution or serious abuse could breach the international legal principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits states from sending people to places where they face severe human rights violations.

Many of the agreements underpinning the programme remain secret or only partly disclosed, Human Rights Watch said, making it difficult to establish the conditions under which migrants are accepted or what incentives are offered to participating governments.

Close 

The global machinery built to carry out Trump's mass deportation drive

The growing network of deportation agreements has also drawn attention to the pressure Washington is placing on African governments to cooperate with its migration policies.

An investigation by French news agency AFP earlier this year found that the US had used diplomatic and economic leverage in negotiations, including threats of higher tariffs, restrictions on the issuing of visas and cuts to development aid.

Burundi became the latest country to sign up this month, becoming the 15th African nation to agree to receive US deportees despite facing severe economic and humanitarian pressures of its own.

World.title: Sudan: Continuing Efforts to Expand the Arms Embargo in Sudan
World.content:
press release

Following close consultations with our Quad partners, allies, and members of the United Nations Security Council, the United States has decided to support a technical rollover of the Security Council resolution on the Darfur arms embargo until December 11. This decision reflects our determination to allow additional space for ongoing diplomatic efforts, including recent initiatives by some of our closest allies, to secure a negotiated settlement, a humanitarian truce, and a durable ceasefire.

This extension is not a lapse in our resolve. It is an opportunity for diplomacy to deliver tangible results and for the international community to intensify its efforts to end the suffering of the Sudanese people, pave the way for a genuine and inclusive national dialogue, and facilitate a credible transition to a civilian-led government.

The United States remains firmly committed to expanding and strengthening the arms embargo to better protect civilians across Sudan from the devastating consequences of this war, including the growing threat posed by drones and other sophisticated weapons. External military support to the warring parties must end. Those fueling this conflict through the continued supply of weapons and military assistance are prolonging the violence, undermining diplomatic efforts, and deepening an already catastrophic humanitarian crisis. Sudan's neighbors must stop allowing their territories to be platforms to further the violence and destruction in Sudan.



The Sudanese people have suffered far too much and for far too long. As called for by President Trump, they deserve an immediate end to the violence, unhindered humanitarian access, and a credible pathway toward lasting peace. Their voices and aspirations must be at the center of any political process.

We thank all members of the United Nations Security Council for their unanimous support for this technical rollover. This consensus sends an important message of unity and shared responsibility, and we look forward to working closely with Council members and our international partners to translate this unity into meaningful progress toward peace in Sudan.

-Massad Boulos, U.S. Senior Advisor for Arab and African Affairs - posted on X

World.title: Zambia: U.S. and Zambia Sign Global Health Partnership under the Trump Administration's America First Global Health Strategy
World.content:
press release

The United States and the Republic of Zambia today signed a five-year bilateral Health Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) under the Trump Administration’s America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), a new model of health partnership built around greater Zambian investment, stronger accountability, and a clear path toward self-reliance.

Building on more than 50 years of U.S. health assistance to Zambia, this MOU represents a $2.49 billion partnership of $1.52 billion in planned U.S. health assistance and a commitment from Zambia to invest $975 million in new funding in its own health system over five years. Under this MOU, the United States also plans to provide more than $13 million in Global Health Security funding to strengthen Zambia’s ability to detect and respond to infectious disease threats. Over five years, Zambia will progressively assume greater responsibility for its health system, including the procurement of health commodities, transitioning U.S.-supported frontline health workers into its civil service, and strengthening systems to track medicines and supplies from production to delivery.

The United States will support Zambia in modernizing its health infrastructure, to include expanding electronic medical records and interoperable data systems for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and disease outbreak surveillance.



The America First Global Health Strategy Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) signed to date represent more than $27.2 billion in new health funding, including more than $16.1 billion in U.S. assistance alongside more than $11.1 billion in co-investment from recipient countries, building on decades of progress fighting HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis, and other infectious diseases around the world.

As of October 8, the State Department has signed 36 bilateral global health MOUs with Angola, Bolivia, Botswana, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cambodia, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Eswatini, Ethiopia, Guatemala, Guinea, Honduras, Kenya, Lesotho, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Panama, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Rwanda, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Southâ¯Sudan,â¯Tajikistan, Tanzania, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia.

World.title: Africa: Museveni Urges African Defence Chiefs to Link Security With Development
World.content:
President Yoweri Museveni has called on African defence leaders to recognise the close link between national security, economic strength and political cohesion.

Closing the inaugural African Conference of Chiefs of Defence Forces on Military Operations Other Than War at Speke Resort Munyonyo, Museveni said a strong defence force cannot be sustained without a strong economy.

He urged African countries to focus on wealth creation through commercial agriculture, industry, services and ICT, while expanding markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and regional integration.

Museveni also called on defence forces to adapt to emerging and non-traditional security threats and play a role in peacebuilding and national development.

"Security and prosperity go together," Museveni said.

He thanked visiting Defence Chiefs, Intelligence Chiefs and Force Commanders for attending the conference in Uganda and wished them a good stay in the country.

World.title: Mamdani demands Trump release illegal immigrant shot by ICE agent as protests erupt in the Bronx

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani demanded that President Donald Trump end all ICE enforcement in the state after a federal agent shot an illegal immigrant in the Bronx on Thursday, sparking protests and confrontations with law enforcement.

At a news conference late Thursday night, Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he spoke with Trump for about two hours following the incident.

Mamdani said he urged Trump to have the man released – an effort that was unsuccessful – and said New York City wants ICE agents out.

"All they do is terrorize this city," the mayor said of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

ICE OFFICER SHOOTS, INJURES MAN DURING TARGETED IMMIGRATION OPERATION IN BRONX: DHS

Mamdani also accused ICE of acting "with impunity" and spreading "chaos and terror" across the country, alleging that ICE has killed more people than it has saved.

"Today's shooting is only further devastating confirmation of what we have long known," the mayor said.

"ICE is rotten to its core," he added.

Mamdani also confirmed that the man who was shot has been transported out of the hospital by ICE agents.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul also said she spoke to Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"Tonight, I spoke with President Trump and DHS Secretary Mullin about the shooting in Marble Hill," she said on X. "I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York. I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."

ICE SHOOTING ROCKS AUSTIN AS DEMOCRAT DEMANDS BODYCAM VIDEO, INDEPENDENT PROBE

ICE was attempting to arrest a wanted man from the Dominican Republic at around 4 p.m. on Thursday when an agent opened fire and wounded him, according to DHS, which did not provide details on what led to the shooting.

"ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation. More information will be shared as it becomes available," DHS said in a statement.

DHS said the man, who was described as an illegal immigrant, had a prior grand larceny conviction and previous arrests involving assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession. The agency also alleged that he had ties to the Trinitarios gang.

Later Thursday night, New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch identified the man as a 28-year-old and said a 5-year-old boy believed to be his son was inside the vehicle with him during the shooting.

"Based on evidence collected at the scene, we know that at least one ICE agent discharged the seven rounds, striking the driver in the neck below his left ear," Tisch said, adding that the boy was not injured and is in the care of a family member.

The agency said the man was arrested by New York City police on Dec. 7, 2023, but was released several days later. DHS blamed New York City's sanctuary policies for his release.

Hundreds of demonstrators gathered outside NewYork-Presbyterian Allen Hospital, where the wounded man was being treated, and chanting "ICE off our streets" and "No justice, no peace." Protesters and police were seen shoving one another during the demonstration as officers began to set barricades, and some demonstrators threw water bottles at the officers.

"From Palestine to Mexico, all these walls have got to go," the group chanted.

World.title: Brian Schottenheimer now sits on hottest seat in NFL after Cowboys collapse against Buccaneers
World.content:
It’s official: Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer has the hottest seat in the NFL.

Schottenheimer was stumped on the sideline at AT&T Stadium on Thursday night as his squad fell 24-16 to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who entered the game 0-4 and started a rookie quarterback in his first career road game.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Jalon Daniels was quite efficient against a reeling Cowboys defense, which came into this game as the third-worst in the league in terms of yards allowed per game (389.5) and fifth-worst in points allowed (28). The defensive side of the ball was a problem during Schottenheimer’s inaugural season leading the Cowboys in 2025, and with 34-year-old Christian Parker as defensive coordinator, it’s more of the same in 2026.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The reason Schottenheimer’s seat is the hottest is because the man facing him on the opposite sideline came into Week 5 in that position first.

Buccaneers head coach Todd Bowles is fighting for his job security after a brutal start to the season. Yes, his starting quarterback, Baker Mayfield, is out, but the Buccaneers did not look good before his injury. And since Tampa Bay couldn’t make the playoffs last season despite a red-hot start, Bowles needs to start stacking wins.

The state of Tampa Bay, and a Dallas victory over the Houston Texans in Week 4, led Vegas to mark the Cowboys as a clear-cut favorite at home. But Dak Prescott never felt comfortable like he did in Week 4, with Bowles drawing up his signature blitzes throughout the four quarters, and the Dallas defense continued to be passive.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Tampa Bay found itself down at halftime, 10-7, but shifty running back Bucky Irving changed the entire momentum of the contest when he sprinted 72 yards on the opening drive of the third quarter to set up an Emeka Egbuka touchdown. In just two plays, the Bucs went 86 yards and took the lead, shocking the sold-out crowd.

To make matters worse, the Cowboys would turn the ball over their next three possessions, leading to a lopsided game. Prescott threw an interception, and Daniels found Tez Johnson in busted coverage for a 64-yard catch-and-run. Irving scored his second touchdown of the game to further the Bucs’ lead, and Prescott wouldn’t even get the ball back after KaVontae Turpin fumbled the ensuing kickoff, which Tampa Bay recovered.

With a Chase McLaughlin field goal making it 24-10, the Cowboys felt desperate at the end of the third quarter, going for it on fourth down near midfield and failing to convert.

There was, however, some hope provided by a key stop from this lackluster defense. On fourth-and-goal from the one-yard line, Bowles decided to go for the kill shot, hoping to punch one into the end zone and make it a 31-10 game in the fourth quarter. But Sean Tucker, their short-yardage specialist in the backfield, was unable to punch it home.

From there, Schottenheimer put on his best play-calling hat and recognized that momentum was shifting toward Dallas despite the Buccaneers’ 99-yard drive. He and Prescott delivered.

George Pickens capped that 99-yard drive with a 17-yard touchdown catch, his first of the season, to make it a one score game after a two-point conversion failed.

The momentum continued, as the Buccaneers went three-and-out, and with ample time as well as timeouts, Prescott could go down the field and perhaps tie the game with a touchdown and two-point conversion. Instead, more disaster for the Cowboys in this primetime matchup, as tight end Jake Ferguson, usually as sure-handed as they come for Dallas, had a Prescott pass go right through his hands, hit his face mask and land in the arms of Buccaneers linebacker Alex Anzalone while in Tampa Bay territory.

This time, Daniels and the Buccaneers’ offense didn’t squander the chance to put the Cowboys away, as Irving picked up the necessary first down to allow his rookie quarterback some victory kneels to end the game.

Sure, the Cowboys' record still reads 2-3 compared to the Buccaneers' 1-4. But Jerry Jones demands winning in Dallas, and this was a brutal loss for a coach already stirring speculation about whether he’s right for one of the most coveted jobs in the sport.

There’s still many games left to play, but it’s truly heating up for Schottenheimer after this one.

World.title: A'ja Wilson wins record fifth MVP as first three-peat in WNBA history strengthens all-time greatness case
World.content:
On Thursday, A’ja Wilson added another line to her already lengthy basketball resume, reaching yet another level of WNBA greatness by becoming the league’s first five-time MVP.

The Las Vegas Aces superstar has claimed the coveted trophy for a third consecutive season, becoming the first player in league history to win three straight MVP awards. It marks her fourth MVP title in the past five years.

Aces coach Becky Hammon believes Wilson’s résumé already places her among the greatest players in basketball. In addition to her WNBA accomplishments, Wilson won an NCAA Division I national championship at South Carolina.

DREAM MOVE WITHIN ONE WIN OF FIRST WNBA FINALS APPEARANCE SINCE 2013 AFTER OVERTIME VICTORY

"(As) I said, take her off Mount Rushmore — she’s Everest," Hammon said earlier in the playoffs. "Now I’m taking her off Everest, and I have to put her on a different planet. She just has all of it."

Hammon also emphasized that talent alone does not guarantee the kind of sustained team and individual success Wilson has achieved. "Because you can be a really talented and skilled basketball player and not win as much as she has, and not become as individually great as she has."

Wilson may not have put together the most statistically impressive season of her career, but she remained dominant across the board.

Her 26.2 points per game led the WNBA in scoring, while her 79 blocks were also a league high. She ranked among the league’s top five rebounders in rebounds per game during the regular season. Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese led the WNBA with 12.1 rebounds per game and was named the 2026 WNBA Defensive Player of the Year.

Other notable former WNBA players with multiple MVP awards

When Wilson won her fourth MVP award in 2025, she broke a tie with Hall of Famers Sheryl Swoopes, Lisa Leslie and Lauren Jackson for the most MVP trophies in WNBA history at the time. The three standout players largely traded the award between 2000 and 2010, winning every MVP except in 2008, when Candace Parker claimed the honor, and 2009, when Diana Taurasi won.



In NBA history, only three players have been awarded at least five MVPs: Bill Russell, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Michael Jordan. With her fifth MVP, Wilson is now among select group of legendary basketball players.

"If you’re able to set a standard, if you’re able to rewrite things, and kind of etch yourself into history books, it means a lot," Wilson said at a news conference in Las Vegas on Thursday. "I’m so grateful that I can share these moments with so many different people. But it’s always fun when you’re able to set the standard, and give people and yourself something to chase after."

Minnesota Lynx rookie Olivia Miles finished second with six first-place votes, followed by Indiana Fever guard Kelsey Mitchell with two. Mitchell’s teammate, Caitlin Clark, received the remaining first-place vote and finished fourth.

A’ja Wilson’s latest challenge is guiding the Aces through unprecedented territory. They would have to become the first team in WNBA history to erase a 2-0 deficit against the Golden State Valkyries and win a best-of-five playoff series. World.title: Tony Romo got disqualified from his Korn Ferry qualifier the same day he 'parted ways' with CBS Sports
World.content:
Man, it has not been a great run recently for former Dallas Cowboys star quarterback Tony Romo.

Romo became the talk of the internet when he was arrested over the summer for operating a vehicle while intoxicated in Wisconsin. Police body cam footage of the arrest went viral, and his mugshot was quickly passed around, with a seemingly endless run of memes made about the 46-year-old.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

As one of CBS Sports' lead football analysts, speculation immediately started about his future on television, with the network announcing that he'd been put on indefinite leave.



That leave turned into a permanent separation in early October, when news broke that the two sides had agreed to mutually part ways. Obviously, not the best news for Romo, who, while he started off hot, had recently come under criticism from fans for his analysis and was still owed tens of millions of dollars on his contract.

Well, the news got even worse for him that same day.

Romo is an accomplished, very talented golfer, to the point where he recently participated in a pre-qualifier tournament for a Korn Ferry Tour event. Far from the PGA Tour, or more likely the Champions Tour, but still impressive for an "amateur" player.

Less impressive? The fact that on the same day he "parted ways" with CBS, Romo was disqualified from that Korn Ferry pre-qualifier.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

While trying, unsuccessfully, to make the cut, Romo was accused of signing an incorrect scorecard.

Per Golf.com, Romo's qualifier was held at the Club at Forest Ridge in Broken Arrow, Okla., where he started with rounds of 76 and 75, putting him well back, 13 strokes to be exact, of the leaders after 36 holes. That score was still good enough to put him in a decent spot to move on to the next stage of Q-School for the Korn Ferry tour. Put in a solid showing on Friday? He'd have given himself a realistic chance to advance.

The problem? Three people had three different versions of Romo's score in that third round.

Romo signed his score card showing that he made a 4 on the 16th hole and a 4 on the 17th hole. But his playing partner and marker, Brandon Rice, put him down for a 4 on the 16th, but a 5 on the 17th. That's odd, but even more bizarre is that a PGA Pro and walking referee told tournament organizers that after being assigned to track Romo's group after they were put "on the clock" for slow play, he recollected Romo having a 5 on the 16th and a 5 on the 17th.

What on earth?

Well, Rob Keller, the pre-qualifier administrator, told Golf.com what he thought happened. Keller believed that the slow-play, inability to make birdies, and "all that was going on with him," Romo simply didn't take the time to thoroughly check his marker's version of his score. Keller also added that Romo "took responsibility" when the two spoke on the phone while being "very complimentary" as to the quality of the tournament.

Romo wouldn’t have made it through given his third-round score, but still, what a day for the former QB. How do you get your scores wrong? Especially when you know you have a marker there observing all of it. Sounds like Romo might be the ideal scramble tournament partner, one where the winning score is in the 40's somehow.

World.title: Rumbling volcano forces immediate trail closures at popular vacation hot spot
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Officials are monitoring renewed volcanic activity at one of Hawaii's most popular tourist destinations as hundreds of earthquakes and rockfall risks prompt temporary trail closures.

The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) issued a volcanic activity notice earlier this week for the Kīlauea volcano at Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, reporting renewed spattering at two vents following recent activity beneath the summit.

The National Park Service (NPS) announced Wednesday that Halemaʻumaʻu Trail and part of Byron Ledge Trail would temporarily close amid increased seismic activity and concerns about rockfalls.

The closures affect a combined 1.3 miles of trails.

HUSBAND AND WIFE GET TRAPPED IN PREMIER HIKING DESTINATION; ONLY ONE OF THEM MAKES IT OUT ALIVE

Over 200 shallow earthquakes were recorded beneath Kīlauea's summit during the past week, according to the NPS, citing the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory. A magnitude-3.4 earthquake on Sept. 30 caused small rockfalls along the caldera's north wall.

Kīlauea remained at an ORANGE aviation color code, the second-highest level on the USGS' four-tier scale, as of Thursday.

The designation indicates heightened volcanic activity and the potential for an eruption, or an eruption underway with limited hazards to aviation.

The intrusion, which occurred from Sept. 30 to Oct. 1, is believed to have caused new cracks along the caldera floor, according to scientists.

Scientists said they cannot forecast when — or if — the volcano's 55th episode of lava fountaining will occur.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Forecast windows for episode 55 fountaining can no longer be modeled due to changes in conditions," the USGS advisory said.

Officials also outlined several hazards for residents and visitors, including potentially dangerous gas emissions and small, glassy volcanic fragments that can cause skin and eye irritation.

"Small glassy volcanic fragments may be remobilized during windy conditions following recent eruptive episodes," the statement added.

"Residents and visitors should minimize exposure to these fragments, which can cause skin and eye irritation."

CLICK HERE TO 

Visitors must also stay out of closed areas and away from unstable cliff edges, which can collapse without warning, according to the NPS.

Kīlauea, one of the world's most active volcanoes, has erupted dozens of times since 1952, according to the USGS.

Eruptive activity was nearly continuous along the volcano's East Rift Zone from 1983 to 2018, a 35-year stretch that ended amid significant eruptive activity and a collapse at the summit, the agency said.

Since December 2024, an eruption has been intermittently active within Halema'uma'u crater at the summit.

The National Park Service has said the number of visits surged during Kīlauea's eruptive episodes, with tourists drawn to opportunities to view the volcanic activity.

Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park recorded more than 1.8 million recreational visits in 2025, according to NPS data.

World.title: 2 foreign nationals breach UK base housing key US, NATO intel hub amid $556M expansion
World.content:

Two Latvian nationals legally living in the United Kingdom were arrested under Section 4 of Britain's National Security Act of 2023 Thursday after allegedly breaching a perimeter fence at RAF Molesworth, a sensitive British military base housing critical U.S. and NATO intelligence operations, Reuters reported.

The arrests triggered a major counterterrorism investigation into the security breach at the strategic installation, which serves as a central intelligence hub supporting American military commanders across Europe and Africa.

The base is also undergoing a $556.5 million expansion centered on the Joint Intelligence Analysis Complex (JIAC), a location designed to consolidate 20 intelligence facilities and accommodate more than 1,000 personnel, according to reports.

IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY

The suspects, ages 32 and 36, were discovered inside the base around 2 a.m. Thursday after an extensive security sweep.

Ministry of Defense Police officers conducting routine patrols first raised the alarm around 10 p.m. Wednesday after finding an abandoned vehicle near the perimeter.

Bomb disposal specialists cleared the vehicle before armed officers discovered a fence breach and located the men inside.

Initially detained on suspicion of trespass and criminal damage, both men were arrested again under the National Security Act for allegedly entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom. They remain in custody as counterterrorism detectives execute search warrants at two residential properties in nearby Peterborough.

Managed by the U.S. Air Force's 423rd Air Base Group, RAF Molesworth is a nonflying installation dedicated to joint intelligence and command operations.

It houses intelligence elements for U.S. European Command, U.S. Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre.

During World War II, the airfield was used by the U.S. 15th Bombardment Squadron. In 1973, the airfield was officially deactivated before transitioning into its current role as an intelligence center.

Construction on the JIAC broke ground April 12, 2024, with onsite work beginning that spring. The facility is scheduled for completion in summer 2028.

FOILED TERROR PLOT AT BOMBER BASE SIGNALS WIDER THREAT TO US MILITARY INSTALLATIONS: EXPERT

A 2024 Defense Department release described the base development as part of the department's overall European Infrastructure Consolidation efforts.

Among others, it will host members of the NATO Intelligence Fusion Centre, Battlefield Information Collection and Exploitation System, U.S. Africa Command, U.S. European Command and U.S. Air Force elements in a cross-agency, multi-mission collaboration."

At the time, Defense Intelligence Agency Deputy Director Suzanne White said the facility would enable "the U.S. and allies’ shared mission of ‘outpacing our strategic competitors and addressing threats together wherever they may arise.’"

The Defense Department designed the project with a two-stage procurement strategy, allowing stakeholder agencies to provide feedback and streamline scheduling requirements.

Following the intrusion, U.S. European Command praised the swift British response.

"While we assess the global security posture, U.S. forces remain at the highest state of readiness," the command said in a statement.

"We would also express our gratitude to the UK for the close partnership with U.S. forces on matters of security."

British counterterrorism officials cautioned against drawing premature conclusions about possible espionage or terrorist motives.

"We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites," Counterterrorism Policing London commander Helen Flanagan said.

Flanagan added that investigators have not established a connection between the Molesworth breach and recent security concerns at RAF Fairford, another British base used by U.S. strategic bombers.

A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., has heard evidence concerning possible false statements former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson made to the congressional committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, Fox News Digital has learned.

Additional evidence could be presented to the grand jury as soon as next week, according to a source familiar with the matter.

The proceedings remain in the grand jury phase, and no final decisions have been made about whether the matter will result in criminal charges, the source said.

During a nationally televised hearing in June 2022, Hutchinson provided testimony about Trump's actions on Jan. 6, including an account she said she heard from another White House official about the president's reaction after being told he could not travel to the Capitol.

Her account of an alleged confrontation inside the presidential vehicle was subsequently disputed by other individuals familiar with the events.

FORMER WHITE HOUSE AIDE CASSIDY HUTCHINSON 'STANDS BY ALL OF THE TESTIMONY SHE PROVIDED' TO JAN 6 COMMITTEE

It remains unclear which portions of Hutchinson's congressional testimony are being examined by the grand jury.

World.title: Sparks fly as Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers face off in first Michigan Senate debate
World.content:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — The two candidates battling for Michigan’s open Senate seat tangled here Thursday over the war in Iran, gas prices and tariffs in a debate that often veered into mean-spirited sniping.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed sought to portray his Republican rival, former Rep. Mike Rogers, as a weak-willed loyalist to President Donald Trump who has recently changed his positions on certain issues out of political necessity.

Rogers tried to frame El-Sayed as a “con man” who is making promises he cannot pay for without raising taxes or other costs.

Each repeatedly taunted the other over real estate — a home Rogers has in Florida and property El-Sayed’s wife owns in the United Arab Emirates. The debate, hosted by NBC affiliate WOOD of Grand Rapids, became so punchy at times that moderator Rick Albin pleaded for the candidates to rein in their attacks.

“I’d like to be a part of the debate, too,” Albin interjected at one point.

Michigan’s Senate race is one of the most competitive and closely watched in the country, and the results could help determine partisan control of the chamber. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is not seeking re-election.

Backed by progressive luminaries such as Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed emerged from a nasty primary against Rep. Haley Stevens, who positioned herself as a more moderate Democrat. Since then, Republicans eager to win a Senate seat in the state for the first time since 1994 have tried to paint El-Sayed as an extremist.

The debate opened with Albin asking both candidates whether, at a time of high gas prices related to the war with Iran, they would support a pause on the federal gas tax. Both said they would support a pause, but the question led into a deeper discussion about the conflict. Rogers, who initially supported the war, recently said he wants it to end swiftly.

“I would support pausing the federal gas tax, but there is one thing that is actually causing this: It’s the war in Iran, a war that has been cheer-led by my opponent since the beginning,” El-Sayed said. “Called it a ‘win, win, win.’ I don’t know about you, but when I go to the gas tank, I don’t feel like I’m winning. I don’t feel like our country is winning.”

Rogers responded by pivoting to El-Sayed’s support for “Medicare for All,” a proposal that Sanders and others on the left have been championing for years. Such a policy, Rogers asserted, would force people off private insurance they might prefer while causing taxes and gas prices to rise.

“It is a disaster,” Rogers said. “We cannot afford Abdul.”

At another point, Rogers said: “Listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today. You’re going to find out that this guy is not what he says he is. He is actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.”

Albin then turned the discussion toward tariffs — another area in which Rogers has recently tried to distance himself from Trump.

New tariffs implemented by Trump took effect last month, placing duties of 15% to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. products exported to Canada. The tariffs are a major issue in Michigan, which borders and trades with Canada. Rogers, who once supported Trump’s push, released an ad this week calling for an end to the trade war.

“I have actually called the White House this week, talked to the secretary of commerce about getting the deal done,” Rogers said during the debate. “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before they started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those. So this is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end.”

El-Sayed countered by noting Rogers’ initial support and a study that estimated how costly the tariffs have been for Michigan households.

“Look, you’re hearing somebody who has cheer-led, again, a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said. “The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.”

El-Sayed added, a moment later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”

The debate presented other contrasts between the candidates, including differences over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which El-Sayed has called for abolishing. When Albin asked whether he believed the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement strategy had ever gone too far, Rogers said this year’s very public operation in Minneapolis, which resulted in federal agents’ shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, was “probably not appropriate.”

“I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago,” he said. “You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems. So that to me was something that they could have done differently.”

El-Sayed was pressed about his criticism of Israel and his recent refusal, in a NewsNation interview, to say whether he sees Israel or Iran as a bigger threat to the U.S. Despite Albin’s prodding, El-Sayed again declined to offer a direct answer.

“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical, because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he replied.

“We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part. I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel,” he added. “I want our money spent here to buy schools and healthcare and childcare here. I don’t understand why that is so inconceivable.”

The debate was the first of two planned between El-Sayed and Rogers, but the candidates have been circling each other for months. Both have leaned into schoolyard taunts, with Rogers mocking El-Sayed’s height and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a “no pads” football game.

Nationally, Republicans have tried to make El-Sayed, with his progressive views and alliances, the new face of the Democratic Party. In their efforts to villainize El-Sayed, they have also emphasized his ethnicity and Muslim faith.

Vice President JD Vance, for example, has urged Republicans who are “running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy” to instead mention El-Sayed. And Trump referred to El-Sayed on Truth Social on Wednesday night as “Mohammed” and described him as someone who “goes back to the days of the Jihad.”

Earlier Thursday, at a lunch event with Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer at a Grand Rapids restaurant, El-Sayed mocked Trump’s antics, including how Trump pronounces his real name.

“Get it right,” El-Sayed said, “because we’re going to teach you how to say it properly with the word ‘senator’ in front of it.”

He added, referring to Trump and Vance: “They keep pointing to my name and my faith because they think that they can distract us from the issues that affect all of us — because my name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford a tank of gas.”

World.title: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico off the trail with the flu
World.content:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.

But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.

His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.

While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.

“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”

While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.

“He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.

“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”

Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.

Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.

“Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”

Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.

Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.

“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”

To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.

At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.

“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”

After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.

“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social.

It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.”

World.title: MAHA fractures deepen as some RFK Jr. followers turn into harsh critics
World.content:
Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

“We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

“What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.”

“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

“To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.”

“I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.”

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

“What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said.

Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Phasing out food dyes

Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?”

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

“If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

“The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”
