World.title: Ithaca city council calls on Cornell to report sexual assault investigations to local police
World.content:
ITHACA, N.Y. — The city of Ithaca called on the Cornell University Police Department to turn over sex and violent crime investigations to the Ithaca Police Department, after the city council voted nearly unanimously in favor of the measure. The decision late Wednesday came as a gang-rape allegation by a former Cornell student took the campus and nation by storm last month.

The Cornell University Police Department has said it did not refer its investigation of the 2024 allegation to the Ithaca Police Department. The former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month detailing the allegations and what she said was a lack of appropriate response by the university and its police department.

The Ithaca Common Council also voted Wednesday to temporarily suspend affiliated student organizations at the university, such as fraternities, from new assemblies, parades and special events “due to public safety concerns.” The moratorium on events would expire on Nov. 5, unless the council were to take further action, according to a meeting agenda.

The resolution passed by a vote of 9-1. The council did not say how the measure would be enforced or what would happen if the university did not comply. Cornell declined to comment, citing pending litigation.

More than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a poll conducted last year. That figure was up from 23% in 2023, according to the university.

The university police department and the local district attorney are under intense scrutiny over how the investigation into Doe’s allegations was handled.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten previously said he based his decision not to bring charges based on a six-page summary made by Cornell police of Jane Doe’s initial interview with police. But, according to reports, that summary was missing some of Jane Doe’s strongest remarks to police.

CBS News New York, citing a transcript of a conversation between Jane Doe and investigators, reported that she told campus police three weeks after the fraternity incident that she had been raped.

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” Jane Doe is quoted as saying.

World.title: Man shot by ICE agent in New York City's Marble Hill, authorities say
World.content:
A man was hospitalized after being shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in New York City's Marble Hill neighborhood on Thursday, according to the Department of Homeland Security and New York City officials.

The shooting occurred at about 4 p.m. local time near West 225th Street and Marble Hill Avenue.

Officials said he was taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

The NYPD was not involved in the shooting, the department said.

Video from the scene showed numerous law enforcement personnel present. A gray vehicle with a bullet hole in the windshield could be seen in the middle of the road.

Two law enforcement sources told CBS News that preliminary information indicated ICE agents were attempting to take someone into custody when another male, who was not the target of the arrest, was shot.

DHS, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement that officers were conducting a targeted enforcement operation to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic who they allege was living in the United States illegally.

In a press conference Thursday night, NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said preliminary information indicates a 28-year-old man was inside a grey Honda at the time of the shooting with a 5-year-old boy. Tisch named the wounded man during the press conference, but the NYPD was unable to confirm the spelling, deferring it to DHS.

Tisch said NYPD cameras captured a vehicle backing into a parking spot in front of a fire hydrant. She says video shows one plainclothes federal law enforcement officer approaching the driver's side window with his gun drawn and a second plainclothes officer approaching the vehicle by the driver's side headlight. According Tisch, the vehicle then moves forward out of view of the camera.

An ICE officer discharged his weapon during the incident, injuring the man, DHS said.

Tisch said the NYPD cameras did not capture the shooting, but based on evidence collected at the scene, at least one ICE agent discharged seven rounds, striking the driver in the neck below his left ear.

"ICE officers immediately rendered aid," DHS said. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation. More information will be shared as it becomes available."

Tisch said NYPD officers who were in the area responded to the scene after hearing reports of shots fired.

"When they arrived, they encountered several men in various forms of attire, including some in construction-style vests, face masks and at least one carrying a long gun," she said.

Tisch said the injured man was handcuffed and seated on the ground. According to Tisch, NYPD officers placed him into an NYPD vehicle, rendered aid and transported him to the hospital.

The child was not injured and is in the care of a family member, Tisch said.

Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat of New York told CBS News in an interview Thursday night that the 5-year-old child was the son of the victim. Espaillat told CBS News that he met with the 5-year-old boy and his mother at the hospital, where the victim received treatment.

Espaillat disclosed the victim was under guard from ICE agents outside his hospital room, and Espaillat was not allowed to see him.

Late Thursday, Mamdani said ICE "put the man in an unmarked vehicle and whisked him away."

DHS alleged that the man had associations to the Trinitarios gang. Tisch said he has two prior arrests. In 2023, he was arrested on a robbery charge and later pleaded guilty to fourth-degree larceny. He was also arrested in 2025 on a charge of criminal sale of a controlled substance, a case that remains pending.

Mamdani said he spent two hours on the phone with President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Thursday night to negotiate for the release of the man ICE agents shot, but those negotiations were unsuccessful.

Federal agencies have taken over the investigation, Tisch said.

There have been at least 30 shootings involving DHS officers during the second Trump administration, according to a CBS News analysis, some of which have turned deadly.

World.title: LAUSD data shows student fights and threats higher than 4 years ago
World.content:
While the Los Angeles Unified School District has made steady improvements to lower the number of students experiencing fights, threats, drug incidents, weapons issues and suicide risks, school safety experts warn the district has more work to do.

Student fights and threats are still significantly up compared to four years ago, according to LAUSD data.

In the 2025-2026 school year, there were 6,131 fights, a 21% jump from four years ago, and 4,015 student threats, an 11.5% increase from the 2022-2023 school year.

Monica Harmon, executive director of Speak Out Against Bullying Inc., says the school district needs to implement stricter measures.

"There's no consequences. There needs to be consequences," she said after an anti-bullying assembly at an elementary school on Thursday. "So many kids get in trouble, the students report it, and then, you know, they're back in school the next day. They're not suspended. There need to be tougher restrictions."

Ronald Stephens, executive director of the National School Safety Center and professor of education emeritus at Pepperdine, reviewed the LAUSD data. He called the numbers "very concerning."

"I will tell you from a litigation standpoint, the questions the school district will be asked if something serious happens is, 'What did you know, and when did you know it, with respect to the fighting and aggression and illegal substance, and then, when you learned of it, what did you do about it?' So, it will be important for the school district to take some steps in terms of enhancing their supervision, or some other type of training or intervention or partnership," Stephens explained.

"The school district does indeed have a safe school plan, but clearly, their existing plan, with these other red flags that are emerging, suggests that they will need to do something else to enhance their supervision and support for students at risk."

Stephens added that the data should inform the school district's protocols moving forward.

"With those kinds of numbers jumping over the last few years, it really suggests to go back to the drawing board and talk with students, with parents, with teachers, and get some good advice on what they might suggest, because most of this work in keeping schools safe is not about rocket science," he said. "It's about having a physical presence and a care for students."

Los Angeles Police Department Capt. Eric Eppolito says his agency is making a focused effort to increase school outreach this year to help prevent smaller problems among students in schools from growing into bigger ones.

"When you talk about bullying, that can lead to a lot of things, from minor to something really serious. You know, as the kids get older, it gets even more problematic. You're dealing with fights and things that escalate from there," Eppolito said. "So, if we can teach someone on the front end to communicate better and to solve their issues through communication, and if that doesn't work, then we can get ahead of the problems."

Over the last five years, police have not had an active presence at LA public schools.

CBS California Investigates took a closer look at the district's safety data, because parents are furious about school safety in the wake of the death of 17-year-old Xavier Nungaray at Franklin High School last week.

LAUSD parents called for more police presence at schools during a rally outside Los Angeles Unified School District Headquarters on Wednesday. This follows the death of 17-year-old Franklin High School student Xavier Nungaray-Martinez. Myung J. Chun

Harmon says she hopes her bullying prevention assemblies, which end with students taking an anti-bullying pledge, will help prevent more tragedies down the road.

"Reinforcing the message to the kids not to be witnesses, rather to speak up and say something," Harmon said. "What I'm seeing on social media, like what happened to the student at Franklin High School, there were students standing around watching, recording. It would have taken one or two students to save that little boy if they stepped up, and we need to get that culture of kids not to be afraid to speak up in the schools."

The new LAUSD data, presented at a school board meeting in late September, also shows that weapons-related incidents and reported incidents of students considering suicide — what the district calls "suicide risk" — have continued to decline significantly over the last four years.

There were 923 weapons-related incidents last school year, down 38% compared to four years ago. Last year, there were 10,055 incidents of suicide risk, down 14% compared to four years ago. Suicide risk, however, has been the most pervasive school safety problem facing students in LAUSD for the last five years in a row.

To read the district's presentations on the data for the 2025-2026 school year, click here. To see the data from the 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 school years, click here.

A spokesperson for the LAUSD wrote the following statement to CBS LA:

"Student safety and well-being remain a priority for Los Angeles Unified. The latest data show decreases in reported fighting and physical aggression, threats, weapons incidents and suicide risks compared with the previous school year. However, we recognize that reports of student conflict remain a concern, and we must continue working to prevent incidents and ensure students have access to the support they need.

"This year, we continue to strengthen prevention efforts through Positive Behavior Interventions and Supports and Restorative Practices, which help schools establish clear expectations, build positive relationships, address conflict and hold students accountable while repairing harm. We are also continuing to provide training and resources for school staff, families and students on mental health supports, healthy relationships, and creating safe, welcoming school environments.

"We work with community partners to support violence prevention and intervention and connect students and families with additional resources. Schools reinforce campus supervision plans and identify areas where additional attention may be needed."

World.title: El-Sayed and Rogers toss insults in Michigan Senate debate
World.content:
In Thursday's Michigan Senate debate, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed called his opponent "weak," "cowardly" and a "sock puppet for the Trump administration." Republican Mike Rogers called his opponent a "glitchy AI chatbot" who is running a "con" and will "say anything to win."

The two candidates in one of the country's most closely watched midterm contests spent the hourlong debate sparring over the Iran war, the trade war with Canada, immigration, healthcare policy and cost-of-living issues. They also tossed insults across the stage in nearly every exchange, accusing each other of flip-flopping and financial entanglements.

After the only commercial break, debate moderator Rick Albin of WOOD-TV in Grand Rapids said the two men were arguing even when they were off-air. At various points, Albin pleaded with the candidates to "work with me" and said: "I appreciate your passion, but please, let's try to keep this orderly."

El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination after a bitter primary in which the former health official clashed with the party's moderate wing over his support for single-payer healthcare and his opposition to U.S. military aid for Israel. A former congressman, Rogers won the GOP nomination with little competition after an endorsement from President Trump, whose rocky approval ratings have posed a vulnerability for his party's midterm candidates.

Most polls show a razor-thin race between the two candidates, who are competing to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The race could be pivotal in determining which party wins control of the Senate.

During the debate, both candidates called for pausing the gas tax as the conflict in the Middle East keeps energy prices high, and questioned the tit-for-tat tariff war with Canada.

On the Iran war, Rogers said "this would be the time to wrap it up." He also argued "we need to end" the trade dispute with Canada by striking a deal with the U.S.' northern neighbor, saying he spoke with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "about getting the deal done."

But El-Sayed pushed Rogers on the Trump administration's trade and Iran policies, accusing him of running at the president's behest and being unwilling to stand up to Mr. Trump.

"He's got a direct line to the president who's making sure the war does not end, and he's not using it," El-Sayed said of the Iran conflict, which he called a "stupid war."

Asked if the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration has gone too far, Rogers said the intense operations in Minnesota earlier this year were "probably not appropriate."

"They made that correction. They made an adjustment," Rogers said, before arguing agents are "targeting murderers and rapists who were here illegally doing bad things."

El-Sayed — who has called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be abolished — was asked whether an undocumented immigrant who committed a violent crime should be deported. He answered: "Yes, but you don't have to do that by violating the whole Constitution."

Meanwhile, Rogers attacked El-Sayed over his support for Medicare For All, calling his views on healthcare "dangerous" and arguing it would involve "taking over your private health insurance and giving it to the government." When El-Sayed said that "if families want to keep their private health insurance, that's fine by me," Rogers interjected: "That is absolutely news to me."

Foreign policy animated much of the debate. El-Sayed frequently criticized the Iran war and cast Rogers as a hawk who "thinks there's a war for everything." El-Sayed said he supports a diplomatic solution on Iran, pointing to the Obama-era deal that limited Iran's uranium enrichment, an agreement that Mr. Trump ended during his first term.

Rogers said he believes the war can end now because Iran's nuclear program and conventional military have been severely degraded.

El-Sayed is a vehement critic of the Israeli government over its conduct during its war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip, and opposes U.S. military assistance to Israel. Asked by the moderator whether he views Iran or Israel as a bigger threat, El-Sayed called it a "ridiculous hypothetical," arguing Israel spurred the U.S. to enter the war with Iran and saying "both of them have proven dangerous in their own way."

Rogers described himself as a staunch backer of Israel. Asked if there is anything Israel could do to cause him to lose support, he said: "If they were talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support. I've never heard them say that, though."

Rogers pressed El-Sayed for not putting out a statement marking three years since Hamas' deadly Oct. 7, 2023, terror attack on Israel, alleging that his opponent "could not bring himself to even acknowledge the pain, the terrorism, the rape, the murders." El-Sayed said he has condemned the attack but "didn't turn it into political theater like you just did." He later told reporters after the debate that he felt whatever he had said about the terror attack would be scrutinized and politicized.

Both candidates pressed each other on campaign donations and questioned each other's finances, with El-Sayed dinging Rogers over a waterfront home that he owns in Florida and Rogers bringing up El-Sayed's wife's rental property in the United Arab Emirates.

"At least Florida is in the United States," Rogers said at one point, prompting El-Sayed to respond, "It's not in Michigan, my guy."

World.title: Hurricane Isaias threatens Gulf Coast with rain, flooding. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias is intensifying and is expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season after strengthening from a tropical storm late Wednesday night.

Isaias is now a Category 2 storm with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour. A hurricane warning is in effect for the northern Gulf Coast, from the Mississippi-Alabama state line, across southern Alabama, to Panama City, Florida.

"Extremely high seas, heavy rains, and damaging winds that accompany tropical storms and hurricanes present serious dangers to the public," the U.S. Coast Guard said in a statement.

Maps show hurricane's path

The core of Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," was located about 260 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, moving northeast at 14 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center's latest update Thursday night. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 25 miles from the storm's center, and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 125 miles.

Forecasters said Isaias could potentially become a major hurricane Friday. A major hurricane is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger, which means it has maximum sustained winds of 111 mph or greater.

Map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

"Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday night," the hurricane center said. "Preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds along the warning area of the Gulf Coast should be rushed to completion."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from the southeast corner of Louisiana to Biloxi, Mississippi, as well as the area around Apalachicola, Florida. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana, across the coasts of Mississippi and Alabama, into the Florida Panhandle.

Map shows the strength of the wind Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring to the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 4 to 8 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast from southern Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and Florida's Big Bend. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall as well.

Tornadoes are also a potential threat Friday night into Saturday in coastal parts of Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle.

Map shows amounts of rain expected through Saturday in some regions of U.S. CBS News

"There's a great chance that this will spin off tornadoes," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a Thursday news conference, noting how twisters can occur far from the center of the storm. "Please be on the lookout. Even if you're way outside the cone, you could still have tornado risks."

Evacuations underway

Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which took effect at noon Thursday.

Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."

Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News that his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community was whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in Florida, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. Government buildings will close in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.

The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: LAPD dog shootings raise questions about police tactics, best practice
World.content:
Neveah Aguilar was 7 years old when a Los Angeles police officer opened fire on her family's dog inside their Hollywood apartment. She was just a few steps away when Kush, a pit bull, was shot in the jaw.

Almost eight years later, CBS California Investigates has looked into the Los Angeles Police Department's use-of-force reports involving dog shootings. The team found dozens of cases in which officers opened fire, which raised questions about when officers use deadly force against animals and whether some of these shootings could have been prevented.

The investigation comes months after a family dog in Canoga Park was fatally shot by LAPD officers. For Aguilar and her mother, Norma Lopez, hearing about the incident brought back memories of what happened to Kush.

Lopez sued the police for unlawfully entering their home during an investigation into a shooting that happened outside their apartment complex. Lopez said officers detained her and her former partner before the apartment search, even though her family had nothing to do with the shooting in the area.

Aguilar alleged that officers tricked her mother, who only speaks Spanish, into letting them in without giving her a chance to secure Kush.

Lopez and Aguilar said they not only want to shed light on their own case, but also on the case of the 2-year-old Golden Saint Bernard Doodle, named Jameson, in Canoga Park. Aguilar said, "I don't want it to happen again."

In June, LAPD officers answered a call about a woman screaming during the NBA Championship game, celebrating a victory.

Body-worn camera footage shows Jameson's owner answering the door when two officers knocked on her door. The officers asked the woman to secure Jameson, but he walked out of the apartment, barking. As Jameson moved toward the officer, he opened fire.

Lopez's attorney, Theida Salazar, said police shootings against dogs were common when he worked on her case in 2018.

CBS California Investigates looked at the LAPD's Use of Force reports over the past 10 years and found the LAPD had 19 cases in which officers shot at dogs in 2016. Of those incidents, 12 dogs died. In 2015, there were 11 shootings, eight of which were fatal.

The numbers have been going down, with only one in 2024. But so far, in 2026, there have been four, resulting in three deaths.

According to LAPD reports, over the past 10 years, officers have shot 67 dogs; 45 have been pit bulls, including Kush.

CBS California Investigates reached out to the LAPD for comment, but the department declined a request for an interview. Instead, a spokesperson emailed a statement saying in part: "At this time, the Department is conducting a comprehensive review of tactics, training, and best practices."

Salazar said his clients settled their lawsuit, but he is unable to share the specific terms.

"If just a little more patience had been exercised, the dog would not have been shot, and I believe in the same instance in Canoga Park," Salazar said.

In the case of Kush, Lopez said the police told her the dog was dead after the shooting. That wasn't true.

She said after the shooting Kush snuck into the bathroom and hopped into the tub. Four hours after the shooting, animal control walked Kush out to their truck. She alleges that "they just let her bleed out."

Kush lived for another couple of years. But Lopez and Aguilar said their once energetic and playful dog was never the same. Lopez said her daughter has had to undergo years of therapy for what she witnessed.

Photos of Kush still hang on Aguilar's bedroom wall. There's also a paw print by her bed. Her mother said she raises her children to respect police, but the now high school freshman said, "It's not that I don't trust them, but I'm still afraid of them, and I feel like they still scare me."

Following the deadly shooting of Jameson, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass ordered a review of dog encounters when it comes to deadly force.

The department said it has not made formal changes to its 'Dog Encounters' Directive that went into place in 2023.

World.title: Guilfoyle associate says when she asked him for $100K, it was "quid pro quo"
World.content:
Businessman Eric Deters said he has "no doubt it was pay to play," claiming Kimberly Guilfoyle, now the U.S. ambassador to Greece and ex-fiancee of Donald Trump Jr., asked him to wire $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of Guilfoyle's Senate confirmation hearing.

In an interview with CBS News, Deters said Guilfoyle should "lose her ambassadorship" over her alleged behavior, after texts between the two of them from last July were published in the Wall Street Journal.

"It was quid pro quo," Deters told CBS News White House correspondent Weijia Jiang Thursday.

Deters said he never gave her the money.

"Unfortunately for Kimberly Guilfoyle, at that time, at that moment in time, I didn't have $100,000 to spare to give to Kimberly Guilfoyle, or I actually would have been a dumbass enough to do it."

Deters said he made up an "excuse" that his wife wouldn't go along with it.

White House officials were told that the text messages between Guilfoyle and Deters were authentic, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. Some Trump aides expressed displeasure about Guilfoyle's actions, they said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported this week that Guilfoyle allegedly reached out to Deters days before her congressional hearing to become a U.S. ambassador, saying she needed $100,000 to pay off her American Express credit debt in a way that wouldn't be publicly visible.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that's all that will show," Guilfoyle wrote to Deters on July 3, according to screen shots of texts provided to CBS News. "I have been officially announced honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote, punctuating the message with a prayer-hands emoji. Her confirmation hearing took place on July 9.

Text alleged by businessman Eric Deters to have been sent to him from Kimberly Guilfoyle on July 3, 2025, days before her confirmation hearing to be U.S. ambassador to Greece Provided by Eric Deters

She sent him "American Express Instructions" in a PDF document.

Eric Deters with President Trump in undated photo Provided by Eric Deters

CBS News has reviewed the texts, which were provided by Deters as part of a 292-page file that included dozens of pages of grievances against Trump world figures, communications with Guilfoyle and others, photos of Deters with Guilfoyle, President Trump, Eric Trump and Trump Jr., and a lengthy excerpt of a book Deters has written.

CBS News has reached out to spokespeople for the State Department and the White House, as well as Guilfoyle.

Deters, a longtime Trump supporter, is a retired lawyer and businessman from Kentucky who was sanctioned by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2021 for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law. He has also run unsuccessfully for Kentucky governor and for Rep. Thomas Massie's U.S. House seat.

For years, Deters has been trying to attract media attention and political support for a push to extradite orthopedic spine surgeon Dr. Abubakar Durrani. The government believes Durrani fled the country while he was awaiting trial for healthcare fraud charges. He was accused of billing Medicare, Medicaid and private insurance companies millions of dollars for unnecessary spinal surgeries that were potentially harmful to patients. Today, Deters said he feels slighted that he never received support for his push to have Durrani extradited to the U.S. from influential Trump world figures.

"I sent Susie Wiles, Don Jr. and Kimberly Guilfoyle an email, and I told them, I said, 'You got until 5 o'clock on Monday to help me out with the Durrani victims,'" he said. "They didn't respond. And I told them, 'If you don't, I'm going to go to the media and try to get the media's help because you're not helping.' So I gave them one last shot, and they ignored me."

In the text messages reviewed by CBS News, Deters, who said he also represents hundreds of Durrani's former patients, may have believed he could benefit from Durrani's extradition to the U.S. He wrote to Trump Jr. and Guilfoyle's podcast producer, Drew Lynch, and suggested, "If anyone in Don Jr or your world has an interest in listening to a pitch on how lots of money could be made for a little money in this Durrani matter let me know."

Deters, who no longer practices law, once stood to gain financially if he were able to successfully sue Durrani.

Just before he took office in 2025 and soon after Guilfoyle and Trump Jr. broke off their engagement, Mr. Trump announced he planned to nominate Guilfoyle to be U.S. ambassador to Greece. But Deters said her influence has waned since her relationship with Trump Jr. ended.

"There was no question that she would do anything for me," Deters said. "The problem was, she was on the outs of the Trump world."

Deters claimed Guilfoyle knew there was something wrong about asking for the payment.

"She knew there was something wrong about it because she kept getting mad at me," Deters said. "I mean, I'm naive, I'm putting stuff in writing, sending it to her. She's getting mad. She wants me to use Signal. I didn't know what Signal was."

In late June 2025, she texted, "Eric, I really wish you would stop papering these things. It's really dangerous and not helpful to you and not helpful to you or me while you could simply just call me on Signal." Deters had just sent her a memo to complain that she had not delivered on things that he had asked of her, including getting him booked on Tucker Carlson's podcast.

Eric Deters alleges Kimberly Guilfoyle sent him this text message

"I generously offered you $1 million dollars when Durrani settles if you got me on Tucker," he wrote. He also complained that he had prepared a "concise summary" for then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, but "I have not received nothing concrete."

Deters also sought a meeting with then-IRS Commissioner Billy Long about a tax issue, and he wanted Guilfoyle to send the lyrics to a song he had written to Kid Rock.

Deters said in the memo, "I am not naive or a sucker. I need results. No results. No need for me to pay."

He prodded her over text soon afterward: "As of this moment, I bet there have been no emails AND phone calls by you to Wells [Tucker Carlson's producer], Bondi, Long."

Guilfoyle said his accusation was "completely false" and sent as proof the PDF of a letter in which she congratulated Long on his confirmation and asked him to give his attention to Deters' tax issue.

Deters claimed he has paid Guilfoyle and members of the Trump family in the past.

"I paid her a total of $300,000," he said. "Don, Jr. $200,000 for two appearances. Eric Trump for $100,000, $125,000 for President Trump's PAC, $100,000 to go to Kentucky Derby with Trump. So, I paid a lot of money to Trump World," he said, adding that he never owed money to Guilfoyle or anyone else around Mr. Trump.

According to the documents he shared with CBS News, he says he paid Guilfoyle a total of $300,000 for appearance fees. And he said his promise of further payments to Guilfoyle and Lynch was to be for their services as consultants.

The Trump administration's response so far

In Greece, where Guilfoyle greeted his plane earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio chastised reporters for asking about the matter.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel," he said. "It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things."

Rubio also declined to comment because the story had only "literally posted a few hours ago," telling reporters that "we don't conduct these things in a press conference, on a tarmac, in a foreign country." As Rubio departed Greece, Guilfoyle was present, but off to the side.

CBS News on Thursday asked Vice President JD Vance about the propriety of a government official asking someone to pay off their debt.

CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs asked: "Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange to access to other government officials?"

"With that hypothetical, obviously I don't love that, but I, you know, I don't know exactly who you're talking about. I don't know the full details," Vance responded.

Deters insisted his relationship with Guilfoyle was purely political.

"Kimberly Guilfoyle and I have absolutely zero personal relationship, nada," he told CBS News.

But Deters is now determined to share his story. He said he wants to draw attention to Dr. Durrani's victims. And he wants Guilfoyle out of her post as U.S. ambassador.

"I'm a tough hombre," Deters said. "I'm going to get to take Kimberly Guilfoyle's deposition."

World.title: NFL urges Supreme Court to decide who should regulate prediction markets
World.content:
The National Football League is urging the Supreme Court to decide whether the federal government or U.S. states should have legal authority to set the rules for prediction markets.

In an amicus brief filed in support of a September petition by the New Jersey attorney general's office, the NFL expressed support for prior court rulings favoring state regulation of prediction markets. Those rulings, from the Sixth and Ninth Circuits, "correctly concluded" that sports-related event contracts are not "swaps," but rather amount to "sports gambling," the NFL said in its brief.

The NFL filed its brief the day after a bipartisan coalition of states made a similar plea to the Supreme Court, asking it to resolve the regulatory dispute over prediction markets.

In its legal filing, the NFL asked the high court to decide whether states or the federal government should regulate prediction markets before the end of the pro football season in January. Any delay will "result in increasing consumer harm and risk to game integrity," the NFL wrote.

Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a federal agency that oversees derivative markets, among other areas. However, at least 10 states have taken legal action against prediction market platforms, alleging that the sports contracts they offer constitute gambling and should be subject to state law.

An NFL source told CBS News that the league has asked the CFTC and prediction markets to adopt safeguards around gambling and insider trading. But neither the agency nor industry players have banned bets that could be susceptible to manipulation or raised the minimum age to bet on prediction markets to 21, the source said, up from the current minimum of 18.

In an email to CBS News, the league source said it is unclear whether the CFTC has the resources or staff to regulate sports betting, a concern echoed by some legal experts.

A Kalshi spokesperson said the company's priority is the integrity of its markets.

"Contrary to the NFL's statements, the CFTC is actively policing sports-related markets, which are now listed on nearly every U.S. commodities exchange," the spokesperson said in an email. "The CFTC's ongoing rulemaking addresses many of the NFL's supposed concerns."

A Polymarket spokesperson told CBS News in an email that the company has built advanced market surveillance tools and is working with the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission to develop a regulatory framework that it believes would be stronger than state laws.

World.title: OpenAI caught Russians and Iranians using ChatGPT for influence campaigns
World.content:
OpenAI caught Russians and Iranians using ChatGPT for influence campaigns

toggle caption i Jeff Chiu/AP

OpenAI said in a blog post on Thursday that it banned Russian and Iranian accounts that were using the company's artificial intelligence tools to help with influence operations in multiple countries. The operatives said they managed to get their false narratives picked up by news outlets, and in once case, prompted a response from a member of the European Parliament, according to internal reports the operations produced using OpenAI's chatbot, ChatGPT.

OpenAI investigated the impact of the different campaigns the accounts mentioned and found that those focused on placing false narratives in established media outlets appeared to have reached a wider audience than campaigns that focused on using fake social media accounts to spread their message.

The Russian operations targeted countries in Latin America and appeared aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and influencing local politics, OpenAI said. The accounts appeared to be mostly using ChatGPT to write reports detailing their work to unspecified higher ups, OpenAI said. The company said one of these reports appeared to describe the widest-reaching influence operation OpenAI has come across so far, because it led to public response from a political figure.

Sponsor Message

In this campaign, the Russian operatives said they impersonated a regional educational authority in Peru and tricked some schools into organizing activities about Ukraine that featured Stepan Bandera. Bandera is a controversial figure, admired by nationalists for leading a drive for Ukrainian independence before and during World War II. He is reviled by others, including in Poland, because his movement sided with the Nazis and killed Poles and Jews. Peruvian outlet Extra reported that one such event did take place at a Peruvian school.

A Polish news report about the school event prompted a far-right Polish member of the European Parliament to suggest banning the entry of people who professed support for Bandera.

"The Russian fake thus both fed on, and fed into, historical tensions between Ukrainians and Poles," OpenAI wrote in its report.

"Russians are constantly engaging in these sorts of active measures," said Darren Linvill, a co-director of Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub who studies online influence operations. "Trying to engage in narrative laundering, creating fake stories, fake persona to either create or spread propaganda that aligns with Russia's worldview and Russia's political agenda."

The Russian internal memos created with ChatGPT also claimed that the operatives ran a fake think tank in Latin America and recruited unwitting researchers to interview experts and compose reports. OpenAI said that effort was similar to a 2020 Russian operation posing as an independent news outlet linked to the late oligarch Yevgeny Prigozhin's Internet Research Agency, which was involved in efforts to influence the 2016 U.S. election.

Sponsor Message

In other instances, OpenAI said, the Russian operatives took credit for events they were not responsible for. The Russians did use AI to generate fake material, OpenAI said, but it was a minority of the workload.

"These Russian underlings were trying to use AI to create a shortcut and do less work in the same way that a lot of us use AI, but in this case it helped get them caught," Linvill said.

While the Russian operatives primarily used AI to update their superiors, Iranian operatives used AI to help them push out content in Persian and English. The campaign mainly focused on the U.S.-Iran war and, to a lesser degree, American politics. OpenAI said the operation's activity "appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign" but that it was unable to identify who that was.

According to OpenAI, Iranian accounts made up seven fake authors to pitch and polish long articles to small media outlets around the world. They published almost 100 articles in this way.

The fake authors published articles in outlets including the progressive U.S. news site Daily Kos and the U.K.-based Middle East Monitor. According to NBC News, the Middle East Monitor published at least 21 articles by four fake authors. The outlet, which didn't respond to a request for comment, has since taken down the author pages.

The Daily Kos wrote in response to NPR's request for comment that its community section, where one of the fake personas posted, is separate from staff reports. Anyone can sign up to post in the community section and posts are "not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication," according to a disclaimer on the site. The community section does have rules for posting, including prohibiting "Pretending to be someone you're not." The posts by the persona are still up.

Sponsor Message

"AI was valuable to them above and beyond just being a shortcut," Linvill said. "It helped them create language that ... looked and felt and read authentic to the point where it was being published by legitimate outlets. And I think that is something that a few years ago, an Iranian operation like this would have struggled a lot more with."

World.title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
World.content:
The long-deployed USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay

toggle caption i Gregory Bull/AP

CORONADO, Calif. — After more than 10 months at sea, thousands of sailors Thursday poured out of the the USS Lincoln on San Diego Bay to thunderous cheers, streaming tears and emotional hugs, marking a homecoming that included new dads who met babies born while they were away on a historic deployment supporting the Iran war.

The reunion followed an emotional rollercoaster for families who described crying and losing sleep after hearing reports of supply shortages and deteriorating mental health among the crew during the deployment that spent a record 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea. Many said they only could communicate with family via the occasional email or rare WhatsApp calls.

Abel Ramirez, 20, was glad to have that all behind him. He walked off the carrier with a big grin, overjoyed that his first deployment was over.

Sponsor Message

"It feels amazing," he said while headed out to search for his parents who traveled from Texas. "There was a certain point when I never thought I would come off."

Cassity Garduque, 14, waved as her mom in her sailor uniform frantically waved back from the top deck after the ship docked at the pier.

"It feels really overwhelming," she said about being seeing her mom again. "She missed most of my seventh grade and my birthday."

She added that she's happy her mom won't be eating ramen almost every day and can celebrate with her now.

toggle caption i Gregory Bull/AP

Capt. Daniel Keeler, the ship's commander, said most of the crew was on their first deployment and that the issues they faced were normal for such a long deployment, adding everyone had access to four meals a day.

"It's a floating city as you can see and at any moment there might be a clogged toilet," he said.

The Navy has downplayed problems on the carrier

The Navy initially downplayed any problems during the deployment, and President Donald Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."

Navy leaders eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the Lincoln on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive.

Sponsor Message

Hegseth told the crew that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

toggle caption i Jae C. Hong/AP

USS Lincoln crew looks forward to family and favorite meals

The Lincoln, which set a record for uninterrupted time at sea, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment during the Iran war and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward, typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

The crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford returned in May from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era. The Lincoln's deployment of 322 days was just shy of that.

Among the first to depart the carrier at the naval base in Coronado were 64 fathers meeting their babies for the first time, the Navy said. With the airwing included, there were 122 new dads, Keeler said.

Waiting for the Lincoln to bring her husband home, sailor Kathy Monterrosa held her 6-month-old daughter, Sarahi, outfitted in a tiny blue and white sailor dress.

"She's our deployment baby," said Monterrosa, of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

It was tough to hear about the ship's conditions while she was pregnant, she said. "I was crying a lot and worried. I wasn't sure if he was OK or not," she said.

When she finally heard from her husband, he told her it was "pretty bad," but now she said she feels blessed to have her family home.

Sailor Steven Rivas beamed as he held is 7-month-old daughter.

Sponsor Message

"I couldn't grasp the reality of it," he said about coming home. He became overwhelmed as they pulled into the bay, "seeing everyone and knowing my family was waiting for me," Rivas said, his voice shaking as his eyes teared up.

toggle caption i Karl Anderson/AP

Alma Solano Velez said her husband gave his family an extensive list of the foods he has been craving over the past 10 months: oxtail, barbecue chicken, broccoli and shrimp empanadas to name a few.

He had told his wife about "the lack of food and showers" on board and was looking forward to seeing their daughter, who turned 4 while he was away, she said.

The carrier left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced for a short time.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Long deployments can tax service members

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed nearly 3,700 combat missions, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

World.title: Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.
World.content:
Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.

My brother took his own life on May 10, 2010. Rarely a day goes by that I don't think of him. But just because I thought about him, it didn't mean I could talk about him. For a long time, I couldn't.

Sometimes when the subject of suicide came up, I would want to — or literally have to — leave wherever I was. Not helpful if you're in the news business.

I've come to realize that I have to talk about it. We have to talk about it.

Why do we have to? Because our silence is not protecting us.

Sponsor Message

Suicide is a public health crisis for the country — but that crisis is becoming acute in the Black community. Black suicide rates are climbing, increasing more than 50% over about the past 10 years according to CDC data. And the suicide rates among Black youth are increasing particularly dramatically. The rate of Black youth suicides by firearms exceeded that of white youth in 2022.

At a time when government-sponsored public health initiatives are retreating from issues that impact different communities differently, we're going there with care, sensitivity and honesty.

I hosted an NPR's Morning Edition live event called Going There: A Matter of Life and Death. It brought together a panel of clinicians, lawmakers and people who have lived with this pain to talk about this epidemic, in front of a live audience who have also experienced it. Speakers include CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor.

It was an attempt to try to find out why this crisis is happening, how it is affecting us, and most importantly, what we can do about it.

Sponsor Message

During the conversation, Super Bowl-winning tight end Vernon Davis shared his struggles with panic attacks and depression.

"I would have these episodes in the game," Davis said, "I would go sit on a bench and breathe hard. I just felt like, for a split second, that I didn't want to be here. I had nothing to live for. It happened so fast, and it was just so sudden."

Davis now says that focusing on his mental health is a daily priority. And, after Davis lost both his brother and sister in quick succession, he started speaking more openly about his experiences with mental health.

"There's people out there who are going through the same thing that I went through," he explained, "they just need to hear that there's someone else out there that is going through the same thing."

Dr. Paul Nestadt is a psychiatrist, medical director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, and a national authority on suicide. He notes that white people still account for the majority of suicide deaths, and the suicide rate has decreased slightly among white Americans. Meanwhile, the rate has gone up among Black Americans. Access to guns accounts for at least part of that increase.

"When that trend in young Black people, especially young Black males, started to go up was also a time when we saw a dramatic increase in firearm ownership in the Black community. That was in 2020, in the context of the pandemic, the murder of George Floyd, and a variety of other things," Nestadt said.

As a result, 2025 survey data shows the lowest rate of self-reported suicide attempts among young Black people in America in years. But, Nestadt said, "the death rate has gone higher than it's ever been. And that just comes down to the fact that when an attempt is made, now with so many more guns in the house, that attempt is fatal."

Sponsor Message

Nestadt emphasized that it is crucial to correct several prevailing myths about suicide: chiefly that only people with long-term mental illnesses are vulnerable and that mentioning that you are concerned that someone might take their own life plants the idea. Neither is true. He says suicide is often an impulsive act, and interrupting that thought can work.

Every panelist brought similar words of wisdom. Among the most important advice:



Reaching out to offer support to loved ones who seem like they might be struggling can be lifesaving.



Free and low-cost resources and treatment options are out there, and are effective.



Remembering those we've lost to suicide as the full people that they were can be healing to those left behind.

There's a lot we can do to support each other and take care of ourselves.

And if you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

World.title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego
World.content:
The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego

The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The Navy initially downplayed problems on the carrier

The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.

Sponsor Message

The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."

The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.

Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Long deployments can tax service members

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

Sponsor Message

The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

World.title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
World.content:
New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture

toggle caption i Ariana Cubillos/AP

NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.

Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.

The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.

"This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."

Sponsor Message

Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.

A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.

The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.

Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.

Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.

Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens

The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.

Sponsor Message

While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.

Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.

Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.

In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito."

"It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations."

Former first lady denied release for medical treatment

Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.

Sponsor Message

They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.

U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.

He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

World.title: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
World.content:
4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space

toggle caption i NASA via Anil Menon

Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.

The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.

Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.

The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.

Sponsor Message

The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day. During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.

Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.

Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13, who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.

During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.

But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.

The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

World.title: White House correspondent April Ryan reflects on reporting while under attack
World.content:
White House correspondent April Ryan reflects on reporting while under attack

Ryan has spent decades pressing presidents for answers. She talks about access, power, race and how asking questions put her in President Trump's crosshairs. Her new book is Notes on a Blacklash. Sponsor Message

World.title: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
World.content:
South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

Sponsor Message

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

Sponsor Message

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.

Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

World.title: Will Ottawa really take Stelco to court? Here's what happened last time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stelco Holdings has days to share a plan to save hundreds of Ontario steel workers from layoffs already underway — or it risks legal action from the Canadian government.

The clock is ticking on what lawyers say is a test of how foreign investors are held to account as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to lure more of them to Canada amid a bitter trade war with the United States.

So, how idle is the threat? And is it likely to save workers' jobs? Here's what we know from the last time the federal government took the U.S. steelmaker to court.

2 decades since Ottawa fought ex-Stelco owner in court

In 2007, Pennsylvania-based U.S. Steel announced a deal to acquire Stelco, then a publicly traded company , for about $1 billion US, and the company was renamed U.S. Steel Canada.

Major foreign investments must benefit the domestic economy, per the Investment Canada Act. So, foreign buyers must give legally binding written commitments — called undertakings — to the federal industry minister to prove the deal provides a "net benefit to Canada."

At the time, U.S. Steel agreed to several such undertakings, including a three-year commitment to maintain Canadian employment levels, and increase steel production in Canada by at least 10 per cent.

However, when the 2008 financial crisis sapped global demand, U.S. Steel closed most of Stelco's Canadian operations and laid off over 1,500 employees.

WATCH | Union says layoffs have begun: Layoffs start at Hamilton Stelco plant, union says | Duration closed caption 7:19 Layoffs at the Stelco steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks, says Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005. Stelco worker Jordan Williams says he received his layoff notice at the end of his shift on Wednesday.

The attorney general of Canada filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel in July 2009.

"As far as the public record shows, it is the only time Ottawa has gone to court over commitments like this," Toronto-based business lawyer Nassira El Hadri told CBC News.

According to a summary of court filings compiled by a lawyer at Toronto-based Torys LLP, Stelco argued the undertakings only required compliance at the end of their three-year term, not before.

Stelco also said that per Industry Canada guidelines, its investors should not be held accountable for factors beyond their control, like the unfolding financial crisis.

WATCH | Stelco worker speaks about his layoff notice: Layoff uncertainty 'a roller-coaster' for Stelco workers | Duration 1:12 Steelworker Jordan Williams describes the frustration he’s feeling after receiving a layoff notice from Stelco. Cleveland-Cliffs — the Ohio-based company that owns Stelco — started issuing individual layoff notices as it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers and idle production at the Hamilton plant.

Last legal battle ended in deal to keep making steel

The attorney general of Canada formally withdrew the lawsuit in late 2011, ending in an out-of-court-settlement before the court could make a judgment.

U.S. Steel agreed to keep production alive in Hamilton and Lake Erie, and to make $50 million in new capital investments by the end of 2015 to modernize its operations. It agreed to new undertakings with Ottawa, but those did not include minimum worker headcount requirements.

But before then, in 2014, U.S. Steel Canada filed for creditor protection, and the American parent company severed ties with its Canadian operations.

In 2016, a New York-based private equity firm acquired the steelmaker. The Stelco name was revived when the company returned to the Toronto Stock Exchange the next year.

The dispute prompted updates to the Investment Canada Act in 2009 and 2012 to make settlement negotiations easier, and strengthen enforcement. The government later raised daily non-compliance fines to $25,000, and tightened reviews for sensitive industries.

What's happening now at Stelco?

Flash forward to 2024, when Ottawa approved Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs' $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal to buy Stelco.

The conditions included a promise to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers, according to a government statement at the time .

Last week, Stelco announced a plan to idle certain production in Hamilton, resulting in up to 500 layoffs company-wide. The union says layoffs are already underway.

WATCH | Layoffs are now underway at Stelco: Stelco layoffs start despite Ottawa's legal threats | Duration closed caption 2:24 Stelco started laying off steelworkers at its Hamilton plant despite government demands that it reveal a jobs-saving plan within five days or face potential legal action.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said the cuts are necessary and justified by the Canada-U.S. trade war, arguing that Stelco's ability to sell steel to the U.S. was an "underlying condition" of the deal.

But in a letter Monday to Stelco president Paul Simon, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave the company five business days to share a job plan, or face legal action.

And on Tuesday, Joly slammed Goncalves's public support of American steel tariffs.

"He's in favour of these U.S. tariffs against steel," she said. "They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure."

Will Stelco fight Ottawa in court again?

El Hadri says the matter is "most likely going to end up in court."

She points out that Joly's letter does not ask Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs for an explanation about why they plan to lay off workers. It states the company's commitments "do not cease to apply simply because business strategy or market conditions have changed."

"It may end up in a settlement as well, but it all depends on the economic conditions, like what's going on inside Stelco," El Hadri told CBC News.

The court has "wide powers" at its disposal, she said, including putting a business up for sale.

"We could end up with new commitments, which is what happened with Stelco in 2009."

Sandy Walker, co-chair of the competition and foreign investment review group at the global law firm Dentons, says it's still possible that Stelco could reverse course on its full layoff plans to avoid going to court.

"That depends on how effective the Canadian government’s threats are," she told CBC News.

"There are many reasons why [it] may not end up in court, but may end up with a variation of its undertakings, or otherwise settling with the Canadian government."

At the same time, Walker says those Industry Canada guidelines on factors beyond a company's control may let Stelco "off the hook" to some extent.

What does this mean for PM's agenda?

Both Walker and El Hadri agree the timing is somewhat awkward, given Ottawa's push for $1 trillion worth of investments across the country over the next five years.

Last month, Carney hosted hundreds of deep-pocketed investors at an investment summit in Toronto in a bid to spur deals, and cut reliance on the United States.

"We are giving a signal to the world that ... you have to respect our rules," El Hadri said.

"It's a difficult balance," Walker said. "The government has got to worry about looking weak."

World.title: B.C. teen rescued from 'Widowmaker' mountain trail says AI isn't to blame
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A B.C. teen making global headlines after being rescued from the side of a mountain says AI is not the reason he became stranded.
