World.title: Juan Manuel Cerúndolo Beats Nicolás Mejía to Set Up Carlos Alcaraz Clash in Shanghai
World.content:
Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerúndolo advanced to the second round of the Shanghai Masters on Thursday with a 6-4, 6-4 victory over Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía, setting up a meeting with world No. 3 Carlos Alcaraz. The 24-year-old Argentine needed just one hour and 22 minutes to get past Mejía, a qualifier ranked No. 119 in the world. Cerúndolo, ranked 55th, recovered from an early deficit and took control of the match with his left-handed serve and consistent baseline play.

He finished with five aces, committed no double faults and won 84% of the points behind his first serve. Cerúndolo converted four of seven break-point opportunities while dropping his own serve twice. The victory was Cerúndolo’s first at the Shanghai Masters after losing in the opening round of his tournament debut last year.

His reward is a considerably tougher assignment against Alcaraz, who enters the tournament as the No. 2 seed and one of the favorites for the title. The Spaniard arrives in Shanghai fresh off winning the Japan Open in Tokyo on Tuesday, defeating Czech player Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7-4), 6-4 in the final.

That victory marked Alcaraz’s first title since returning from a lengthy absence caused by a wrist injury. The 23-year-old has steadily regained his form in recent months and is looking to win the Shanghai Masters for the first time. His best previous result at the tournament was a quarterfinal appearance in 2024.

Saturday’s second-round meeting will be the first official tour-level match between Alcaraz and Cerúndolo, although the two players have faced each other before. They met at the 2021 Next Gen ATP Finals in Milan, where Alcaraz defeated the Argentine 4-0, 4-1, 2-4, 4-3 (7-3) during the group stage. Alcaraz went on to win that tournament, which featured some of the leading young players in men’s tennis.

Cerúndolo has since developed into an established presence on the ATP Tour, with several notable performances against higher-ranked opponents. His biggest victory came at this year’s French Open, where he stunned then-world No. 1 Jannik Sinner in the second round. The Argentine rallied from two sets down to win 3-6, 2-6, 7-5, 6-1, 6-1 after Sinner began struggling with physical problems while leading in the third set. The result ended the Italian’s 30-match winning streak.

Cerúndolo followed that victory with a nearly six-hour win over Spain’s Martín Landaluce to reach the fourth round of a Grand Slam for the first time. Those results added to a career that began attracting international attention in 2021, when Cerúndolo won the Córdoba Open in Argentina as a 19-year-old qualifier making his ATP Tour debut.

Thursday was also a productive day for Argentine tennis in Shanghai. Sebastián Báez recovered from a slow start to defeat American Marcos Giron 1-6, 6-3, 6-4. Thiago Tirante advanced with a 6-4, 6-2 victory over Serbia’s Hamad Medjedovic, while Camilo Ugo Carabelli rallied past qualifier Ilya Simakin 2-6, 6-2, 7-5.

The four victories gave Argentina a strong opening to the ATP Masters 1000 tournament, although Cerúndolo now faces the highest-profile challenge of the group. For Alcaraz, Saturday’s match offers an opportunity to extend his recent winning run. For Cerúndolo, it is another chance to test himself against one of the world’s best players just over four months after producing one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 season.

World.title: Study Counts More Than 557,000 Costa Rican Children in Poverty
World.content:
More than 557,000 children and teenagers in Costa Rica are classified as living in basic or extreme poverty, according to a study released by the National Council of Rectors (Conare), the body that represents the public universities. The study, titled La deuda de Costa Rica con sus niños, niñas y adolescentes (Costa Rica’s Debt to Its Children and Adolescents), was written by Ana Teresa León Sáenz, a psychologist, retired Universidad Nacional (UNA) professor and former executive president of the National Children’s Trust (PANI).

Conare presented the work on Sept. 24 after two years of research. The poverty figure is drawn from 2024 records of Sinirube, the national registry the state uses to identify people who receive or may qualify for social assistance. Of 810,394 minors evaluated in that system, 290,026 were classified in extreme poverty and 267,167 in basic poverty, a combined 68.8%. Another 253,201 were classified as not poor.

The numbers are not a national child poverty rate. León has noted that Costa Rica’s population under 18 is roughly 1.3 million, and because Sinirube records people who are current or potential recipients of state aid, the 557,193 total describes children already identified by the welfare system rather than a representative sample of all minors.

Younger children make up the largest share. The study counts 371,610 poor children between birth and age 12, of whom 200,236 are in extreme poverty and 171,374 in basic poverty. Among adolescents ages 13 to 17, 185,583 are classified as poor, including 89,790 in extreme poverty and 95,793 in basic poverty.

Alajuela and San José hold the largest numbers of poor children ages 12 and under. In Alajuela, more than 50,000 children in that age group fall into extreme poverty and some 35,000 into basic poverty, while in San José both figures are close to 45,000. The sharpest concentrations appear at the local level. In Sarapiquí, 78.1% of registered children and 75% of registered adolescents are in some form of poverty, according to the study.

Puntarenas, Coto Brus, Buenos Aires and Osa are among the areas where more than 30% of households face economic deprivation. In Coto Brus, Buenos Aires, Corredores and Golfito, fewer than half of minors have their material needs met under the UNICEF Child and Adolescent Wellbeing Index used in the research.

Education gaps follow a similar map. All 11 areas in Guanacaste register average schooling below six years, and six of them fall below five years. The study also flags coverage, connectivity and access problems across the Northern Region. León has described poverty as perhaps the most critical factor in the lives of the children studied. She explained that stress, poor nutrition and harmful surroundings associated with poverty can impair brain development, slowing language skills in ways that later show up in school performance.

She also warned that early childhood contains critical periods in which nutrition, stimulation and care are essential, and that opportunities missed then are extremely difficult and costly to recover. In her view, a generation that does not receive that attention and protection now will struggle to be productive later, and families cannot carry the burden without outside support.

The study links the deterioration to budget decisions since the 2018 public finance law, Law 9635, and the fiscal rule it created, arguing that spending limits have cut programs for minors and eliminated some, particularly those focused on prevention. It cites recommendations from the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child urging Costa Rica to protect child-related budget transfers, including a Constitutional Chamber ruling that requires 7% of income tax revenue to be allocated to PANI.

The research also documents pressure on the child protection system. PANI records examined for 2022 include 59,469 cases classified as failure to attend to a child’s integral development and 44,909 classified as neglect, which together accounted for 77.6% of that year’s caseload.

On sexual violence, the study lists 2,109 PANI case files in 2022, 2,607 in 2023 and 1,857 in 2024. The Costa Rican Social Security System (CCSS) separately recorded 11,768 outpatient consultations for sexual abuse of patients under 18 in 2024. The study cautions that the figures come from different administrative records and cannot be added together or read as a count of victims.

Mental health is another concern. Citing the 2018 Third National Youth Survey, the study reports that 8.6% of respondents ages 15 to 17 said they had wanted to end their lives and 4.8% said they had attempted to do so.

All of this is unfolding as Costa Rica’s child population shrinks. Minors fell from about 33% of the national population in 2012 to roughly 25% in 2023, a trend that has left Costa Rica facing a future with far fewer children. The study argues that a smaller cohort does not reduce the need for services and should instead be treated as a chance to strengthen them.

Among its proposals for early childhood are “Cajas Cuna,” baby boxes paired with parenting education for mothers, and “Bebetecas,” mobile services that teach positive parenting to families with children under 4. It also recommends mobile units running parenting academies, early intervention centers in high-need communities and wider coverage of the national childcare network for children up to age 12.

For adolescents, the study proposes clubs that combine tutoring, sports, arts and psychological care, along with more public spaces for recreation. It calls for an evaluation of whether Avancemos, the state’s cash transfer for secondary students, is keeping young people in school and whether payment amounts meet family needs.

The study further recommends strengthening PANI by reviving its children’s observatory, creating a unit to monitor programs and expanding its regional and cantonal presence, as well as giving the National Council for Children and Adolescents greater capacity. Rather than a single national plan, it sets out three-year investment estimates and projected beneficiaries for each province.

Conare President Jorge Herrera Murillo said public universities have a responsibility that goes beyond training professionals and includes producing evidence on the main challenges. He said the study offers a clearer view of the conditions in which Costa Rica’s children live and should inform decisions aimed at guaranteeing their rights.

León wrote that she hopes communities, local development associations, municipalities, institutions and authorities in all three branches of government will weigh what she calls a growing debt to the children and make the decisions within their reach to change the course of thousands of young lives.

World.title: Booking a Red Taxi on Uber in Costa Rica Can Cost 2.5 Times More
World.content:
If you open Uber in Costa Rica and tap the red taxi option, check the price before you confirm. On a longer ride, it can cost you two and a half times what the same trip costs on UberX. The gap showed up in side-by-side fare checks by a local news crew this week. A ride from Alajuela’s central park to the entrance of Poás Volcano, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) and roughly 50 minutes, came to ₡10,590 (about $23) on UberX. The same trip by red taxi through the app cost ₡26,686 (about $58).

That is a difference of roughly ₡16,100, or about $35, for one ride. Short trips show a smaller gap in money, but not in proportion. A 3-kilometer (1.9-mile) ride from the National Theater to the University of Costa Rica, about 10 minutes, cost ₡1,890 (about $4) on UberX and ₡3,655 (about $8) by red taxi. That is close to double.

The reason is the meter. Red taxis booked through the app still have to charge the official taxi fare, the same rate you would pay if you flagged one down on the street. The app shows you an estimate before you book, but the final charge follows that official fare, and UberX drivers are not bound by it.

Laura Santillán, Uber’s manager for Central America, said Uber Taxi fares are the same ones taxis charge on the street, so riders pay what they would for a cab hailed at the curb. Uber says about 300 red taxi drivers have signed up. Red taxis became bookable through Uber only recently, and not everyone in the taxi sector is on board. Rubén Vargas of the Costa Rican Taxi Drivers Union said the price comparison is unfair.

Vargas said licensed taxi drivers pay for vehicle inspections, insurance, a special operating license and taxes. He argued that platform drivers pay no taxes and charge prices too low to make a living on.

Before you confirm a ride, compare the UberX and Uber Taxi estimates. On a short hop across San José, the red taxi costs you a few extra dollars. On a long trip out of the city, the gap grows fast. If you get around Costa Rica without a car, that difference adds up over a month of rides.

The rules could change. A bill in the Legislative Assembly would bring ride-hailing platforms under state regulation in a free-market model. Companies would have to set up locally and pay taxes. Under the bill, drivers and vehicles would have to be registered with the road safety council, carry insurance and pass technical inspection. Drivers would also need to be registered with the tax authority and the social security system.

Until lawmakers decide, the fare you pay depends on which button you press. The estimate is on the screen before every ride.

World.title: US Flags Costa Rica Again Over Illegal and Unreported Fishing Concerns
World.content:
Costa Rica is once again under scrutiny from the United States over shortcomings in the monitoring of its fishing fleet, less than three years after receiving a positive certification for correcting earlier problems. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) identified Costa Rica for illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing in its 2026 Report to Congress on Improving International Fisheries Management.

Costa Rica was one of six countries identified in the latest report, alongside Grenada, Mexico, Morocco, China and Russia. The designation does not mean that the United States has imposed sanctions on Costa Rica or concluded that all Costa Rican fishing activity is illegal. Instead, the finding begins a consultation period during which Costa Rica will have an opportunity to address the problems identified by U.S. authorities before NOAA makes a future certification decision.

At the center of the U.S. concerns is Costa Rica’s failure to meet international requirements for independent observers aboard larger longline fishing boats. NOAA said Costa Rica failed to ensure the required observer coverage during 2022, 2023 and 2024 for longline vessels operating in waters managed by the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission.

Under the applicable rules, at least 5% of fishing activity by longline vessels longer than 20 meters must be monitored by scientific observers. According to NOAA, Costa Rica had not implemented a national onboard observer program by the end of 2024 and had no observer coverage for its longline fleet operating in the commission’s convention area.

Costa Rica also had not provided required summary reports or operational data concerning the observer program for at least five years. Costa Rica told the commission in July 2024 that it had 21 longline vessels measuring more than 20 meters, although only eight had carried out fishing operations during the previous year.

Authorities said difficulties establishing an observer program included the relatively small size of some vessels, continuous work schedules and Costa Rican labor rules governing working hours. NOAA acknowledged that Costa Rica has since taken steps toward addressing the issue.

Information supplied to U.S. and international fisheries authorities in June 2025 said Costa Rica was developing a pilot program combining human observers and electronic monitoring. Costa Rica said it expected that system to allow it to reach the required 5% monitoring level. Costa Rica’s National Fisheries and Aquaculture Development Plan for 2025-2030 also calls for the creation of an onboard observer program.

However, the U.S. report said those efforts had not yet resolved the deficiencies that led to the new identification. NOAA also raised concerns about gaps in fishing data. The agency said Costa Rica does not appear to have reported catches of relevant species to the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission for any year after 2020, despite more than 150 Costa Rican-flagged longline boats appearing on the commission’s vessel registry.

The lack of independent observers also means there may be limited information about accidental catches of protected species, including sea turtles. Scientific observers can record the species caught, fishing locations, the amount of fishing effort and interactions with marine wildlife, providing information that fisheries managers cannot obtain solely from reports submitted by vessel operators.

The latest finding comes after Costa Rica had previously appeared to make progress on the same broader issue. NOAA identified Costa Rica in its 2021 report over problems with fisheries management and the submission of required information to international fisheries organizations.

Two years later, the United States gave Costa Rica a positive certification after determining that Costa Rica had taken corrective steps. That 2023 certification was based in part on Costa Rica presenting plans to establish a national onboard observer program. The new 2026 identification concerns more recent activity and covers the 2022-2024 period.

That distinction means Costa Rica did not lose or reverse the earlier certification. Instead, the United States has opened a new evaluation cycle based on subsequent monitoring failures. NOAA said it will now hold consultations with Costa Rican authorities. When the United States makes its next certification decision, it will consider whether Costa Rica has implemented its observer program, achieved the required monitoring coverage aboard larger longline boats and submitted the required reports.

A negative certification could eventually result in restrictions on access to U.S. ports for some Costa Rican fishing boats and potentially affect imports of certain seafood products. Costa Rica is not currently subject to those sanctions. For now, Costa Rica remains in the consultation stage, giving authorities an opportunity to demonstrate that the monitoring and reporting problems identified by NOAA have been corrected.

The 2026 finding is significant for Costa Rica that promotes marine conservation as an important part of its environmental identity and has expanded protection of large areas of its Pacific waters in recent years. It also places renewed attention on how Costa Rica monitors commercial fishing outside its protected areas and whether regulators have enough independent information to determine what boats are catching at sea.

NOAA says the results of its consultations with Costa Rica and the other countries identified in the 2026 report will be announced in a future Report to Congress.

World.title: Shain Young granted $6,000 bail after nearly four months on remand for alleged sexual assault of 12-year-old girl
World.content:
Shain Young granted $6,000 bail after nearly four months on remand for alleged sexual assault of 12-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 33-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl during a family swimming trip has been released on bail after spending nearly four months on remand at the Belize Central Prison.

Shain Young, a resident of May Flower Street, appeared before a magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday, October 7, where he was granted bail of $6,000, with two sureties of $3,000 each, subject to conditions imposed by the court.

Young met bail later that afternoon and is scheduled to return to court on October 30, 2026.

He was initially arraigned on June 9, 2026, on a single charge of assault of a child by penetration. No plea was taken at the time, and he was remanded after the prosecution strongly objected to bail.

The charge stems from an alleged incident on May 31, 2026, when Young accompanied several family members, including the 12-year-old complainant, on a swimming trip to a pond in the Blackberry Ridge Estate area.

According to police reports, the child alleged that Young, who was known to her family, inappropriately touched and sexually assaulted her while they were in the water.

During his initial arraignment before Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison, prosecutor Sergeant Christopher Smith objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the allegation and concerns about possible interference with the complainant, given Young’s familiarity with the family.

Those objections were upheld, resulting in Young’s remand to prison until his release on bail this week.

The criminal proceedings against Young remain ongoing, and he has not been convicted of the alleged offence.

World.title: Sentencing delayed again for two men who pleaded guilty in 2018 killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez
World.content:
Sentencing delayed again for two men who pleaded guilty in 2018 killing of police constable Osbourne Martinez

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Nearly four years after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the killing of Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, Tyrique Myles and Glen Lopez remain behind bars awaiting sentencing after another adjournment in the High Court on Thursday.

The two men appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim on October 8, but sentencing could not proceed because the agreed facts and formal plea agreement had not yet been filed with the court.

Justice Pilgrim gave the parties until Friday, October 9, to submit the necessary documents and adjourned the sentencing proceedings to October 27, 2026.

Both men were represented in court by attorney Norman Rodriguez.

Myles and Lopez pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter in November 2022 before then-High Court Justice Ricardo O’Neil Sandcroft. However, their sentencing has remained outstanding for almost four years.

The case stems from the November 2, 2018 murder of 27-year-old Police Constable Osbourne Martinez, who was fatally shot while responding to an armed robbery at the Belcove Hotel on Regent Street West in downtown Belize City.

Martinez and other officers responded to reports of an armed robbery involving three men. During the confrontation, Martinez was shot and later died while undergoing treatment at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital.

Myles, Lopez and Rayford Mejia were subsequently arrested and jointly charged with murder. While Myles and Lopez eventually pleaded guilty to manslaughter, Mejia maintained his innocence and proceeded to trial.

In May 2023, Justice Sandcroft found Mejia guilty of murder, determining that the prosecution had proven his involvement in the killing.

The latest adjournment means Myles and Lopez must remain in custody for another 19 days before their sentencing proceedings are scheduled to resume, nearly eight years after Martinez was killed in the line of duty.

World.title: Anthony Carballo Jr. faces life imprisonment with minimum 20 years before parole if he pleads guilty to murder
World.content:
Anthony Carballo Jr. faces life imprisonment with minimum 20 years before parole if he pleads guilty to murder

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Anthony Carballo Jr., one of two men accused of the 2023 murder of Sylvian Nigel Swift in Belize City, has been informed that he could face life imprisonment with a minimum of 20 years before becoming eligible for parole if he chooses to plead guilty.

The sentencing indication was delivered on Thursday, October 8, by High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim, following a request made by Carballo Jr. through his attorney, Nazira Myles-Espat, during a case management conference on September 29.

Justice Pilgrim considered the circumstances of the murder, agreed facts, sentencing guidelines, and relevant aggravating and mitigating factors before arriving at the proposed sentence.

Carballo Jr. has until Friday, October 23, 2026, to inform the court whether he will accept the sentencing indication and enter a guilty plea. No guilty plea has been entered at this stage.

Meanwhile, his co-accused, Christopher Pitts Jr., continues to maintain his innocence and intends to proceed with a trial before a judge sitting without a jury.

The two men are charged jointly with the murder of Swift, who was fatally shot on Antelope Street on April 27, 2023. Reports at the time indicated that Swift was standing near his home shortly before 8 p.m. when two men riding a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the arm and neck. Police subsequently pursued the suspects and recovered a motorcycle and a 9mm firearm.

Carballo Jr. was initially arraigned on May 2, 2023, followed by Pitts Jr. on May 8. Both men were jointly indicted for murder before the High Court in March 2025.

The case is expected to return to court on October 23, when Carballo Jr. must indicate whether he intends to plead guilty or proceed to trial.

World.title: UB hosts AI discussion with renowned Belizean Mathematician Dr. Arlie Petters
World.content:
UB hosts AI discussion with renowned Belizean Mathematician Dr. Arlie Petters

By Zoila Palma: The University of Belize (UB) welcomed internationally renowned Belizean mathematical physicist and New York University Abu Dhabi Provost, Dr. Arlie Petters, for a panel discussion on artificial intelligence (AI) and higher education on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at the UB Conference Center.

The discussion explored the implications of AI for teaching and learning, as well as the opportunities and challenges it presents for the future of universities. UB faculty and staff, students and representatives of Belmopan Comprehensive School were invited to participate in the timely conversation.

UB’s President, Vice President for Academic Affairs and guests from Tuskegee University also attended the discussion. Dr. Petters, who is internationally recognized for his pioneering contributions to the mathematical study of gravitational lensing, continues to represent Belize through his achievements in science and education.

UB also recognized the contributions of IT lecturer David Garcia and Faculty of Management and Social Sciences lecturer Dr. Yasmine Andrews, who shared their perspectives during the panel.

World.title: Skiff stolen from Marina in Ladyville Village
World.content:
Skiff stolen from Marina in Ladyville Village

By Zoila Palma: A 43-foot fiberglass skiff was reported stolen from the Rusty Anchor Marina on Yellow Snapper Drive in Ladyville Village, Belize District, during the early hours of Wednesday, October 7, 2026.

The vessel, named OCEANICA, has a white hull with green stripes, a blue bottom and a cabin. It is equipped with two 200-horsepower Yamaha outboard engines and is registered as BZ-0428.

Police are asking the public to be on the lookout for the vessel and to report any information about its whereabouts.

Anyone with information can contact Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 App, or report to the nearest police station.

World.title: Minister Chebat says his approach will be of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service
World.content:
Minister Chebat says his approach will be of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service

By Zoila Palma: Today, Minister Michel Chebat issued a statement extended gratitude to Prime Minister John Briceno for the confidence entrusted to serve as Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports.

“I accept these responsibilities with a clear understanding of their importance to the security, stability and continued development of our nation. These portfolios touch directly on the safety of our citizens, the strength of our institutions, the resilience of our economy and Belize’s ability to meet both present and emerging challenges.

At the heart of our national security are the men and women who serve our country every day. I look forward to working closely with the Belize Defence Force, the Belize Police Department, the Coast Guard, our border and security personnel, and all those who dedicate themselves to protecting our people and our sovereignty,” Chebat said.

Chebat added that National security, however, does not stop at our borders. The challenges facing Belize—from transnational crime and maritime security to trafficking, cyber threats, disaster preparedness and energy security—require strong cooperation with our neighbors and trusted international partners.

“I therefore look forward to strengthening Belize’s relationships with our regional counterparts in Central America and the Caribbean, as well as with our longstanding security and development partners. Cooperation, intelligence sharing, training and mutual respect will remain essential to keeping Belize and our wider region safe.

Our ports and energy infrastructure are equally important to our national security and economic future. I intend to work closely with the professionals, regulators, private-sector stakeholders and communities involved in these sectors to ensure that they are secure, efficient, resilient and positioned to support Belize’s long-term development,” Chebat explained.

Chebat says that his approach will be one of partnership, professionalism, accountability and service.

Chebat pledged to engage constructively with stakeholders, and to build upon the important work already being done.

Minister Chebat says he plans to meet with the leadership and personnel across the respective portfolios, reviewing key priorities and gaining a full appreciation of both the challenges and opportunities.

World.title: Minister of Agriculture eyes Wambugu Apple research for local production
World.content:
Minister of Agriculture eyes Wambugu Apple research for local production

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Agriculture Rodwell Ferguson visited Jamaica last week to explore the potential of cultivating Wambugu apples in Belize.

Minister Ferguson also visited the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) in Jamaica to examine research into the tropical fruit.

Ferguson believes the research could provide a blueprint for Caribbean countries seeking to diversify agricultural production and strengthen food security.

During his October 1 visit to CASE, Ferguson inspected the Wambugu apple and expressed interest in the possibility of producing apples in tropical climates, the Jamaica Observer reports.

He noted that apples are traditionally associated with colder regions and are largely imported into Belize from countries such as the United States and Canada.

Ferguson said growing apples locally could reduce reliance on imports while creating new opportunities for farmers and agricultural businesses. He also called for greater investment in agricultural research, pointing to Brazil as an example of how innovation and research can help countries achieve food self-sufficiency while expanding their agricultural exports.

The minister was accompanied during the visit by Senior Advisor Hugh O’Brien, Latoya Panton, managing director of Summit Apple Orchards and My Jamaican Food Forest, which imports and distributes Wambugu apples from Kenya to Jamaica and other Caribbean markets.

Panton said the variety has been performing well in Jamaica, with farmers and backyard gardeners successfully cultivating the fruit, and expressed hope that production can eventually be scaled up to commercial levels across the Caribbean.

World.title: International News: Maduro and wife face new US charges over alleged torture
World.content:
International News: Maduro and wife face new US charges over alleged torture

By Zoila Palma: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been charged by U.S. prosecutors with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding new allegations to the drug trafficking case they already face.

A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court details alleged torture involving nine people, including three U.S. citizens, Reuters report.

Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured in Caracas on January 3 during a U.S. military operation and taken to New York to face drug-related charges. Prosecutors allege that thousands of Venezuelans were threatened, arrested, tortured or killed by state forces between 1999 and 2025, with several of the alleged incidents occurring during periods of political unrest.

According to the indictment, Maduro allegedly ordered the 2013 arrest of a Venezuelan military officer suspected of plotting a coup, who prosecutors say was subsequently subjected to electric shocks and other forms of abuse. Prosecutors also allege that a U.S. citizen detained in Venezuela in 2022 was beaten and subjected to electric shocks after being accused of plotting to assassinate Maduro.

Both Maduro and Flores deny the new allegations. Maduro’s attorney said the former president looks forward to his day in court, while Flores’ lawyers also rejected the charges.

World.title: Jamaica hosts first Caribbean staging of OPANAL nuclear disarmament course
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Senator the Honourable Kamina Johnson Smith (front row, centre), shares a photograph with Permanent Secretary, Ambassador Sheila Sealy Monteith (front row, second right), Ambassador Shorna-Kay Richards (front row, second left), other senior Ministry officials, course facilitators and participants at the opening of the 15th OPANAL Course on Nuclear Disarmament and Non-Proliferation. The opening ceremony took place at the Ministry’s headquarters in Kingston on October 7, 2026.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica is hosting the 15th edition of the Agency for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean (OPANAL) Course on Nuclear Disarmament and Non-Proliferation from October 7 to 9, marking the first time the programme is being held in the Caribbean.

The three-day course, organised by the Government of Jamaica in collaboration with OPANAL, is being hosted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.

According to a release, the programme was officially opened with remarks from Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Senator Kamina Johnson Smith, and a video message from OPANAL Secretary-General, Ambassador Juan Carlos Ojeda Viglione.

The initiative underscores Jamaica’s commitment to advancing nuclear disarmament education, strengthening regional cooperation and increasing the participation of Caribbean countries in international discussions on nuclear non-proliferation.

It also provides a platform for diplomats, government officials and other professionals to deepen their understanding of nuclear disarmament issues while exchanging knowledge and experiences.

Throughout the course, participants will examine the Treaty of Tlatelolco, which established Latin America and the Caribbean as a nuclear-weapon-free zone, alongside key aspects of the international nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation framework.

Discussions will also explore the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and the importance of gender and youth participation in global disarmament efforts.

The programme features contributions from Jamaican experts representing the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, the International Centre for Environmental and Nuclear Sciences (ICENS) and the Earthquake Unit at the University of the West Indies.

Specialised sessions will also be delivered by the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean (UNLIREC) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

As part of the programme, participants will visit ICENS to gain first-hand insight into how nuclear science and technology are being used for peaceful purposes in Jamaica.

The course forms part of OPANAL’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the technical knowledge and capacity of professionals across its member states, particularly in matters relating to nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.

In hosting the event, Jamaica and OPANAL have reaffirmed their commitment to the full implementation of the Treaty of Tlatelolco and to promoting greater regional collaboration in nuclear disarmament education.

The Kingston staging is also expected to strengthen cooperation between Jamaica and OPANAL while supporting broader international efforts to achieve a world free of nuclear weapons.

World.title: No connection between JLP councillor and Brown’s Town Community College, says witness
World.content:
Kim Brown Lawrence (Photo: Facebook/Kim Brown Lawrence)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Principal of Brown’s Town Community College, Claudeth Haughton testified Wednesday that the school had never hired or had any formal relationship with Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) councillor Kim Brown Lawrence.

Haughton was called by the prosecution at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court to give evidence in the $25 million fraud case of Brown-Lawrence, former Education Minister Ruel Reid, former head of the Caribbean Maritime University Fritz Pinnock and Reid’s wife and daughter, Sharen and Sharelle Reid.

Haughton shared information on the operations of the school, with the prosecution focusing specifically on whether lunches were provided for certain students engaged in the nine-month-long Customer Engagement Operation Training programme.

The principal, who has served in the capacity for 11 years, since 2015, addressed the period of time from 2017 to 2019.

The prosecution asked a series of questions, including whether during the period the school offered the course alongside a Joseph Martin, or engaged him to provide meals. The prosecution also asked if Kim Brown Lawrence, who is the councillor for the Brown’s Town Division, was engaged to provide meals for the Brown’s Town Community College students, in general or those enrolled in the programme, to which the witness repeatedly responded “No.”

She added, “We do not provide meals for students”.

When asked by Justice Sanchia Burrell if this meant the school did not undertake the expense, Haughton responded, “Yes, your honour.”

The prosecution also asked how students would have obtained meals, to which she responded that students were at liberty to purchase meals from a restaurateur which she identified as operated by a Carol Brown, who rented the canteen on the college’s main campus in Brown’s Town to provide meals to students, staff and visitors.

Similarly, the witness was asked if the school had ever engaged Optimum Customer Service Consultancy in the Customer Engagement Operation Training programme to which she responded it had not.

While she indicated she knew Kim Brown Lawrence, who was introduced to her only as ‘Kim’ on one other occasion, Haughton indicated that neither she nor any of the other two parties mentioned during questioning by the prosecution, had been contracted by the school for any reason during the period.

Haughton admitted that there were certain occasions where food would be provided for students, such as honour roll events, and that the restaurateur on campus would’ve been contracted during that period to prepare refreshments.

During cross examination, Brown Lawrence’s attorney Senior Smith asked whether it was the principal’s impression, based on questions asked by the prosecution, that his client had said she was a supplier of food for Brown’s Town Community College or its students, to which an objection was raised by the prosecution.

Burrell allowed the question to be posed, and the witness indicated she had not formed any impression based on the questions.

Haughton told Senior Smith that while she was familiar with Brown’s Town in general and Brown’s Plaza, she was not familiar with any restaurants operated by Kim Brown Lawrence and her husband at said plaza.

She also said that the college has allowed in the past both major political parties to host events, but indicated that any catering done would have been handled by the parties themselves.

Under further cross-examination by Senior Smith on whether Kim Brown Lawrence had used the premises of the college for a Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) divisional meeting in early 2018, Haughton said “I cannot confirm.”

Upon further questioning from Senior Smith, who queried whether she was “not saying it did not happen”, the witness repeated: “I cannot confirm that, sir.”

The principal also maintained that she had never been shown any statement purported to be that of Kim Brown Lawrence by police.

The principal confirmed that she had been visited by a cop on April 9, 2019, after which she gathered certain documents relating to the registration of students in the programme and indicated those documents would have been prepared by the bursars office.

Under cross-examination, she indicated that the records were made by the school’s then bursar, Delroy Palmer, but said that Palmer would not necessarily have been the first point of contact for programmes and events entered into at Brown’s Town.

Rather, that would have been handled by the vice principal if the query was academic or the requisite financial professionals.

The trial continues on Monday, at 10:00 am, where additional witnesses are expected to be called.

— Dana Malcolm

World.title: Rent row retreat
World.content:
The Digicel headquarters building in downtown Kingston where the Government has leased space for the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority. (Photo: Observer file)

PRIME Minister Dr Andrew Holness has announced that the Government will initially limit the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) to one floor of the Digicel building, cutting the amount of office space originally planned for the agency following public outrage over the roughly $115-million annual rental cost of its headquarters.

But in an immediate response to the Jamaica Observer on Wednesday, Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson rejected the Government’s decision, saying it did not go far enough.

“My view is that it’s not good enough. I think the lease must be cancelled fully and the Government must find existing office space. The Government has hundreds of thousands of square feet of office space around the country. A lot of it is not being fully utilised and they must use space that exists instead of renting space. There’s no justification for that in this climate,” Robinson said.

He also dismissed the Government’s argument that NaRRA needs a disaster-resilient building to carry out its work, questioning whether that requirement falls within the authority’s mandate.

“Jamaica is in the worst fiscal position we have been in for about 10 years. We are $31 billion below budget. Our borrowing is almost $70 billion more than projected. There are people who are living in Westmoreland, St Elizabeth, and St James and they’re under tarpaulin, and we’re going to spend their money to lease an office and we don’t even reach the cost of NaRRA in terms of staff and all of that. Madness!” he said.

Holness, on Wednesday, said the move is intended to reduce the immediate cost of establishing NaRRA, while allowing the authority to begin its work with a smaller operation.

“Instead of doing the two floors where you would roll out the organisation as quickly as you can, we’ll start with one floor, and people there will have to double up and work fast and earn the credit of the trust,” Holness said during an Office of the Prime Minister retreat at Terra Nova hotel in St Andrew.

The decision follows public backlash over the cost of the five-year lease for NaRRA’s proposed headquarters at 14 Ocean Boulevard in downtown Kingston. The authority announced on Monday that the lease was based on a rate of US$26 per square foot, with an annual cost of US$725,972, equivalent to about $115 million.

The controversy has unfolded as thousands of Jamaicans remain in need of assistance following Hurricane Melissa — which demolished large sections of western Jamaica last October — including people awaiting roof grants and others still without shelter.

Holness said he understood why the cost of the lease had caused concern, particularly when placed alongside the outstanding needs of hurricane victims.

“The announcement of the lease is understandably met with concern. Because it could appear as if the Government is giving expenditure priority to the establishment of NaRRA versus paying the grants and taking care of persons who have not yet received any benefits from the Government or are now currently without shelter,” he said.

Holness maintained, however, that the decision to use the Digicel building was not based on comfort or luxury, but on the need for NaRRA to continue functioning during a disaster.

He said the authority, which is responsible for supporting Jamaica’s reconstruction and resilience efforts, needs headquarters that can withstand hurricanes and earthquakes, remain operational after a disaster, and accommodate its various functions in one location.

He said the Digicel building was originally designed for a utility company and was therefore built to support a high level of operational continuity.

Holness also defended the cost of the lease.

“The price of the building, you know, that is a market reality. When you look at where it fell in terms of the range, it’s average. In fact, before NaRRA could have engaged in the lease, my understanding is that it would have had to be reviewed by the National Land Agency,” he said.

He added that while he believed there could have been further negotiations, the Government ultimately had to reach an agreement because NaRRA needed to begin operating.

The prime minister said the greater concern now was not simply the rental cost, but the effect the controversy could have on public confidence in the new authority.

“I spent a lot of time this morning going through it with [NaRRA CEO] Ambassador [Antony] Anderson and the team, and we have decided to seek a review of the lease with the leasing company to revise the lease, and to also scale the staging of NaRRA,” Holness said.

He shared the Government had initially intended to move quickly with a full launch so that NaRRA could begin delivering projects as soon as possible. However, he said the controversy over the cost of the headquarters could become a distraction and weaken public support for the authority.

Meanwhile, Information Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon, speaking at the post-Cabinet press briefing, also on Wednesday, confirmed that the Government had instructed NaRRA to reduce the amount of space it will use.

She said the change could also mean that the authority hires fewer people at the start and takes longer to reach its intended level of operations.

“Having listened to the sentiments of Jamaicans, there would have been meetings between yesterday and this morning in terms of how to move forward. So the plan is wherever NaRRA is, it will be using less space. Right now it’s looking like it will still be in that same building, but scaling down the scope and the size of space that will be used,” she said.

Morris Dixon also addressed questions about why NaRRA could not use other Government space, including the building previously occupied by the Ministry of Legal and Constitutional Affairs on Fairway Avenue in St Andrew.

She said that the ministry had since been merged with the Ministry of Justice and that the former office space was no longer being used because of problems with the building.

“They had to come out of the lease for that specific space that you’re speaking to, and from my checks this morning, it had to do with issues of leaking in the building, and also significant electrical problems in the building,” Morris Dixon explained.

“So that staff is actually now being housed in a gym in the offices of the Ministry of Justice. So I always say you have to get your information from credible sources. This morning, I had to reach out to the Ministry of Justice to get an understanding of that because I saw that on social media. But that team is no longer in that building because that building was not suitable, even for the team that was there,” she added.

Morris Dixon also said original space requirements for NaRRA were based on an expected workforce of between 100 and 120 employees, along with engineers and consultants who would periodically come to Jamaica as part of reconstruction efforts.

For now, Holness said the Government’s priority was to reduce the immediate cost while ensuring that NaRRA could still begin its work.

“So the public can be assured that we are not wasting your funds. We hear what you say. We will cut it back. It will have an impact on how we will be able to deliver the things you actually want. But we understand that,” he said.

World.title: Enough of the absences
World.content:
PINNOCK... former head of Caribbean Maritime University

Clearly frustrated by disruptions caused by the repeated absence of a defence attorney, Justice Sanchia Burrell on Wednesday told co-accused Fritz Pinnock that he may have to cross-examine a witness himself if no legal representation is present for him when the delay-plagued Ruel Reid fraud trial resumes next Monday.

“I’m expecting that counsel will be here and that you will be assisted or represented in so far as proceedings are concerned. It may, however, be that you will have to apply those doctoral muscles and ask questions in cross-examination,” Burrell told Pinnock, former head of Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

Pinnock was in the dock alongside his co-accused — Reid, the former education minister; his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle Reid; as well as Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence (Jamaica Labour Party, Brown’s Town Division).

The five are before the Half-Way-Tree Parish Court in the high-profile $25-million trial.

The judge’s comments followed the departure of a witness, who was placed on hold for the possibility of cross-examination by Pinnock’s attorney Hugh Wildman.

It was highlighted that at least two witnesses have now been deferred for cross-examination by the lawyer.

Burrell, in fielding the Crown’s concerns about the arrangement, maintained that the court could not defer every witness, noting that it impacts how the evidence flows and how the court is organised.

While she impressed upon Pinnock that she would be present to assist him, if necessary, reminding him that she is an independent arbiter, the judge made it clear she expected an attorney to be present to give him the representation he deserved.

“If not, Mr Pinnock, please come prepared to type or write and prepare cross-examination,” she said.

The directive followed statements made by Justice Burrell Wednesday morning about the way in which Wildman was communicating his absences to the court. She described it as piecemeal, disjointed communication that was unhelpful at best.

The trial had resumed Wednesday morning with one attorney, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Reid’s daughter Sharelle, present via Zoom. Oswest Senior-Smith, who represents Brown Lawrence, also joined late during the trial via Zoom.

Chuck briefed Burrell on the absences of several others, including Linda Wright, who represents Reid; Shannen Clarke, who represents Reid’s wife, Sharen; and Wildman, who had asked Chuck the day before to hold for him in the matter.

When she indicated that she was unable, she said Wildman had advised that he would ask another attorney to hold in his stead; but no one turned up.

Chuck went on to share that Wildman had indicated that he could also have challenges with being present next week as he was given time off from the Supreme Court to deal with the arrangements for his mother’s funeral.

Justice Burrell, acknowledging the sensitivity of the matter, extended condolence to Wildman’s family. However, she queried why this had not been communicated before.

“I don’t take lightly that Mr Wildman is making funeral arrangements for his mother, and my condolences go out to him and his family, but early information sharing makes a huge difference,” she maintained.

“I have to be very sensitive because all of us who are here either have a mother or had a mother at some point …but I am not understanding the lack of communication; the lack of communication is very unhelpful,” the judge said.

Emphasising that the case impacts four other accused, Burrell said Wildman and Pinnock are not entitled to an infinite supply of the court’s resources.

The judge’s comments come on the one-year anniversary of the official start of the trial, which has been plagued with scheduling challenges.

“It cannot be that Mr Wildman avoids appropriate and adequate communication and expects to get what he asks for,” she said.

“How can the rights of four other people be expected to continuously and infinitely, at this point in time, … be expected to yield to Mr Wildman’s failure — I am using the word failure — to organise himself?”

The judge impressed upon the court her sympathies for Wildman, but also highlighted that the attorney had secured time off from the Supreme Court, not the Parish Court, making it likely he had not intended to be present in the trial anyway, and that prior communication or arrangements should have been made, allowing the Parish Court to arrange itself accordingly.

“It should not have to be said, but counsel should only take on a workload that their chambers can support,” Burrell said.

The Crown expects to call more than 90 witnesses in the case and Burrell maintained that the witnesses are real people with lives of their own which must also be considered.

Wednesday’s witness, Brown’s Town Community College Principal Claudeth Haughton, shared information on the operations of the school, with the prosecution focusing specifically on whether lunches were provided for certain students.

The principal, who has served in the capacity since 2015, addressed the period of time from 2017 to 2019.

She told the court that the school has a number of courses, including customer engagement operation training.

Questions from the prosecution surrounded whether food was ever provided for the students of this course by the school, to which Haughton responded, “No.”

The prosecution also asked how students would have obtained meals.

The principal responded that students were at liberty to purchase meals from a restaurant, which she identified as operated by a Carol Brown, who rented the canteen on the college’s main campus in Brown’s Town to provide meals to students, staff, and visitors.

The principal confirmed that she had been visited by a police officer on April 9, 2019, after which she gathered certain documents relating to the registration of students in the programme.

While she indicated she knew Kim Brown Lawrence, who was introduced to her only as Kim at the time, Haughton confirmed that the community college had no relationship with either Kim Brown Lawrence, an individual cited as Joseph Martin, or Optimal Customer Service Consultancy.

She indicated that the college had not contracted any of these people to provide meals for the students or for any other purpose during the period 2017 to 2019.

Haughton admitted that there were certain occasions, such as honour roll events, when food would be provided for students and that the restaurateur on campus would’ve been contracted during that period to prepare refreshments.

Senior Smith, who represents Brown Lawrence, during cross-examination, asked whether it was the principal’s impression, based on questions asked by the prosecution, that his client had said she was a supplier of food for Brown’s Town Community College or its students.

The question prompted an objection by the prosecution.

But Justice Burrell allowed the question, and the witness indicated she had not formed any impression based on the questions.

Haughton told Senior Smith that while she was familiar with Brown’s Town in general and Brown’s Plaza, she was not familiar with any restaurants operated by Kim Brown Lawrence and her husband at said plaza.

She also confirmed that the college has, in the past, allowed both major political parties to host events, but indicated that any catering done would have been handled by the parties themselves.

Under further cross-examination by Senior Smith on whether Brown Lawrence had used the premises of the college for a Jamaica Labour Party divisional meeting in early 2018, Haughton said, “I cannot confirm.”

Upon further questioning from Senior Smith, who queried whether she was “not saying it did not happen” the witness repeated: “I cannot confirm that, sir.”

The principal also maintained that she had never been shown any statement purported to be that of Kim Brown Lawrence by police.

More witnesses are expected to be called in the case on Monday.

Brown Lawrence and the other four accused are before the court to answer to allegations that between March 2016 and October 2019 they participated in a scheme with others unknown, which siphoned off a revised figure of more than $25 million from both the Ministry of Education and CMU.

It is alleged that this money was funnelled through transfers to various accounts either owned or controlled by the accused, or handed over in cash, with the recipients either knowing, or reasonably should have known, that it was criminal property, resulting in charges of acquisition of criminal property.

Pinnock and Reid are accused of using their roles as public servants to mastermind and effect a scheme in which individuals were being paid on a regular basis by CMU, without knowledge that they were being paid; and in which invoices for goods and services were generated, but not by the individuals being paid, who did not, at any time, provide the stated services or goods to CMU, resulting in charges of conspiracy to defraud.

The two are also charged with acts of corruption under Section 15 of the Corruption Act.

World.title: Here comes Fudgie…30 years later
World.content:
Mr G

Dancehall artiste and producer Mr G, aka Goofy, credits his breakthrough 1996 hit Fudgie for opening several doors for his career.

The deejay, who started his Young Blood Records label in 1999, went on to score major success as a producer.

“Fudgie changed my life drastically,” he told the Jamaica Observer in a recent interview.

“Mi buss [got the breakthrough] at the end of August and, within months, I signed a deal with EMI/BMG Records in the United Kingdom. Early the next year I was able to purchase my first apartment in Kingston,” Mr G recalled.

Fudgie, produced by Danny Browne of Main Street Records, opened the floodgates for subsequent hits, including I Don’t Give a Damn, Big Man Little Yute with Red Rat, Buff Bay, Normal, Nah Stoop Low (with Chico), and Brush Yuh Teeth from Mawning.

Mr G shared the back story behind the origins of Fudgie and how the song became a hit.

“Me and [recording artiste] Mad Anju were walking along Donmair Road when a fudge man rode by on his bicycle. Mad Anju said, ‘Here comes Fudgie’, and I asked him if I could use the line in a song. My ears always indicated to me when I heard something special,” said Mr G.

He indicated that while it was not easy-going, he always had confidence in the track.

“I always knew Fudgie would have been a hit. I voiced the song three times for three different producers before it became a hit. I did it in 1994 for Junior Fender, who was my first manager, then I recorded it for Collin Fat, but he didn’t release the song,” he said.

He headed over to Main Street Records, a fledgling label at the time that had among its roster the likes of Papa San, General Degree, Richie Stephens, and Lady G. There he presented the song to Browne, who told him that he had a rhythm for up-and-coming artistes to ‘voice on’.

Mr G later accompanied Richie Stephens and General Degree to a stage show that was being held at a nightclub at the foot of Spur Tree Hill heading to St Elizabeth. There he tested the song Fudgie to see what the response would be like.

“The song mash up the show. Monday after the show I went to Arrows [studio] to cut a dub plate for the song and I bought a fudge horn downtown and included the horn in the song. After that, I jumped on a taxi from Spanish Town and went all the way down to Irie FM in Ocho Rios and gave the dub plate to Big A (Ainsworth Higgins). He said the song would change my life. And it did,” Mr G shared.

While travelling in the taxi on his way back to Kingston, Mr G heard the song being played several times. This continued for the next few days and, within a week, a promoter contacted Main Street Records wanting to book Mr G for his very first performance at Orchid Great House in Westmoreland.

“Fudgie gave me my first paid show at Orchid Great House in Westmoreland and, from there, everything fell into place. Hits after hits,” said Mr G.

Last month he released his latest musical juggling, titled I Shall Be Released rhythm, on his Young Blood Records imprint. It features the songs Weh Mi Woulda by Eminoxx, If You Love Me by Little John, Broken Promises by Phalcon, Baby Mother by Renigad, Mind Over Matter by Spanner Banner, You Don’t Deserve by Pinchers, If You Were Mine by Christopher Martin and Jesse Royal, No Substitute by Romain Virgo, and Free Up Di Youths by Mr G and Richie Spice.

I Shall Be Released rhythm is a remake of the beat accompanying the song of the same name by The Heptones, which was released in 1969.

“What I try to do, as a producer, is to preserve our culture and, by preserving our culture, sometimes we revisit some rhythms and give them a fresh sound, a fresh energy, whether it’s the artistes that are established or new artistes. We try to do things that will spark and create that buzz and resonate with people,” Mr G reasoned.

Mr G’s credentials as a producer are impeccable. Among the hits he has produced are 100 Dollar Bag by Beenie Man; Wah Dis Fada, the breakthrough hit for Mad Anju; Eva Clean by Beenie Man; Breath of Fresh Air by Warrior King; Ben Ova by RDX; Oh, My Lord by Chuck Fenda; Wife and Sweetheart by Christopher Martin and Romain Virgo; and Martin’s collaborative hit Leave People Business Alone.

World.title: Scotia going private
World.content:
Scotia Group Jamaica (SGJ) Chairman Vernon Douglas reads the result of the vote at Wednesday’s extraordinary general meeting. Observing from the head table are SGJ executives Audrey Tugwell Henry (left) and Maia Wilson.

Scotia Group Jamaica Limited (SGJ) is set to become a private company in the coming months as minority shareholders on Wednesday approved an offer by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited (SCH) to acquire their shares for $63.50 billion (US$397.84 million).

The decision was taken at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) called by the financial conglomerate at AC Hotel Kingston under a scheme of arrangement as directed by the Supreme Court of Jamaica.

At the meeting, minority shareholders were asked to vote on the offer by SCH to purchase their shares for $75 per share and take the company private. The vote was reviewed by scrutineers PwC Corporate Services (Jamaica) Limited.

“The resolution was approved by a majority in number of the stockholders being 77 per cent holding 97 per cent of stock units voting in person or by proxy at this meeting, which means preliminarily, the vote has been approved on both counts,” stated SGJ Chairman Vernon Douglas as he delivered the results to a round of applause.

The shareholder meeting was attended by more than 300 people comprising mainly older shareholders such as pensioners and a few young investors. Several shareholders asked about a better offer for their shares, with one older shareholder saying the $75 was not good enough, while another said that SCH should go and find more money for the offer.

However, institutional shareholders, like pension funds and managed funds, voted to support the offer.

There were 334 proxy forms submitted prior to the EGM, with SGJ’s second-largest shareholder, Sagicor Pooled Equity Fund, voting in favour of the scheme.

SGJ disclosed last Tuesday that some institutional shareholders entered into voting support arrangements for the offer, which was adjusted from $61.50 to $75. These shareholders represented 21.12 per cent of the minority shares in SGJ.

“Today’s shareholder support marks an important milestone and validates the strength of the proposal we put forward. This is a decisive statement of the Caribbean’s strategic importance to Scotiabank and of our confidence in Jamaica’s long-term future. Jamaica is a priority market, and we will continue investing in our business, our people, and the communities we serve,” a press release quoted Scotiabank Dominican Republic and the Caribbean President Jabar Singh on Wednesday.

Following the conclusion of the EGM, Scotia executives, including Audrey Tugwell Henry and Maia Wilson, attorney Gina Phillipps Black, and former Scotia Investments Jamaica Limited CEO Lissant Mitchell celebrated with hugs.

With the resolution approved by minority shareholders, SGJ and SCH will now return to Justice David Batts on October 30 for the final court hearing to sanction the scheme of arrangement. If the scheme is sanctioned, the court order would be filed with the Companies Office of Jamaica to make the scheme effective.

SCH would remit the funds to minority shareholders and become the sole shareholder of SGJ. Shareholders must submit a physically signed currency election form prior to the effective date to be paid in United States dollars. Also, shareholders who own more than 13,334 ordinary shares need to ensure that they have an electronic dividend mandate to be paid over $1 million as, since September 1 Jamaica has stopped processing cheques over that amount.

The Jamaican subsidiary will delist from the Jamaica Stock Exchange (JSE) after more than 57 years as a listed company partially owned by Jamaicans. SGJ is currently the most profitable company on the JSE as measured by net profit attributable to shareholders as it reported $16.18 billion.

SGJ represented 10.55 per cent of the JSE Main Market and 9.83 per cent of the entire Jamaican dollar equity market as of September 30. It was worth $226.75 billion as of Wednesday, making it the largest company on the JSE by market capitalisation.

World.title: 200 Cubans back in public health system
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton speaking at Wednesday's post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House.

THE Government has re-engaged 157 Cuban medical professionals months after the collapse of a long-standing bilateral health-care arrangement with Cuba, bringing the number of health-care workers from the neighbouring Caribbean island now serving here to 200.

Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton made the disclosure at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House, saying the latest arrivals had been appropriately deployed across the public health system.

“The renegotiated agreement with our Cuban health-care workers has resulted in, to date, an engagement of some 157 Cuban medical professionals, including doctors and nurses, who have returned to Jamaica to support health-care delivery across the island,” Tufton said.

The largest complement, 69 professionals, has been assigned to the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), while 28 have been deployed to the Western Regional Health Authority and 26 to the Southern Regional Health Authority.

Another 25 have been assigned to University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), while nine are serving within the Ministry of Health and Wellness and the North East Regional Health Authority.

The 157 are in addition to 43 Cuban health-care workers who opted to remain in Jamaica after the Government ended the previous country-to-country arrangement and offered them the option of continuing to work under individual contracts.

Tufton said the latest re-engagement brings the number of Cuban medical professionals in Jamaica to 200, compared with 277 before the renegotiated arrangement.

“We basically gave them an offer. We said, we can’t do the arrangement as was the case, but if you return and it’s your option, your choice, we would engage you in a direct contract,” he said.

“So, we are close to where we were, and they have been appropriately deployed.”

The development comes after Jamaica announced that it would discontinue the existing technical cooperation arrangement with Cuba after both governments failed to reach an agreement on the terms of a new framework.

The previous agreement had expired in February 2023, but Cuban medical professionals continued working in Jamaica while negotiations for a replacement arrangement continued. In March this year, the Government said it was willing to engage the professionals individually under Jamaican labour laws to ensure continuity of services.

At the time, the health system had about 260 Cuban health-care workers, with the largest group consisting of 97 assigned to SERHA. Others were deployed across the western and southern regions, UHWI and specialised services, including the Jamaica-Cuba Eye Care Programme.

The end of the bilateral arrangement subsequently exposed staffing gaps at some public facilities. At Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James, for example, 27 Cuban health-care workers, including nurses, doctors and radiotherapists, left with the hospital having to recruit locally and look overseas for specialised personnel to fill some vacancies.

The Cuban programme has been a major component of Jamaica’s public health-care system for decades, with the eye-care programme in particular providing specialised services to Jamaicans since 2010.

Tufton on Wednesday expressed appreciation to the Cuban professionals who had chosen to return.

“I want to thank those who have chosen that option because the system needs them,” he said.

World.title: Golding, Chuck trade blows over Gun Court data
World.content:
GOLDING : I think that must be a critical deliverable of the Ministry of Justice to track how this legislation is impacting the justice system

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck and Opposition Leader Mark Golding clashed in Parliament on Tuesday over data on the Gun Court.

The exchange was sparked after Golding questioned why the justice ministry had not determined whether the 2022 Firearms Act was affecting guilty pleas and case backlogs.

Both legislators also engaged in a joust over Chuck’s response to a question about juveniles and people with no previous convictions who may have received the mandatory 15-year sentence for possessing imitation firearms, with Golding arguing that the minister should have obtained the information from the relevant agencies.

The exchange came during the House of Representatives’ Questions and Answers to Questions segment on Tuesday, after Opposition spokeswoman on Justice Zulieka Jess put seven questions to Chuck about the operation of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022.

One of Jess’s questions was whether the Government had assessed the extent to which the 15-year mandatory minimum sentence had reduced the incentive for early guilty pleas and what specific effect that had had on the trial backlog in the Gun Court.

Chuck’s answer was brief.

“Answer no,” said the justice minister.

Golding then rose to ask a supplementary question, challenging Chuck over the absence of an assessment on an issue he said should be central to the justice ministry’s work.

“I was shocked by that because I think that must be a critical deliverable of the Ministry of Justice to track how this legislation is impacting the justice system. And I’m asking you, why is it that you don’t have that information? How is it that you don’t have the data as to what impact this legislation is having on the flow of cases through the court system?” Golding queried.

Chuck defended the ministry’s position by pointing to the time it takes for criminal cases to move through the Gun Court.

“First of all, [when] all of these matters come into the gun courts, most of these matters tend to last two or three years before they’re tried. So to say that over the past four years, I should have figures when most of these matters would not even be tried after the Gun Court Act…and with due respect, all the material that would come to the Ministry of Justice would be two, three years.

“They would not be indicating what has been the impact of the 2022 legislation. So you should know that most of these figures would only come after three, four years,” explained Chuck.

Golding, however, pointed to information already being produced by the Court Administration Division, saying the issue was not necessarily whether cases brought under the 2022 law had already been completed, but whether available case-flow information showed an effect on the backlog.

The disagreement then moved to the treatment of juveniles and people with no previous criminal records.

Jess had asked the minister whether any juveniles, or people without prior convictions, were serving or awaiting trial for the mandatory 15-year sentence solely because they possessed an object classified under the law as an imitation firearm.

Chuck initially answered that those statistics were held by other agencies.

But Golding argued that the minister should obtain the information rather than leave the question unanswered.

“You say that doesn’t lie in your ministry. But it’s your obligation to answer the question. So if you don’t have the information in your ministry about sentencing or in the courts, which fall under your ministry, you should get it from whatever source there is,” charged Golding.

Chuck later clarified his position, saying he was aware juveniles might be before the courts, but he had not been informed of any juvenile who had been convicted under the Act and was serving a 15-year sentence.

The explanation was challenged by Golding who argued that Chuck’s response appeared inconsistent with his earlier answer that the information rested with other agencies.

“Your answer was that you can’t provide an answer because that information resides elsewhere. Then, on your feet, you are saying, to the best of your knowledge, there has been no case where somebody has been convicted in those circumstances. So those are two different answers,” argued the Opposition leader.

“…And unless you’re just going to arrogantly dismiss the questions that have been asked, which is really how it felt like, to be honest, you would be expected to find out from whatever ministries… I mean, these questions were tabled just recently, and you’re providing the answers already without any real attempt to find out the information to answer the question, and I think that was unbecoming of a minister of your stature,” Golding added.

Chuck then explained that he had requested more recent information, but had not received it.

He said the ministry’s statistician is a consultant and, to his knowledge, was behind on some of the data.

According to Chuck, even after the information is obtained, the ministry would have to compare recent figures with those from previous years before determining the effect of the 2022 law.

He acknowledged that the comparison had not yet been completed.

The exchange took place against the background of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which replaced the previous firearms law and introduced tougher provisions governing firearms offences.

The Act is set to be reviewed by the Government after members of the defence bar staged a protest to push for changes.

World.title: EU faces gas supply shortage as winter looms
World.content:
Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday.

Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe's buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU's gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter.

With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found.

While that doesn't necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable.

The EU's record-low reserves leave the bloc "with less of a buffer" against global supply disruptions, leaving it "vulnerable to price spikes," Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA's lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added.

The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can't be easily tapped into.

World.title: Elif Eralp und Friedrich Merz’ neues Berlin-Problem
World.content:
Ein drohender Linksruck in der Hauptstadt sorgt für handfesten Ärger auf Bundesebene. Während SPD und Grüne in Berlin ernsthaft mit der Linkspartei sondieren, blickt Friedrich Merz mit Sorge auf eine mögliche Regierende Bürgermeisterin Elif Eralp. Welche radikalen Forderungen im Raum stehen und warum der Antisemitismus-Streit in der Linken die Regierungsbildung zur Zerreißprobe macht, analysiert Maximilian Heimerzheim.

Beim Dauerbrenner Rentenreform verhärten sich die Fronten zwischen Union und SPD zusehends. Ein neues Sherpa-Treffen soll nun klären, ob das Rentenpaket aufgespalten wird oder langfristig gar ein Renteneintrittsalter von 70 Jahren droht. Rasmus Buchsteiner ordnet ein, welche Kompromisse der Kanzler bis Weihnachten erwartet und wer in den Verhandlungen auf der Bremse steht.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview spricht CSU-Forschungsministerin Dorothee Bär über das europäische Kräftemessen im All. Parallel zum Staatsbesuch von Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier und Emmanuel Macron in Bordeaux erklärt sie, wie sich Deutschland in der Raumfahrt behaupten will und warum Europa beim Flug zum Mond mehr Selbstbewusstsein gegenüber der NASA braucht.
