World.title: Berechenbare Risiken – unberechenbare Politik? Warum Deutschland jetzt aus Worten Gesetze machen muss
World.content:
Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet.

Dazu gehört auch, dass wir uns ehrlich machen: Die finanzielle Schieflage der Kassen entsteht durch strukturelle Ineffizienzen im System, nicht durch medizinischen Fortschritt. Ganz im Gegenteil: Innovative Medizin ist kein Kostenfaktor, sondern eine Investition in die Zukunft. Der konsequente Einsatz modernster Diagnostik, digitaler Prozesse und innovativer Therapien könnte schon heute jährlich über 40 Milliarden Euro freisetzen – direkt im Gesundheitssystem und indirekt als positiver Effekt auf Wirtschaft, Wachstum und Wohlstand.

Die Politik hat jetzt die Chance, einen Perspektivwechsel einzuleiten. Eine Expertenkommission hat jüngst konkret vorgeschlagen, wie Unternehmen, die in Deutschland investieren, von einem Teil – wohlgemerkt: nur einem Teil – jener zusätzlichen Belastungen ausgenommen werden können, die mit dem GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetz eingeführt wurden. Diese Vorschläge zur Verknüpfung des Herstellerabschlags mit einer sogenannten Standortklausel liegen nun auf dem Tisch. Und sie sind schon bemerkenswert: Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet. Ein Ansatz, der Industriepolitik, Sozialpolitik und Geopolitik endlich zusammendenkt.

Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit.

Dabei wird uns keineswegs etwas geschenkt: Die Kassen werden mit einem erhöhten Herstellerabschlag von 15,5% weiterhin auf Rekordniveau durch die Industrie gestützt – Unternehmen, die nachweislich vor Ort Werte schaffen, Arbeitsplätze sichern und Forschung verankern, erhalten lediglich die Chance, die zusätzlichen Belastungen zu reduzieren. Das ist kein Geschenk – sondern die Korrektur einer massiven Fehlsteuerung. Eine vorausschauende, ressortübergreifende Standortstrategie hätte von vornherein auf positive Anreize gesetzt, statt bestehende Strukturen zu schwächen. Umso wichtiger ist es, dass daraus nun schnell ein wirksames, unbürokratisches Gesetz wird – und dass weitere Schritte folgen. Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit. Denn milliardenschwere Investitionsentscheidungen in die Zukunft Deutschlands folgen keinen Kommissionspapieren – sondern verlässlichen Taten, die die Grundlage für eine Pharma-Strategie werden können, die Deutschlands Wettbewerbsfähigkeit wiederherstellt und den internationalen Herausforderungen gerecht wird.

Hinweis

World.title: Is the EU ready for the next pandemic?
World.content:
Five years after the height of the Covid pandemic, how much better prepared is the EU for the next health crisis?

Host Sarah Wheaton is joined by POLITICO health reporter Helen Collis and global health expert Michel Kazatchkine to discuss the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, and what it tells us about international health cooperation and transparency.



They look at what became of Brussels’ post-Covid ambitions — from the EU’s HERA health-emergency authority to better coordination of research — and at Donald Trump’s push to bring down US drug prices by putting pressure on Europe to pay more.



Plus: As Brussels tries to compete with the U.S. and China on biotech and new medicines, is it focusing on the innovation patients actually need?

Questions? Comments? Let us know on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

World.title: Green Leader Polanski’s Westminster gamble fails in Holborn and St Pancras
World.content:
It is a symbolic early boost for Starmer’s replacement Andy Burnham, who has shifted the ruling Labour Party to the left since taking charge and toughened the U.K.’s stance on Israel by announcing plans to sanction West Bank settlements last month.

The north London seat has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983 — but the left-wing Green Party poured significant resources into trying to get its high-profile leader elected. The Greens took 33% of the vote to Labour’s 45% on a turnout of 38.8%.

Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the U.K. as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was “deeply personal” and vowed to work with Burnham to tackle homelessness. She said she wants to see Thames Water — the giant private water company that serves her constituents — brought into public ownership.

Labour Party candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali is hugged by a supporter after winning the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in London on Oct. 9, 2026. | Carl Court/Getty Images

A defeated Polanski said he would stay on as party leader, telling broadcasters: “I’ve taken a loss tonight, but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion.”

His rival for the Green candidacy Hamza Chowdhury — a Green councillor in Camden — said: “This is a fucking win mate. Labour might be celebrating now but wait till 2029 when we wipe the floor with them.”

U.K. polling expert John Curtice said the Holborn result is “still by far and away [the Greens’] second best ever result in a parliamentary by-election” — but warned the Greens are “now operating in a more politically competitive environment.”

World.title: When politicians write bad erotic fiction
World.content:
Politicians can, of course, make great writers, and several have won Nobel’s literature prize, including Britain’s Winston Churchill in 1953, and Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010. The latter — who ran for president in 1990 — won the prize “for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual’s resistance, revolt, and defeat.” But has he ever referred to British Conservative grandee Jacob Rees-Mogg as a “Haunted Pencil”? No, he has not.

There are, however, a lot of very bad books written by politicians.

Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson — very much the “Winston Churchill if you ordered him off Temu” — published a book in 2004 called “Seventy-Two Virgins — A Comedy of Errors” (the last four words also being the summary of his Covid policy) about a terrorist group targeting the U.S. president on a visit to London. It was described in the Guardian some 15 years later — after Johnson became prime minister — as ” sexist, racist, fundamentally undiplomatic.”

But the undisputed king when it comes to politicians letting out their inner writer is France.

In 2023, Bruno Le Maire, then the country’s economy and finance minister, published the novel “Fugue Américaine,” which drew instant criticism and mockery, mainly because of an explicit sex scene (unhappy French people were quick to point out that they had been screwed by the government for years).

Then there’s Marlène Schiappa, former government minister and writer of raunchy books under the pen name Marie Minelli, with titles such as “Osez les sexfriends,” “Sexe, mensonge et banlieues chaudes” and “Comment transformer votre mec en Brad Pitt en 30 jours.” When she was junior social affairs minister, Schiappa appeared on the cover of Playboy, although she was not naked in the magazine (great news for those who buy Playboy only for the articles).

World.title: ‘Not great, not terrible’: Why nobody trusts Russia to tell the truth about plague
World.content:
The World Health Organization, which leads global response to international health threats, got in touch with Russian health authorities on Oct. 3. It requested more information using one of the tools laid out in the International Health Regulations, which Russia is signed up to. Under the IHR, countries have 24 hours to respond to the WHO — though Russia sent its response on Oct. 6.

Russian authorities said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk” and “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”

World Health Organization epidemic and pandemic management head Maria Van Kerkhove, who said "we still don't know exactly how this person died, at a press briefing in Geneva on Oct. 7, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images

As of Thursday, Russian health authorities maintain that there is no “epidemic risk” in the region. Rospotrebnadzor said that it had concluded health inspections and found “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms.” It had also completed monitoring of 90% of the contacts, without identifying any infections, the agency added. Simultaneously, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov slammed media reports about the case as false and said Russia has been communicating with global health authorities.

Yet the WHO insists there’s still much left unknown about the events inside Russia.

“We don’t know exactly how this person died,” said Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management, during a press briefing Wednesday. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case. We understand that some laboratory tests have been done. They haven’t found the causative agent. This is why we need more information.”

The WHO said it requested further details on what laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, which further analyses are being done to determine the patient’s cause of death — if not plague — along with more details on any potential lab incident and the 200 contacts.

World.title: EU cyber and science researchers are testing Chinese AI models
World.content:
AI safety and security — topics currently under intense scrutiny following a series of incidents in which advanced AI models hacked real-world networks during testing activities — are not the core focus of the JRC’s testing activities, according to a different Commission official, who was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive material.

Open-weight models are those whose core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to run the model and study how it works. China’s approach to AI has leaned more towards open models than the United States. Some major U.S. tech and AI companies, including chips giant NVIDIA, are investing in open-weight models.

Forced to choose

The U.S. and China are locked in a race to dominate in the technology, with Europe largely sitting on the sidelines. Without a viable European frontier model, European private and public organizations may be left to choose between American and Chinese providers for advanced AI applications.

In a recent speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested Europe should not try to win the frontier AI race. A top German tech company told POLITICO this week it was dropping Europe's leading AI lab Mistral in favor of open-source Chinese models.

The JRC has not entered into any “bespoke access” or licensing negotiations with the relevant Chinese developers, Berestecki said. The models are run on the center’s “secure, on-premises scientific infrastructure” and the Commission is not intending to use Chinese models for its own purposes, he added.

EU cyber agency ENISA — which has gained access to advanced models from top U.S. AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and Google — is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models, its executive director Juhan Lepassaar confirmed in an interview on Wednesday.

JRC and ENISA have been tasked with working together to set up an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, the European Commission's attempt to respond to the growing concerns after a series of incidents involving AI systems breaking out of testing environments and breaking into other organizations' digital systems.

World.title: Graphene opens new way to detect brain damage after stroke
World.content:
An international team of scientists has developed a graphene-based technology that makes it possible to monitor brain activity and identify the areas at greatest risk of sustaining additional damage after a stroke. The breakthrough, tested in mice, could help drive the development of more precise treatments for stroke.

 

The research, published in the scientific journal "Brain (source in Spanish)", involved the participation of Spain's National Research Council (CSIC), the University of Manchester, the Catalan Institute of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology (ICN2) and the German company Multi Channel Systems.

When a person suffers an ischaemic stroke, a blockage interrupts the blood flow to part of the brain. However, the lesions can continue to spread because of waves of disturbed electrical activity, known as spreading cortical depolarisations, which move through the affected brain tissue.

Until now, accurately detecting these signals has been a challenge, as conventional technologies struggle to record the extremely slow electrical changes that occur during this process.

Graphene helps identify the brain's most vulnerable areas

Using high-sensitivity graphene sensors placed on the brains of mice, the researchers succeeded in recording these electrical waves with an unprecedented level of detail. The results showed that the characteristics of the signals made it possible to distinguish between relatively healthy brain tissue, tissue at risk and tissue that had already suffered severe damage.

The scientists also found that these signals could anticipate the blood-flow response. While in healthier areas it increased to support recovery, in vulnerable regions it could fall even further, worsening the injury.

The team also discovered that a low dose of ketamine, a drug already used in medicine, reduced the duration of the harmful electrical waves, improved the blood-flow response and reduced the extent of brain damage in animal models. These findings point to a possible neuroprotective effect of ketamine after a stroke, although it has not yet been shown to offer the same benefits in humans.

A potential tool to improve treatments

"In broad terms, the study shows how cutting-edge technologies can not only improve the way brain activity is measured, but also reveal new and important information about how brain lesions develop and how they might be treated", explains Rob Wykes, a researcher at the University of Manchester.

For his part, Anton Guimerà-Brunet, a CSIC researcher at the Institute of Microelectronics of Barcelona, stresses that recording low-frequency brain activity is still a challenge for current technologies. "We have been developing our graphene-based technology for years, with our first results published in 2018, and the challenge has been to standardise and refine it for use in relevant preclinical studies", he says.

The breakthrough is part of a scientific collaboration launched years ago between institutions in Spain and the United Kingdom to develop graphene devices capable of recording brain signals.

Although the technology is still at the preclinical research stage, the scientists believe that in future it could make it possible to monitor in real time the condition of brain tissue during a stroke, identify patients at greatest risk of additional injury and contribute to the development of new treatments.

World.title: El Niño could weaken the polar vortex. Does a scorching summer mean a freezing winter?
World.content:
Experts have warned that this year’s El Niño event could be the “strongest in living memory” – increasing the likelihood of 2027 becoming the hottest year on record.

 

Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño events, and the weather phenomenon isn’t expected to peak until late autumn or early winter.

Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate that the extreme heat associated with El Niño could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths. The extra warming also paves the way for more extreme weather impacts, such as wildfires and floods.

South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced heightened flood risks during previous El Niño events – while droughts and wildfire risks rise across large parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries such as Indonesia.

But in Europe, El Niño’s weather impacts tend to be much more indirect and less severe. The natural phenomenon could increase the chances of more unsettled conditions later in the year, such as a milder, wetter and windier autumn and early winter.

So, why are fears growing that Europe will be cast into a deep freeze this winter?

What is a Sudden Stratospheric Warming event?

Every year in winter, strong westerly winds circle around the pole high up in the stratosphere – which extends from an altitude of about 10 to 50 km above the Earth’s surface.

This is referred to as the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and it circulates around cold air high over the Arctic.

However, following a peak in El Niño, the SPV can become weaker. This can increase the likelihood of a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event, which would subsequently increase the potential for cold weather.

A SSW is where temperatures rapidly increase (up to about 50C in just a couple of days) in the stratosphere. As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere.

“Typically this will form over the North Atlantic and Scandinavia,” the UK Met Office says.

“This means that northern Europe, including the UK is likely to get a long spell of dry, cold weather, whereas southern Europe will tend to be more mild, wet and windy. On the boundary of these areas, cold easterly winds develop and in some cases the drop in temperatures leads to snow.”

Will El Niño trigger a ‘deep freeze’ in Europe?

Multiple newspapers have recently warned of a “deep freeze” hitting Europe due to the risk of El Niño peaking and weakening the polar vortex.

However, winter weather across the UK and mainland Europe is influenced by a wide range of factors – including human-caused climate change. For example, a 2025 study from Newcastle University found the burning of fossil fuels is accelerating winter rainfall changes in the UK and Europe, almost 25 years sooner than expected.

Many of the factors that impact Europe’s weather cannot be predicted so far in advance. In fact, meteorologists can only reliably forecast individual SSW events about a week ahead.

“While there is a known teleconnection between El Niño and a colder end to the UK winter, this outcome is by no means guaranteed,” Grahame Madge, a Met Office climate spokesperson, tells Euronews Earth.

“There are many other drivers of UK winter weather including El Niño, and it is the balance of these drivers that determines the winter forecast rather than any single one.”

World.title: Russia slashes cancer care as defence spending hits post-Soviet record
World.content:
Russia is cutting funding for its national cancer programme nearly twelvefold in 2027, from 44.9 billion roubles (€470.5m) to 3.87 billion roubles (€40.5m), according to the draft federal budget, as defence spending reaches its highest share since the collapse of the Soviet Union.

 

The reduction is even sharper compared to last year: the programme received 148.5 billion roubles (€1.5bn) in 2025, meaning federal spending on cancer control would have fallen roughly 38-fold in two years if the budget passes as proposed.

Funding is projected to recover partially thereafter — rising to 5.76 billion roubles in 2028 and 12.78 billion in 2029 — but both figures remain far below current levels.

Since its launch, the federal cancer project has funded diagnostic equipment, cancer centres, and early screening programmes.

Under the new 2027-2029 budget, the remaining money is expected to go mainly to diagnostic and radiology equipment, while specialised units in smaller towns and rural areas face cuts, a distribution likely to deepen an already significant gap between cancer care in major federal centres and outlying regions.

Rerouting roubles

Officials have said some costs will be transferred to the compulsory health insurance system (OMS) and other budget lines rather than eliminated entirely.

Patient organisations and some experts have questioned whether the new mechanisms could fully offset the federal reduction, and noted that shifting costs to regional budgets and the OMS ties the quality of care more directly to the financial strength of individual regions.

The proposed cuts come as new data show Russian cancer patients are already bearing a growing share of treatment costs.

A study by the NGO Movement Against Cancer found that between 2019 and 2025, patients bought roughly one in every six or seven packs of cancer medicines out of pocket. In 2025 alone, household spending on anti-tumour drugs rose from 8.8 billion to 11.4 billion roubles, and the number of packs bought independently increased from five million to 5.8 million.

Around 94% of those drugs are on the list of essential medicines and should be provided free of charge.

The study's authors attribute the out-of-pocket spending not to patients choosing more expensive options — most purchases involved generics — but to supply disruptions and gaps in provision.

Russian law guarantees cancer patients free access to the medicines they need, but in practice, patients and doctors have long reported procurement delays and regional budget shortfalls.

State procurement remains substantial: official figures show the government bought 32.8 million packs of medicines worth 336 billion roubles through the OMS system in 2025. But the trajectory in out-of-pocket spending suggests the burden on patients is already rising ahead of the planned federal cuts.

Defence spending in the 2027 draft budget is set to reach 17.1 trillion roubles, or roughly 35% of all federal expenditure — a post-Soviet record.

More than four years of Moscow's all-out war in Ukraine have progressively shifted Russia's public spending, with civilian programmes including healthcare and medical infrastructure taking a backseat to continued expansion of defence outlays.

World.title: Santorini: Wine, gastronomy and unique experiences beyond the famous sunsets
World.content:
With a new digital campaign built around 32 short videos, Santorini is seeking to broaden its international tourism profile, highlighting experiences that are often overshadowed by its famous sunsets and luxury accommodation.

 

The Greek island, renowned for its whitewashed houses perched above the volcanic caldera and its unique views over the Aegean, aims to attract travellers interested in gastronomy, wine, culture, nature and everyday local life.

The new initiative was unveiled at the GNTO Santorini Tourism Forum 2026, held from 5-8 October, with the participation of representatives of the Greek National Tourism Organisation (GNTO), local authorities, industry professionals and around 30 journalists from international travel media.

During the forum, GNTO executives active in key European markets presented the travel trends they are recording in their countries, looking for ways to link Santorini’s already powerful reputation with different types of experience and trips outside the peak summer season.

From volcanic vineyards to gastronomy and culture

Santorini boasts a distinctive wine-making tradition, closely tied to the island’s volcanic soil and climatic conditions.

For centuries, winegrowers have used the technique known as the "kouloura", training the vines into low, circular basket-like shapes to protect the grapes from strong winds and intense sunlight.

The local Assyrtiko grape variety has gained international recognition, and many wineries now offer tours of their vineyards, visits to production facilities and wine tastings.

Santorini’s culinary identity also features hallmark products such as fava, tiny cherry tomatoes and white aubergine, all cultivated in the island’s distinctive terrain.

The importance of local gastronomy has also been recognised by the Michelin Guide, which announced in December 2025 that Santorini and Thessaloniki will be added to its Greek selection for 2026, alongside Athens.

Beyond food and wine, visitors can explore the archaeological site of Akrotiri, a prehistoric settlement preserved beneath layers of volcanic ash, discover traditional villages such as Megalochori, or follow hiking trails overlooking the caldera.

Local authorities also want to strengthen activities such as cooking and pottery classes, which allow travellers to connect with local production and culture.

"Visitors do not simply tick off a standard sightseeing itinerary; they go home holding on to the moments that moved them," said Georgia Nomikou, president of the Municipal Council and the Tourism Committee of Thira, speaking to the Athens-Macedonian News Agency.

She revealed that production is already under way on 32 short social media videos, focusing on the moments and experiences a visitor can enjoy on the island.

Santorini’s famous sunset AP Photo/Petros Giannakouris/File

What travellers from European markets are looking for

The diversification of travel preferences was a central theme of the forum’s discussions, with GNTO representatives outlining the trends they observe in Europe’s main markets.

In the United Kingdom, one of Santorini’s key markets, head of the GNTO office Eleni Skarveli noted that luxury remains a strong element of the island’s image, but interest is growing in gastronomy, wellness, family trips and holidays that combine several Greek islands.

Similarly, GNTO's representative in France, Emmy Anagnostopoulou, stressed the appeal for visitors who want to discover local cuisine, wineries and cultural heritage.

"These are not tourists who stay shut inside a hotel wearing an all-inclusive wristband; they get out, explore and spend money in the local economy," she said, describing the preferences she observes in the French travel market.

She also underlined that demand for travel outside July and August can help attract more visitors in spring and autumn.

In Austria and Germany, according to GNTO representative Stavroula Skaltza, there is clear interest in wine tourism, gastronomy and wellness, while repeat visitors are looking for new experiences in a destination they already know.

For the Scandinavian markets, GNTO representative Eftychia Aivalioti highlighted the importance of nature, hiking and activities linked to quality and sustainable tourism.

These assessments are based on reports from GNTO offices in the respective countries and reflect the trends that the organisation’s staff identify in their markets.

Santorini’s stunning view AP Photo/Kristi Eaton/File

More visitors in spring and autumn

One of the main goals of the new strategy is to boost tourism activity outside the peak summer months, attracting visitors who are interested in experiences that go beyond a traditional beach holiday.

The development of wine tourism, cultural visits and nature-based activities can offer additional reasons to travel to Santorini during periods with fewer tourists.

Air connectivity is also a key factor. According to the GNTO representative in France, Transavia flights to Santorini have been extended until November, improving options for autumn trips.

New connections are also planned from the British market. Jet2 has announced weekly flights from Leeds-Bradford Airport to Santorini, from 6 May to 7 October 2027.

World.title: From barbershops to nature courses: How community-driven campaigns are rethinking men’s mental health
World.content:
At a small barbershop in Brixton, south London, men’s lives are being transformed. Not just through a new haircut or fresh beard trim — but by opening up about their mental health.

 

“People confide in barbers and often share things that perhaps they wouldn't with their partners or friends,” Ben Theophanous, owner and co-founder of Curfew Grooming, told Euronews Health.

“The relationship is often strong, but there is an element of superficiality that provides a unique platform for sharing feelings,” he added.

Curfew Grooming is one of more than 100 barbershops across the United Kingdom to receive Mental Health First Aid (MHFA) training through the 12th Man Campaign — a community-driven initiative founded in 2013 by mental health nurse Nick Little and his late friend Oz Osborne.

The campaign takes its name from the football term for a team’s fans and provides support for men by normalising talking about mental health in everyday spaces.

These spaces include barbershops and tattoo studios — places where there’s already a one-on-one dynamic. Employees who volunteer take an online course, which guides them through how to spot signs that a customer might be struggling; how to ask meaningful questions and how to direct them to the right resources if needed.

Workers attending a mental health trainins session provided through the 12th Man Campaign. Nick Little

“We're just handing the responsibility to men in society to look out for their friends and their family. To recognise mental health more in their lives and to talk about it,” Nick Little told Euronews Health.

Nearly 1 in 7 people around the world are living with a mental health condition, but men are still less likely than women to reach out for help — and three times more likely to die by suicide, according to the Office of National Statistics.

Those who are looking for professional help encounter another issue: long waiting times. For example In the UK, people were eight times more likely to wait for over 18 months for mental health treatment on the National Health Service than those waiting for physical health treatments, according to data analysed by the charity Rethink in 2025.

Increasingly, community-led initiatives are stepping in as a way to fill these gaps in the system — not to replace professional services, but to put more preventative measures in place before people reach crisis.

“Let's put trust in society and invest in our community businesses, because that's the front line,” Little said.

Engaging men with nature

Similar community-based and male-focused initiatives are happening all across Europe.

In Denmark, many of these have used the Vildmandsprojektet (Wild Man) project as a blueprint; a 9- to 12-week nature-based rehabilitation program for men in crisis.

Co-founded by nature psychologist Simon Høegmark in 2014, its development was partly inspired by Høegmark’s own personal experiences with mental health.

Over a decade ago, he travelled to Norway to hike and regain his “footing.”

“After several days of heavy thoughts, I reached the summit of a mountain overlooking Lysefjord. For a brief moment, the thought of jumping crossed my mind,” he recalled.

But as quickly as these thoughts took over, the views of Lysefjord became awash with light — and something inside Simon shifted.

“The sun broke through the clouds, illuminating the entire landscape. I experienced a moment of self-forgetfulness, a sense of connection, and a love for life,” Høegmark told Euronews Health.

While the experience did not immediately resolve his psychological crisis, it allowed the beauty of nature to take over — its stillness settling the thoughts in his head and replacing them with a sense of hope.

“I saw my situation more clearly. I decided to investigate why encountering nature can affect people so profoundly, and how nature can be professionally utilised as a framework for recovery and rehabilitation,” he said.

The Vildmandsprojektet (Wild Man) project in Denmark. Simon Høegmark

After launching the Vildmandsprojektet project in 2014, Høegmark conducted many studies alongside a team of researchers to monitor its effects. One such study involved 114 men, who showed significant improvements in their physical and mental quality of life, as well as a reduction in self-perceived stress symptoms after taking the course.

“These improvements were evident immediately after the course and — on several measures — six months later,” Høegmark said, also noting a lasting sense of community even after the courses had ended.

“This serves as a vital bridge between a time-limited public program and everyday life, where habits and relationships need to endure,” he added.

The project ran from 2014 for a period of over eight years, during which time around 700 men participated in its courses. Since then, its Nature, Body, Mind, and Community (NBMC) method has been adopted by more than 50 Danish municipalities and adapted for both men and women.

While Høegmark cautions that Vildmandsprojektet was never intended to replace psychiatric treatment, it has proved itself to be an accessible format for men that might otherwise be reluctant to engage with mental health services.

“My professional interpretation is that [the NBMC method] can strengthen participants' sense of agency and ownership regarding their own wellbeing,” said Høegmark.

“However, the method must be used as a supplement within a cohesive health service framework that includes clear referral pathways should a participant require more specialised care,” he said.

An event hosted by the 12th Man Campaign. Nick Little

The growing importance of community-driven care

Alongside local initiatives, nationwide healthcare systems have also begun looking into community-driven care as a tool to alleviate wait times.

One example of this is social prescribing, which the NHS has been offering as a way to connect patients with activity groups. These can include gardening, walking, art and crafting clubs — anything that encourages reconnection with the outside world.

“The reason I'm so in favour of this more community-driven style of support is that the format can be more relevant to everyday life, more aligned with people's hobbies and things that they normally would do anyway,” Stella Chan, a professor of evidence-based psychological therapies at the University of Reading in England, tells Euronews Health.

“It's less stigmatising and also easier to assess,” she added, which can in turn help ease resistance.

While some have argued that social prescribing is not enough — and avoids addressing more serious underlying societal issues like economic inequality — research suggests it’s become an important way to bridge medical and non-medical support.

“Mental ill-health and mental disorders are among our major global health challenges, and we need both robust treatment and far more prevention,” Høegmark said.

World.title: Six injured as heavy rains batter Chile's capital, sweeping away cars and flooding homes
World.content:
Heavy rains battered Chile’s capital Santiago and its surrounding regions on Thursday, triggering mudslides that swept cars through streets, flooded homes, forced residents to evacuate and injured at least six people, according to authorities.

 

Chilean President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in Las Condes, a wealthy suburb east of Santiago, giving government agencies more power to respond as torrential rains turned key roads into impassable waterways.

Vehicles are partially inundated in muddy floodwaters after heavy rains caused flash flooding in the Las Condes district of Santiago, Chile, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 Esteban Felix/Copyright 2026. The AP. All rights reserved

The district's mayor, Catalina San Martín, said 14.4 centimetres of rain had fallen in recent days — about nine times the average October rainfall — leaving the area “totally drenched.”

The Mapocho River, which runs through Santiago, overflowed, prompting evacuation orders.

Chile’s disaster-response agency put 10 other districts on high alert for more landslides and ordered schools to close on Friday.

A rescue worker walks through muddy debris in a shop damaged by flash flooding caused by heavy rains in the Las Condes district of Santiago, Chile, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 Esteban Felix/Copyright 2026. The AP. All rights reserved

Rain storms earlier this week had already damaged a few dozen homes across central Chile and left nearly 12,000 customers in Santiago without power, officials said. The downpours were expected to ease on Friday.

No deaths were reported on Thursday as a result of the heavy rains. The injured however included a one-year-old child, who suffered broken bones. Firefighters said they'd rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people.

A man is pulled to safety by rescue workers after heavy rains caused flash flooding in the Las Condes district of Santiago, Chile, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026 Esteban Felix/Copyright 2026. The AP. All rights reserved

The floods come as a powerful El Niño gains strength.

The naturally recurring warming of tropical Pacific waters scrambles rainfall patterns worldwide and often brings wetter springs to the Southern Hemisphere.

The World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday that this year’s El Niño was expected to peak in December and could be among the most intense since at least 1950.

World.title: Police boost presence and detain 17-year-old after 'Bloody Friday' threat to Polish schools
World.content:
On Thursday, social media were flooded with claims about alleged planned attacks on schools. Among pupils and parents, screenshots and recordings have been circulating, warning of a so-called "bloody Friday", said to fall on Friday 9 October.

 

The reports appeared after a series of serious incidents in schools in the Mazovia region.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old attacked nine people with a knife at a school in Ostrołęka. The following day in Leszczydole-Nowinach, a 15-year-old former pupil attacked three people, where a 37-year-old school employee died from her injuries.

Boosted police presence in schools

In response to mounting concern, police have announced reinforced preventive measures. National Police Commander-in-Chief Marek Boroń said officers would be present around schools from Friday morning to help combat the threat and ease anxiety.

"The police will do everything to ensure these schools are secure" – Boroń told Polish media outlets.

He added that patrols had already appeared near school premises on Thursday and were in contact with their representatives. On Friday, officers are expected to work with principals, teachers and local authorities.

The police chief also appealed to pupils and parents to report any credible suspicions of planned violence to teachers or law enforcement directly.

Boroń added that after the attack in Ostrołęka, the number of reports about potential threats has risen sharply. He also urged caution in spreading information about alleged attacks.

Social media-induced panic

One of the main reasons behind the growing anxiety was a video that began circulating on social media platforms in the country.

According to Polish news outlets, the material referred to alleged plans to attack schools as part of "bloody Friday", after its author had announced a "massacre in Przasnysz".

Officers in Przasnysz quickly took up the case. They detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz county, who is believed to be the likely author of the video.

"Officers detained a 17-year-old resident of Przasnysz county, who is the probable author of the video circulating online. Activities with the man are under way" Mazovian police reported.

Schools closed on Friday

Alarming reports have also emerged in other localities.

In Sierpc, police detained a 17-year-old who had said he intended to hurt someone at school. Two knives were found on the teenager. In this case, pupils and teachers played a key role in his detention by reporting information about his behaviour to the police.

On Thursday, there was also a tragic attack in Leszczydole-Nowinach near Wyszków.

A 15-year-old former student attacked a caretaker, the principal and a teacher with a sharp tool, likely a knife. The 37-year-old school employee succumbed to their wounds while two other victims were injured.

Authorities have decided that primary schools in the Wyszków municipality will not hold classes on Friday as a result of the attacks and further safety-related concerns.

The institutions are however still expected to provide care for their pupils. Local media reported that on Friday all secondary schools in Ciechanów will operate remotely. In-person classes will also not take place in schools in the district of Pułtusk.

World.title: Podcast: AI in France, translators fight back, musicians' mentor
World.content:
Artificial intelligence is everywhere in France but who's using it, and how? We also look at its impact on translators and how they're striving to keep humans at the helm. And Nadia Boulanger – the pioneering French composer and conductor who taught generations of musical greats.

Advertising

AI is widely used in France, despite many peoples' misgivings. Tech consultant Frederic Cavazza says adoption is being driven by individuals, rather than a coherent or systemic approach. That results in a paradox: the technology is everywhere, but guidance and confidence in it is lacking. (Listen @2'40'')

One field that is heavily impacted by generative AI in France – and the non-English-language world – is translation. Low-cost translation agencies are increasingly using machines to deliver first drafts and relying on humans for ungratifying, poorly paid "post-editing". But translators are fighting back. The En chair et en os collective and the recently-launched STEF union for translators in publishing marked last week's World Translation Day with symbolic strike action. They gathered to find collective ways of keeping humans at the heart of the translation process, including an initiative to "sabotage" the post-editing system. (Listen @17'50'')

The story of French musician Nadia Boulanger, a talented composer and the first woman to conduct some of the world's top orchestras. Today she is best remembered for teaching an extraordinary number of the 20th century's most famous musicians, from Aaron Copland to Philip Glass, Burt Bacharach and Quincy Jones. (Listen @10'30'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war
World.content:
Officials from Ukraine, Europe and the US are meeting in Miami to discuss ways to break the deadlock in the war. The meeting comes as Russian strikes on Ukraine killed more than 70 people this week.

Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.

Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.

More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.

The capital Kyiv again came under attack this week Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?

"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."

Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.

"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.

"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.

Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting civilians, which the Kremlin denies Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout/Anadolu/picture alliance

Zelenskyy blames US for inaction

Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.

"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at ‌the negotiating table," he said.

Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.

"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.

NATO members in Kyiv: 'We stand unwavering with Ukraine' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked

Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.

"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on ​the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.

Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.

World.title: Man injured after New York shooting involving ICE
World.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has condemned the incident and urged Donald Trump to end ICE actions in the city. The man was being treated at a nearby hospital, New York police said.

A man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent during an arrest in New York City, US federal authorities and Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday.

The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. local time (2100 GMT) in the Marble Hill neighborhood of Manhattan.

The New York Police Department said its officers were not involved in the incident and that the man was conscious and receiving medical attention at a nearby hospital.

US President Donald Trump's administration has scaled up ICE raids in major US cities to detain and deport people who are in the US illegally.

Protesters slammed the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Image: Charly Triballeau/AFP

Mamdani urges Trump to end ICE actions in NYC

New York City Mayor Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he had contacted President Trump.

Mamdani added that a five-year-old child was reportedly in the car during the shooting, but that the child was "physically unharmed."

"This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," Mamdani said in a post on X. "I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities."

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken with Trump and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the shooting. DHS is the parent agency of ICE.

"I expressed outrage on behalf of New Yorkers and urged them to halt ICE enforcement operations in New York," Hochul said. "I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."

Federal govt says 'criminal illegal alien' in hospital receiving treatment

In a post on X, DHS had confirmed that an "ICE officer discharged his weapon" during an attempt to arrest a "criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic" with ties "to the Trinitarios gang."

DHS said the man had a prior conviction for grand larceny and had been arrested "multiple" times for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession.

DHS noted ICE officers immediately rendered aid after the man was injured. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital," the statement said, adding that the FBI was on the scene.

Democrat hopeful for the US House, Darializa Avila Chevalier (center-left), joined a rally outside the hospital where the man was being treated Image: Eduardo Munoz/REUTERS

ICE, CBP fatal shootings raise alarm in second Trump term

Deadly ICE and Border Patrol shootings have drawn major controversy during Trump's second term, particularly regarding the training and oversight of the agents.

An ICE agent killed a 37-year-old US citizen, Renee Good, during their operations in Minneapolis in January, triggering demonstrations there and in several other US cities.

Later that month, Alex Pretti, another US citizen, was killed by two US Customs and Border Protection officers agents in Minneapolis following an altercation.

World.title: US to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution: Pentagon
World.content:
US Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth had said that Nidal Hasan would be executed by firing squad and that it would be done "in public." Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961.

The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.

The confirmation came a day after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said Hasan's execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in "public."

Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.

What did Pete Hegseth say about Nidal Hasan's execution?

In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said Wednesday that Hasan would get "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public."

Hegseth was speaking to right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which ended a nearly 10-month deployment on Thursday.

"People need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth said.

Hasan's execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and will be the first to be done by firing squad since World War II.

Hegseth added: "I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win."

What do we know about the Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan?

US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.

A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.

During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.

The announcement that Hasan will be executed by firing squad comes amid the fallout of the botched execution of Christa Pike.

World.title: Ex-German Chancellor Schröder attends Putin's birthday bash
World.content:
Former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder still maintains a friendship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Tensions are high between Germany and Russia as the invasion of Ukraine continues.

Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder attended Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday party, the Kremlin said Thursday.

Putin celebrated his 74th birthday in Moscow on Wednesday. The Kremlin said Putin learned that Schröder was on a business trip in the Russian capital via Russian media reports.

"The president invited his old friend to his home," the Kremlin said, with the Russian government releasing pictures of Schröder and Putin smiling and clasping hands.

Schröder was visiting Hyperglobus branch after joining board

Schröder, who is 82 years old, was in Moscow visiting one of the branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain. The ex-German chancellor was named to the chain's supervisory board last week.

Schröder was visiting a branch of Russian retailer Hyperglobus on Wednesday, the same day as Putin's birthday celebration Image: RBC/Handout/REUTERS

Hyperglobus was originally part of German retail company Globus Holding, which operates the Globus supermarkets in Germany and the Czech Republic.

Globus Holding also had supermarkets in Russia, but divested its stake last year, with those stores thus being spun off into seperate company Hyperglobus.

What backlash has Schröder faced in Germany over his Russia ties?

Schröder, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), served as Germany's chancellor from 1998 to 2005.

Since leaving the chancellery, Schröder has worked for Russian state-owned energy firms and has also maintained personal contact with Putin.

Why Putin turned to ex‑German chancellor as a peace broker To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Schröder's fondness for Russia has drawn controversy, particularly since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Schröder's tax-payer financed Berlin office was closed in 2022 over his involvement in the Russian energy sector, and he has also faced calls by fellow party members to be expelled from the SPD.

Schröder, however, has survived the attempt to be kicked out of his party.

World.title: UK: Two Latvian men arrested for breaking into RAF base
World.content:
The men were arrested for breaching a perimeter fence at a UK air base that houses US and NATO intelligence operations. The incident comes after an alleged terror plot at another air base in England was foiled recently.

Two Latvian men have been arrested for breaching the perimeter fence at an RAF base used by the US military, UK police said Thursday.

The two UK residents, aged 36 and 32, were arrested by counterterrorism police at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Molesworth base in southeastern England, 70 miles north of London.

Police said they were being held on suspicion of trespassing, causing criminal damage and entering a prohibited place "for a purpose prejudicial to the UK."

A former World War II airbase, RAF Molesworth, is now a non-flying facility that is managed by the US Air Force.

It houses intelligence personnel from US Africa Command and the NATO Intelligence Fusion Center, which provides information to the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.

The incident comes after several men were arrested amid an alleged terror plot at another UK air base last month.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know about the incident at RAF Molesworth?

According to a statement from Counter Terrorism Policing London, officers from the Ministry of Defense Police and Cambridgeshire Constabulary began investigating an incident at approximately 10 p.m. local time on Wednesday after an abandoned vehicle was found near the edge of the base.

Police later discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence and arrested the two suspects at around 2 a.m. on Thursday.

The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage. They were later arrested on charges of entering a prohibited place with the intent to harm the UK.

Both men remain in police custody. Due to the nature of the offense, the matter is being investigated by counterterrorism police.

Is this related to the RAF Fairford incident?

On September 27, authorities discovered three suspicious vans near RAF Fairford, a British air base from which US bombers launched strikes against Iran. This triggered a widespread investigation that led to seven arrests.

Last weekend, the US Air Force brought home all the bombers deployed to the base.

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of the counterterrorism unit, said that while UK authorities are "very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites", there is "nothing to suggest" the incident at RAF Molesworth is related to what happened at RAF Fairford last week, although she added that the investigation was still in its "very early stages."

The US European Command acknowledged the incident but declined to comment on specific force protection measures.

World.title: Afghan women facing arrest for dress code violations: UN
World.content:
In recent months, the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan have arrested or detained dozens of women for alleged violations of dress codes and for appearing in public without a male guardian.

At least 52 women and one girl were arrested or detained in the Afghan cities of Herat and Kabul between July and September of 2026, according to a statement released by the United Nations on Thursday.

"Women were detained for not wearing a chador [an all-enveloping, cloak-like garment], having visible hair, wearing colourful scarves or makeup, or being in public without a mahram [male chaperone]," the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said.

According to the mission, the detained women were released after being held for several hours. It also warned that the number of cases could be higher due to underreporting.

In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UNAMA said it was "gravely concerned" by the arrests, detentions, and threats of arrest.

The mission stated that the detentions violate women's and girls' rights to freedom of movement, expression, and autonomy. The detentions also expose them to severe social stigma in traditional Afghan society, UNAMA said.

In June, Afghan authorities opened fire on a rare protest in Herat over the arrests and detentions of women for alleged dress code violations. According to witnesses and the UN mission, at least one person was killed and several others were injured.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What restrictions do women in Afghanistan face?

Since seizing power in 2021 as US-led forces withdrew from Afghanistan, the Taliban government has imposed severe restrictions on women and girls, including banning them from attending school beyond the primary level and limiting what they can wear and where they can go.

In public, women must wear a full hijab, which includes a headscarf, a long robe that covers the body, and a face covering. The Ministry for the Propagation of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice enforces these rules.

Earlier this week, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued four arrest warrants for senior Taliban officials, accusing them of committing crimes against humanity by systematically depriving women and girls in Afghanistan of their rights.

Hovewer, the Taliban rejected the decision, calling it a politically motivated violation of Afghanistan's sovereignty.

World.title: US suspends Microsoft, Adobe from filing for green cards
World.content:
The Trump administration cut off tech firms, including Microsoft and Adobe, from filing for green cards for their foreign workers.

The Trump administration on Thursday said it was suspending major tech firms, including Microsoft, from applying for a program that allowed their foreign workers to work permanently in the US.

US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling accused those tech firms of abusing the program — the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) — that had so far been a legal pathway for workers to apply for green cards.

"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labor Certification Program some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said.

Sonderling said the suspensions were due to ongoing federal investigations into those firms.

There are good reasons that Indian media firms covered the issue so urgently because many of those firms are either Indian or rely on thousands of Indian professionals who've moved to the country.

Trump administration accuses Microsoft of abusing program for green cards

Vice President JD Vance said the PERM system required companies to advertise work in the US before they applied for green cards for foreign workers due to a lack of qualified American job applicants.

"They'll put an  in a small-town newspaper. They'll go out there and say that 'We have advertised for a position with our company, and nobody is responding to it.' And they will use that lack of response to then go and replace American workers with what is effectively foreign indentured servants," Vance claimed.

President Trump presenting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation on October 8. Image: Evan Vucci/REUTERS

"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has used this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.

The announcement came hours before US President Donald Trump was scheduled to award the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

Microsoft says majority of its workers are Americans

Microsoft said in a statement that it looked forward to providing the administration with additional information, saying the majority of its workers are Americans and that a large part of the H-1B filings have to do with the status of people already based in the US.

"We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings," the company said.

The H-1B visa program is another part of the Trump administration's crackdown on immigration, as concerns have long persisted that the visa for skilled workers has displaced Americans in favor of lower-cost foreign labor.

Microsoft employs 125,000 US workers and 103,000 international workers, according to the company's 2025 annual report .

World.title: South Africa: Anti-migrant protests turn violent
World.content:
A court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications reignited violent protests against immigration in South Africa.

Anti-migrant protests erupted in South Africa on Thursday as tensions over immigration were reignited by a court order requiring the government to resume processing asylum applications.

Some of the protests turned violent, according to local media reports. This included incidents in the coastal city of Durban and the Soweto township of Johannesburg, where cars were set on fire and gunshots were heard.

What do we know about protests in South Africa?

The unrest in Durban reportedly followed a protest by a group demanding that a refugee center stop processing asylum applications. About 10 vehicles were overturned and set on fire. Foreign-owned shops were also looted.

Meanwhile, in Soweto, residents clashed with foreign shop owners, and gunshots were heard, according to the broadcaster Newzroom Afrika.

At least nine vehicles were torched, said Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department spokesman Superintendent Xolani Fihla in an interview with SABC television.

"It's reported that there were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals," he said. "At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported."

Police fired rubber bullets when clashes erupted between protesters and foreign nationals in Durban Image: Rajesh Jantilal/AFP

What has the court decided?

The court ruling that sparked the flare-up of xenophobic tensions deemed certain provisions of the government's refugee policy to be unconstitutional.

The court explained that this was because the provisions prevented individuals from accessing the asylum system on procedural grounds, such as entering the country illegally.

Recently, this ruling has led hundreds of people, reportedly including those who do not qualify for asylum, to flock to government refugee centers.

On Wednesday, the government emphasized that the judgement "does not grant refugee status or permanent residence automatically to anyone who enters South Africa."

Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Xenophobic sentiment in South Africa

South Africa has experienced months of anti-immigrant protests this year. Populist and anti-immigrant groups have demanded that undocumented foreign nationals leave by June 30.

Amidst international criticism, tens of thousands of people have fled the country, while some were repatriated by their governments.

Although South Africa has a third of its population unemployed, it remains the largest economy in Africa and continues to attract migrants.

Migrants are often blamed for taking jobs, fueling crime, and straining public services. However, social scientists have said these accusations are not supported by evidence.
