World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, finds UN study
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte. The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study. “Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte. 📉Facts matter. Refugees from Ukraine contributed 2.4% of Poland’s GDP in 2025, says new analysis by UNHCR and Deloitte. This is what happens when people forced to flee are given the opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity. The full report: https://t.co/egUp8jjCwc pic.twitter.com/CSNONqdKGU — UNHCR Polska (@UNHCRPoland) October 1, 2026 The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025. Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further. The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before. The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data. The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens. However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens. Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland. Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise. The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million. Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity. Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”. Indeed, in 2025, they paid around 2.8 billion zloty more in health-insurance contributions than the cost of the services they received. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives. Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work. Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded. The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2025 The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status. Meanwhile, surveys show a weakening of refugees’ intentions to eventually return to Ukraine. Research by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) found that the proportion who plan to settle permanently in Poland rose from 21% to 25% between 2024 and 2025. However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine. World.title: Poland to review Paramount takeover of TVN through acquisition of Warner Bros
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will examine whether Paramount Skydance can take control of TVN, one of the country’s leading broadcasters, following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns TVN. The review is being conducted under a law that requires state approval for ownership changes of companies designated by the government as strategic and protected from takeovers deemed to threaten the national interest. TVN was added to the list in 2024, following reports of its possible sale. Minister Aktywów Państwowych zajmie się przejęciem TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance#PAPinformacjehttps://t.co/FxxDnozx9i — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) October 6, 2026 Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest mergers in the global media market, brings together major US media assets including Paramount’s CBS and MTV and Warner’s HBO, CNN and Discovery Channel. After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover. The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”. The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares. “I assure you that it will be an entirely substantive and objective administrative procedure, carried out in fulfilment of a statutory obligation, and nothing more,” Balczun told broadcaster Kanał Zero on Tuesday. The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest. That move came amid reports that Warner Bros. Discovery was considering selling TVN and that a businessman linked to Hungary’s then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Poland’s conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, was seeking to buy it. 🎙️Minister @wbalczun w @OficjalneZero o przeprowadzeniu postępowania ws. przejęcia TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance: bardziej bym skupił się na organie, czyli ministrze aktywów państwowych. To jest odpersonalizowana procedura administracyjna, która wynika z ustawy o kontroli… pic.twitter.com/jp3J9zC0jh — Ministerstwo Aktywów Państwowych 🇵🇱 (@MAPGOVPL) October 7, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time the move was intended to protect the broadcaster from hostile foreign takeovers and prevent foreign interference in Poland’s media and elections. TVN, which was originally founded in 1995, has been in American hands since 2015, when it was bought by US broadcaster Scripps, which was in turn acquired by Discovery in 2018. The station, which is known for taking a liberal position on many issues, has long been a target for Polish conservatives. In 2021, the then-PiS government passed a law that would have forced Warner Bros. Discovery to sell its majority stake. However, that was vetoed by then-President Andrzej Duda. Poland is adding the country’s two largest private TV stations, Polsat and TVN, to its list of “strategic companies” under special protection. That allows the government to block the sale of the firms to owners from “hostile states”, says PM @donaldtusk https://t.co/TwK9IFRPrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2024 Some in Poland have expressed fear that Paramount could push TVN in a more conservative direction, as it has been accused of doing with other media outlets it has acquired, notably US broadcaster CBS. Paramount’s owner, David Ellison, is a Trump ally, as are PiS and Poland’s current president, Karol Nawrocki. On Sunday, the Journalists’ Association, a Polish organisation representing journalists, called on TVN’s management to establish an editorial independence council similar to those being created at CNN and CBS under the settlement deal that paved the way for the merger in the US. Media reports claim that President Trump tried to persuade Poland's defence minister to leave the government and form a coalition with the right-wing opposition. We outline what is known so far and how the government, including PM @donaldtusk, has reacted https://t.co/m04H8VgoSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 5, 2026 In July, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) also raised concerns about the potential impact of the merger on TVN’s editorial independence, citing the new ownership structure and the risk of political interference. The NGO called for guarantees protecting the channel as a condition of approval for the takeover from the European Commission. The EU executive, however, approved the deal in July without imposing such conditions, following an antitrust review. The commission’s approval covered the entire European Union, meaning that national competition authorities have no grounds to challenge the deal, Tomasz Chróstny, head of Poland’s consumer protection authority UOKiK, told news service Wirtualna Polska before the transaction was completed. World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: 15-year-old boy beaten with branches in Hungary after refusing to give up his property
World.content:
A 15-year-old boy suffered serious-looking injuries after several youths allegedly attacked him with willow branches in a park in Pilis, near Budapest, on Wednesday. The boy had reportedly refused to hand over a carabiner attached to his keys. His friend was also injured.

According to a report by TV2 Híradó, the incident happened in broad daylight in a park that also contains a playground. The confrontation reportedly began when another teenager took an interest in the carabiner attached to the 15-year-old’s keyring and tried to take it from him.

The boy refused and managed to take back his property. Several people then allegedly attacked him.

The attackers reportedly broke branches from a nearby willow tree and used them to hit the two boys. The 15-year-old was left with long, bloody marks across his back and what appeared to be a large red handprint, while his friend suffered an injury to his calf.

Photographs taken after the incident showed the extent of the injuries.

Mayor arrived before authorities

The injured boy’s family remained in contact with him by phone before asking Pilis Mayor Attila László for help. The mayor said he and his colleagues reached the scene before municipal wardens.

“We arrived before the wardens and told the group that nobody could leave the area,”

László told TV2 Híradó. He said he took photographs and videos at the scene and gathered information about what had happened. According to the mayor’s account, the boy had attempted to defend himself after the carabiner was taken from him and eventually managed to recover it.

A crowd soon gathered at the park, including relatives of both the injured boys and those allegedly involved in the attack. László later addressed the incident on social media, saying that the town should have zero tolerance for violent acts. He called for the circumstances to be thoroughly investigated and for anyone found responsible to face the consequences under the law.

Police investigation expected

The mayor also raised concerns about information allegedly given to the victims’ families at the Monor Police Station. According to his account, one parent was reportedly told that a criminal complaint could be made after obtaining medical documentation of the injuries, but that little would come of the case because the alleged perpetrators were under 16.

László questioned this information, pointing out that the general minimum age of criminal responsibility in Hungary is 14. Being under 18 can result in different procedures and sanctions, but does not automatically rule out criminal responsibility.

He called on the Monor police to clarify exactly what information had been given to the parents and what action would be taken. The mayor later said he had been contacted by the Monor Police Station and informed that proceedings would be launched against those allegedly involved.

The investigation will determine the precise circumstances of the incident, including whether the initial attempt to take the boy’s property and the subsequent assault could amount to robbery or other offences.

The case also comes with a political and social controversy, as László’s public statement included inflammatory comments about the alleged attackers’ ethnic background and called for members of their community to leave Pilis and Hungary. Those remarks are separate from the factual question of what happened during the alleged assault, which will have to be established by the authorities.

World.title: Orbán-era oligarchs reportedly seek immunity deals as corruption arrests grow
World.content:
Some members of Hungary’s former economic elite are reportedly looking to make deals with the new Tisza government, with one wealthy oligarch allegedly offering to return assets and money in exchange for protection from prosecution.

Oligarch reportedly offers assets in exchange for immunity

Some members of the economic elite associated with the former Orbán era are already seeking ways to reach an agreement with Hungary’s new government as several prominent figures face criminal investigations and arrests, according to the latest edition of the VSquare newsletter Goulash.

A senior member of the Tisza government told VSquare that one unnamed, wealthy and influential oligarch has reportedly been sending messages to the government through intermediaries. According to the source, the businessman would be prepared to return assets and money in exchange for immunity from prosecution.

The source did not identify the oligarch or specify the amount of money or assets allegedly involved. It is also unclear whether the government led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar is willing to consider such an arrangement.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Another oligarch reportedly chooses a different strategy

According to the same source, another member of the former economic elite has chosen a different approach. Rather than attempting to negotiate immunity, the oligarch is reportedly keeping a low profile, returning whatever the government demands and trying to remain in business through bids from foreign subcontractors.

The source compared this strategy to that previously used by Austrian construction company Strabag, which operated while being placed on a blacklist by the previous Orbán government. The reports come amid a series of high-profile arrests involving figures linked to Hungary’s former political and economic establishment.

High-profile arrests shake former elite

In September, Dániel Jellinek, Hungary’s seventh-richest person and CEO of property company Indotek, was detained together with former state asset manager chief Norbert Szivek over alleged bribery linked to public transport bus purchases.

A court ordered Jellinek to remain in pre-trial detention for a month. His company has denied wrongdoing on his behalf, and the detention order is under appeal.

Two weeks later, former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták were arrested within hours of Parliament lifting their immunity. Courts subsequently ordered 30 days of detention for both men in separate corruption-related cases.

The arrests have contributed to growing uncertainty among members of the economic elite who built their fortunes or political connections during the previous governing era.

Will the new government make deals?

The VSquare source said it remains unclear how willing Magyar’s government will be to negotiate with former oligarchs and potentially spare them from prosecution in exchange for the return of assets. Any such agreements would raise significant questions about accountability and the treatment of wealth accumulated during the previous political era.

World.title: Wizz Air cancels several Eastern flights for the entire winter season
World.content:
Wizz Air has scrapped its planned winter return to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, citing ongoing airspace restrictions that have made the routes commercially unviable.

Wizz Air postpones Middle East return

Wizz Air will not resume its planned flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai this winter after cancelling all services to and from the two UAE destinations for the season. The airline had originally planned to operate the routes between 25 October and 27 March, following an earlier announcement that it would return to the UAE alongside services to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan.

The latest decision comes just days after Wizz Air initially announced that some Abu Dhabi routes would be postponed until January following updated safety guidance from Europe’s aviation regulator. The airline has now cancelled the Abu Dhabi and Dubai services for the entire winter season.

Longer routes make flights too expensive

Wizz Air said the decision was prompted by regional airspace restrictions that were extended on 30 September. The restrictions mean aircraft would have to take significantly longer routes to reach their destinations, increasing both flight times and operating costs.

According to the airline, the resulting costs make operating the routes commercially unviable under current conditions, including with its Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft.

“We regret the disruption to travel plans and will continue to monitor developments, reassessing operations as safety guidance and operating conditions evolve,” Wizz Air said in a statement to The National.

The airline also confirmed that its planned flights to and from Amman are affected by the latest conflict-zone guidance from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace.

Have you heard? Wizz Air rethink could reshape ticket prices and routes across Europe

Wizz Air had planned a major Middle East comeback

The cancelled UAE services were part of a much bigger planned return to the Middle East. For the winter season, Wizz Air had announced plans for 12 routes and 49 weekly flights connecting nine European cities with destinations in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

The planned network would have offered around 470,000 seats across the three countries. Wizz Air had suspended its European-operated Middle East services in late February following the escalation of the regional conflict.

The planned return came after the airline’s low-cost subsidiary Wizz Air Abu Dhabi ceased operations in September 2025. The continuing airspace restrictions have also forced other international airlines to adjust their schedules and routes across the region.

For passengers who had been planning to fly Wizz Air to Abu Dhabi or Dubai this winter, the latest announcement means the airline’s much-anticipated return will have to wait.

World.title: Ecuador brings its culture to Hungary as the two countries celebrate 80 years of diplomatic ties
World.content:
In the framework of the celebration of the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Republic of Ecuador and Hungary, the Embassy of Ecuador successfully hosted a magnificent series of cultural events last week. These celebrations were meticulously curated to commemorate this historic bilateral milestone, bringing the rich, diverse, and vibrant heritage of Ecuador directly to the heart of Central Europe. Through cinema, traditional music, fine arts, and gastronomy, the Embassy highlighted the enduring friendship, strategic cooperation, and mutual admiration that have characterised the diplomatic ties between the two nations over the past eight decades.

The commemorative week officially commenced with a grand celebration of Ecuadorian cinema in Budapest. The Embassy of Ecuador proudly inaugurated the 2026 Latin American Film Festival at the highly emblematic and prestigious Uránia National Film Theatre. The opening night featured a special screening of the acclaimed Ecuadorian film, “Puka Urpi”. The event drew a distinguished audience, including prominent local authorities, enthusiastic members of the Ecuadorian community residing in Hungary, and numerous international cinema lovers. The compelling narrative of “Puka Urpi” served as a powerful medium for cultural exchange, allowing the Hungarian audience to immerse themselves in the visual storytelling and profound cultural landscapes of Ecuador.

Photo: Embassy of Ecuador in Hungary

Following the success of the film screening, the celebrations continued with an unforgettable evening at the renowned Eötvös10 Cultural Centre in Budapest. The Embassy orchestrated a cultural gala centred around the “Misa del Chimborazo”, an event that masterfully intertwined Ecuador’s musical heritage, visual arts, iconic floral exports, and world-class coffee. The event was met with overwhelming enthusiasm, boasting a full house of more than 180 attendees. It was a profound honour to share these cherished traditions with the beloved Ecuadorian diaspora, members of the diplomatic corps, respected Hungarian authorities, and local friends deeply enamoured with Latin American culture.

The centrepiece of the evening was the majestic “Misa del Chimborazo”, a monumental Andean and choral composition by the esteemed Ecuadorian composer Mario Godoy. This breathtaking musical journey was brought to life through a collaborative performance featuring the virtuoso Francisco “Paco” Godoy, the magnificent Pesterzsébet Mixed Choir, and the celebrated traditional music group, Los Andinos. The audience was captivated by an emotional repertoire that transcended borders, taking listeners on a musical voyage through exquisite choral pieces, traditional melodies rooted in the majestic Andean highlands, nostalgic pasillos, and vibrant urban mestizo rhythms.

Photo: Embassy of Ecuador in Hungary

If you missed it: The heart of Ecuador is back in Budapest – photos

Complementing this auditory feast was a stunning visual showcase by Ecuadorian plastic artist Daniela Godoy, whose colourful and evocative painting exhibition elegantly dressed the venue’s lobby, showcasing the profound artistic talent of the nation. Furthermore, the atmosphere was beautifully enhanced by the unmatched elegance and vibrant colours of Ecuadorian roses, generously provided by Naranjo Roses, which transformed the space into a sensory garden. Attendees were also treated to a warm and inviting tasting of exquisite Ecuadorian coffee, courtesy of Flor’d Café, allowing guests to savour the authentic, world-renowned flavours of the country’s highlands.

The week of cultural festivities culminated outside the capital at the historic Esterházy Palace in Fertőd, widely celebrated as the “Hungarian Versailles.” The Embassy of Ecuador, acting in synergy with other Latin American embassies, proudly participated in the highly anticipated first edition of the Latin American Festival in Fertőd. This majestic 18th-century Baroque architectural jewel – historically significant for hosting much of the illustrious career of classical composer Joseph Haydn – provided an unparalleled and evocative backdrop for celebrating Latin American roots in Hungary.

Photo: Embassy of Ecuador in Hungary

Ecuador’s prominent presence at the festival was marked by a highly dynamic and engaging national stand, which offered comprehensive information about the country, interactive games for children, and exciting prizes for attendees. To further promote the nation’s biodiversity and attractions, the Embassy conducted an inspiring tourism promotion seminar, inviting the local public to discover the wonders of Ecuador. The country’s representation was further enriched by vibrant displays of painting and art by Ecuadorian Hungarian painter Gina Altamirano, alongside spectacular and joyful musical performances featuring Los Andinos, Paco Godoy, Mario Godoy, whose rhythms resonated through the historic palace grounds.

As the Embassy of Ecuador reflects on a week of unprecedented cultural engagement, these events stand as a testament to the robust, dynamic, and ever-growing relationship between Ecuador and Hungary. As both nations celebrate 80 years of shared history and diplomatic cooperation, the universal languages of art, music, and cinema continue to forge an unbreakable bridge of understanding and fraternity between their peoples.

World.title: Hungary and Türkiye restart structured diplomatic cooperation after government change
World.content:
Hungary and Türkiye are restarting structured cooperation between their foreign ministries and opening a new dialogue on security policy, Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said following talks in Ankara on Thursday.

The meeting marked the first Hungarian-Turkish foreign ministerial talks since Hungary’s new government took office, according to Orbán. The two sides held several hours of discussions, during which the Hungarian-Turkish Joint Planning Group also met in Ankara for the first time.

The group is responsible for coordinating key issues between the two countries and helping organise high-level meetings.

New dialogue on security and EU affairs

Orbán said Hungary and Türkiye would relaunch structured professional cooperation between their foreign ministries and initiate a new dialogue on security policy.

Hungary will also provide practical assistance to Türkiye in EU-related matters. Through the TAIEX programme, Hungarian EU experts will share their knowledge and experience with Turkish institutions as part of the two countries’ cooperation.

TAIEX is an EU technical assistance programme that helps partner countries align their legislation, institutions and practices with EU standards.

If you missed it: Hungarian FM: Viktor Orbán’s influence still entrenched as government dismantles former system

Energy and defence industry cooperation to continue

The two countries also agreed to continue developing their energy cooperation, while strengthening economic and defence industry ties. Orbán said Hungary and Türkiye would also take further steps to expand transport connections between the two countries.

One recent development is the direct Budapest–Ankara flight, which began operating in April 2026. Orbán also noted that the Hungarian Parliament has ratified a new air services agreement with Türkiye. Once the agreement enters into force, Hungary expects air traffic between the two countries to develop further.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan holds joint press conference with Hungarian Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Photo: Anadolu Agency Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan holds joint press conference with Hungarian Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Türkiye’s wider security concerns

The talks also took place against the backdrop of a number of international security issues. At a joint press conference, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Türkiye had completed preparations to submit its Mecca defence agreement to parliament for approval. He stressed that the agreement is defensive in nature and provides for mutual support if one of its parties comes under attack.

Fidan also discussed the war in Ukraine, warning against the conflict spreading into the Black Sea and highlighting the impact of attacks on shipping and navigational safety.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan holds joint press conference with Hungarian Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Photo: Anadolu Agency Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan holds joint press conference with Hungarian Deputy PM and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. Photo: Anadolu Agency

The Turkish minister additionally addressed the situation in Gaza and the West Bank, saying Türkiye would continue its diplomatic efforts to support humanitarian aid and a lasting peace.

For Hungary, however, Thursday’s meeting marked a restart of bilateral diplomatic cooperation, with energy, defence industry, EU affairs, security policy and transport links among the key areas identified for closer cooperation.

World.title: Billions for defence? New international bank puts Hungary in the spotlight
World.content:
The proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank could add a new financing channel for defence production, military mobility and critical infrastructure. A new analysis argues that the real question is not political symbolism, but whether the model can lower financing costs and improve market access for Hungarian companies.

A new multilateral financial institution designed specifically to finance defence, security and resilience investment is moving closer to reality – and the debate over its potential role in Central and Eastern Europe is now reaching Budapest.

The proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) is still in its establishment phase, but the initiative has already attracted public support from nine governments. Canada is the prospective host country, Luxembourg is developing a role as its European financial hub, and the political objective is for the institution to begin operations in 2027.

Ahead of the next stage of that debate, a new analysis by Halftermayer & Partners, authored by Dr Ferenc Antal, examines what the emerging institution could mean for Europe and, more specifically, whether Hungary could use it to finance investments it will increasingly need to make anyway at a lower all-in cost and with greater domestic industrial value creation.

Budapest to host international defence finance forum on 21 October

The discussion will also move from research to the conference table later this month. On 21 October, Budapest will host the International Defence Finance Conference – Financing Defence, Security and Resilience in Hungary and Central & Eastern Europe, an invitation-only executive forum organised by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hungary.

The event is expected to bring together senior Hungarian and Canadian government representatives, representatives of the proposed DSRB initiative and the Central Bank of Hungary, commercial banks, multilateral finance institutions, legal and advisory experts, and industry leaders.

One of the central purposes of the conference is to move the debate around the DSRB from institutional concept to practical financial questions: how lending and guarantee instruments could work in practice, what banks would need in order to use them, how defence and resilience projects can become bankable, and where Hungary and the wider Central and Eastern European region could fit into the emerging system.

The programme is intended to combine an international defence-finance discussion with a Hungary and Central and Eastern Europe-focused session, followed by a smaller closed-door executive consultation. The event is not an official DSRB conference: it is a broader defence-finance forum in which the proposed bank will be one of the central subjects of structured knowledge-sharing and market consultation.

The event is also supported by leading international organisations, including global professional services firm PwC and ING Bank, the latter of which is actively involved in the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) initiative at an international level.

If you missed it – Billions at stake in NATO’s new pledge: how much of the defence spend stays in Hungary?

So what exactly is the DSRB?

Despite its defence focus, the proposed institution would not be a NATO bank or an EU fund. Its model is closer to a specialised multilateral development bank: member states would provide capital, the DSRB would raise money on capital markets in its own name, and that funding could then be deployed through long-term loans, guarantees, co-financing and other risk-sharing instruments.

Public DSRB material currently envisages a capital structure consisting of 20% paid-in capital and 80% callable capital, with financing capacity potentially reaching five to eight times the institution’s capital base. The bank would seek a high credit rating – ideally AAA – although the Halftermayer & Partners study stresses that such a rating remains an objective rather than an established fact.

Public reporting has referred to an ambition to mobilise up to approximately USD 135 billion for defence and resilience projects. The study cautions that this should not be confused with money already committed or lending capacity that currently exists. The actual scale will depend on capital subscriptions, leverage, market access and the eventual credit rating of the institution.
