World.title: Russian strike on civilian buses kills 33 in Ukraine
World.content:
At least 33 people have been killed and another 18 injured after Russian glide bombs struck two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine, according to Ukrainian officials and rescue workers.

Civilian buses hit in Kramatorsk

Two buses carrying civilians were hit in a Russian glide bomb attack in Kramatorsk, Donetsk region, Ukrainian authorities said.

Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said 33 people were killed and 18 others wounded. He accused Russia of deliberately targeting passenger buses in an attempt to cause as many civilian casualties as possible.

The BBC reported that images released by local prosecutors showed the burned-out remains of one of the buses and debris scattered across the road. Moscow had not commented on the attack at the time of publication.

Filashkin urged residents who remain in the Donetsk region to leave for safer parts of Ukraine. Public transport has also been ordered to stop in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk following the sharp deterioration in security.

“We have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers,” Filashkin said, stressing that the safety of civilians was the priority.

The strike targeted two civilian buses, killing 30 people in Kramatorsk, while shelling in nearby Bilenke claimed three more lives, bringing the total regional casualties to 33 dead and 18 injured. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Kramatorsk under growing pressure

Kramatorsk and nearby Slovyansk form part of a defensive belt in the Donbas that Russia is seeking to capture as its forces advance through eastern Ukraine.

Kramatorsk has served as an important logistics and supply hub for Ukrainian forces throughout much of the war. The city is now facing increasingly frequent Russian attacks as Russian troops move closer.

Glide bombs have been used repeatedly against both Kramatorsk and Slovyansk. These weapons are fitted with wings that allow them to glide towards their targets after being released from an aircraft.

Kramatorsk City Council described the latest attack as a “horrific crime” against civilians, saying there were no military targets at the location that was hit. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also condemned the attack and said it would receive a response.

Doctors are now fighting to save the lives of people injured in the Russian strike on Kramatorsk. As of now, 30 people have been confirmed killed, and sadly, that number may rise. The Russian bomb effectively hit two city minibuses. Some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries. My condolences to all their families and loved ones. Another 18 people were injured in the strike. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged. This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace. — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 8, 2026

If you missed it: Pneumonic plague fears grip Russia after lab worker dies, quarantine measures imposed

Kyiv also hit as schools and public transport disrupted

Russian air raids continued over Kyiv on Thursday, with air-raid sirens sounding throughout the day. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said three people had been killed and 14 wounded in attacks on the capital, with two of those injured reported to be in critical condition.

The strikes have disrupted daily life across the city. Schoolchildren have been sent to shelters, businesses have closed and public transport has been affected.

Attacks on energy infrastructure have also caused power cuts and disrupted water supplies. Local water authorities warned that water pressure was falling across parts of Kyiv’s right bank because of electricity shortages.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Civilian deaths surge as Russian attacks intensify

These attacks come after a sharp increase in civilian casualties in Ukraine. According to the United Nations, more Ukrainian civilians had been killed by August this year than during the whole of 2025. On Wednesday, a Russian strike destroyed part of a five-storey residential building in Pryluky, east of Kyiv, killing 22 people, including five children. Three of the children were just one year old.

British Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who met Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the Pryluky attack demonstrated Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “evil intent and evil strategy”. He also announced additional UK sanctions targeting Russia’s war effort, including its shadow fleet, oil companies, cryptocurrency and other sources of war financing. The UK, Lammy said, would continue to support Ukraine “as long as it takes”.

Ukraine calls for more air defence

Zelensky has called on Ukraine’s international partners to provide concrete support, including new defence packages to protect the country from Russian attacks. Ukraine has faced shortages of interceptor missiles as Russia and Ukraine have both intensified long-range strikes in recent months.

Russian attacks have increasingly targeted Ukrainian infrastructure, including energy facilities, data centres and logistics sites, while Ukrainian forces have continued to carry out strikes against targets inside Russia. For civilians in cities such as Kramatorsk and Kyiv, however, air-raid warnings and shelters are among the few available protections against incoming attacks.

World.title: Polish-Hungarian friendship meets a new challenge: who pays for the power grid?
World.content:
A Polish-Hungarian friendship dating back centuries may seem far removed from today’s electricity bills, but a recent energy forum in Budapest offered an unexpected connection between the two.

At the Polish-Hungarian Energy Forum, American creator Ray Brown of Magyar Minute found himself among Polish and Hungarian energy specialists discussing a very modern challenge: how should the costs of maintaining and expanding the electricity grid be shared as more households and businesses produce and store their own energy?

Brown attended the Budapest event with the help of Alpár Kató, founder of Daily News Hungary. The following account is his personal perspective on the forum and the issues discussed there.

From an old friendship to a modern energy challenge

Poland and Hungary have a long history of close relations, but the forum showed how cooperation between the two countries can also have a practical role in dealing with today’s energy challenges.

Energy security, regional cooperation and the future of Europe’s electricity system were among the issues discussed. One particularly interesting question concerns who should ultimately pay for the infrastructure that connects electricity producers and consumers.

The question is becoming more relevant as the energy system changes. Traditionally, electricity has largely flowed from centralised power plants through the grid to consumers. However, households and businesses are increasingly able to generate electricity themselves, for example through rooftop solar panels, while batteries and other storage technologies are also becoming more common.

That raises a question that goes beyond simply producing electricity: if customers increasingly generate some of their own power, how should they contribute to the cost of the network they continue to rely on?

Photo: Alpár Kató/Daily News Hungary

Where does Paks fit into the picture?

Hungary’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant is central to the country’s electricity supply and was also discussed in the context of energy security.

Paks produces nearly half of Hungary’s domestically generated electricity, according to MVM. This does not mean that the plant supplies nearly half of all electricity consumed in Hungary, as the country also imports electricity.

The distinction is important when considering Hungary’s overall energy system, particularly at a time when supply security and the resilience of the electricity network are becoming increasingly important.

Europe’s grid faces a major investment challenge

The debate is not limited to Hungary or Poland. Eurelectric’s Grids for Speed study estimates that distribution grids in the EU and Norway could require investments of up to EUR 67 billion per year through 2050. The report also notes that more efficient planning and greater flexibility could reduce the investment required.

Contrary to one interpretation raised during the discussion, the study does include distributed generation and energy storage in its modelling. The broader concern discussed at the Budapest forum was instead how changing customer behaviour and the growth of self-generation could affect the way network costs are shared.

In other words, producing electricity at home may reduce a customer’s reliance on the grid at certain times, but it does not eliminate the need for the infrastructure itself.

Screenshot: Magyar Minute Screenshot: Magyar Minute

The complicated question of cutting electricity demand

Another topic discussed was Hungary’s efforts to reduce electricity consumption during periods of pressure on the system.

Figures reported in connection with voluntary demand reductions need some context. MTI reported on 2 August that companies had initially pledged around 250 MW of reductions, with the figure potentially rising to 400–500 MW.

Separately, consumption by businesses, public institutions and households was around 500 MW below MAVIR’s forecast on the previous day.

These figures describe different things: company commitments, the difference between actual consumption and a forecast, and verified reductions attributable to particular groups should not be treated as interchangeable measures.

A shared network means shared responsibilities

The discussion ultimately returns to a simple but increasingly important issue. Europe’s electricity system is changing. More renewable generation, household solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles and flexible consumption are creating new opportunities, but they are also changing how electricity moves through the network.

The grid still has to be maintained, upgraded and expanded — even when the people connected to it are producing some of their own electricity.

For countries such as Hungary and Poland, cooperation on energy security is therefore not only about where electricity comes from. It is also about how the infrastructure behind the system is financed and adapted to a changing energy landscape. An old friendship may have brought the countries together, but the challenge facing their electricity networks is decidedly modern.

World.title: Serbian Watchdog Claims Voters’ Rights Under Threat Ahead of Elections
World.content:
Serbian election watchdog CRTA asserted on Thursday that citizens’ electoral rights and freedoms are being undermined by intimidation, violence and unlawful surveillance ahead of the October 25 parliamentary elections.

CRTA’s election monitoring report claimed that opposition figures have been subjected to unlawful surveillance and police operations.

It also claimed that pro-government politicians and media had spread “manipulative narratives” about alleged opposition plans to incite unrest and overthrow the constitutional order.

CRTA’s monitoring found that nearly 1,500 articles in pro-government online media warned of chaos and violence on election day, while an average of seven articles daily portrayed opposition activities as an attempted “colour revolution”, referencing the popular revolts that toppled authoritarian, pro-Moscow governments in Ukraine and elsewhere.

CRTA programme director Rasa Nedeljkov said another key issue was “widespread electoral engineering” , which “clearly involves Serbia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs”.

According to CRTA, around 22,000 Serbian citizens living abroad could effectively be denied the right to vote because of the decision not to open polling stations in all countries where sufficient numbers of voters had registered.

“The ministry made a poorly explained, vague and unconvincing decision not to open polling stations in countries where a sufficient number of voters had registered to vote,” Nedeljkov said.

Nedeljkov said another example of “electoral engineering” was the “unrealistic decision by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) requiring voters in all time zones to cast their ballots according to Serbian time, making it even more difficult for them to exercise their right to vote”.

The new rule rule obliging voters abroad to follow polling hours based on Central European Time means some diaspora Serbians would have to cast ballots in the middle of the night.

The report also highlighted unequal media coverage, saying opposition parties have received half as much airtime as the ruling parties on national television, much of it negative. On the public broadcaster, RTS, the opposition has received just 15 per cent of airtime devoted to political actors, largely due to mandatory election coverage segments.

Nedeljkov said the mission was alarmed by persistent efforts to incite hostility towards independent election observers like CRTA.

“Allegations that first appear on marginal social media accounts, often newly created, quickly gain traction in pro-government media outlets and even in statements by senior state officials. CRTA is portrayed as a tool of foreign intelligence services, a covert political actor and a participant in a conspiracy to overthrow the state,” Nedeljkov said.

He said such actions threaten not only citizens’ rights and freedoms but also the safety of everyone “who wishes to devote their time and energy to election monitoring in the interest of democracy in this country, with the aim of ensuring free and fair elections”.

CRTA reported that one in three campaign activities by the ruling “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list monitored on the ground had involved elements of manipulation or potential legal violations, including suspected signature forgery, misuse of public resources and public office, and offering money, assistance or jobs in exchange for political support.

The watchdog also accused the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, and the Anti-Corruption Agency of contributing to the ruling party’s advantage by failing to consistently enforce the law.

World.title: Bosnia Charges Catholic Cleric with Glorifying War Criminal
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

The Bosnian state court on Thursday confirmed an indictment alleging that Father Petar Barbaric, a Catholic priest, gave a speech glorifying Slobodan Praljak after the unveiling of a monument to the deceased war criminal at a cemetery in the city of Capljina in November 2025.

“The speech was broadcast by various electronic media outlets and internet portals, garnering a large number of views, as well as reactions from the public and citizens,” the state prosecutor’s office said in a statement.

The indictment charges Barbaric with glorifying an individual who had been convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, under a final verdict, of crimes against humanity and war crimes, thereby committing the criminal offence of “provoking ethnic, racial and religious hatred, conflicts and intolerance”.

The investigation was opened in November last year after a photograph began circulating of the unveiling in Capljina of the monument to Praljak, wartime commander of the Main Headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council, the Bosnian Croat wartime military force.

The monument features Praljak’s likeness carved into stone, with the inscription: “Praljak, Croatian General,” his place and year of birth – “Capljina, 1945” – and the year and place of his death: “The Hague, 2017.”

In November 2017, the Hague Tribunal convicted Praljak, along with five other high-ranking officials of the unrecognised Croat-led wartime statelet of Herzeg-Bosnia, sentencing him to 20 years in prison for crimes against Bosniaks. During the reading of the verdict, Praljak took poison and died the same day.

Under amendments to the Bosnian Criminal Code imposed in July 2021 by the High Representative, the international overseer of the continuing implemetation of the Dayton Peace Agreement, denying genocide and other war crimes was outlawed.

It also became a punishable offense to bestow honours or awards, or erect monuments or any other form of memorial, to a person convicted under a final verdict of genocide, crimes against humanity or war crimes.

When news of the installation of a monument to Praljak first emerged, Emir Hajdarevic, president of the Mostar Association of Camp Inmates, said it showed that some still see war criminals as heroes.

“This is yet another crime against the victims of Herzegovina committed in Capljina, which is known for the crimes at Gabela and Silos [wartime detention camps in the Herzegovina area],” Hajdarevic said.

World.title: Albanian Criminal Procedure Bill Slammed as Bid to ‘Neuter’ Anti-Graft Body
World.content:
Prosecutors in Albania were taken aback last week when the government unexpectedly unveiled a bill running to 106 articles and revising roughly a fifth of the country’s Code of Criminal Procedure.

The bill proposes scrapping pretrial detention in criminal cases carrying a maximum sentence of five years in prison, introducing new requirements for prosecutors in the conduct of investigations, and strengthening rules governing investigative secrecy. It would further prohibit the public disclosure of the fact that a person is under investigation.

In 2016, Albania introduced sweeping reforms to its justice system that established the Special Prosecution Office Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK. This body has since brought a string of cases against senior officials from the ruling Socialist Party and its main rival, the Democrats.

World.title: Bosnia’s 2026 Elections: Fewer Votes, Familiar Winners
World.content:
The biggest, if not the only, real novelty in Bosnia’s October 4 election was that the first preliminary results were announced on election night, before all the polling stations had even closed.

For a country with such a complex administrative system as Bosnia and Herzegovina, this came as a major surprise.

It was welcomed by most politicians, media and ordinary people alike, who formerly had to wait days or weeks before the Central Election Commission, CEC, announced the preliminary results in all the key races.

However, for many Bosnians, the excitement generated by this technical novelty was quickly replaced with disdain on hearing the actual results.

As soon as the CEC officials started listing them, they revealed the continued domination of Bosnia’s main Serb and Croat ethnic parties, as well as a major comeback by their Bosniak counterpart.

World.title: Justina Shiroka Pula, Another Woman at Kosovo’s Helm
World.content:
Justina Shiroka Pula was having a peaceful evening on Tuesday, taking with “guests from Sarajevo” when she hung up a phone call from a TV studio running a prime-time political debate.

She was not aware that she was the pick for Kosovo’s top state position at a dramatic moment, less than two hours before the deadline to elect a President expired.

“We will hear [about this] a bit later,” she said, switching off.

Minutes later, in another call, she sounded like she was coming to terms with her new situation.

World.title: Moldova Speeds Up Construction of Trump-Named Power Line
World.content:
Moldova’s government on Wednesday approved a draft law declaring the construction of a high-voltage power line linking Moldova with Romania a national public utility, allowing acquisition of land and other procedures required for the project to be accelerated.

The 400-kilovolt line will be about 190 kilometres long, with around 70 kilometres on Moldovan territory and 120 in Romania, according to government officials. It is expected to strengthen Moldova’s integration with Romania and the wider European electricity market.

Construction of the new power line is backed by a $130 million investment from the US and is expected to be completed in 2032.

The US embassy in Chisinau meanwhile announced on Monday that the planned line will be named the “Trump Liberty Line”, making it the latest infrastructure project to bear the name of the US President.

Moldovan authorities have stressed that the project will reduce vulnerability to energy pressure from Russia. “This is a very important project for Moldova’s energy security … and we are grateful to the American side for its support,” Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said during Wednesday’s government meeting.

Moldova, one of Europe’s poorest countries and an EU candidate, relies heavily currently on electricity imports from Romania and Ukraine.

But Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have repeatedly disrupted regional electricity supplies in recent years, exposing Moldova’s vulnerability to instability and underscoring the need for stronger and more reliable connections, particularly with Romania.

There has been no significant critical reaction in either Moldova or Romania to the planned name of the new power line connecting the two countries. The announcement has attracted little public controversy, with attention focused instead on the project’s potential to strengthen Moldova’s energy security.

Moldova meanwhile joins a number of other countries where local infrastructure projects have been associated with Trump’s name, as governments seek to highlight ties with the US administration.

In Eastern Europe, other examples include a planned Donald Trump Romanian-American Friendship Park in Bucharest, Romania, which is expected to be inaugurated early next year, and a proposed US military base in Poland that was previously promoted under the name “Fort Trump”.

World.title: Mayor of Turkey’s Third-Largest City Joins Ruling Party
World.content:
Izmir Metropolitan Mayor Cemil Tugay on Wednesday joined President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, giving it the mayoralty of Turkey’s third-largest city, which it has never won in an election.

Tugay was elected mayor as a candidate of the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, in 2024. He received his AKP badge at the party’s parliamentary group meeting.

“I welcome Izmir Metropolitan Mayor Cemil Tugay, who joined us, the AKP family, today,” President Erdogan announced. “I want to emphasise that we will support him with all our means in his efforts to serve Izmir, the pearl of the Aegean, and our fellow citizens in Izmir.”

Tugay said: “I love Izmir very much,” adding: “Very good things await Izmir” and calling Erdogan’s “the greatest leader”.

Izmir, a major economic hub on Turkey’s Aegean coast, is home to some 4.5 million people and has been a stronghold of the opposition for decades.

Tugay’s move follows a wider realignment within Turkey’s opposition. Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas left the CHP on September 23 following months of turmoil that split the party between the leadership, now restored to Kemal Kilicdaroglu, and the New Party, Turkey’s new main opposition party, established by the former CHP leader, Ozgur Ozel.

Yavas has remained an independent, however.

In the 2024 local elections, Tugay, running for the CHP, won 49 per cent of the vote, almost 12 per cent ahead of Erdogan’s AKP candidate, who received 37 per cent.

The balance of power on the metropolitan council remains heavily in favour of the opposition. The New Party holds 93 seats, compared with 38 for the AKP, 33 for the CHP, 12 independents and seven for AKP-allied Nationalist Party members.

New Party leader Ozel mocked Erdogan’s seeming victory in parliament on Wednesday. “You have never won Izmir at the ballot box, and you never will,” he said, addressing President Erdogan.

World.title: Kosovo Avoids New Deadlock With Last-Minute Presidential Election
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Newly elected President Justina Shiroka Pula takes oath in Kosovo Parliament, October 7, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Shqipron Xhema

After a roller-coaster of proposals for the vacant post of Kosovo’s President, MPs pulled off a last-minute save just before midnight on Tuesday, avoiding a constitutional deadline that would have triggered parliament’s dissolution and the fourth parliamentary election in less than two years.

Justina Shiroka Pula, a 73-year-old economist, former minister and MP and current head of the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo, was announced as the new President with 81 votes in favour and two votes not valid.

“I pledge to dedicate all my strength to safeguarding the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Kosovo,” Shiroka-Pula declared.

She is the third woman President of Kosovo.

She has directed the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo since December 2025. From 2008 to 2011, she was Minister of Energy and Mining in a government led by Hashim Thaçi. She was part of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK’s, parliamentary group from 2011 to 2014.

Shiroka Pula was nominated by Prime Minister Albin Kurti at a press conference just before midnight, after earlier candidates did not get the backing of the opposition PDK.

The issue of electing the President had become tangled up with demands for law changes to curb the powers of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which sparked anger after it convicted four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes last month.

PDK leader Bedri Hamza said in a press conference after the election that “we do not want to hinder justice, we want to establish justice. The President is the people’s representative, I believe she will do her job with honour and high responsibility.”

The PDK and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, AAK, had called for draft amendments to the law governing the Chambers to be passed on a second reading before they would agree with the government on electing a President.

Kurti had claimed that electing a President was the priority – until he proposed voting through the law amendments prior to electing the President as a solution.

The law change was then adopted in an extraordinary session close to midnight on Tuesday just before the election of the President. It crucially limits the jail sentences the court can impose to 15 years.

On September 16, the court sentenced former Kosovo President Thaci and three other former KLA chiefs, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes.

The sentences caused outrage in Kosovo, where many considered the verdict went against the just war against the Serbian regime in the 1990s. Protests became violent on Monday as protesters clashed with the police.

The adoption of the law by the parliament and the election of the President were welcomed with fireworks and patriotic music by protesters outside parliament in Pristina.

However, the election of the President could be subject to constitutional interpretation as, while the session started on October 6, which was the last day to elect a President, the results were not announced until 13 minutes after midnight.

World.title: EU Seeks Strict Classification of Toxic Compound Found in Croatian Subjects
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The EU is seeking much stricter classification of the toxic compound discovered in the blood of Croatian subjects.

The European Chemicals Agency has announced that its Committee for Risk Assessment recommends that trifluoroacetic acid, known as TFA, and its inorganic salts be classified as substances toxic to reproduction. Index reports that this is one of the concerning PFAS compounds that was recently found in the blood of all 110 participants in a study conducted by the Greens/EFA group in the European Parliament. Among the test subjects were ten people from Croatia, from Gospić, Knin and Pula.

It is important to emphasise that ECHA has not yet adopted a final, legally binding ban or classification. The Committee for Risk Assessment (RAC) adopted an expert opinion and sent it to the European Commission, which still has to decide whether to introduce such a classification into European legislation.

what is being sought?

RAC recommends that TFA and its inorganic salts be classified in category 1B for adverse effects on development and in category 2 for adverse effects on sexual function and fertility. Their classification as persistent, mobile and toxic substances (PMT) and as very persistent and very mobile substances (vPvM) has also been recommended. This means that they are difficult to break down, move easily through soil and water, and can pollute water resources over a long period. Such a classification does not mean that every measured amount of TFA will automatically cause a health problem in humans. It indicates the hazardous properties of the substance itself, while the actual health risk also depends on the level and duration of exposure.

tfa was discovered in the blood of all 100 subjects

The Greens/EFA study covered 110 volunteers from nine European countries. TFA was detected in the blood of all participants. The authors of the study emphasise that this is an exploratory study that is not representative of the population of individual countries and that the results should be interpreted with caution. There is currently also no appropriate health reference value for the concentration of TFA in blood serum on the basis of which it could be concluded from the finding alone that an individual is health-endangered. In the Croatian part of the testing, ten people from Gospić, Knin and Pula participated, who travelled to Brussels for testing organised by Možemo! MEP Gordan Bosanac.

should the ec react more quickly?

After ECHA’s announcement, Bosanac called on the European Commission to speed up the procedure. “I welcome this decision of the European Chemicals Agency, which comes a few days after our study showed that TFA is present in the blood of European Union citizens,” he said. He announced that together with Greens/EFA MEPs he will demand that the Commission react within the next three to six months, instead of the procedure, as he claims, being stretched out until the end of the decade. Bosanac had earlier also requested a broader restriction of PFAS compounds, the gradual phase-out of their production and use, and European funds for more extensive population testing.

ECHA’s expert opinion is now with the European Commission. If the Commission, after consultations with Member States and other interested parties, accepts the recommendation, TFA and its salts would receive a harmonised and legally binding classification at EU level. Such a decision could then trigger additional restrictions under European chemicals regulations and other sectoral laws.

World.title: Friends of Animals Demand a Ban on Loud Pyrotechnics in Croatia
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – The Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) Association is seeking a ban on all loud pyrotechnics in Croatia after the Netherlands set the ball rolling.

Friends of Animals have called on the Croatian Government to further restrict the use of loud pyrotechnics, after the Netherlands banned citizens from buying, possessing and using category F2 and F3 pyrotechnic products from the 1st of August this year. Index reports that in Croatia, firecrackers and string firecrackers from those categories have been banned for personal use since 2021, but other F2 and F3 products are still permitted under prescribed conditions. The association is demanding that the ban be extended to all category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics whose main effect is a strong explosion and noise.

“It isn’t logical to ban one product because of the noise and allow others that produce an equally strong or even stronger bang, just because they are not called a firecracker but, for example, an aerial bomb,” said Snježana Klopotan Kačavenda from Friends of Animals.

According to the association, the Dutch ban covers entire categories F2 and F3 for private users, while citizens still have access to category F1 pyrotechnics, which pose a very low risk and produce negligible noise. Professional fireworks remain possible under special conditions, and exceptions can be approved for some organised New Year’s celebrations. Friends of Animals believe that such a model would reduce the number of injuries, fires, material damage, noise and stress for people and animals.

The association has already proposed amendments to the Act on Explosive Substances and the Production and Trade of Weapons to the Ministry of the Interior. In addition to the ban on loud category F2 and F3 pyrotechnics, they are demanding that the use of the remaining permitted pyrotechnics for citizens be limited to only two hours around midnight on New Year’s Eve. They also propose that sales be allowed only on the 29th, 30th and 31st of December, that advertising of pyrotechnics and their sale in mixed-goods stores be banned, and that places of use and the number of public fireworks displays be further restricted.

Friends of Animals state that their petition for a ban on loud pyrotechnics has so far been supported by more than 40,000 citizens. “Croatia already has experience with the ban on firecrackers, a concrete proposal for amendments to the law and more than 40,000 citizens’ signatures for a ban on loud pyrotechnics,” the association concluded.

World.title: More Issues Arise for Ambitious Croatian Toll Collection System
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – More issues have arisen for the ambitious future Croatian toll collection system due to come into function in March 2027.

Croatian Motorways (HAC) has now cancelled the public procurement procedure for the development of a sales web portal, a mobile application for end users and an integration data bus as part of the new Crolibertas toll collection system. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this raises the question of whether the new system can indeed start operating on 1 March 2027, as prescribed by the Toll Collection Act.

how will crolibertas work?

The new Crolibertas toll collection system should completely change the way motorway tolls are paid in Croatia. Instead of stopping at toll booths, vehicles will pass without stopping, and collection will be carried out via ENC devices or automatic reading of registration plates. A total of 212 portals with cameras and antennas are being installed on the motorways, along with new IT infrastructure and data processing centres. The main contract for the implementation of the system, worth almost 80 million euros excluding VAT, was signed by HAC with the consortium of SkyToll and TollNet. According to the government’s decision, of the total 160.5 million euros, 115.6 million euros of eligible costs will be financed by non-repayable funds from the Recovery and Resilience Mechanism, while 44.9 million euros of ineligible costs will be borne by Croatian Motorways.

what procurement issues have arisen?

After the cancellation of the procurement procedure, the question now arises whether it will be possible to implement it on time at all. In May, HAC initially selected the consortium of Bos Projekt, Infinum and the British AMR CyberSecurity, whose bid amounted to 329,500 euros excluding VAT. The estimated value of the procurement was 330 thousand euros. The State Commission for the Control of Public Procurement Procedures cancelled the initial selection decision following an appeal by the Zagreb company Abysalto, whose bid amounted to 379,000 euros excluding VAT, and returned the matter to HAC for a new decision.

hac has now also rejected the bid it initially chose

HAC rejected this bid because it was higher than the estimated value of the procurement, while it also rejected the bid it had initially selected. The minutes state that this consortium did not meet the conditions for key experts. For two mobile app development engineers, diplomas from the Faculty of Organisation and Informatics in Varaždin were submitted, and for one database engineer a diploma from the Faculty of Science in Zagreb. The tender, however, required diplomas in the field of technical sciences. The consortium of bidders, according to the minutes, did not satisfy the condition relating to the quality standard. The submitted ISO 9001:2015 certificate relates to cybersecurity and assurance services, and it is not evident from it that it covers software production and the integration of information and communication solutions.

The third bid, from the Zagreb craft H&D Info i trgovina, amounted to 410,000 euros excluding VAT. It was rejected because the bidder did not meet the conditions for key experts, and the price was higher than the planned funds.

deadlines are now the big issue

In the cancelled procedure, HAC envisaged six months for the realisation of the work. It should be said that the cancellation decision is not yet final because the appeal deadline is ongoing, and any new procedure could follow only after the completion of that part of the procedure. Less than five months remain until the legally prescribed start of Crolibertas operations, which is a potential problem. HAC has previously emphasised that this is an implementation-complex and multidisciplinary project that requires the coordination of technological, legal and operational segments. Precisely for this reason it is clear that after this additional complication time is increasingly running out, and there is less and less room for new delays.

Jutarnji reported back at the beginning of September, citing a source, that the procurement had been incorrectly set up from the beginning. According to the claims, the development of the application was initially included in the tender for the selection of the contractor for the new toll collection system, but was subsequently, for unknown reasons, separated and a separate procurement procedure was decided upon for it. It is also stated that DKOM accepted the appeal because HAC did not adhere to the conditions it itself prescribed. In the event of the cancellation of the tender, HAC can contract this service by direct agreement with a contractor who will carry out the work for a lower amount than the estimated value in the tender and guarantee that everything will be completed by January next year.

hac: the project is proceeding according to plan

We contacted HAC and asked them whether the new toll collection system can still start operating on the 1st of March 2027, when they plan to launch a new procurement procedure, and whether that date will remain final or whether there is a possibility of it being postponed. We also asked them whether the web portal, mobile application and integration data bus are necessary for putting Crolibertas into operation. “In accordance with the Public Procurement Act, the decision on the cancellation of the procedure has not yet become final and the deadline for lodging an appeal is ongoing. Therefore, at this moment HAC cannot comment on possible further steps or models for the realisation of the subject functionalities.

The project of the new electronic toll collection system is being carried out according to plan, and HAC is undertaking all necessary activities so that the system is established within the deadline established by the Toll Collection Act. The public will be timely informed about all future decisions and activities,” Croatian Motorways explained. The question also arises at what stage the remaining parts of the infrastructure are, how many systems are already interconnected and how much time will be needed for final testing before commissioning.

According to the latest information published in the media, of the total of 212 planned portals, 111 have been installed. But the portals are only one part of the infrastructure. HAC officially states that the project also includes cameras, antennas, advanced IT equipment, construction works and back-office centres for data processing, and after the installation of all portals and related equipment a comprehensive system test will follow at the level of the entire network.

the deadline has already been postponed once before

It should also be noted that the deadline for the introduction of the system has already been postponed once. When the main contract with SkyToll and TollNet was signed in September 2024, HAC stated a works completion deadline of 24 months, i.e. until September 2026, and the Government at that time announced that the new system would be in function after the summer of 2026. The Act later set the start of full application for the 1st of March 2027, which is now once again under a very large question mark.

World.title: Rijeka Saw More Tourists in September 2026 Than September 2025
World.content:
October the 9th, 2026 – Rijeka recorded 22,690 tourist arrivals in September, which is two percent more than in September 2025.

In addition to encouraging growth in arrivals, Rijeka’s number of overnight stays remained almost unchanged at 61,672. The strongest growth was achieved among domestic guests. Index reports that there were 4,035 of them recorded in September, or 17 percent more than last year, and they recorded 7,604 overnight stays, a rise of 15 percent. Foreign tourists accounted for 82 percent of all arrivals in September, and domestic guests for 18 percent.

From the beginning of the year to the end of September, Rijeka achieved 193,716 tourist arrivals and 568,868 overnight stays. The number of arrivals remained at last year’s level, while overnight stays were one percent lower. Domestic tourists also recorded strong growth in this period. They achieved 38,747 arrivals, 14 percent more than last year, and 76,655 overnight stays, a rise of 13 percent. Foreign guests recorded 154,969 arrivals and 492,213 overnight stays and account for 80 percent of all arrivals and 87 percent of overnight stays.

Among foreign markets, Germany leads with 71,764 overnight stays in the first nine months. It is followed by Poland with 56,842 overnight stays, Italy with 41,053, Hungary with 30,437 and Austria with 25,932 overnight stays. In September, Germans were also in first place with 9,945 overnight stays, ahead of Poles, Italians and Austrians. The most overnight stays in the first nine months were recorded by guests aged 19 to 30, a total of 137,776, or 24.22 percent of all overnight stays. They are followed by guests aged 41 to 50 with 103,645 overnight stays and those aged 31 to 40 with 97,749.

Foreign tourists in Rijeka stayed on average 3.18 days, domestic guests 1.98 days, while the overall average was 2.94 days. The largest share of overnight stays was recorded in private accommodation – 335,776, or 59.02 percent of total traffic. Hotels had 145,876 overnight stays, hostels 41,573, and non-commercial accommodation 43,094 overnight stays. The data shows that Rijeka still achieves the largest part of its tourist traffic from foreign guests, while the domestic market is recording noticeably faster growth this year.

World.title: Hvar in Conde Nast Top 10 Islands for 8th Consecutive Year
World.content:
October 8, 2026 – More strengthening of the American love for Croatia’s premier island, as Hvar once more in top 10 islands in Europe in Conde Nast Traveler Readers Choice Awards.

These are good times for the relationship between Hvar Town and the sought-after American tourism market, with a marked shift in approach resulting in a boom in American tourism arrivals in recent years. According to official statistics, American tourists were the biggest number of arrivals and overnight stays in the town last year, and those numbers show no sign of slowing, with overnight stays from the USA in September up an impressive 17.83% year on year.

The success has been down to a number of key factors, including better promotion to the USA market, the introduction of the first direct flight from New York to Split this April, meaning one can get from New York to Hvar (with the aid of a good speedboat) in under 10 hours. So successful has the flight connection been that plans are being discussion to prolong the flight season as well as frequency of flights for 2027.

An additional factor has been the positive media coverage that the town has been attracting since moving away from its party focus in search of more upmarket tourism focused on families and couples, as well as adventure tourism. Arguably the most influential travel publication for American travellers is Conde Nast Traveler, which every year holds the prestigious Conde Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards, a publication which known Hvar very well.

Often named one of the 10 most beautiful islands in the world, that claim has its roots in a Conde Nast award in the late 1990s (you can see a list of the islands on the map on the Jelsa waterfront), and the American publication’s readers’ love for Hvar has been pretty constant ever since. Indeed, this year’s 9th place as the best island in Europe is the 8th consecutive year that Hvar has featured in the sought-after top ten list, including 2019 and 2021, when Hvar was voted the best island in Europe.

Breakfast at Sirena Resort

American interest has been mirrored by a raising of standards in the hotel sector, which is also attracting plenty of international column inches. The latest addition is the superb Sirena Resort from Suncani Hvar Hotels, 1.4 km north of the town, set in an idyllic bay without neighbours, and offering access to the vibe of Hvar Town, as well as the laidback calm of the nature of Hvar, the island. Within weeks of opening, Sirena Resort was featured in the New York Times as one of the top 5 new hotels in Europe for an autumn getaway.

The main season may be over, but there is still plenty of life in the town, with this weekend hosting the Spartan World Championship, with around 3,000 competitors expected. All the signs are there for a bumper 2027 for Americans visiting one of Europe’s most perfect spots.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport Could Surpass 3.2 Million Passengers
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Airport might surpass the figure of 3.2 million passengers, with passenger numbers climbing even during the month of September this year.

Dubrovnik Airport continued its passenger traffic growth throughout September this year as well. According to data from the airport itself, Dubrovnik Airport handled 474,212 passengers in September, which is almost 31 thousand more passengers than in the same month last year. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that for comparison, in September 2025 a total of 443,444 passengers passed through Dubrovnik Airport.

Compared to September 2025, the number of passengers increased by 6.9 percent, while the number of operations also rose. Dubrovnik recorded 3,718 operations in September this year, compared to 3,564 operations in the same month last year, which represents growth of approximately 4.3 percent. Growth is also recorded in the first nine months of this year. From the beginning of January to the end of September 2026, Dubrovnik handled a total of 2,820,860 passengers. In the same period last year 2,692,873 passengers were recorded, meaning that Dubrovnik handled almost 128 thousand more passengers in the first nine months of this year, or 4.8 percent more.

Last year, the airport handled a total of 3,090,245 passengers, which means that by the end of September 2026 more than 91 percent of last year’s total traffic had already been achieved, and the airport still has three months ahead of it. While significantly lower traffic is expected in November and December, October should bring strong numbers. Consequently, it would be no surprise if Dubrovnik Airport already matches last year’s figures by the end of October.

World.title: Radioactive Strontium in Gospić Jumps by a Staggering 961%
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – Radioactive strontium found in the soil in the Gospić area has jumped by an extremely concerning 961 percent, but what is being done about it?

In the surface layer of soil at the measuring point in Gospić last year, an almost 11 times higher concentration of radioactive strontium-90 per square metre was recorded than in 2023, according to the regular annual reports of the Zagreb Institute for Medical Research and Occupational Health (IMI), published on the Ministry of the Interior’s website. Slobodan Mufic reports for Index that the published activity per square metre rose from 24.5 to 260 becquerels, or by as much as 961 percent. The concentration of strontium-90 (Sr-90) per kilogram of material at the Gospić measuring point also rose drastically: from 0.605 becquerels per kilogram in 2023 to 4.08 becquerels in 2025, or almost seven times.

has radioactive contamination occurred?

It should be emphasised immediately that there is no evidence pointing to a connection between strontium-90 and the illegal waste at the former PPK Velebit in Bilajska Street in Gospić, nor does this change in itself mean that radioactive contamination has occurred or that the health of residents is endangered. The measuring point in Gospić is located about 7.6 kilometres southwest of PPK Velebit and so far there is no evidence that would confirm a link between the two locations.

Strontium-90 is a radioactive form of the chemical element of the same name, a silvery-white metal. This means that its atomic nucleus decays over time and in doing so releases radiation that can damage living cells. Strontium-90 does not exist originally in nature, but is created by the fission of atomic nuclei, for example in nuclear reactors and during nuclear weapons explosions. “All Sr-90 in the environment on Croatian territory is a consequence of the Chernobyl disaster back in 1986. Sr-90 has a half-life of 28.8 years. After the half-life has elapsed, the activity and quantity of the radionuclide fall to half of the initial amount, so it is not surprising that Sr-90 is still present in Croatia – there is still approximately 38% of the quantity that was initially deposited.

This radionuclide is anthropogenic; it is created by the fission of uranium-235. Sr-90 entered the environment from the atmosphere, via the radioactive cloud, and accumulated in the surface layer. Therefore it is not surprising that it is most present there, because it spreads into deeper layers by the slow process of diffusion,” states the response of IMI’s Radiation Protection Department.

Gospić is the only area to record an increase since 2023…

The origin of strontium-90 has been explained, but there is no adequate answer as to why its concentration on the surface has enormously increased only in Gospić over the last three years. Among the five measuring locations we compared, Gospić had the lowest surface value of strontium-90 in 2023, and two years later the highest. While between 2023 and 2025 that value fell in Zadar, Osijek, Buzet/Pula and Opuzen, in Zagreb it rose by approximately 92 percent, and in Gospić by 961 percent. Becquerel per kilogram (Bq/kg) indicates how much radioactivity is concentrated in a kilogram of soil, while becquerel per square metre (Bq/m²) indicates how much total radioactivity of Sr-90 exists under one square metre of surface. Since Bq/kg can fluctuate considerably if the sample one year is a little lighter, denser or richer in organic matter, Bq/m² is to some extent a better indicator.

If there is no new input or soil erosion, the total Sr-90 expressed in Bq/m² should mostly gradually decrease due to radioactive decay, and not increase as in the Gospić case. It should also be added that in the deeper layers of the earth, below the surface five centimetres, the opposite occurred: the concentration of Sr-90 is strongly declining.

The Radiation Protection Department offered this answer to the question about the professional interpretation of the increase in Sr-90 concentration: “In Gospić soil Sr-90 is continuously monitored, with a break in the period 2014–2022. It was reintroduced into the environmental radioactivity monitoring programme in the Republic of Croatia in 2023 and continues to be monitored. The measured values varied and no year-on-year upward trend was observed. For example, in 2003 440 Bq/m² was measured, in 2004 280 Bq/m², in 2005 180 Bq/m², and in 2007 270 Bq/m². In order to establish whether the increase in the period 2023–2025 represents the beginning of an upward trend, more time needs to pass.” The last measured and published value of 260 Bq/m² is not in itself a historical maximum in Gospić, but such a sudden jump from 24.5 to 260 in only two years is shocking. An additional problem is that IMI did not carry out measurements in Gospić from 2007 to 2023.

Although IMI wrote in its 2024 report that only in Gospić “is the activity concentration of Sr-90 is several times higher than last year’s”, there’s no data that because of this obvious anomaly, which was repeated in 2025, a new control measurement was proposed or requested.

nobody requested or paid for additional monitoring

“Sampling within the framework of environmental radioactivity monitoring is carried out in agreement with the client of the work, in this case the Ministry of the Interior. IMI cannot itself define where and how often sampling will take place. We have not received a request from the client for additional or extraordinary sampling in Gospić.

Every year, sampling for the following year is agreed with the Ministry of the Interior. We may propose the mentioned, but the Ministry of the Interior will decide. That is open for now. It should be emphasised that it is possible to carry out detailed research outside the regular monitoring; we have often done that so far. Someone has to order and pay for it,” the Radiation Protection Department replied to the question whether it would recommend to the Ministry of the Interior more sampling points, more frequent sampling, analysis of water, vegetation, food or sediment. An interpretation of this sensitive issue was sought from a renowned Croatian scientific institution, without revealing what it was about. A radioactivity expert, who requested not to be named, answered the question whether a multiple increase in the concentration of strontium-90 on the soil is possible without a new source of contamination: “NO. That would be a perpetual motion machine.”

When we explained to him what it was actually about, he said that the only reasonable explanation could be deficient sampling, or inadequate laboratory analysis: “Measuring low activities is very delicate and it can happen that laboratories have different instrumentation, so measurements near the detection limits can deviate significantly. This is especially the case with measuring Sr-90, which is quite complicated. The analysis takes about three weeks.”

no answers have come from institutions about potential health risks…

From the existing data, it is not possible to draw a concrete and reliable conclusion about the impact of the strontium-90 concentration on people in Gospić. The surface increase refers to activity per square metre of soil, and not to the radiation dose received by citizens. To assess the health risk it is necessary to determine what dose residents receive due to radiation from the environment and the possible intake of radioactive substances through food, water and inhalation of particles. The soil finding alone is not sufficient either for the claim that there is a danger to health or for the claim that it is completely ruled out.

Interestingly, the Radiation Protection Department did not want to comment on the possible danger to human health: “The assessment of the threat from a particular radionuclide, which includes the ways of its propagation through the environment and the food chain, is not part of our contract in monitoring environmental radioactivity. That topic is quite complex and requires an interdisciplinary approach that would consider all relevant aspects.”

There was no concrete answer from the Croatian Institute of Public Health to Index’s inquiry. Unofficially we received the message: “We do not deal with that.” And the Ministry of the Interior’s Civil Protection Directorate completely ignored several inquiries on this topic; that is, even after two weeks no answer arrived. The key question in this story is not the concentration of strontium-90 itself and its possible impact on human health, but the inertia and disinterest of the competent institutions in reacting and additionally checking findings that clearly deviate from trends and expectations. Just as in the case of the illegal waste at Bilajska 50.

World.title: For 75% of Croatians, a Dignified Salary Starts From 2,000 Euros
World.content:
October the 8th, 2026 – For 75% of Croatians, a dignified salary starts from 2,000 euros, but the reality of what salaries are actually paid out in Croatia is starkly different.

The topic of the average wage in Croatia is a frequent topic, and we talk about the minimum wage most often when another increase is announced. The real question for many, however, is just how much should a Croatian wage be to enable workers a fully dignified life? What some would be one in which, after paying rent, utilities and food, there remains room for socialising, going to the cinema, an annual holiday or putting some savings away for a rainy day. A life in which an unexpected expense does not mean that we have to spend the rest of the month counting every single euro.

Alma Career Croatia, the international company known for the MojPosao/MyJob brand, addressed precisely this question in a new survey in which more than 500 people participated. Poslovni reports that just two years ago participants said that a dignified wage should not be less than 1,500 euros. Given the constant increases in the cost of living, we checked where they set that boundary today.

Is 1,500 euros enough for a month, but not for a peaceful life? The minimum wage in Croatia currently amounts to 1,050 euros gross, or around 800 euros net, depending on the worker’s tax circumstances. But the legal minimum and the amount that survey participants consider sufficient for a dignified life are clearly quite distant, because none of them chose a wage lower than 1,000 euros. The next range did not receive many more votes either. Only 3% of participants believe that it is possible to live with dignity on a wage between 1,000 and 1,500 euros.

A somewhat larger number, approximately every fifth person (22%), chooses the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros. For them 1,500 euros is the lower limit which, with inflation and rising living costs, still leaves the possibility of a life above merely covering obligations. Everything below that, they believe, means living ‘from month to month’. Everything below 2,000 euros is not enough for the vast majority.

The largest number of participants, 50% of them, place a dignified wage in the range from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. However, they note that even that amount does not tell the whole story. A lot depends on whether we have solved our housing situation or whether every month we have to set aside money from the same wage for rent or a loan. For every fourth person (25%) the boundary is even higher. A dignified life in Croatia, they emphasise, requires a monthly wage of at least 2,500 euros.

Compared with the survey from 2024, the change is visible. Then the largest number of participants, 47% of them, chose the range from 1,500 to 2,000 euros, while a third selected amounts from 2,000 to 2,500 euros. Today precisely that higher range gathers half of the answers.

World.title: Estonian government approves several updates to primary healthcare rules
World.content:
Health centers in Estonia will have to provide up to three months' temporary coverage when a family doctor leaves a practice, among several new rules approved Thursday.

A bill of amendments the government greenlit Thursday will require health centers to find a replacement for a departing family doctor for up to three months, with the option to stay on longer by agreement.

If no permanent doctor is found to take over the previous doctor's practice list within that time, the Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) would step in.

A family doctor planning to leave a health center with their practice list would generally have to give six months' notice, although the doctor and center could arrange an earlier departure by agreement. The change is intended to give health centers time to reorganize.

Among other changes, the Health Board will be able to take over a doctor's practice list after 30 days, down from the current 60, if their patients have gone without family medical care.

Patient caps to be raised

The practice list cap will also be raised to 2,000 patients, or 2,400 if an additional doctor is available, although the bill still recommends a maximum of 1,600 patients.

Doctors with more than 1,600 patients will be able to turn away new patients if another family doctor in the area has fewer than 1,600. They will also have to direct patients to information on available practice lists.

The changes are intended to more evenly distribute patients among practices.

Pending Riigikogu approval, the amendments are set to take effect next March 1.

At the start of this year, 77 practice lists covering more than 132,000 patients across Estonia still lacked a permanent family doctor, with nearly one in 10 residents receiving primary care from temporary replacements.

World.title: Gallery: Estonian conducts charity Hamburg shows with Calum Scott, Kontra K
World.content:
On October 1–3, conductor Kristjan Järvi led three Hamburg charity concerts with the Lufthansa Orchestra featuring British pop star Calum Scott and German rapper Kontra K.

The three-night run at Hamburg's Deutsches SchauSpielHaus was part of Channel Aid – Live in Concert 2026, with seven musicians from Järvi's band Nordic Pulse also joining the orchestra.

The concerts with Kontra K marked his first time performing his music with an orchestra, selling out many of the more than 200 movie theaters across Germany, Australia and Switzerland that streamed them live.

Calum Scott's concert, with orchestral arrangements by Järvi's team, drew nearly 100,000 viewers worldwide on YouTube and TikTok.

'Estonians are already making a mark'

The collaboration was based on Järvi's developing orchestral rituals approach, in which musicians from Nordic Pulse perform as part of the host orchestra rather than as a separate ensemble.

Manager Nora Liisa Suislepp said the Hamburg project clearly shows the scale of what Estonian musicians and creators are doing internationally.

"We often talk in Estonia about how our artists could reach a wider global audience, but sometimes it's worth recognizing Estonians are already doing really exciting things and making a real mark internationally," Suislepp said.

Channel Aid – Live in Concert is a charity concert series supporting children, youth and disabled people, with proceeds from its digital channels funding projects run by the Lufthansa Group nonprofit help alliance.

World.title: Migration pressure could rise sharply in coming weeks, PPA chief says
World.content:
Migration pressure could rise sharply in the coming weeks as people try to leave Belarus ahead of winter, Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) chief Egert Belitšev said.

Belitšev said Russia has deliberately eased entry requirements and increased flights from countries like Ethiopia. Its ally Belarus facilitates onward travel to Europe. Travel is organized right up to the EU border and can cost up to €10,000 per person.

Estonia does not border Belarus. Latvia does. Most of the nearly 200 illegal migrants apprehended in Estonia since summer came via that route.

Estonia has a population of 1.3 million. Ethiopia has 130 million. More than a million refugees from neighboring countries live there.

Speaking to "Esimene stuudio," Belitšev said six direct flights a week operate between Ethiopia and Moscow, with no Russian visa required. Passengers intend to reach the EU.

"The Russian Federation has deliberately made entry requirements significantly easier for these countries and increased the frequency of flights," Belitšev said.

From Moscow, people travel by bus to Belarus. The authorities there make no pretense of stopping them. They help.

Russia is using Belarus to pressure Europe. "Is it dependence, or the feeling that working alongside the 'master' will bring wealth and success? This is the path Belarus has chosen," Belitšev said.

Organized crime generates substantial profits

Human trafficking is the preserve of organized crime, and it is highly profitable. The authorities in Russia and Belarus take a cut.

"If you think about someone using the migration route through Belarus to reach Europe, it is not simply a matter of buying a ticket to Moscow and arranging the rest yourself," Belitšev said. Criminal organizations handle the whole journey. Each person pays €5,000 to €10,000.

On Tuesday, news emerged that the PPA had caught migrant smugglers red-handed. "Figuratively speaking, it is impossible to stop any pattern of criminal activity without cutting off the heads at the top," Belitšev said.

The main tactic is to detain them, hold them in custody and bring them to trial quickly. Where possible, criminal proceeds are seized. In mid-September, a court sentenced a convicted smuggler to seven months in prison and a six-year ban on entering the Schengen Area.

Local governments and administrative courts not accustomed to workloads

The PPA is under considerable pressure, but has not yet had to leave tasks undone. "However, many other institutions are also affected by the migration attack," Belitšev said.

Many arrivals claim to be minors, attempting to exploit EU child protection systems. That creates problems for local governments, which are responsible for guardianship. The first-tier administrative courts are also unaccustomed to such heavy workloads.

Belitšev said the situation could get more complicated in winter, when migration pressure has usually declined. Few people want to hide in Belarusian forests in sub-zero temperatures.

"Our advantage is that we have four seasons," he said.

World.title: Defense agency launches €195M tender for arms and ammunition
World.content:
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has launched a tender for weapons, ammunition, components and training with an estimated value of up to €195 million.

The procurement is split into five lots — three for ammunition worth €145 million and two for weapons worth €50 million — with seven-year framework agreements for each.

The sum makes it among the larger defense procurements the RKIK has issued to date.

Under the terms of the tender, the RKIK intends to conclude a framework agreement to purchase 40 mm and 23 mm weaponry plus 76 mm, 40 mm and 23 mm ammunition. The tender also covers the purchase of various types of these weapons and ammunition and their components, along with training and instruction, as well as life-cycle support services.

The ammunition types include blank rounds, training and practice ammunition, as well as a range of live ammunition with various lethal and non-lethal projectiles.

The products must be manufactured in EU or NATO member states and currently be in use as standard equipment by conventional military units or special forces in EU or NATO countries. Products currently being introduced into service in these countries are also eligible.

The RKIK will conclude framework agreements with a maximum estimated total value of €195 million.

Under the draft contract, the seller may, in justified cases, request an advance payment of up to 30 percent of the contract value, but RKIK retains the right to refuse the advance payment.

If an advance payment has been made but the seller fails to fulfill its obligations, it must immediately refund the advance payment, including VAT, to the buyer.

The RKIK is accepting tender bids until November 13 this year.

Estonia's largest defense contract so far remains the €400 million IRIS-T SLM air defense system, signed jointly with Latvia in 2023. A HIMARS deal in 2022, worth over $200 million, was described at the time as the largest weapons procurement in Estonia up to that point.

World.title: Rally Estonia put on WRC calendar also for next season
World.content:
FIA and the WRC promoter unveiled the calendar for next season's World Rally Championship on Thursday, with Rally Estonia also included. The event will take place on the roads of southern Estonia from July 22-25.

In August this year, the FIA World Rally Championship's promoter changed hands, with French automotive technology company Cosmobilis and private equity investor Park Square Capital acquiring WRC Promoter GmbH. The new owners aim to make the championship and its individual rounds even more attractive, turning each rally into a major event offering a wide range of entertainment alongside exciting racing.

The championship's new CEO, Eric Boullier, also visited Delfi Rally Estonia this summer and was highly impressed by what he saw. He praised the high standard of organization and the organizers' ambition and ability to combine world-class rallying with a comprehensive sports and entertainment experience.

Following this year's rally, the Rally Estonia team held several further meetings with representatives of the promoter. These discussions resulted in an agreement for Rally Estonia to remain a round of the World Rally Championship in 2027.

"Rally Estonia's continued inclusion in the WRC calendar is a major recognition of everyone who has contributed to the event's success. A big thank you to the Estonian state, local governments, private sector sponsors and the entire organizing team and of course to local residents, rally fans, drivers and teams," rally director Urmo Aava said.

"WRC Delfi Rally Estonia is much more than four days of top-level racing. It is a major international event that boosts Estonia's economy, supports regional development, generates tax revenue for the state and provides memorable experiences for tens of thousands of spectators along the stages and hundreds of millions of viewers across various platforms. The desire of foreign visitors to return to Estonia and recommend us to their friends creates value long after the rally weekend has ended," Minister of Culture Heidy Purga added.

WRC Rally Estonia will be the ninth round of the 2027 FIA World Rally Championship, taking place from July 22–25. The 2027 WRC calendar will feature a total of 15 rounds.

The WRC is set to become even more global in the coming years, with the United States also hosting a championship round in 2027. The series will also enter a new era with the introduction of new Rally1 cars and technical regulations. Several new private teams are expected to join the championship, while Ford recently announced that it would return as a factory team after a decades-long absence. These developments promise to make the championship even more exciting and competitive.

Of the 43,894 unique spectators who attended this year's WRC Delfi Rally Estonia, foreign visitors accounted for 31.9 percent or 14,002 people. According to a study, the event generated an estimated €44.9 million in additional revenue for Estonian businesses, up 36 percent from 2025. Direct tax revenue associated with this turnover was estimated at €8.3 million.

World.title: Gold coins seized at Estonian-Russian border put up for auction
World.content:
Nearly €400,000 worth of gold coins found hidden in a truck seat at Estonia's Luhamaa border checkpoint are now up for grabs after authorities put them up for auction.

The Estonian Tax and Customs Board (MTA) is auctioning 157 gold coins, valued at about €390,000, that were seized at the southeastern border crossing last year.

Customs officers found the coins, weighing nearly 4.8 kilograms, hidden inside a truck seat on August 8 as they inspected the vehicle before it left Estonia.

A criminal investigation was opened over an alleged attempted sanctions violation and to determine who owned the coins. After the owner could not be identified, a court ordered the coins forfeited to the state.

The coins are being auctioned in small lots through Osta.ee, a local online auction site similar to eBay. Bidding on the first eight coins runs through October 14.

World.title: Estonian Spa Association: There may not be enough customers for all new spas
World.content:
Several new spas are set to enter Estonia's market in the coming years, but Aire Toffer, CEO of the Estonian Spa Association, warns that there may not be enough solvent customers to fill both the new and existing facilities.

Toffer said that the completion of several new spas is planned for the end of next year and the beginning of 2028. In her view, an incorrect impression may have formed about the spa market, as if large amounts of money were circulating there.

"These perceptions have arisen from the fact that during school holidays and on Saturday evenings the prices in spas are very high," she explained. Toffer said these are isolated days when visitors have time to go to the spa, which makes it possible to charge higher prices.

She said that starting spa entrepreneurs may lack an understanding of what the cost side of spas looks like, such as electricity and water consumption. "It's worth looking at companies' financial reports — the accommodation sector is not a very profitable business," Toffer noted.

Still, she is optimistic that every product has a consumer if it is created in the right place and is distinctive and innovative. But at present, according to Toffer, Estonia does not have enough solvent customers to fill all spas.

Spa center (photo is illustrative). Source: Anna Aurelia Minev/ERR

Gross: if you do it well, there should be enough customers

Next year, a spa hotel will rise by Lake Viljandi, owned by Lääne‑Virumaa entrepreneur Oleg Gross. He said that if you do something, you must do it very well. "And if you do it very well, there should be enough customers," he added.

Gross noted that a spa must offer a premium‑class product. "Besides, life has shown that Estonians have started going to spas more," he said. Gross explained that although foreign tourism has decreased, Estonia's climate encourages Estonians to visit spas more. He stated that a spa hotel is not a profit project but rather an emotion project. "But that it would start running losses — I don't believe that," he said.

According to Gross, there is room on the spa market for one more spa. At the same time, he noted that many developers have built a hotel with a spa only with bank loans and have no other business. "But we have a parent company in food retail," he said.

Oleg Gross Autor/allikas: ERR

Gross said that if the spa should run a slight loss in its early years, he does not plan to sell or close it, and the spa will be kept alive by force if necessary. "It will get going in any case, there is no doubt about that," he noted.

According to Toffer, whether every spa will have enough guests does not depend solely on Estonian visitors. "Many other things also play a role here — for example, how accessible Estonia is, whether we have flight connections, what will happen with airBaltic," she explained. Toffer stated that when designing a tourism service, foreign visitors are always considered as well.

Foreign visitors are also needed

"Certainly, we also need to do something at the national level to find visitors from other target markets outside Estonia who would come to Estonia because of the spas," she said. Toffer explained that this requires better marketing messages and promoting Estonia even more as a health‑oriented country.

While it is often visible how various companies close their doors because customers do not have the money to visit them, this is not seen much with spas. "Perhaps spa entrepreneurs have been more patient and have become accustomed to the fact that this is not a very profitable business," Toffer suggested.

She explained that in the current economy most entrepreneurs are trying to make ends meet, and if many more spas are added, it is not excluded that someone may have to close their doors.

"Entrepreneurs have a very high tax burden, and our VAT is unreasonably high compared to neighboring competitor countries," Toffer said. She added that if someone decides to end their activity in the current economic environment, they cannot be blamed for it.

World.title: Estonia's military conscription no-show rate falls to 2%
World.content:
The number of young adults failing to report for conscript service in the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF) has fallen steadily in recent years, reaching 2 percent in 2025.

A total of 63 call-up selectees failed to report for conscription last year, down from 4 percent in 2024 and 6.6 percent in 2023, the Defense Resources Agency (KRA) said.

KRA Conscripts Office director Krista Juhanson told ERR that those who repeatedly skip required medical assessments without good reason can be subject to official orders and an enforcement fine.

She said fines for failing to attend a medical assessment, which are intended to encourage compliance, are currently capped at €640, with the exact amount depending on the circumstances. Next year, however, the cap will double to €1,280.

"It's important to note that paying the fine does not exempt you from having to attend the medical assessment," Juhanson said.

KRA can impose fines repeatedly, but if that proves ineffective, the agency can seek to suspend a selectee's driver's license or fishing, hunting and firearms permits.

So far this year, the KRA has sought the suspension of 57 driver's licenses. Juhanson said that in practice, these extra measures generally work.

"Once call-up selectees grasp that failing to fulfill their obligations can result in additional consequences, they usually come in for the medical assessment," she said, adding that the goal is to encourage compliance, not punitive.

More flexible medicals

The KRA official also attributed the decline in no-shows in part to a more flexible approach, including a digital pre-assessment review of health records and allowing call-up selectees to choose when and where to have their assessment done.

"That means no more having to spend all day waiting your turn outside a doctor's office," Juhanson said.

Being summoned to a medical assessment doesn't automatically result in a conscription order either, she added, as when and where a selectee will be sent for conscript service are decided only after the assessment.
