World.title: PM Carney says Canadians will decide their future after Elon Musk expresses support for separatism
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday (October 8, 2026) that Canada's future will be decided by Canadians, pushing back on Elon Musk's call for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada.

“The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec,” PM Carney said when asked about Mr. Musk's comments.

Mr. Carney said Canadians should be free to live according to their languages and cultures, without interference "from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

Mr. Musk weighed in on Canada's separatist debates on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) in a post on X about Quebec Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose separatist Parti Québécois won Monday's provincial election.

The PQ's victory was not a mandate for independence. The party won about 28% of the popular vote and fell short of a majority of the seats in the Quebec legislature. Support for Quebec independence remains at about 30%, said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. He said the election was driven more by a desire to oust the Coalition Avenir Québec government than by support for separation.

“Good. Quebec should separate,” Mr. Musk wrote, adding that “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

Alberta is scheduled to hold a vote October 19 on whether the province should remain in Canada or move toward a future referendum on separation. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will vote to remain in Canada.

Mr. Smith said that separatist sentiment in her province has weakened as her government and Mr. Carney's have worked to address Albertans' concerns.

“The federal government has changed. Their approach to us has changed and they're willing to work together on addressing those issues,” Mr. Smith said in Edmonton.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe responded to Mr. Musk on X with a single word: “No.”

MMr. musk, the world's richest man and first-ever trillionaire, is a South African-born Canadian-American.

World.title: After speculation over political appointees, government to send senior career officer to Kathmandu
World.content:
The government’s decision to forward the name of Sudhakar Dalela, one of the most senior officers in the diplomatic service, as Ambassador to Nepal is an indication of the importance of the India-Nepal relationship, as well as the delicate situation the relationship is in at present.

Sources confirmed to The Hindu that the agreement or proposal for Mr. Dalela was forwarded to Kathmandu on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) and is expected to be approved soon by the Balen Shah government. Mr. Dalela, the Secretary (Economic Relations) not only has experience at managing ties with the neighbourhood from the Centre, in both the Ministry of External Affairs and the Prime Minister’s Office, but also from the ground, where he was India’s previous Ambassador to Bhutan. He also has a higher rank than former Ambassadors to Kathmandu, who were at Additional Secretary rank.

More than the qualifications, the government’s move suggests a change in thinking, favouring diplomatic experience over political flair. Speaking at the 11th Heads of Missions conference in April this year, Prime Minister Narendra Modi had, according to sources present, expressed his “disappointment” at the slow reaction time of missions in the neighbourhood to a series of political developments, indicating the street protests and government changes in Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Maldives in recent years. Pointing to India’s then newly appointed High Commissioner to Bangladesh, former Minister Dinesh Trivedi in the audience, Mr. Modi had said that the government would henceforth prefer “Anubhavi” (seasoned or experienced) diplomats in the neighbourhood- leading many to speculate that the government would also send a politician to Nepal when the term of the outgoing Ambassador Naveen Srivastava ended.

In particular, the government is understood to have worried that the new Nepal Prime Minister Balen Shah, known for his unorthodox style, would not deal as well with a professional diplomat. In his first few weeks in office, Mr. Shah declined to meet the Ambassadors of India and China, representatives of the two most important relationships, except in a larger group, and also would not confirm a meeting with the Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who subsequently put off his visit.

In the run-up to the decision on Indian envoy, media reports in Delhi and Kathmandu had floated the names of several senior BJP leaders, particularly from Nepal- neighbouring states Bihar and Uttar Pradesh for the position. However, since that time, relations with Bangladesh have taken a turn for the worse, and the last-minute cancellation of the visit of Bangladesh Prime Minister Tariq Rahman in August this year is being ascribed to miscommunication between the political appointee and the more protocol-bound MEA officials. As New Delhi plans for a possible visit by Mr. Rahman in November, it is also hoping to host Nepal PM Shah in November-end, and appears to have decided on a sure pair of hands rather than defying convention again.

Also Read : New and raw: On Nepal-India ties

“Traditionally, atleast for the past three decades, only professional diplomats have been posted as heads of missions in India’s neighbouring countries,” explained Vivek Katju, former Indian Ambassador to Afghanistan, Myanmar and Thailand. “These are very sensitive posts and they require quiet and deft handling which only a career diplomat can usually bring,” he said.

Mr. Dalela, a soft-spoken 1993-batch officer who has served as the Secretary (Economic Relations) since September 2025, was most recently in the news for his role as Sherpa and for forging a joint declaration at the BRICS Summit despite differences within the grouping over the Iran war. During his posting as Ambassador in Thimphu (2022-2025), he was instrumental in pitching for Bhutan’s Gelephu Mindfulness City project (GMC), often travelling to India with the Bhutanese leadership to discuss investments for the project. He also managed differences over Bhutan’s border talks with China, hydropower pricing issues, and Bhutan’s moves to curb low-end mass tourism from India.

He has considerable experience at the MEA’s ‘North’ desk, for Bhutan and Nepal ties, first as Director (North) (2006-7), and then as Joint Secretary (North) (2016-19) and would be the first time an officer with as much experience on the desk will also have helmed the embassies in Thimphu and Kathmandu. Interspersed with Mr. Dalela’s neighbourhood experience have been three stints in the U.S., including as Consul General in Chicago and two postings at the Embassy in Washington, where he was the Deputy Chief of Mission. In addition, he has worked twice at India’s mission to the World Trade Organisation and ran the Trade policy desk at the Commerce Ministry earlier.

World.title: Opposition leaders ‘pray’ at Rajghat for government to ‘get wisdom’ to remove CEC; say protest will continue
World.content:
For the third day in a row, leaders of the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA) on Thursday (October 8, 2026) protested in Delhi against alleged “vote chori [theft]” and demanded the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, staging a symbolic satyagraha at Mahatma Gandhi’s memorial at Rajghat.

Also read | The Rahul Gandhi show and the Congress’s INDIA bloc dilemma

Following two days of face-offs with the Delhi Police, the Opposition leaders were allowed to hold a peaceful protest at Rajghat without being prevented from reaching there.

The leaders offered floral tributes and “prayed at the memorial”, with Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge saying “they prayed for the BJP government gets the wisdom to stop vote chori, remove the CEC and protect the citizen’s right to vote”.

The INDIA bloc will continue its protest on Friday (October 9) and is likely to march towards Rashtrapati Bhavan after assembling at Parliament House in the morning. Senior leaders, including Mamata All India Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee, may join the march, even though President Droupadi Murmu has not yet given an appointment.

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Mr. Kumar of “hijacking” the country by allegedly indulging in vote theft.

Lunch at Connaught Place

In a replay of Wednesday’s (October 7) outreach, Mr. Kharge hosted a lunch for Opposition MPs and leaders at Moets restaurant in the Outer Circle of Connaught Place. In a show of Opposition unity, leaders of the Samajwadi Party, Shiv Sena (UBT) and the Nationalist Congress Party (Sharadchandra Pawar) were present at Thursday’s (October 8) lunch.

Interacting with reporters after the lunch, Mr Gandhi targeted Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat and Mr. Kumar, accusing them of “destroying” the Constitution.

The Opposition leader claimed that around 300 MPs wanted to hold a peaceful dharna on the first day, but were stopped near the Election Commission’s office, while on the second day, they were prevented from going to Jantar Mantar and were “beaten up”. “They will be brought to justice. This is our guarantee, and you will see it happen,” he said.

From Connaught Place, the Opposition leaders travelled to Rajghat in air-conditioned buses.

Congress general secretary (organisation) K.C. Venugopal said the INDIA bloc had sent a message by holding the protest at Rajghat. “Mahatma Gandhi led the freedom fight for India. The entire democracy has been completely finished by Mr. Modi and Mr. Shah through Gyanesh Kumar. We have come here to pray to the Mahatma. This is one of the most powerful agitations,” Mr. Venugopal said.

Besides Congress leaders such as Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and Kodikunnil Suresh, Abhishek Banerjee of the Mamata Trinamool Congress, John Brittas of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), P. Sandosh Kumar of the Communist Party of India, and Manoj Jha of the Rashtriya Janata Dal were also present at the Rajghat protest.

World.title: Government rejects ‘omnibus’ claims of enrolment of NEET-UG protestors’ biometrics on criminal database
World.content:
The union government has opposed Rajya Sabha MP A.A. Rahim’s “sweeping” assertion that the biometric data of “thousands of protestors” has been enrolled on national criminal databases.

An affidavit filed by the Home Ministry through the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) said blanket allegations of indefinite retention, storage and sharing of biometric information were not based on foundational facts.

The NCRB said allegations of violation of fundamental rights to privacy, free speech and expression must be based on factual foundation of the alleged infringement.

The government said the MP has not identified a single biometric record of any identified person which was unlawfully collected at Jantar Mantar, transmitted to NCRB, which had in turn processed or retained the information in breach of any law.

An “omnibus” assertion that biometrics of the NEET-UG protestors were captured and stored cannot substitute for proof that it was actually done, the Home Ministry said.

Mr. Rahim, represented by advocate Subhash Chandran, had challenged the alleged use of Facial Recognition Technology (FRT) and biometric surveillance by law enforcement agencies during public demonstrations, particularly at Jantar Mantar. He had alleged that the biometrics of the protestors were illegally retained and passed on to third parties.

The petitioner had sought comprehensive directives to stop biometric scanning of peaceful protesters and requested the deletion and erasure of collected biometric details from the National Automated Fingerprint Identification System (NAFIS), the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), other allied security databases.

“The petitioner’s prayer seeking deletion and erasure of biometric information from NAFIS, CCTNS and every allied database is in its present form wholly omnibus. Such a prayer would necessarily require the identification of the particular category of record, the database in which the record is maintained, the authority responsible for creating and transmitting the record, the criminal proceedings, if any, to which the record relates and the statutory regime governing its retention or destruction,” the NCRB affidavit pointed out.

A nodal officer would also consider the plea for destruction of the record and verify if the biometrics were linked to any other active cases.

The NCRB said the allegations that it had an interface to share biometric information with private entities were at best vague.

The MP has not placed any record in court to show a specific agreement, authorisation, or data-processing arrangement to back a claim that NCRB had granted access to, custody of, or control over biometric records alleged to have been collected from persons attending the NEET-UG protests.

“The petition discloses no order or act of the NCRB whereby any person at Jantar Mantar was subjected to facial recognition, biometric collection, drone surveillance or fingerprint matching. The mere existence of a statutory framework governing records of measurements [biometrics] and their processing or matching does not make NCRB the author, controller or supervisor of every alleged field-level collection undertaken by a police or investigating agency,” the affidavit said.

World.title: PM under 'GyaneshGate' siege, will not retaliate to U.S. visa crackdown: Congress
World.content:
Attacking the government over the U.S. government's actions affecting Indian IT professionals, the Congress on Friday (October 9, 2026) said India has a number of options to retaliate but a "thoroughly compromised" Prime Minister Narendra Modi, now under "siege" on "GyaneshGate", will not do so.

The Opposition party also said that the appeasement of bullies never pays.

In a post on X, Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh said, "That appeasement of bullies never pays is once again proven by the U.S. government’s actions yesterday targeted directly against Indian IT professionals."

This has come shortly after the Modi government went out of its way to please U.S. President Donald Trump by imposing UPI MDR charges that will clearly and directly benefit American companies, Mr. Ramesh claimed.

"India has a number of options to retaliate under laws already passed by Parliament like the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its Rules. But a thoroughly compromised PM now under siege on GyaneshGate will not do so," the Congress leader said in a reference to the Opposition's push for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged SIR irregularities.

The U.S. on Thursday (October 8, 2026) suspended eight IT firms, including Microsoft, Tata, Infosys and Wipro, from a programme to apply for green cards for foreign workers, contending that the practice has shut out Americans from the job market.

The announcement was made by Vice President J. D. Vance, Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling, and Attorney General Todd Blanche as part of the action under the aegis of the U.S. Anti-Fraud Task Force.

"I am hereby suspending from the Permanent Labour Certification Programme some of the largest IT outsourcing firms in the world, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini," Mr. Sonderling said.

He said the Department of Labour is also suspending Microsoft and Adobe from the programme due to multiple active federal investigations.

"There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft," Mr. Vance said.

"Microsoft laid off 6,000 American workers in 2025 after certifying that it could not find qualified American employees yet the company was approved for more than 6,000 H-1Bs and filed 3,682 PERM applications, including nearly 1,000 applications for the same positions as the laid off American workers, the Vice President said.

Indian professionals account for over 70% of all approved H-1B petitions annually.

The Vice President referred to foreign workers hired on H1-B visas as foreign indentured servants and the companies using the programme as visa mills.

Mr. Vance also announced an investigation into the J-1 visa programme for research scholars utilised by nine major universities, including Yale, Harvard, Stanford and Caltech.

The J-1 programme allows foreign nationals to enter the U.S. as exchange visitors for activities, including research, teaching, study and specialised professional work.

World.title: PM Shehbaz condemns fresh Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, reiterates commitment to kingdom's security under Makkah pact
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday condemned recent Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to the Gulf state’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.

The defence pact , of which Turkiye is also a part, was signed on August 7 and aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them.

In a post on X, the premier condemned attacks targeting Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, noting resulting civilian casualties.

He also commended the “vigilance and professionalism” of the Saudi armed forces and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen for interception of ballistic missiles.

PM Shehbaz expressed “unwavering” solidarity with Saudi Arabia.

“In line with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and recent decisions taken by its Strategic Political and Defence Committee, our commitment to the Kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security is resolute,” he wrote on X, adding that Pakistan fully supports Saudi Arabia right to self-defence.

He called on the Houthis to immediately cease attacks.

“We will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with Saudi Arabia in the face of these threats.”

On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that they had struck the Saudi capital’s main international airport with a ballistic missile, in another attack on the kingdom claimed by the group.

The attacks came as the Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom and are targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Both sides have claimed strikes on each other as tensions remain high.

On Wednesday, Saudi authorities said three people were killed and 36 injured in attacks on two of the kingdom’s international airports, including in the capital, Riyadh, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed to have fired on both transport hubs.

For its part, a Saudi-led coalition that backs pro-government forces in Yemen said on X that it “destroyed the ballistic missile launch platform” used in the attack on Riyadh.

The Houthis, who control most of the country’s northwest, are battling for territory against the Saudi-backed forces after the civil war reignited in July and they captured swathes of coastal land.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government this week declared a major counter-offensive and said Houthi fighters were pushed out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.

But the Houthis say they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.

Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia.

On October 5, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Defence Alliance in Riyadh.

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and was asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, to which he said both Turkiye and Pakistan had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations.

On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”.

Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries.

World.title: Saudis reel from attacks as allies debate ‘involvement’
World.content:
• Houthis fire missiles at Riyadh airport, airbases; kindergarten, clinic complex damaged by debris

• Lufthansa, Air India suspend flights to Saudi capital; half of all departures cancelled

• Nothing in Makkah pact bars members from joining Yemen fight, says Kh Asif

• Ankara calls accord ‘purely defensive’, rules out sending troops; Syria weighs deployment

RIYADH: Yemen’s Houthi forces escalated their campaign against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, attempting to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that disrupted flights and damaged a kindergarten and medical complex.

Lufthansa and Air India said on Thursday they will suspend flights to Riyadh as the Yemeni group renewed threats against airlines, after claiming a third attack on King Khalid International Airport.

According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, 49.7pc of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday across all Saudi airports.

Flight tracker FlightRadar24 also showed numerous delayed arrivals and departures. The airport did not acknowledge the disruption, pointing only to the “necessity” of contacting airlines before travelling.

A thick black column of smoke and flames rose from Riyadh airport in a video verified by Reuters. A witness and three people briefed on the matter said a stationary commercial plane had caught fire and caused the smoke, though the fire was later put out.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched two ballistic missiles at Riyadh’s airport, one at an airport in Najran and another at an airbase in Khamis Mushait. Saree also ordered workers at Saudi oil facilities to evacuate days after the group hit a major refinery south of the capital.

Around the same time, the Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and another toward Khamis Mushait.

Shortly after, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency posted on X that “interception debris” had fallen in Riyadh, causing material damage to a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex, without specifying if there were any casualties.

After loud booms echoed across Riyadh on Thursday morning, several multinational firms in the King Abdullah Financial District told staff to work from home or evacuated employees, according to people familiar with the matter.

Diplomats were instructed to shelter in place at their embassies, and at least one international school sent children into a basement for safety.

Defence pact

As Saudi Arabia pushes for allied support to reverse Houthi gains, regional states are weighing their involvement under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.

Following an emergency alliance meeting in Riyadh earlier this week, members have agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in the kingdom.

But while both Ankara and Islamabad have pledged support for Riyadh, Turkish and Pakistani officials offered contrasting interpretations on Thursday regarding whether the pact is strictly limited to territorial defence, or permits direct military involvement.

In Turkiye, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan ruled out sending troops to confront the Houthis. “This is a defence agreement,” he said. “If one of the countries is attacked, you support its defence. This is not an offensive agreement.”

Turkiye “will not send its troops to another country’s territory to launch an attack,” he stressed.

Meanwhile in Pakistan, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told ARY News on Thursday that no stipulation in the Makkah pact bars alliance members from getting “directly involved” if one member faced a threat.

“To defend one of the member countries, the remaining two would get involved as if they were defending themselves,” Mr Asif said, though he separately told Geo News that while Pakistan and Turkiye had a “presence in the theatre”, only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations.

Separately, the Ministry of Information on Thursday dismissed a New York Times report claiming Pakistan Air Force aircraft were being used against the Houthis as “fake and fabricated”, having earlier termed a Reuters report claiming the deployment of 30,000 to 40,000 Pakistani troops as “speculative”.

“International media houses are again asked to avoid speculative reporting with regards to employment of Pakistan’s military forces under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” it added.

Meanwhile, Damascus is also said to be considering options for military support, including defensive aid for Saudi Arabia or an offensive deployment against the Houthis, according to US and Syrian defence officials.

“Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries,” the diplomat said.

On Thursday, oil prices jumped more than five per cent, then pared gains after President Donald Trump said the US will not launch an attack on Iran before midterm congressional elections in November.

Brent crude futures were up $3.48, or 3.5pc, at $103.73 a barrel by 1641 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained $2.69, or 3.1pc, to $91.

Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

World.title: Direct shipping link with Europe restored
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Direct shipping connectivity bet­­ween Karachi and major European ports has been restored, providing relief to exporters facing longer transit times and incre­ased freight costs due to disruptions on international shipping routes, Federal Maritime Affairs Minister Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry announced on Thursday.

In a statement, the minister noted that the Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) had “reinstated its PREMIUM IPAK service” in response to exporters’ demand for a dedicated and direct Europe service.

Under the restored service, MSC will make wee­kly calls at Karachi Gate­way Terminal Inter­nat­ional (KGTI), connecting the port city to key Euro­pean destinations, incl­u­ding Felixstowe, Rott­er­dam, Hamburg, Brem­erhaven, Antwerp, Le Havre and London Gateway via Colombo.

“Previously we had no tra­nsshipment service from Karachi Port. However, now we have a full-swing service as Pakistan has emerged as the transshipment hub of the region,” the minister said.

He added that the restoration of a dedicated Europe service was an important development for the country’s export-oriented industries, particularly the textile sector, which had been facing increased transit times and logistics costs because of disruptions to international shipping routes.

The minister referred to his meeting with textile exporters who had recently informed him about the difficulties caused by changes in shipping routes, particularly those linked to the situation in the Red Sea.

“Exporters had earlier expressed concern that longer vessel journeys were increasing transportation costs and delivery times for shipments to European and US markets. These additional costs and delays have affected the competitiveness of Pakistani exporters,” he said.

“The restored service will improve connectivity with major European ports and provide exporters with greater options for planning and moving their shipments,” he said.

The minister, however, noted that the reinstatement of the service should not be viewed as a resolution of the wider challenges affecting international shipping routes.

“Disruptions to established shipping routes continue to have implications for global trade. We will continue working with the shipping industry and exporters to address connectivity and logistics issues and to strengthen Pakistan’s position in international trade,” he said.

Risk-based inspections

In another development, the KPT chairman proposed standardised 24/7 electronic delivery orders, risk-based inspections, non-intrusive scanning, joint inspections and common sampling.

He was chairing a meeting of the Working Group on Shipping Connectivity and Optimisation at the KPT head office, focusing on removing physical and regulatory bottlenecks and making cargo clearance faster and more predictable.

Terminal operators exp­ressed readiness for night inspections, while Pakis­tan Customs was reques­ted to facilitate round-the-clock operations.

Published in Dawn, October 9th, 2026

World.title: US to livestream Army firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon says
World.content:
The US will livestream the army’s upcoming firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, the Pentagon said, in what would be an unprecedented broadcast of a US execution.

Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.

The execution is scheduled for December 3 at the same sprawling Texas base where Hasan opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility. It comes amid heightened debate in the US over the death penalty following the botched lethal injection of a Tennessee woman last week.

“It will be livestreamed. Details will follow,” a Pentagon official told Reuters, speaking on the condition of anonymity.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who championed the push to execute Hasan by firing squad, confirmed plans to livestream the execution in an X post.

Media have sought to televise US executions in the past but have been blocked by the courts. No other country is known to televise or livestream a legal execution, experts said.

Public executions have become exceedingly rare worldwide. Among countries known to conduct them in recent years are Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.

Extrajudicial lynchings in the United States, often by white mobs targeting Black Americans, were public spectacles well into the 20th century. The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in 1936, death penalty experts said. Thousands watched that 1936 hanging of a young Black man who had been convicted of raping a white woman.

Hegseth told the Human Events Daily program that deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1:00pm the approximate time, day of the week and location of the 2009 shooting was a “no-brainer.”

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public. Because people need to understand that… there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

Asked if Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth said: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

President must approve firing squad execution

A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralysed and confined to a wheelchair from being shot by police during his arrest.

Under US military law, a US president must approve an execution by firing squad. President Donald Trump did so on Hegseth’s recommendation, the Pentagon said on Monday.

The White House declined to say whether Trump supported the livestreaming, referring questions to the Pentagon.

The group Death Penalty Action, which opposes capital punishment, said Hasan’s execution would be the first military execution since 1961.

According to the Death Penalty Information Centre, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging.

The last known executions by US military firing squads were in 1945, the centre reported.

“It would be extremely, extremely strange” to livestream the event, said Eugene Fidell, a lawyer, author and military law expert who lectures at Yale Law School.

While firing squads have a long history in American military law, as far as he knew it would be unprecedented to livestream or televise an execution, Fidell said, adding that Hasan would need to sue in federal court if he wanted to block a public display of his death.

“The Supreme Court has never addressed this question, and it’s an interesting question whether the current Supreme Court would put on their originalist hat and say, ‘Well, it was OK in 1790, so what the hell?’” Fidell said.

Jonathan Lurie, an author and historian of military justice, said there are no compelling reasons to make the execution public.

“What’s the point of it? Who would want to see that?” said Lurie.

At least five states have firing squads on the books, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. In 2025, South Carolina carried out the first such execution in the United States in 15 years.

Death by firing squad is one of several forms of capital punishment the Trump administration recently added to permissible forms of execution for the gravest of federal crimes, along with electrocution and gas asphyxiation.

The number of federal execution options was expanded in part because of increasing difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections, which have also sometimes proved challenging to carry out.

Plans by the state of Tennessee to execute a woman for the first time in more than 200 years went awry last week when prison personnel botched attempts to administer a lethal injection, leaving the death-row inmate, Christa Pike, alive but hospitalised.

Her lawyers said on Wednesday she awoke “angry and confused” in a hospital. Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, they said.

World.title: Govt, PTI trade barbs over KP governance issues
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The government and PTI traded accusations on Thursday over governance and the deteriorating security situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as federal ministers continued to blame the provincial government for allegedly failing to combat terrorism, and focusing instead on the party’s long march, while the opposition accused the Centre of scapegoating KP for the consequences of “flawed federal policies”.

The PTI also asked the federal government to rein in its ministers if it was genuinely serious about negotiating a settlement to the ongoing political impasse, saying daily press conferences, “provocative statements” and “non-sensical rhetoric” were creating an atmosphere of confrontation and undermining the prospects of meaningful dialogue.

PTI Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said the government could not simultaneously call for negotiations and “allow its cronies” to appear before the media every day to “spew venom” against PTI leadership and the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government.

He said that the government should demonstrate its seriousness about dialogue by accepting PTI’s straightforward demands.

He also rejected attempts to place the responsibility for widespread terrorism on the KP government or Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.

Meanwhile, Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani on Thursday expressed serious concerns over the sharp rise in terrorist incidents in KP, insisting that the province had increasingly turned into a war zone while alleging that the provincial government was fai­ling to play its due role in combating terrorism, APP reported.

Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam on Thursday urged the KP government to focus on resolving public issues instead of pursuing a protest march.

He said terrorist attacks continued in the province while the provincial leadership was busy with political activities.

Referring to PTI’s protest march, the minister said its route kept changing while people in KP continued to face difficulties due to blocked routes.

World.title: Iran weighs US response as Trump rules out attack before midterms
World.content:
• Araghchi says Tehran can reply to proposal within days; Iranian atomic chief vows not to give up enrichment

• Centcom terms Hormuz closure claims ‘false’

TEHRAN: Iran announced on Thursday that it was still reviewing Washington’s response to a proposal under which the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within seven days, as US President Donald Trump indicated that he will not attack Iran before November’s midterm elections amid ‘productive talks’.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran could reply within days, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency, emphasising that “the diplomatic process is still continuing”.

Trump wrote on Truth Social that Washington will not strike Iran prior to the Nov 3 midterm elections, calling talks with Tehran “productive”.

“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition … we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on Nov 3,” Trump wrote.

Meanwhile, Trump said that his special envoy Steve Witkoff is “doing very well” in negotiations with Iran, though he indicated that an agreement is not his preferred outcome, Anadolu reported.

“He’s working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn’t really something that I want to do, but they’re willing to offer us anything to stop,” Trump told supporters at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, adding that Tehran “will never have a nuclear weapon”.

Trump described Witkoff as “a great negotiator” who has “done some phenomenal things”, citing the ceasefire deal in Gaza, and said he expects the war with Iran to end soon.

“That war ends — it’s going to be very soon. It’s got to be very soon,” Trump said, descr­ibing Iran as “a failed nation”.

He also reiterated his claim that Iran has been defeated “economically and militarily” and said the US naval blockade will remain in place, while claiming that oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in “record numbers” with 22 million barrels passing through Wednesday night.

Despite the ongoing talks, Iran will not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium, state media reported Thursday, citing Mohammad Eslami, the head of Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation.

Dismissing renewed US threats aga­inst Iran’s nuclear facilities as “nothing new”, he said enrichment was “an inseparable part” of the nuclear process.

On the aviation front, the first commercial flight operated by a foreign airline to fly into Iran since the outbreak of the Middle East war landed on Thursday, state media repo­rted, after the United States granted a sanctions waiver for Iraq’s national carrier.

The waiver applies to pilgr­ims travelling between Iran and Najaf, alongside a separate agreement allowing Iran­ian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate daily flights on the route.

At sea, Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, warned that military forces are ready “with crushing weapons to deliver a decisive response to any attempt at unauthorised passage in the Strait of Hormuz,” Fars reported.

US Central Comm­and rejected Iranian claims that the waterway is closed. However, shipping data from analytics firm Kpler showed the number of vessels transiting the strait fell to seven on Tuesday, the lowest in more than two months, before edging up to 10 on Wednesday, after tanker attacks reached a wartime high last week.

“Crude crossing the strait fell 27 per cent from a wartime high the week before, to at least 10.1 million barrels a day,” Kpler analysts Emma­nuel Belostrino and Yui Torikata wrote Tuesday, though rising exports from the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea kept overall Middle East crude exports at pre-war levels.

World.title: Capital Development Authority plans to execute 11th Avenue project in two phases
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Capital Development Authority (CDA) is planning to execute the 11th Avenue project in two phases, starting the first phase from E-11 to Srinagar Highway.

Recently, CDA’s DWP approved PC-I worth Rs24.5 billion for the construction of the highway from Margalla Avenue to IJP Road.

According to the PC-I, the 7.5km road, with three lanes on each side, will be completed within a year. Officials of the engineering wing said around 17 bridges and overpasses were part of the project.

However, sources said that now CDA has decided to execute 11th Avenue in two phases. In first priority phase, the 3.5km road will be constructed from E-11 interchange to Srinagar Highway, including an interchange at Srinagar Highway.

DWP recently approved PC-I worth Rs24.5 billion for construction of highway from Margalla Avenue to IJP Road

“Recently, during a meeting it was decided that this project will be carried out in two phases. Hopefully, the project will be formally started within two months as currently we are working on pre-tendering process,” said an engineer of CDA.

He said that when this phase will be completed, Srinagar Highway will be connected with Margalla Avenue and overall traffic load will be divided on both Margalla Road and Srinagar Highway.

To a query, the engineer said that overall PC-I worth Rs24.5 billion had been approved, so “I guess for this portion of 3.5km with an interchange roughly Rs11 to 12 billion will be earmarked. This is a guesswork as proper working is in progress,” he said.

It is relevant to note here that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, during his first stint, had laid the foundation stone of 11th Avenue in June 2023, but the project was not started.

The avenue is supposed to start from IJP ll allRoad and after passing between I-10 and I-11, G-10, G-11, F-10 and F-11, culminate at the E-11 interchange. From E-11 to D-12, a portion of the road has already been completed and is known as Iran Avenue.

After the construction of 9th Avenue decades ago, the CDA could not construct any major road. Work on the construction of 10th Avenue was started in 2022, but after completion of around 50pc of the work, the project was halted last year.

CDA officials told Dawn that besides focusing on 11th Avenue, the authority should also complete the stalled 10th Avenue project, as the structure of the incomplete road was deteriorating. They said 10th Avenue was a federally funded project and, due to the non-release of funds, it had been left abandoned.

The officials said the CDA had requested the federal government several times for release of fund, but to no avail.

According to the CDA, the total cost of the 10th Avenue project was Rs10.2 billion, but the government had released only around Rs4 billion. That was why the project was halted, they said.

They said that under the original plan, the project should have been completed by December 2024, but the federal government did not allocate any funds for the public welfare project in its 2024-25 and 2025-26 budgets.

On the other hand, earthwork and structure from I.J.P to H-9 have been decaying and also causing inconvenience for public. The officials said with little funding, at least this portion could be brought under use with asphalt work.

World.title: Rs26m each given to families of Pakistanis killed by Somali pirates
World.content:
KARACHI: Sindh Governor Nehal Hashmi on Thursday distributed cheques for Rs26 million each among the families of three Pakistanis who were martyred while in the captivity of Somali pirates on hijacked oil tanker MT Honour 25.

The financial assistance cheques were presented to the families of Mahmood Ahmed Ansari, Syed Kashif Umar and Rafiullah Khan on the special directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, said a Governor House statement.

It said the bereaved families thanked the prime minister, saying that the government had stood by them and provided support during this difficult time.

Last week, PM Shehbaz announced financial support for the families of the deceased, including free housing and free education for their children.

A Governor House spokesperson said the prime minister had announced Rs12.5m in financial assistance and a plot for each family. “Cheques for Rs12.5m and Rs13.5m for plot purchase have been presented to each family,” he added.

World.title: Department store in Berlin to offer high-end Japanese rice on trial basis
World.content:
Germany’s largest department store in Berlin, Kaufhaus des Westens (KaDeWe), will sell high-end brand rice from Japan on a trial basis for about two weeks this month, sources said Thursday.

The move comes as the Japanese side approached the department store about handling high-grade Japanese rice, at a time when the country aims to expand sales abroad through retail stores and people in Germany are increasingly interested in washoku Japanese cuisine.

Six varieties, including Yumepirika from Hokkaido and Koshihikari from Niigata Prefecture, will be available to purchase during the trial, set to run from Monday through Oct. 24.

Tastings will be available to allow customers to compare the flavors of the different rice varieties and produce from different regions. A leaflet on how to cook rice will also be distributed.

“We want people (in Germany) to find that rice flavors vary by production area, just like wine and olive oil,” an official from the Japanese side said.

The official added that the planned trial is also intended to raise awareness of high-quality Japanese rice as cheap non-Japanese rice is often used at washoku restaurants in Germany.

Between January and August, Japanese rice exports to Germany rose 15% compared to a year earlier to 699 metric tons, the largest among European countries.

World.title: Extreme rain is testing Japan’s flood defences
World.content:
When Shuji Nishizawa and his wife bought their semi-basement apartment in 2003, the tiled garden terrace was the main draw. On Aug. 13, it became the floodwater’s way in.

Now, pointing to muddy lines that run across the walls 1.8 meters above the floor of his apartment, Nishizawa, 60, explains how the water rapidly rose during the torrential downpour that struck his neighborhood that evening.

Nishizawa, a self-employed web specialist, was in the common area of Sanctus Shinmatsudo, a 10-story apartment complex in Matsudo, Chiba Prefecture, when his wife rushed in to tell him that rainwater had begun gushing down the steps from ground level and pooling on their terrace.

World.title: Rakuten Medical eyes U.S. market for its novel idea to conquer cancer
World.content:
Biotech startup Rakuten Medical is eyeing the U.S. market for its novel idea to conquer cancer — light illumination therapy.

The treatment, based on photoimmunotherapy — a combination of drug administration and illumination with red light — has long been in development as part of its Alluminox platform.

“We believe this could become a new platform for cancer treatment,” Minami Maeda, who became CEO of Rakuten Medical in July, said in a recent interview with The Japan Times.

World.title: Hard-hitting Guardians beat White Sox to force decisive fifth game in ALDS
World.content:
Jose Ramirez and Patrick Bailey homered and had two hits each as the Cleveland Guardians topped the Chicago White Sox 9-5 on Thursday to force a decisive fifth game in the AL Division Series.

Guardians pitchers registered 12 strikeouts while White Sox pitchers issued seven walks.

Game 5 is Saturday in Cleveland, with the winner advancing to oppose the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL Championship Series.

World.title: Nvidia-backed Lumentum sold out of AI server parts till 2029
World.content:
Lumentum Holdings’ optical components are “completely sold out” through early 2029 on demand from tech companies clamoring for faster artificial intelligence data centers, according to its chief executive officer.

Lumentum is unable to meet about 70% of demand for some products through next year, and won’t be able to address 30% of demand for some other products through 2028, Michael Hurlston said in an interview in Tokyo on Friday. Just six months ago, Hurlston said Lumentum was on track to sell out its capacity by 2028.

The company, which received an investment of $2 billion from Nvidia earlier this year along with rival Coherent, supplies advanced indium phosphide devices that help enable high-speed cloud computing and data transmission. Analysts on average expect Lumentum’s sales to more than double this year.

World.title: Dozens protest in Tokyo after U.S. Marine accused of murder in Okinawa
World.content:
Dozens of protesters lined up in front of the Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a U.S. Marine was accused of killing a woman in Okinawa Prefecture, with many holding signs decrying crimes by U.S. service members.

The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fueled unease over the large U.S. troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China, with U.S. officials warning it could undermine ties vital to security in East Asia.

Public reaction to Anna Yagi’s killing, however, has been muted compared with the mass demonstrations that followed the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three U.S. servicemen in 1995.

Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha last weekend and taking her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.

Leaders of Thursday’s protest spoke over loudspeakers about abuses by U.S. service members and called on the government to respond, with others in the crowd rattling noisemakers in assent.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the killing “extremely brutal and heinous,“ and Tokyo said it had strongly protested to the U.S. and demanded measures to prevent a repeat of such incidents.

Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of U.S. forces globally. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the U.S. held from the end of World War II until 1972.

That presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel.

The U.S. on Wednesday began a 48-hour pause of military operations and a ban on alcohol while troops undergo training on standards and discipline. Service members have also been given a monthlong curfew for a “period of reflection.”

World.title: Alcohol makers in Japan tap into U.S. ready-to-drink market
World.content:
Japanese alcoholic beverage makers have entered the growing U.S. market for ready-to-drink (RTD) products, including those known as canned chūhai in Japan, but not canned beer.

While U.S. consumers are steering away from alcohol amid the soaring cost of living and rising health consciousness, RTD beverages are increasing their presence.

According to British beverage market research firm IWSR, yearly alcohol consumption in the United States fell by 1%, on average, between 2015 and 2025, with beer and wine seeing significant declines in recent years.

On the other hand, the consumption of RTD products, mostly canned beverages that are premixed and ready for immediate consumption, grew by an average of 14% per year during the same period.

The popularity of RTD products was ignited by the introduction of hard seltzers, which are carbonated alcoholic beverages that are not as sweet as other RTD options. According to IWSR President Marten Lodewijks, hard seltzers became a hit among U.S. consumers looking for an alternative to beer.

Last year, RTD products accounted for 8% of all alcohol servings in the country, up from 2% in 2015. The market size reached $22 billion.

In light of the growing popularity of RTD products, Japanese companies have introduced U.S. versions of popular RTD products in Japan.

In 2023, Suntory Holdings started selling its -196 Vodka Seltzer series in some U.S. states. The drinks became available nationwide in 2025.

Asahi Group Holdings released Zeitaku Shibori products tailored to the U.S. market last December, while Kirin Holdings started selling some Hyoketsu products in March.

Although RTD products currently hold only a small share of the U.S. alcoholic beverage market, Japanese makers believe that these products are promising and are rushing to establish foundations for sales in the United States, at a time when alcohol consumption in Japan continues to decline.

IWSR’s Lodewijks, however, highlighted fierce competition within the RTD market, saying that although there are a lot of RTD brands in the United States, only a few have been successful.

He also warned that the growing presence of RTDs could cause sales declines for beer and other makers.

Lodewijks added that Japanese beverage makers have “done very well” by associating their RTD products with Japanese food but added that they “haven’t really gone beyond that.”

Citing the rise of tequila as a symbol of Mexican culture, he added that Japanese beverage makers’ success hinges on whether their products can represent Japanese culture as a whole, including movies and music, because a simple link to Japanese cuisine has limited effects.

World.title: Japan deal drought cuts IPO fundraising to lowest in 14 years
World.content:
Fundraising through initial public offerings (IPOs) in Japan is drying up, in contrast to a dealmaking boom across Asia, after regulatory changes and a dearth of artificial intelligence related companies depleted up the listings pipeline.

The number of first-time offerings fell to 32 this year through the end of September, the lowest nine-month tally since 2012, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. The amount of funds raised by companies including taxi app provider Go slid to a four-year low, even as fundraising surged in the rest of Asia.

While companies along the AI supply chain have driven dealmaking around the world, Japan is yet to match the wave of startups that can capture the imagination of investors, like in China. Some IPO hopefuls were also deterred by the Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE)’s plan to raise the bar for companies to remain listed in its startup section, as part of its effort to attract more quality issuers.

World.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: youth-led charity supports young cancer patients
World.content:
Timothy Chan Chi-fung was 19 when a testicular tumour sent him into a Hong Kong hospital system largely designed for children or much older adults.

Neither door quite fitted. His experience eventually led him to found Youth Cancer Hong Kong, a contribution that has earned him a place as a finalist in the community category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards.

The awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, were launched in 2013 to recognise individuals and organisations whose work contributes to Hong Kong and its communities.

Chan was diagnosed in 2019 with a mixed germ cell tumour of the testis. He underwent surgery within two weeks of his diagnosis, followed by two cycles of chemotherapy. He lost his hair and his studies at university were interrupted. But he eventually recovered.

World.title: Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: firm uses 3D-printed tiles to restore coral reefs
World.content:
In 2014, a University of Hong Kong research team watched two years of reef restoration work collapse in Sai Kung.

The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department had asked the researchers to speed up coral recovery. Cement structures were placed on the seabed and coral began to grow. But as the colonies became larger, they became unstable.

“They have no roots,” said Vriko Yu Pik-fan, then a doctoral student on the project. “The bigger they got, the less stable they were.”

World.title: Hong Kong national security police charge man over seditious social media posts
World.content:
Hong Kong national security police have charged a man with publishing seditious material on social media, while court proceedings did not reveal details of his posts.

The force’s national security department said on Friday it had charged a 52-year-old man for posting seditious material with the intent to provoke hatred towards the central Chinese authorities, the Hong Kong government and the judiciary.

The defendant had attended the first hearing on Wednesday afternoon, according to the force’s statement.

Contrary to its usual practice when charges under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance are filed, the department issued no media statements when it brought the defendant before West Kowloon Court.

World.title: Former Greentown China head charged for taking bribes over stake in real estate project
World.content:
Hong Kong’s corruption watchdog has charged the former head of a listed company for allegedly accepting HK$20 million (US$2.5 million) in bribes from a mainland Chinese property developer in exchange for acquiring a stake in the developer’s real estate project.

Zhang Yadong, 58, who was chairman of Greentown China Holdings from 2019 to 2025, faced a count of conspiracy to accept advantages, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Friday.

The case was mentioned at Eastern Court on Friday.

Prosecutors alleged that between January 2020 and March 2023, Zhang conspired with his son, a middleman, a shareholder of an estate developer in Dailian, Liaoning province, and others to accept bribes totalling HK$20 million from the shareholder in exchange for Greentown China acquiring equity interests in the developer’s project.

World.title: Hong Kong and Shenzhen confirm Huanggang Port to open on Monday
World.content:
The revamped Huanggang border crossing between Hong Kong and Shenzhen will open on Monday, after both sides confirmed the facility was ready for service.

Confirming an earlier South China Morning Post report, the Hong Kong government said on Friday that the new Huanggang border crossing would commence operations at 6.30am on October 12, replacing the current Lok Ma Chau-Huanggang port as the sole round-the-clock clearance point

“Acceptance inspection of the new port building of the Huanggang Port has been completed. Following the completion of a series of system tests, trials and emergency drills by both Hong Kong and Shenzhen, it has been confirmed that the port is ready for opening,” it said.

An opening ceremony is due on Sunday, with the government gazette stipulating that only “bona-fide staff, guests and participants” of the event could enter the Hong Kong port area of the facility from 4am to 10pm that day.

World.title: 27 people, groups named finalists for 14th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards
World.content:
Twenty-seven individuals and groups have been named finalists for the 14th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards , which recognises the unsung heroes of the city who have made major contributions to society.

This year’s shortlist for the awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post, is divided into nine categories: community, culture, innovation, sustainability, perseverance, teamwork, youth, nurturing and entrepreneurship.

“The self-effacing yet extraordinary efforts of these wonderful individuals have made positive differences on the lives of others, making our beloved city a more compassionate, vibrant and special place,” said Daryl Ng Win-kong, chairman of Sino Group.

World.title: Hong Kong police to launch international academy, reveal details of new degree
World.content:
Hong Kong’s police have revealed they will launch an academy offering specialised courses for overseas officers and shared new details about the force’s bachelor’s degree programme, with classes expected to start next March.

Kelly Cheng Lai-ki, director of the Police College, said establishing the Hong Kong International Academy of Policing would consolidate generations of frontline wisdom handed down within the force into an international exchange hub.

“These exchanges can showcase our strengths to the world and we can also learn others’ best practices from this platform, fostering mutual learning,” Cheng said.

World.title: From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
World.content:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.

“I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said.

World.title: ‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019087/‘Healing’ Chickens vs. Hungry Thieves: Art Students’ Project Ends in Tears
World.content:
The thieves came in the dead of night in late August — seven ghostly figures illuminated only by the glow of their flashlights and burning cigarettes. When they left, tucked under their arms were 10 chickens and two geese.

The next day, watching footage of the theft recorded by a security camera, Xu Lingni’s heart sank. It was the end of a dream.

The poultry had been kept overnight in a hilltop coop at the bucolic Huxi campus of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute (SCFAI), in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing, and belonged to the Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative, a student-led club aimed at rebuilding the bonds between humans and nature.

The group had intended to use the project to promote interest across campus and beyond in food-waste conversion, community-supported agriculture, plastics consumption, and other sustainability issues.

For Xu, the club’s leader, those plans vanished along with those 12 birds. Yet worse was to come.

After a brief investigation, the Chongqing police discovered that several workers hired by SCFAI for a summer construction project had taken the poultry and eaten them. Their crew manager agreed to pay 7,000 yuan ($1,040) to compensate for the financial loss and the students’ emotional distress.

However, the theft drew widespread attention and sparked fresh criticism over raising animals on campus. Facing mounting pressure, the school’s leadership decided to ban the practice. The cooperative was over.

Hatching a plan

The Happy Chick Feeding Cooperative was a key part of the Healing Garden Project, which inhabits a patch of land on campus once piled high with construction waste. Seven years ago, Jin Lipeng, an associate professor in SCFAI’s School of Experimental Art, led students in repurposing the debris to pave paths and build planting beds. He envisioned an area that could restore nature and nurture people.

At the time, the campus cafeteria was sending hundreds of kilograms of food scraps — often mixed with unsorted plastic waste — to an incinerator dozens of kilometers away. Jin and his students began to use these leftovers as compost, converting roughly 40 tons of food waste into fertilizer over the years.

The idea for the cooperative stemmed from a graduate student’s thesis project in spring 2025 that looked at permaculture and the role of foraging chickens in loosening soil, eating pests, clearing weeds, and providing eggs. To test a theory, the student purchased five chickens of a local breed with red combs and black skin. They were allowed to roam freely through campus and returned at night to their hilltop coop.

Xu, an undergraduate majoring in sculpture, was already involved in the garden project and began informally caring for the chickens, buying them grain and taking them to the veterinarian.

In summer last year, as temperatures soared above 40 degrees Celsius, one bird died of heatstroke, and three others disappeared. Fearing that the sole survivor would get lonely, Xu bought a new one from the market. Then one of the escapees returned.

A few days later, Xu found six new adolescent chickens in the coop. A school janitor, who had bought them to raise for their meat, agreed to sell the birds to the students. These were soon joined by a common chicken brought from a roadside stall, a Plymouth Rock chicken, a new hatchling, and a wuhei black-boned chicken. (Two birds died before the theft — one from hypothermia, the other from a wild animal attack. The wuhei chicken was the only one left behind by the thieves; its dark plumage likely made it hard to spot at night.)

As the flock grew, the birds began producing more eggs than the students could eat. Jin, whose research area includes labor issues, proposed creating the cooperative as a student club and asked Xu to lead it. Soon, the students were dividing up their responsibilities: caring for the animals, sourcing and selling merchandise, writing articles, and managing social media channels. In June this year, several attended an international conference to introduce the cooperative’s work.

Those who joined the project felt that caring for the chickens brought them “healing energy.” Xu recalls one classmate who would often hold the birds and cry. “The theft this summer hit her especially hard, and she wasn’t the only one,” Xu says, adding that the cooperative not only fostered friendships but also helped some members find meaning.

While she doesn’t exactly share Jin’s grand ideals, Xu believes that through her work she came to understand seemingly distant but deeply personal issues such as permaculture and climate change.

“Most university students have no idea where eggs come from, what happens to food waste, or why rubbish gets incinerated,” she said in a speech at a climate change forum in May. “Dorm rooms are piled with takeout plastic. Delivery workers risk heatstroke in extreme temperatures. Yet few students have enough awareness to connect these to drought, heat, and carbon emissions.

“Our work lets people feel the pressure and causes of climate change firsthand,” she added, “and shows that through campus community-supported agriculture we can mount a small resistance.”

Making a mess

The cooperative began selling eggs for about 2 yuan each to residents on and around campus this March. The chickens laid two to eight eggs a day. Xu stored them in her apartment’s refrigerator, took orders through an online group chat, and delivered them to customers on her electric bike. She calculates that this brought in just over 500 yuan in total.

Fans of the project were kept up to date through the club’s channel on the lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, which has more than 6,300 followers. In addition, the cooperative sold themed merchandise including fridge magnets, tote bags, and silk scarves, which brought in about 2,000 yuan.

Not everyone was supportive, though. The most common complaint was that the free-roaming chickens often defecated on the pathways and at the entrance to the student dormitories. To prevent this, this summer the birds were fenced in on the hillside.

In 2022, Chongqing introduced regulations prohibiting the raising of livestock and poultry in urban areas. However, the restrictions apply only to commercial-scale farming, while exceptions can be made for educational purposes and scientific research.

While the number of chickens at SCFAI was far below commercial scale, the activity fell outside the definition of “backyard rearing,” putting it in a gray area. As such, the school took an open-minded approach, requiring only proper fencing and separation, despite repeated objections from others in the campus community.

The cooperative used old bamboo posts and tall netting to enclose the poultry on the hilltop. But the gate was never locked. “This is a public welfare project. Anyone was welcome to come in to spend time with the chickens,” Xu explains.

For security, the group installed an infrared camera to watch the flock at night and raised two goslings to guard the coop. “Geese bite hard. Once I went up the hill in a raincoat, and they didn’t recognize me, so they bit me,” Xu adds. “We’d thought the intruders would be stray cats or weasels — never thieves.”

Ruffling feathers

The theft sparked an outpouring of grief online. “Come home, little ones” and “My babies are gone” were typical comments posted by students in the aftermath.

In the coming weeks and months, Xu and her classmates had planned to step up marketing and sales, offer egg-based food delivery services, and write a handbook on community supported agriculture that could inspire other schools and universities.

That’s now all been scrapped. This fall, the school’s leadership announced a ban on keeping poultry on campus.

In a statement, it also said that officials had learned during mediation that the maintenance workers who took the birds had endured long hours of intense labor in hot weather, with limited food and lodging. Some students strongly objected to this version of events, arguing that chicken meat is cheap and widely available — and that the workers weren’t “desperate,” they just wanted to taste free-range birds.

“Pioneering ecological practice is inherently accompanied by trial and error and waiting,” the statement read. “We will review and consolidate, continue deepening our existing work, and wait for the right conditions to restart explorations.”

The cooperative maintained that its activities “filled a gap” in the school’s labor education by giving students hands-on experience as well as teaching responsibility and empathy. But there was no overturning the decision.

The sole survivor of the theft, the wuhei chicken, was moved to a student’s home for safekeeping and has quickly adapted to her new environment. Xu says the bird is even laying eggs again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Xu Lingni is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Kong Lingyu.

A version of this article originally appeared in FoodThink. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Kiong Xin Xi; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.
