World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.title: China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019100/China’s DeepZang AI Aims to Improve Tibetan Translation
World.content:
DeepZang, China’s first Tibetan-language large language model, is being upgraded to better adapt to Tibetan dialects, enable real-time translation between Tibetan and Mandarin Chinese, and support offline use.

At a Monday seminar in Hohhot, capital of northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, the model’s developer unveiled a series of upgrades scheduled between October and December. The seminar featured representatives from companies, research institutions, and universities.

DeepZang, developed by local technology company Choknor, was launched in March in Lhasa, capital of the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. Its app supports AI-powered conversations, translation, and speech transcription in Tibetan, Mandarin Chinese, and English.

At the model’s launch, organizations including the Xizang branches of China Mobile and the People’s Insurance Company of China, as well as Sichuan Minzu Publishing House, signed agreements with Choknor to promote its adoption.

According to Choknor, DeepZang has attracted nearly 400,000 users across Xizang, the northwestern Qinghai and Gansu provinces, and southwestern Sichuan province, where most of China’s Tibetan speakers reside.

The company has said the model has cut the time needed for some Tibetan-Chinese translation tasks involving two or three people from 40 minutes to just over 10 minutes for one person. It also reported that the model has been used in such varied settings as helping non-Tibetan-speaking doctors communicate with local patients, generating Tibetan-language contracts for yak sales, and assisting grassroots officials in drafting Tibetan work reports.

The model has been trained on nearly 70 million pairs of standardized Tibetan and Chinese texts, along with more than 30,500 hours of Tibetan speech covering its three major dialect groups — Ü-Tsang, Kham, and Amdo. The team collected the data from libraries, medical institutions, and monasteries, among other settings.

At Monday’s seminar, Choknor unveiled plans to develop offline language packages for Tibetan, Chinese, and English, allowing the app to function with limited or no internet access. The company also plans to pilot 50 simultaneous interpretation devices among at least 300 participants in Lhasa this December.

Tenzin Norbu, Choknor’s founder, said the company aims to bring DeepZang into “pastoral tents, tourist service counters, and grassroots hospitals,” enabling Tibetan speakers to “enjoy the benefits of artificial intelligence on an equal footing.”

Choknor said on Sunday that beyond fostering exchanges and integration among ethnic groups, DeepZang could help ensure the accuracy of Tibetan-language information and contribute to social stability and long-term security.

Founded in 2016, Choknor specializes in Tibetan-Chinese bilingual speech technology, scanning and translation tools, and optical character recognition. Its products include smart computer mice, scanning and translation pens, and an AI-powered Tibetan subtitling system.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Prosecution drops bribery case vs Sara Duterte
World.content:
House prosecutor Keith Flores listens to the testimony of a witness during Day 32 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on October 1, 2026.

'The decision to not proceed with the bribery [charge] had nothing to do with the strength of the case,' prosecutor Keith Flores says

MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution will no longer present its bribery case against Vice President Sara Duterte in a bid to expedite her trial.

House prosecutor Keith Flores told the media on Friday, October 9, that the prosecution had informed the impeachment court about its decision in a filing on Tuesday, October 6.

“The decision to not proceed with the bribery (charge) had nothing to do with the strength of the case. We’re conscious about the timetable that the prosecution set for us to prosecute the entire articles of impeachment. But it no longer fit the timetable that we set to ourselves,” said Flores, who leads the team on the bribery case.

This means that the prosecution will end its presentation of evidence with its case on her alleged unexplained wealth. The prosecution had been mulling over the possibility since early September.

During the House good government committee inquiry in 2024, then-DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda claimed that when the Vice President was education chief, she ordered him to give cash to school superintendents through their bank accounts.

The prosecution initially requested eight trial dates to present its bribery case, and listed four potential witnesses. They include those who allegedly received or were offered bribe money from Duterte’s office in DepEd, namely former DepEd undersecretary Gloria Jumamil-Mercado, and former bids and awards committee chair Resty Osias.

Malacañang previously sounded the alarm over the prosecution panel’s possible move to abandon the bribery case against the second-in-command.

“If they withdraw the bribery case against the Vice President, wouldn’t Filipinos who want to know the whole truth be shortchanged or be disadvantaged?” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro had been quoted as saying. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] The Senate’s Villar problem
World.content:
Putting former DPWH secretary Mark Villar in charge of the oversight desk looks less like legislative stewardship and more like institutional conflict of interest

As flood-control scandals raise uncomfortable questions about billions in infrastructure spending and his family’s corporate empire faces regulatory and legal scrutiny, Senator Mark Villar’s sudden leap to the majority—and into the public works committee chairmanship—puts a big question mark on the Senate’s institutional independence.

There are moments when the Senate seems bent on discovering just how far it can stretch the public’s capacity for disbelief.

While the floor was consumed by Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment proceedings, Senator Mark Villar executed a quiet migration from the minority to the majority. He did not arrive empty-handed. Without a peep of floor resistance, he walked away with two key levers of institutional influence: a seat on the Commission on Appointments and the chairmanship of the Senate committee on public works.

Meanwhile, across the aisle, his sister Camille stayed behind in the minority. It is the classic maneuver Filipinos know by instinct—namamangka sa dalawang ilog (playing both sides). Navigating both rivers at once guarantees that whatever current sweeps the chamber, the Villar family remains anchored on both banks.

They alone can speak to whether the split was coordinated, but in the transactional arithmetic of Philippine politics, having a foot in every camp is a survival strategy for any dynasty facing institutional heat. (READ: SEC chief Francis Lim to Villars: No family is too powerful to sue)

What makes this trade-off impossible to ignore is what Villar was handed: the legislative gavel over the very department he ran. (READ: DPWH post: Can Mark Villar rise above business interests?)

From 2016 to 2021, Mark Villar served as secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) under Rodrigo Duterte. Those years sit squarely inside the timeline under review in the flood-control scandal, where billions of pesos in public funds yielded little more than submerged communities and unbuilt defenses. (READ: What’s a flood control project, anyway?)

When he was summoned to answer for projects greenlit under his watch, Villar denied improperly favoring family-linked contractors. Facing questions is not a finding of guilt. But it strains credibility to ask the public to trust that a Senate committee chair will fearlessly investigate his own administrative legacy. (READ: Firm owned by Senator Mark Villar’s uncle bagged P390M in flood control projects)

A committee chairmanship is not decorative. It sets the agenda, marshals witnesses, decides which scandals get dragged into daylight, and determines which files gather dust in an archive.

Even if Villar cannot award contracts from the rostrum, he holds the power to shape the inquiry. At an hour when taxpayers are demanding cold accounting for catastrophic flood projects, putting the former secretary in charge of the oversight desk looks less like legislative stewardship and more like institutional conflict of interest.

The legal entanglements do not end at the DPWH. Just this past September, the Ombudsman opened preliminary investigations into graft and administrative complaints against Villar family members, local water officials, and executives of PrimeWater over joint-venture agreements alleged to be disadvantageous to the public. Both Mark and Camille were named.

The family denies wrongdoing and insists it will defend itself through legal channels, but the fact remains: those agreements intersect directly with the years Mark sat in the Cabinet and held a seat on the Local Water Utilities Administration board.

Then came the afternoon’s corporate timing. Within an hour on Thursday, October 8, three Villar-controlled flagships—Vista Land & Lifescapes, Vistamalls, and VistaREIT—abruptly filed notices that their boards had cleared their long-overdue 2025 audited financial statements.

These filings come after severe reporting delays led to trading suspensions across six Villar-linked firms. Board approval is not the same as audited accounts hitting the public tape, nor does it resolve overdue quarterly obligations.

Timing alone does not constitute evidence of backroom coordination, yet the optics are jarring: at the precise moment political power consolidated in the Senate, the family’s embattled business empire fired off a signal of operational survival.

This saga started in May 2025 when Vantage Point exposed the staggering arithmetic behind Villar Land—a P1.33-trillion property revaluation and an asserted profit of nearly a trillion pesos that quickly evaporated.

The subsequent reversal revealed the chasm between paper accounting and hard reality. Regulators soon disciplined the appraisal firm and launched complaints citing misleading disclosures, alleged market manipulation, and insider trading. The family denies wrongdoing, and due process must run its course, while AllDay and AllHome shutter retail outlets and Vista Land races to refinance debt.

This underscores the danger of letting private commercial distress collide with legislative oversight. Did Senate leaders ask a single hard question before handing him the committee? Did they demand recusal commitments for projects tied to his tenure or family enterprises? Who monitors the overseer?

Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri dismissed concerns by stating Villar’s party shift was unrelated to the impeachment fights. That may answer one concern, but it does nothing to clear the fog surrounding the public works gavel. When essential committees are handed out as political accommodations, legislative credibility disappears.

Filipinos have already paid the bill for suspect infrastructure, delayed dikes, and broken water projects. They should not also have to wonder if the Senate is running oversight with an eye toward preserving alliances. Like any citizen, Mark Villar is entitled to due process. But due process does not guarantee anyone the right to police their own past. The question is not whether he has the freedom to sit with the majority; he does. The real question is why the Senate decided to sacrifice the integrity of its own oversight just to give him a seat at the head of the table. – Rappler.com

World.title: Mans Carpio calls self ‘collateral damage’ in Sara Duterte trial
World.content:
PRIVACY. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, arrives at the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office along with his legal counsel, to file a criminal complaint against BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr., AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura, and members of the House Committee on Justice over alleged violations of banking privacy and data protection laws, on April 27, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Carpio tells a crowd in Bukidnon that he feels like he's the one who was impeached

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – Lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, said he felt he was being targeted amid the impeachment proceedings against his wife, describing himself as “collateral damage” as the couple’s finances came under scrutiny.

Speaking at a 1Bukidnon4 Sara Duterte Movement event in Valencia City on Thursday, October 8, Carpio said he felt he was being treated unfairly.

“Medyo gidaogdaog man ta karon,” Carpio said in a video clip posted on local broadcaster RMN-Malaybalay’s Facebook page.

(I feel like I’m being persecuted a bit now.)

“Tanan sa gobyerno gigamit,” he added, saying “Murag ako ang gi-impeach da,” Carpio said.

(Government resources were being used…. It’s as if I’m the one who was impeached.)

Carpio described himself as “collateral damage” and said he was praying that the situation would pass.

His remarks came as the impeachment proceedings against Duterte brought the couple’s finances to public scrutiny as the trial entered its 36th day. The impeachment court continued tackling their taxes and documents from the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) on Friday, October 9.

House prosecutor Jordan Keith Flores, a Bukidnon congressman, said Carpio’s inclusion in the impeachment trial was not personal, but stemmed from his marriage to Duterte. He was responding to Carpio’s remark in Bukidnon that he was “collateral damage” in the ongoing proceedings.

House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega put it more bluntly: “It’s not personal, it’s conjugal.”

Carpio and his wife’s lawyers had fought to keep the couple’s financial records out of public view, invoking confidentiality rules. Carpio had argued that he was a private citizen, and that his finances should remain private.

Carpio’s name has been repeatedly mentioned by the prosecution in its presentation of the unexplained wealth case against the Vice President.

Earlier this week, a witness from the Anti-Money Laundering Council told the court that, of the P4.4 billion in large and suspicious transactions that flowed through the couple’s bank accounts from 2007 to 2025, P749 million was attributed to Carpio alone.

The witness also said Carpio withdrew P41 million in cash through multiple over-the-counter transactions in a single day in 2024.

The findings are significant because Duterte declared minimal to zero cash on hand and in bank accounts in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) over the years.

The AMLC also said Cale88, a food company Carpio founded, received P319 million in remittances from Chinese corporations.

The company’s corporate filings no longer list him in its general information sheet as of 2025, but the BIR said it has no record of him having sold the company.– Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte’s arraignment for grave threats postponed again
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.

The Vice President was also supposed to be arraigned on September 11, but it was deferred after her camp sought to inhibit the judge from the case

MANILA, Philippines – Vice President Sara Duterte’s grave threats case has again been delayed after her arraignment at Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98 was postponed on Friday, October 9.

Duterte is facing three counts of grave threats filed by the Department of Justice last August due to her alleged assassination threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

Arraignment is the stage in criminal proceedings following a respondent’s arrest or surrender.

Play Video

This is when the court reads the accused the case and asks for either a guilty or not-guilty plea. If the accused enters a guilty plea, the case will immediately move to conviction, usually with a lower sentence.

But the arraignment did not push through again because of the Duterte camp’s pending motion for partial reconsideration of Presiding Judge Maria Angelica de Ramos’ resolution that junked Duterte’s bid to inhibit her from the case.

The Vice President was also supposed to be arraigned on September 11, but it was deferred after her camp sought De Ramos’ inhibition.

“Minabuti ng presiding judge na pag-aralan muna lahat ng bagay na ‘to at i-reset, i-cancel muna ang hearing today at i-reset to some other date. Now that other date, hindi ko muna babanggitin, pasensya na. I would rather na manggaling ‘yon sa court,” Duterte’s lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, told reporters outside the court.

(The judge decided to study all of these first and reset, cancel the hearing today, and reset it to some other date. Now that other date, I will not disclose it for now, I am sorry. I would rather have the court to announce it.)

On top of this, the Duterte camp also has a pending petition for certiorari with the Supreme Court challenging the court’s jurisdiction over her case. Certiorari is a legal action based on possible grave abuse of discretion, or a review of another body’s decision.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) initiated criminal investigation against Duterte after her infamous midnight press conference on November 23, 2024. There, in response to a supporter’s question, she told them not to worry about her security and that she had already “talked to someone” who would assassinate Marcos, the First Lady, and Romualdez if she were killed.

Play Video

In August, the Department of Justice charged Duterte before the court after it found enough evidence or prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction in the case.

De Ramos ordered Duterte’s arrest on September 4 after she found that there was probable cause – or enough evidence – to believe that the Vice President committed the crime. Duterte posted bail on September 5, where she dropped her now-controversial line about “not feeling safe.”

The Vice President is also in the middle of an impeachment trial at the Senate that could remove her from her position and bar her from running in the 2028 presidential election. This grave threats allegation is also part of the articles of impeachment or allegations against Duterte in the impeachment trial. – Rappler.com

World.title: Zelenskyy accuses US of inaction as Russian strikes kill over 70 in 2 days
World.content:
STATEMENT. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy looks on as he delivers a statement along with Bavarian federal state prime minister Markus Soeder (not pictured), chairman of the Munich Security Conference Wolfgang Ischinger (not pictured), Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (not pictured) during the Munich Security Conference MSC, at the Residenz of the former Bavarian Kings, in Munich, Germany, February 14, 2026.

The ongoing Russian air assaults intensify, with significant civilian casualties reported, prompting Zelenskyy to call for increased sanctions on Russia and support from European partners

KYIV, Ukraine – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday, October 7, killed at least 35 people in the east, bringing the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to more than 70.

Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelenskyy criticized Washington’s efforts to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war.

City authorities reported a new drone attack in the evening that killed two people. That brought the total death toll in the city to 35.

Local authorities reported that a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk, while one person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk.

The attacks were launched a day after a mass Russian drone and missile assault killed dozens across Ukraine — 22 of them in a residential building in the central town of Pryluky, about 130 km east of Kyiv.

Speaking in the early evening, Zelenskyy said 78 people had been killed and 215 wounded by strikes across Ukraine over the past two days.

Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to grant his requests to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic missile launchers.

‘That’s called unwillingness’

“Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran … I’ve said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said in an emotional statement.

Ukraine has in recent months aimed to wrest the battlefield initiative from Russia, whose gains have slowed this year, but is still suffering from Moscow’s increasingly brutal air war.

“So where’s the truth here, where’s the honesty? Where’s the stalemate? … That’s called unwillingness,” he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s assertion earlier on Thursday that the war was at a stalemate and that the United States would keep working toward a settlement.

“One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, while on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of … diplomatic stalemate,” Zelenskyy added.

Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered Russian gas to Germany before Moscow invaded Ukraine, Reuters reported on Thursday.

Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the US on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelenskyy added, urging US President Donald Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia.

Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv that he expected Kyiv’s European partners to join the talks with the US. He also said Ukrainian negotiators would raise the issue of air defenses in light of near-constant Russian attacks.

Intensifying strikes

Twenty people were wounded in the Kramatorsk strike, one of the biggest single attacks by Russia this year. Moscow has denied targeting civilians but regularly pounds cities with missiles and drones.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible,” regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.

Images posted by officials showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris and the charred shell of a bus. Some bodies had not yet been identified, Zelenskyy said, adding that the attack would not go unanswered.

Separately, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said four people were killed and 19 wounded in morning attacks on the Ukrainian capital. Water and electricity supplies were disrupted, and officials said it would take time to restore them.

Russia has unleashed relentless drone strikes against Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses and data centers while renewing its campaign against Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter.

Russian technology and AI company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored. Zelenskyy did not refer specifically to the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was “mirroring” Russian attacks on data centers. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] The problem with DOE’s Mid-Merit Natural Gas Capacity Auction Program
World.content:
Natural gas can provide useful mid-merit and balancing services. That capability does not justify a uniform gas procurement across grids with different supply conditions and cost structures.

The first-ever centralized “Mid-Merit Natural Gas Capacity Auction Program” of the Department of Energy (DOE) has a catch. While it sounds highly beneficial on paper as laid out under Department Circular No. DC2026-06-0013, it overlooks the hidden complications and risks resulting from its strict condition of limiting the power source exclusively from natural gas only, which in effect largely passes over the economics of the current structural architecture of the energy systems in the areas involved.

The “mid-merit” term in the energy market refers to power sources that operate between constant baseload generation and short-term peaking units (as in power plants that only run during times of peak electricity demand) to supply variable electricity demand during daytime and evening hours. Hence, they are the power sources that bridge the difference between minimum round-the-clock demand and high daytime surges.

These energy sources are flexible in schedule of use, as they can be easily turned on and off quickly to handle supply gaps anytime when daily activity starts in the morning and scales down at night. Technically, it operates at a moderate capacity level, higher than “peakers” but lower than baseload.

In the case of the present mid-market capacity auction program, the DOE specifically designated natural gas capacities only as the bridge to maintain grid stability.

Auction program and issues

The DOE plans to auction off a total of 3,840 megawatts (MW) of mid-merit capacity covering existing and upcoming generation capacity in Luzon and Visayas. And, instead of letting individual power utilities negotiate separate, fractured contracts, the DOE is implementing a centralized, transparent auction mechanism.

For existing capacities in Luzon, the DOE is targeting the immediate delivery of 1,400 MW from existing gas facilities in 2026, followed by an additional 500 MW in 2027. For new builds in both Luzon and Visayas, this begins in 2028 with 440 MW of liquefied natural gas (LNG) mid-merit plants deployed specifically to Cebu and Panay in the Visayas. By 2031, newly built plants are expected to deliver another 1,000 MW to Luzon and a further 500 MW to Cebu.

Luzon may have weak gas capacity but it has enough power supply. As reflected in the August 2026 billing period, the Independent Electricity Market Operator of the Philippines (IEMOP) reported that Luzon maintained sufficient generation despite outages. Its supply margin increased by 632 MW, while its average Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) price declined from P7.30 per kWh to P4.80 per kWh.

Obviously, while the figures show that Luzon may need more flexibility, they do show that the DOE should not equate a flexibility requirement with an immediate requirement for additional gas capacity, according to market players.

Under the new rules, too, the DOE decides how much power capacity to auction based on the entire country’s grid needs, rather than looking at what individual electric cooperatives and power companies say they need. Once a power company’s share is included in the auction and a contract is awarded, they cannot back out. The agreement becomes legally binding for the entire delivery period.

This strict approach creates a major risk: if the DOE overestimates how much power is needed, consumers will be forced to pay for unnecessary electricity through a long-term financial obligation.

Moreover, auction-backed gas in Luzon would compete against existing generation, new renewable energy, storage, and other flexible resources. If the gas plant’s all-in price exceeds the value of the energy it displaces, the framework can raise rather than lower system cost. Additional gas for Luzon should, therefore, have to prove that it can reduce total electricity cost, not merely that it can provide electricity.

The Visayas presents a materially different case. During the August 2026 billing period, available supply declined while demand increased slightly, reducing the regional supply margin to only 62 MW. IEMOP recorded 86 hours of Yellow Alert and 53 hours of Red Alert. Prior to the implementation of the regional secondary price cap by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), the average WESM price reached P18.59 per kWh in the region, compared with P4.80 per kWh in Luzon.

Transmission constraints also limited access to lower-cost Luzon generation. IEMOP reported that the Luzon-Visayas interconnection was constrained to exchange power for about 86 percent of the August billing period. The resulting regional shortage increased reliance on higher-cost local oil-based plants and battery resources. The ERC’s September 2026 action to implement a regional secondary price cap further confirms that the Visayas faced an exceptional price and supply problem distinct from Luzon.

In this setting, gas can have a credible economic role if it is located where the grid needs it and displaces diesel or other oil-based generation at the margin. The relevant comparison is the all-in cost of gas against the high-cost generation and reliability interventions it would replace. The case still depends on transmission access, plant availability, fuel contracting, and delivered price, but the underlying capacity and flexibility need is clearer.

More auction policy complications

The auction only forces companies to compete on their building and operating fees (the Gas Auction Price). The actual cost of the imported Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) is treated as a “pass-through” cost. Even if the government double-checks that the fuel wasn’t artificially overpriced, consumers still have to pay the full global market price for that gas. The auction cannot stop a completely legal and necessary purchase of LNG from becoming brutally expensive when global prices spike.

Global events directly dictate local electricity rates. For example, due to Middle Eastern supply disruptions in September 2026, Asian LNG prices skyrocketed to US$26.00 per MMBtu. When combined with a weak exchange rate of P62.67 to $1, just the fuel alone costs a gas plant P11.40 to P13.00 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). This does not even include the company’s profit or building fees. When global fuel shocks happen, the electricity bills immediately soar. This already happened in March 2026, when emergency measures were triggered as market electricity prices jumped from P5.00 to over P9.00 per kWh.

If a winning gas plant produces electricity but the daily market (WESM) has plenty of cheaper power available (like solar or coal), the gas plant will lose money in the open market. Under the auction rules, consumers are forced to pay the difference. If the market value of the energy drops below what the government guaranteed the gas plant, the shortfall is collected directly from your monthly electricity bill. Therefore, a “low winning bid” in the auction does not guarantee cheap electricity for the public.

Likewise, four features of the bidding framework create upward pricing pressure or leave major risks with consumers. The fuel component is passed through separately from the Gas Auction Price, leaving consumers exposed to LNG and foreign exchange volatility. The settlement mechanism compensates winning bidders based on the auction formula rather than the WESM energy value, with shortfalls collected from customers. A system-wide capacity determination can exceed the requirements identified by individual utilities if the underlying need assessment is too broad or outdated. Binding participation limits a utility’s ability to withdraw after award even if demand, technology costs, or market conditions change.

It could leave consumers to bear the financial risk of expensive imported gas. Imported LNG creates a continuing exposure to global commodity prices and foreign exchange movements.

A competitive auction can discipline the non-fuel portion of a bid, but it cannot make imported LNG cheap or stable. The government should first establish the service the grid requires, the location and duration of that requirement, and the cost of competing solutions. If the objective is flexibility, the auction should test the full range of technologies that can provide it rather than presume that the fuel has already been chosen.

Image from Department of Energy website

The circular separates the “gas auction price” from the fuel component. Winning bidders are compensated for energy delivered using the gas auction price plus a fuel cost determined under the ERC-approved gas price benchmarking methodology. The fuel component is a pass-through, subject to verification of whether the cost is actual, reasonable, and prudent.

This structure limits the effect of competition. Bidders compete on the Gas Auction Price, while consumers remain exposed to the cost of LNG used to produce the electricity. The Circular encourages least-cost fuel procurement and preferably long-term supply agreements, but it does not remove the underlying commodity and foreign exchange risk. Verification can prevent unreasonable charges; it cannot prevent an otherwise prudent LNG purchase from becoming expensive when global prices rise.

This exposure is material. The ERC reported that the weighted-average landed cost of LNG in the Philippines increased from $14.90 per MMBtu in the first quarter of 2024 to $17.30 per MMBtu in the first quarter of 2025, even as international benchmark prices declined. The risk became more pronounced in 2026: Asian spot LNG prices reached approximately $26.00 per MMBtu in September – around 150% higher than in February – amid severe disruptions to Middle Eastern supply.

At $26.00 per MMBtu and an exchange rate of P62.67 to $1, a combined-cycle gas plant with an illustrative heat rate of 7 to 8 MMBtu per MWh would incur approximately P11.40 to P13.00 per kWh in fuel cost alone. This excludes the Gas Auction Price and other applicable costs. The calculation is illustrative, but it demonstrates how imported LNG prices and their exposure to global supply disruptions and foreign-exchange movements can dominate the all-in cost of gas-fired power and ultimately translate into higher electricity rates.

The risk is not theoretical. In March 2026, the DOE imposed emergency measures as international fuel prices rose and supply risks intensified. IEMOP simulations cited by the DOE indicated that average WESM prices could exceed P9.00 per kWh from a pre-crisis level of P5.00 per kWh or less. The episode demonstrated how quickly imported-fuel shocks can affect Philippine electricity prices.

The settlement design adds another concern. If the WESM value of the winning plant’s output is below the auction settlement amount, the shortfall is collected from customers. In a grid with adequate lower-cost supply, this can socialize the difference between the market value of the energy and the amount guaranteed under the auction. A low winning bid on the Gas Auction Price does not establish that the total charge to consumers will be low.

These features may be justified where the auction secures a needed resource at a lower total cost than the alternatives. They are difficult to justify where capacity is already adequate and the new resource is likely to be more expensive than the energy it displaces.

Lastly, several commercially available resources can provide all or part of the flexibility attributed to gas. They differ in duration, location, construction time, and system function, so no single technology is a universal substitute. That is precisely why the comparison should be technology-neutral and based on the service required.

Level playing field

Natural gas can provide useful mid-merit and balancing services. That capability does not justify a uniform gas procurement across grids with different supply conditions and cost structures.

The Visayas has a demonstrated regional supply and flexibility problem. Gas may lower costs if it displaces diesel and other oil-based generation, is located where the grid can use it, and is procured at a competitive all-in price. Luzon is different. Recent data show adequate margins and materially lower market prices. Procuring additional auction-backed gas without proving the need could add a fuel-indexed resource whose settlement cost exceeds the value of the energy it replaces.

Therefore, instead of choosing natural gas in advance, the government should let all technologies compete on a level playing field. The grid’s need for flexibility should be opened to competing technologies, like solar or wind paired with Battery Energy Storage System or BESS, hydro, and geothermal. And the technology option that provides the lowest total cost and lower risk should win.

For safety measures, treat Luzon and Visayas separately. The Visayas is facing severe power shortages and genuinely needs localized plants to replace costly diesel. Luzon already has an oversupply of cheap energy and does not need extra gas. Stop letting gas companies pass 100% of fuel price hikes to consumers. Force them to absorb some of the global market shocks. And ban any new gas projects in Luzon unless the government can mathematically prove it will lower total consumer electricity rates. – Rappler.com
