World.title: Trump says US will not attack Iran before midterm elections in November
World.content:
CRISIS. US and Iranian flags are seen in this illustration taken March 23, 2026.

'We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,' says Trump

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump said on Thursday, October 8, that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before November’s US midterm congressional elections, asserting that the two countries are having “productive” talks about ending the six-month-old war.

“We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd.”

The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November’s election.

Some 60% of Americans — including one in four Republicans — disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.

Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but he has not offered a detailed plan for exiting the war.

Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran’s latest offer.

Iran’s state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country’s Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make “meaningful” reductions in its enrichment capacity.

The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Bridges Distances With Major Transport Upgrades
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan built, reconstructed and repaired more than 19,000 kilometers of roads between 2023 and 2025, while expanding railway infrastructure and domestic flight connections to improve regional connectivity and strengthen its transit capacity.

The modernization program includes major infrastructure projects and digital technologies aimed at reducing travel times, improving passenger mobility and accelerating freight transportation along international corridors, according to the Kazakh government’s press office.

Road upgrades improve regional access

Road construction, reconstruction and repairs covered 5,656 kilometers in 2023, increasing to 7,306 kilometers in 2024 before reaching 6,178 kilometers in 2025.

In 2026, work is underway on more than 11,000 kilometers of roads, including 3,400 kilometers of national highway construction and reconstruction, 5,000 kilometers of major and medium-scale repairs on national roads and 2,400 kilometers of local road repairs.

The upgrades come amid growing demand for road transport. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the number of passengers transported by road rose from 1.5 billion in 2023 to 1.7 billion in 2024 and 1.9 billion in 2025. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure reached 1.3 billion, up 3.9% from the same period in 2025.

Efforts to improve rural accessibility have also advanced. Between 2023 and 2025, work was completed on 10,200 kilometers of local roads, including 556 kilometers of newly built roads, providing year-round connections to district and regional centers.

The government expects 95% of national highways and 92% of local roads to meet technical standards by the end of 2026, up from 92% and 86%, respectively, in 2023. The targets for 2029 are 97% and 94%.

Major highway projects are expected to further reduce travel times and expand interregional and transit connections. Among them is the 896-kilometer Center-West route, which will connect Astana with western Kazakhstan through Arkalyk and Yrgyz.

Railway expansion strengthens passenger and freight transport

Kazakhstan has laid 911 kilometers of new railway tracks over the past five years, with another 800 kilometers under construction and approximately 2,600 kilometers of existing tracks undergoing modernization.

Railways carried a combined 60.2 million passengers between 2023 and 2025. Since the beginning of 2026, Passenger Transportation, a national passenger rail operator, has served 7.5 million passengers, with the highest passenger volumes recorded in Almaty, Astana, Shymkent and the Abai, Aktobe, Karagandy, Kyzylorda and Zhambyl Regions.

Passenger services have also become more accessible. Women-only carriages now operate on 13 routes and have carried 946,000 passengers since their introduction. Passengers with disabilities and their companions are eligible for a 50% fare discount on socially significant routes, while 396,000 tickets for designated accessible spaces were issued in the first seven months of 2026.

Digitalization is also accelerating international freight transportation. The Digital Trade Corridor platform integrates railway systems in Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Georgia along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, through a single-window system.

Its Tez (fast in Kazakh) Customs module enables paperless customs transit procedures, reducing clearance times from eight hours to 30 minutes. Combined with other infrastructure and operational improvements, cargo delivery times along the corridor have fallen from 38 days to 13-17 days, according to the government. The next target is to achieve consistent delivery times of 10-12 days for shipments from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Domestic aviation network expands to 890 weekly flights

Kazakhstan’s domestic aviation network has grown steadily, with airlines operating 630 weekly flights across 51 routes in 2023. This increased to 669 flights across 57 routes in 2024 and 821 flights across 60 routes in 2025. As of September 2026, approximately 890 weekly flights operated across 60 domestic routes.

The expansion has been accompanied by the restoration of regional airports. On Aug. 22, subsidized flights began operating between Arkalyk and Astana, Almaty and Kostanai following the reopening of Arkalyk Airport. Each route operates twice a week, with flights between Arkalyk and Astana taking approximately 40 minutes.

Airport modernization is continuing elsewhere in the country. The runway at Pavlodar Airport was upgraded in 2026, while construction of new airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and the Kenderli resort area is scheduled for completion by the end of the year.

Further runway construction and reconstruction projects are planned through 2029 in Astana, Almaty, Shymkent, Taraz, Aktobe, Oral and Zhezkazgan, alongside terminal upgrades at major airports.

To support air cargo transportation, the government has introduced a 12-year duty-free regime for cargo aircraft and simplified export procedures for selected goods, including aviation-related products, to countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Nuclear Legacy Offers Lessons in Age of AI and Geopolitical Rivalry
World.content:
ASTANA – Thirty-five years after Kazakhstan closed the Semipalatinsk nuclear test site and began giving up the nuclear arsenal it inherited from the Soviet Union, the world is moving back toward a security environment in which nuclear weapons are again seen by some as an answer rather than a danger. That was one of the central concerns raised during the Sept. 22 online discussion dedicated to what Kazakhstan’s nuclear experience can teach the world today.

Organized by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and the Council on Strategic Risks, the discussion brought together Kazakh and United States officials and experts who were directly involved in the nuclear threat reduction efforts of the 1990s. Their focus was not only on what Kazakhstan did after independence, but on whether the lessons of that period can still work in a world defined by geopolitical rivalry, weakening arms control and rapidly developing artificial intelligence.

The answer was not straightforward. The environment that allowed Kazakhstan and the U.S. to cooperate on eliminating nuclear dangers was unusually favorable. Today, major powers are again competing militarily, key arms control agreements have lapsed or been abandoned, and new technologies are making strategic calculations more complex. But Kazakhstan’s experience offers one lesson that remains relevant: security does not necessarily become stronger when a country possesses more nuclear weapons.

When a nuclear arsenal was seen as a risk, not an asset

When Kazakhstan became independent, it inherited the world’s fourth-largest nuclear arsenal. The country also inherited the consequences of the Soviet nuclear program. Between 1949 and 1989, the Soviet Union conducted 456 nuclear tests at the Semipalatinsk site, affecting approximately 1.5 million people. Kazakhstan closed the site on Aug. 29, 1991, and subsequently relinquished the nuclear weapons and delivery systems left on its territory.

For Laura Holgate, former U.S. ambassador to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the significance of that decision goes beyond disarmament. She noted that Kazakhstan’s leaders recognized that the weapons were not necessarily an asset that would protect the newly independent country. They could instead make Kazakhstan more vulnerable to confrontation with other major powers.

“To recognize that that was a source of weakness or risk of insecurity rather than a source of security,” Holgate said, was an “incredibly bold and courageous decision.”

That point is particularly relevant today because nuclear deterrence continues to shape how states think about security. Magzhan Ilyassov, Kazakhstan’s ambassador to the U.S., recalled a conversation he had as a young exchange student in the U.S. in the early 1990s. Americans he met had grown up fearing that the Soviet Union might attack them. Kazakh Soviet people had grown up with a similar fear of the U.S. Yet on both sides, nuclear weapons were understood as defensive.

“I never thought that we would drop it on you. It was our defense,” Ilyassov recalled.

That contradiction remains at the heart of the nuclear debate: if every country sees its own nuclear weapons as defensive, but another country’s arsenal as a threat, the logic of deterrence can become an argument for more proliferation.

Ilyassov warned that the more countries come to believe they need nuclear weapons for deterrence, the more difficult it becomes to maintain the credibility of the system itself.

“The whole deterrence concept sounds solid,” he said, but the more countries seek nuclear weapons, “the whole deterrence thing starts losing its credibility.”

Corey Hinderstein, vice president for studies at the Carnegie Endowment, similarly noted that nuclear weapons should not be discussed as a stand-alone security issue. In countries where public support for acquiring nuclear weapons is rising, she said, the question changes when people are asked to consider what that choice would mean for national spending, alliances, economic stability and society.

“It’s not a nuclear trade-off. It’s a societal trade-off,” Hinderstein added.

That is one of the lessons Kazakhstan’s experience puts back on the table: nuclear disarmament was not simply about removing weapons. It was about redefining what security meant.

From a Soviet nuclear legacy to a role in global security

Kazakhstan’s decision did not end with the closure of Semipalatinsk. The country worked with the U.S. under the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program to dismantle nuclear weapons and delivery systems, eliminate nuclear infrastructure, seal test tunnels and secure dangerous materials.

One of the most significant operations was Project Sapphire in 1994, when nearly 600 kilograms of highly enriched uranium were removed from Kazakhstan: enough material for approximately 25 nuclear weapons. The operation was carried out through close cooperation between the two countries and was kept secret until the material had been safely transported.

Andrew Weber, former U.S. assistant secretary of defense for nuclear, chemical and biological defense programs, was directly involved in that effort. He described Project Sapphire as an example of what can happen when governments focus on solving a specific security problem rather than allowing political differences to prevent cooperation. The operation, he said, required technical and security cooperation over several weeks to safely package and transport the material.

For Corey Hinderstein, the broader lesson was that Kazakhstan’s leadership in the anti-nuclear field was not something imposed on the country by its Soviet past.

“The nuclear legacy was imposed on Kazakhstan from Moscow. Kazakhstan didn’t have to do what it did. It certainly did not have to give up its inherited nuclear weapons. But even once that moment and that decision came, nuclear leadership was selected, was embraced and has been sustained,” she said.

That distinction matters because Kazakhstan did not simply dismantle an inherited arsenal and move on. It continued to build its role in nuclear non-proliferation, including through the IAEA low-enriched uranium bank, its participation in international negotiations on Iran and its support for the global nuclear non-proliferation regime. The country’s experience could again become relevant in dealing with Iran’s nuclear material.

Ilyassov said Kazakhstan remains ready to provide a neutral venue and, if Washington and Tehran reach an agreement, potentially assist with the secure handling of Iran’s enriched uranium under international legal, technical and verification arrangements. Weber said such a process would need to involve international partners and UN and IAEA supervision rather than being treated as a unilateral U.S. operation. That willingness is part of what Weber described as Kazakhstan’s “tremendous moral authority” on nuclear issues.

The forgotten public movement behind the decision

The discussion also highlighted a part of Kazakhstan’s nuclear history that receives less international attention: the role of civil society. Ilyassov pointed to the Nevada-Semipalatinsk movement, which brought the consequences of nuclear testing into public debate and created pressure for political action. The movement, he said, did not itself make the political decision to close the test site. But it put the issue on the political agenda and made it impossible for politicians to ignore.

“That was a public driving force that actually didn’t make the politicians take the decision, but it put this topic onto the agenda,” Ilyassov said, adding that this grassroots dimension deserves renewed attention today.

Nuclear weapons have become strangely disconnected from everyday public debate despite their continued existence. Social media can turn relatively trivial subjects into global trends within hours, while nuclear disarmament rarely becomes a mainstream issue among younger generations or public figures.

“This is your world. This is real. These weapons exist,” Ilyassov said.

The challenge is therefore not only diplomatic. It is also political and societal: how to make nuclear risks visible enough for the public to understand the stakes before a crisis forces the issue back into the headlines.

AI makes human responsibility more important

The most difficult question for the future may be how nuclear security will work once artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in military decision-making. AI can improve analysis of satellite imagery, identify unusual activity, support safeguards and help detect illicit networks. But the same technology can accelerate decision-making, amplify false information and make deception more convincing. In a nuclear crisis, that could reduce the time available for diplomacy and increase the consequences of a technical error.

For Kazakhstan, the lesson is not that AI should be excluded from nuclear security. It is that technology cannot replace the person who ultimately has to take responsibility for an irreversible decision. Ilyassov put the distinction bluntly: an algorithm can calculate the probability of escalation, but it cannot understand its human cost. It does not feel fear, grief or hesitation, and it cannot carry moral responsibility. That is why, he said, “meaningful human control” and clear accountability must remain central to decisions involving nuclear weapons.

The issue is becoming more urgent as the global nuclear consensus weakens. Hinderstein warned that the idea that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” is itself losing ground. Discussions of limited nuclear war, tactical nuclear use and contained exchanges can make nuclear use appear more manageable than it actually is.

At the same time, countries without nuclear weapons are increasingly reconsidering whether they should acquire them, particularly when confidence in security guarantees declines. Hinderstein said that a broader public discussion of the economic, social and political costs of nuclear weapons could change that calculation.

That concern was echoed just days later at the UN General Assembly, where Kazakh Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi linked the country’s nuclear disarmament experience to the current erosion of international trust.

“Our experience of renouncing the world’s fourth largest nuclear arsenal did not weaken our state. To the contrary, through international trust, it strengthens sovereignty, enhances security and promotes development,” he said.

For Kazakhstan, the experience of the 1990s offers a different reference point. She highlighted that the country did not have to keep the nuclear weapons it inherited. It chose to give them up. It did not have to become a long-term advocate of nuclear threat reduction. It chose to take on that role. And it did not do so through one decision alone. The process involved political leadership, public pressure, international cooperation and years of practical work.

The circumstances today are very different from those of the previous millennia. The U.S., Russia and China are strategic competitors, arms control mechanisms are under pressure, and AI is adding a new layer of uncertainty to nuclear decision-making. But the question raised by Kazakhstan’s experience remains much the same: whether security is best achieved by accumulating more instruments of destruction, or by finding ways to make those instruments less necessary. For Kazakhstan, the answer was decided 35 years ago. The discussion in Washington suggested that the rest of the world may need to revisit that choice.

World.title: Jackie Chan Highlights Kazakhstan’s Film Potential After ‘Armour of God IV: Ultimatum’ Shoot
World.content:
ASTANA – Filming of the international action film “Armour of God IV: Ultimatum,” starring legendary actor Jackie Chan, has concluded in Kazakhstan, showcasing the country’s potential as a destination for major international film productions.

The project, Salem Entertainment’s first international production, was filmed in Almaty and the Almaty and Mangystau Regions, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information and China Film Group Corporation.

Speaking at a press conference on Oct. 6, Chan said the idea was first discussed during a meeting with Kazakhstan’s Vice President Erlan Karin in China in 2017 or 2018, when Karin served as State Counselor, Kazinform reported.

“I was surprised that the team had already started working on the script and selected a director,” Chan said, noting that the project moved from an initial proposal to production much faster than he had expected.

He also praised the shoot’s organization and government support.

Kazakh actor and producer Rustem Omarov said Chan sustained a shoulder injury and later fractured a rib during filming. Despite doctors advising him to rest, Chan returned to the set within days.

Filming will continue in Shanghai, with the film scheduled for international release in 2027.

The project is expected to promote Kazakhstan’s tourism and cultural potential and help attract further international film productions to the country.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Stronger Regional Cooperation at Central Asia-Azerbaijan Summit
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for stronger economic integration, transport connectivity, water cooperation and artificial intelligence partnerships among Central Asian states and Azerbaijan at the eighth Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Avaza on Oct. 8.

Held in the year marking 35 years of independence of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan, the meeting focused on expanding regional cooperation and strengthening stability amid growing geopolitical tensions, Akorda reported.

Trade and connectivity

Tokayev proposed increasing intraregional trade from approximately $13 billion to at least $20 billion and called on governments to develop a joint action plan to achieve this target.

He also highlighted the potential of border trade and logistics hubs, as well as industrial cooperation centers, to create regional value chains.

Tokayev stressed Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen transport connectivity, noting the nearing completion of the Moyynty-Kyzylzhar and Darbaza-Maktaaral railway lines and the planned opening of the Bakhty-Ayagoz route next year.

He underscored the growing importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, and said World Bank estimates indicate that cargo traffic across the Caspian Sea could increase almost fourfold by 2040 if planned infrastructure projects are implemented.

Tokayev also proposed discussing the possible integration of the Middle Corridor with the TRIPP transport initiative at the expert level.

Water and AI cooperation

Water security was identified as another key priority. Tokayev called for new approaches to managing transboundary water resources and proposed advancing a Framework Convention of Central Asia on Water Use.

He also reiterated Kazakhstan’s initiative to establish an International Water Organization under the auspices of the United Nations.

In the technology sector, Tokayev proposed creating a Central Asian Partnership Program on Artificial Intelligence to facilitate cooperation among universities, research centers and technology companies.

He also suggested developing a Declaration on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence by Central Asian States and Azerbaijan.

Security and humanitarian ties

Tokayev stressed the importance of coordinated efforts against terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, organized crime and other transnational threats, including the misuse of digital technologies by criminals and terrorists.

He also called for stronger cultural and humanitarian ties through youth exchanges, academic cooperation and a common information space.

Among the proposals were a regional television channel based on Kazakhstan’s Silk Way TV, a 2027 Youth Forum on Volunteering, and a common calendar of major cultural, scientific, sporting and tourism events.

Focus on implementation

Tokayev urged greater attention to implementing regional initiatives, noting that more than 200 initiatives have been put forward since 2018, while only a small proportion have been implemented.

He proposed that foreign ministries inventory existing initiatives and assess their relevance and prospects.

A Joint Statement was adopted following the eighth Consultative Meeting of Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Government Securities Added to J.P. Morgan Watchlist for Potential GBI-EM Inclusion
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government securities have been placed on J.P. Morgan’s Index Watch – Positive list for potential inclusion in the Government Bond Index – Emerging Markets (GBI-EM), marking further progress in integrating the country’s government securities market into international capital markets.

Market accessibility under review

The status was assigned as part of J.P. Morgan’s 2026 index classification review. Over the next 12 months, the Finance Ministry said it will assess international investors’ access to Kazakhstan’s government securities market, the ministry reported on Oct. 8.

The review will include investors’ access through international clearing and settlement infrastructure, as well as the liquidity of bonds meeting the index’s eligibility criteria.

The move reflects joint efforts by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Finance and National Bank to develop the government securities market, strengthen market infrastructure and improve international investors’ access to Kazakh financial instruments.

Potential to broaden investor base

Placement on the positive watchlist marks a new stage in assessing Kazakhstan’s potential inclusion in the GBI-EM.

If Kazakhstan’s government securities are ultimately included in the index, the move could broaden the country’s foreign investor base, support greater market liquidity and help reduce borrowing costs.

The GBI-EM is a widely followed benchmark for local-currency government bonds issued by emerging-market economies.

World.title: Kazakhstan, UK Reaffirm Commitment to Expanding Strategic Partnership
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev received UK Minister of State for Trade Lord Anas Sarwar on Oct. 7 to discuss strengthening bilateral trade and investment ties and expanding cooperation in energy, transport, digitalization and artificial intelligence.

Strong trade and investment ties

Tokayev highlighted the importance Kazakhstan attaches to developing relations with the United Kingdom, noting constructive political dialogue and growing contacts between the two countries, Akorda reported.

“Kazakhstan and the United Kingdom are connected by constructive political dialogue and active contacts at various levels. I am confident that we have significant potential to expand cooperation,” Tokayev said.

The UK remains one of Kazakhstan’s key trade and investment partners. Bilateral trade increased by 83% in 2025 to more than $1.6 billion, while more than 500 British companies currently operate in Kazakhstan.

President Tokayev also underscored the importance of developing human capital alongside trade and investment, calling on Kazakhstan’s younger generation to broaden their international outlook and strengthen foreign-language skills, notably English.

Tokayev conveyed his warm wishes to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and invited him to visit Kazakhstan.

Lord Sarwar welcomed the continued development of the strategic partnership and thanked President Tokayev for supporting British business projects and efforts to maintain a favorable investment climate.

“We closely follow Kazakhstan’s dynamic development and highly value the closeness of our approaches to key topics on the international agenda. We are united by our commitment to open and trusted partnership, innovation, mutual confidence and free trade,” Lord Sarwar said.

Cooperation in emerging and priority sectors

Tokayev and Sarwar also discussed prospects for expanding cooperation in energy, transport and logistics, digitalization and artificial intelligence, while also highlighting the importance of strengthening humanitarian ties, academic exchanges and joint education initiatives.

The discussions continued during a separate meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin and Lord Sarwar, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

Zhumangarin described the UK as an important and reliable strategic partner, noting that the British delegation’s visit provides fresh momentum for bilateral relations and creates opportunities to translate existing agreements into concrete projects.

Lord Sarwar reaffirmed the UK’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Kazakhstan, and both officials expressed commitment to open, constructive dialogue and to advancing priority areas of partnership.

World.title: Kazakh FM Takes Part in CIS and Regional Meetings in Turkmenbashi
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi took part in a regular meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and a meeting of the Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan in Turkmenbashi on Oct. 7.

CIS ministers prepare for upcoming summit

The CIS foreign ministers discussed pressing topics on the international agenda and prospects for multilateral cooperation within the commonwealth.

Tileuberdi outlined Kazakhstan’s approaches to cooperation within the organization and put forward several proposals aimed at strengthening the CIS’s potential, the ministry’s press service reported.

A key focus of the meeting was preparations for the upcoming CIS Summit, which will bring together the leaders of the Commonwealth’s member states in Turkmenistan on Oct. 9.

The ministers approved statements by the heads of state marking the 35th anniversary of the CIS and addressing the preservation of historical memory.

They also endorsed draft documents to strengthen cooperation in security, economic, cultural and humanitarian affairs, as well as transport, science, space and information and communication technologies.

The meeting concluded with the participants reaffirming their commitment to implementing the agreements reached and enhancing the effectiveness of multilateral cooperation mechanisms.

Central Asia and Azerbaijan discuss regional cooperation

Tileuberdi also participated in the meeting of the Foreign Ministers of the Central Asian States and Azerbaijan, where the participants discussed regional cooperation within the framework of the consultative meetings and current regional and international topics.

Tileuberdi highlighted the progress achieved since the first consultative meeting of the Central Asian Heads of State in 2018, noting that political dialogue had contributed to stronger mutual trust and closer ties between the Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan.

“Thanks to the political will of our Heads of State, relations between our brotherly nations have reached a qualitatively new level. The consultative meetings have provided significant momentum for deepening cooperation across trade, industrial cooperation, energy, transport, logistics and digital technologies,” Tileuberdi said.

Following the meeting, the ministers agreed on the draft agenda and outcome documents to be signed at the eighth consultative meeting, scheduled for Oct. 8 in Turkmenbashi.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is also in Turkmenistan for a working visit on Oct. 8-9 at the invitation of President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.

World.title: Central Asia Has UK, US Investors’ Attention But Understanding Still Lags Behind Interest
World.content:
Kazakhstan remains the region’s economic anchor and its largest recipient of foreign capital. At the same time, Montfort Eurasia’s Investor Perception Report 2026 for the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (U.S.) suggests that Central Asia and the Caucasus are moving beyond a traditional foreign direct investment story toward a broader capital markets story.

Yet the report identifies a growing gap: investor appetite is advancing faster than investor understanding.

“Investors’ self-assessed knowledge of the region has plateaued,” the report notes, with average scores of 6.63 out of 10 among UK respondents and 6.79 among those in the U.S. At the same time, the proportion of investors expressing strong or moderate interest remains elevated at 67.1% in the UK and 65.5% in the U.S.

This is the central message of the 2026 survey: Central Asia has moved into a more serious phase of international investor attention, but it now needs to convert visibility into informed, committed capital.

From discovery to deliberation

Montfort Eurasia’s report covers 273 respondents — 137 in the UK and 136 in the U.S. The research used a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative questions with open-ended responses. The results were then benchmarked against the 2024 and 2025 surveys to identify changes in investor priorities, risk perceptions and strategic outlooks.

The year-on-year comparison is revealing. Investor knowledge has increased significantly from the roughly 4.9 level recorded in 2024, but the sharp improvement seen in 2025 has not continued. Instead, the region appears to have reached a higher baseline of familiarity.

The same pattern is visible in overall interest. The report describes the current stage not as one of discovery, but of “deliberation”. In other words, investors already familiar with the region are increasingly evaluating Central Asia and asking harder questions about political risk, market access, regulation, investment security and the quality of available information.

That is a meaningful change in audience. Two years ago, much of the international discussion around Central Asia still focused on whether global investors would notice the region at all. Today, the more relevant question is whether governments and businesses can provide enough reliable information for investors to move from interest to due diligence and eventually to transactions.

The report itself captures that transition. Financial analysis has overtaken international media as the leading source of information about the region, cited by 68.6% of UK respondents and 56.6% of U.S. respondents. That suggests that the market is becoming less dependent on headlines and more dependent on numbers.

Kazakhstan remains the anchor

For Kazakhstan, the report reinforces a familiar position while adding an important new dimension. The country remains by far the largest economy and the leading recipient of foreign capital in Central Asia. According to the report, Kazakhstan attracted around $440 billion in total FDI between 2005 and 2025 and continues to account for close to 70% of all FDI entering Central Asia. Real GDP growth accelerated to 6.5% in 2025, compared with 4.8% in 2024, with strong contributions from industry, transport, construction and trade. Construction expanded by 15.9%, while transport grew by 20.4%.

The report also points to Kazakhstan’s large infrastructure pipeline. The National Infrastructure Plan envisages more than 200 projects with a combined value of around $81 billion through 2029. The government is targeting economic growth to $450 billion and an additional $150 billion in FDI over the same period.

These figures help explain why Kazakhstan continues to occupy a different position from its regional peers.

Among UK respondents, Kazakhstan was identified as the most business-friendly Central Asian market, selected by 10.9% of investors, compared with 2.9% among U.S. respondents. For UK investors, ease of market entry and existing trade links were each cited by 60%, followed by a stable environment at 46.7% and corporate governance at 33.3%.

The distinction between the UK and U.S. views is important. Kazakhstan’s position is stronger among UK respondents, while its standing among U.S. investors has weakened compared with last year. The report notes that Kazakhstan fell from 8.5% to 2.9% among American investors, suggesting that broader geopolitical narratives may be affecting perceptions of the country despite its economic weight.

This is a perception issue rather than an economic one, and those two things increasingly need to be considered separately. Kazakhstan’s fundamentals remain substantial, but investors do not assess fundamentals in isolation. The country is part of a region exposed to the Russia-Ukraine war, tensions around energy infrastructure, changing global supply chains and intensifying competition over critical minerals.

That explains why investment security and political stability remain at the top of the investor agenda. Investment security was a concern for 72.3% of UK respondents and 64.7% of U.S. respondents, while political stability was cited by 56.2% and 52.9%, respectively. For Kazakhstan, the implication is straightforward: scale alone is no longer enough.

The capital markets story is becoming more important

One of the report’s most significant developments is the growing importance of capital markets. Kazakhstan has long relied heavily on FDI, particularly in oil, mining and infrastructure. But the emergence of a broader regional capital markets ecosystem is changing how Western investors view the region.

Vladimir Mikhailovsky, Partner, Capital Markets at Sidley Austin LLP, points to increased Kazakh bond activity in 2026, including debut transactions. He expects diversification to remain a key market feature.

“The popularity of “dim sum” or offshore RMB offerings is likely to continue to grow, as Kazakh issuers seek to diversify their investor base and capitalize on the favorable interest rate environment, ” he said.

This matters because capital-market access can signal financial maturity. A country that can attract investors not only into physical assets but also into bonds, equities and other financial instruments is gradually becoming integrated into a more sophisticated international capital ecosystem.

The regional picture is also changing quickly. In May 2026, Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund completed the country’s first international equity listing, with the offering more than four times oversubscribed. Sovereign credit ratings across the region were upgraded, while critical minerals moved higher on the strategic agenda of both the U.S. and the European Union (EU).

For Central Asia, that is a notable transition: the story is no longer exclusively about attracting greenfield investment into resource projects. It is increasingly about building investable financial instruments and institutions around the region’s economic expansion.

Critical minerals are changing the conversation

The renewed international focus on Central Asia is also inseparable from the global race to secure critical minerals and diversify supply chains.

Kazakhstan remains particularly well positioned because of its role in uranium and its broader mining potential. The report describes the country as the world’s leading uranium supplier, accounting for 40% of global output in 2025. Mining exploration spending reached a decade high of $127 million in 2025, with almost half directed toward copper projects. Uzbekistan, meanwhile, is emerging as another important mining center, with newly announced deposits of tungsten, lithium and germanium as well as 14 rare-earth sites.

This is where economics and geopolitics increasingly intersect. The report points to the November 2025 C5+1 White House Summit, which generated more than $130 billion in commercial commitments, as well as the EU’s commitment of up to 12 billion euros through Global Gateway. Both developments are presented as evidence that Western governments are no longer viewing Central Asia purely through the lens of traditional development or trade policy.

The region is becoming strategically relevant to discussions about energy security, supply-chain resilience and access to critical raw materials. For Kazakhstan, that creates an opportunity but also raises expectations. Resource wealth can attract capital, but investors increasingly want to know how resources are governed, processed and integrated into longer-term value chains.

Uzbekistan is becoming harder to ignore

While Kazakhstan remains the region’s economic anchor, Uzbekistan is becoming increasingly important to the investor story. The country’s first international equity listing by the National Investment Fund was one of the report’s defining transactions. The offering was more than four times oversubscribed, demonstrating that international investor appetite is not limited to Kazakhstan’s established market position.

The report also highlights the planned launch of the Tashkent International Financial Center, alongside Uzbekistan’s growing mining potential and efforts to deepen its financial infrastructure. But perhaps more importantly, Uzbekistan offers a different investment proposition: a large population, a rapidly transforming economy and the possibility of expanding the region’s consumer and industrial base.

Executive Chairman of East-West Group and Founder and Board Member of the Europe-Uzbekistan Association for Economic Cooperation Oybek Shaykhov argues that international investors still face an information deficit.

“Transparent, consistent and credible communication is not simply a reputational tool; it is a fundamental pillar of investor confidence,” he said.

That observation applies to the wider region, particularly to countries trying to attract investors beyond the traditional circle of state-backed or resource-focused projects.

The geopolitical premium and discount

For Central Asia, the external environment has become more favorable and more complicated at the same time. Associate Director at the Eurasia Center of the Atlantic Council Andrew D’Anieri notes that Central Asia’s growth outlook for 2026-27 looks relatively strong compared with regions more directly exposed to the fallout from the Iran war and higher energy prices. He also points to Russia-related instability and growing water pressures as tests of the region’s resilience.

That combination is likely to define the next stage of the region’s investment story. Central Asia is gaining strategic importance precisely because the international system is becoming less predictable. Supply chains are being redesigned, competition for critical minerals is intensifying, and governments are looking for alternative transport and energy routes.

But the same geopolitical environment also raises the risk premium. The Montfort survey shows that investors are willing to engage with the region despite these uncertainties. The harder question is whether that interest can translate into long-term commitments.

This is where Kazakhstan’s next phase of economic development becomes particularly important. Maintaining high growth is one objective. Converting growth into deeper capital markets, greater financial diversification and more international investor participation is another.

The report suggests that the opportunity is there. Interest among Western investors is dramatically higher than it was two years ago, even if the extraordinary surge of 2024–25 has now stabilized. The challenge is that investors are becoming more sophisticated just as the region competes for larger, more strategic pools of capital.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

World.title: ‘Pink Lung’, or why claim that Abkhazia has no good wine is outdated. VIDEO
World.content:
Wine in Abkhazia

For a long time, Abkhazia was known mainly for its basic range of wines. The region’s unpredictable climate, with annual rainfall of up to 2,000 mm, was seen as a challenge, as was the popularity of mass-produced semi-sweet wines.

However, modern winemaking practices have challenged this perception. Today, Abkhaz wine producers are shifting their focus towards premium wines.

The Association of Winemakers is actively reviving local indigenous grape varieties. It says fermentation control and modern scientific methods now make it possible to produce delicate, dry and fresh rosé wines.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Wine in Abkhazia

World.title: European Parliament resolution on banning opposition parties in Georgia: what it says
World.content:
On 8 October, the European Parliament adopted its latest — and seventh — critical resolution on Georgia. This time, it focuses on the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban five opposition parties and political groups.

In the resolution, the European Parliament strongly condemns the attempts to outlaw these opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them.

The draft resolution also once again calls for the release of political prisoners and sanctions against those responsible for Georgia’s democratic backsliding. It specifically names Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, party secretary-general Kakha Kaladze, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili.

The document says that the actions of Georgian Dream have caused the situation in Georgia to deteriorate further. Democracy and media freedom have declined, while human rights and the rule of law face growing violations. The document says this increasingly conflicts with Georgia’s international obligations and responsibilities, including the Copenhagen criteria.

The draft resolution also notes that two German foundations — the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation — had to close their offices in Tbilisi after the authorities rejected their funding applications under the grants law.

The draft resolution also again refers to the persecution of journalists in Georgia who covered the authorities’ repression of the opposition and civil society.

According to the draft resolution, the European Parliament:

Strongly condemns the attempt to outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them. It stresses that a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that using judicial mechanisms to eliminate legitimate political opposition is incompatible with democracy. It notes that banning the only opposition party represented in the Georgian parliament undermines the government’s previous narrative that it targeted only parties “under boycott”;

Timeline of European Parliament resolutions on Georgia

Since October 2024, the European Parliament has adopted six critical resolutions concerning the Georgian government. In these documents, MEPs have criticised Georgian Dream’s policies on democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the country’s European integration.
