World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
UNHRC resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories

On 7 October, the UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution in Geneva concerning Georgia‘s occupied regions.

According to Georgia’s Foreign Ministry, the resolution, entitled “Cooperation with Georgia”, addresses the human rights situation in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The UN Human Rights Council calls for unhindered access to the occupied territories for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as international and regional human rights mechanisms.

The resolution also condemns Russia’s actions aimed at annexing Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

It expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in the Russian-occupied regions.

The document also highlights the importance of the Geneva International Discussions, established under the ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008.

The resolution, submitted by Georgia, was adopted by consensus, as it was last year.

World.title: ‘No right to enter classroom’: Teacher beats pupil at Armenian school
World.content:
Teacher beats pupil at school in Armenia

A video showing a teacher beating a second-grade pupil at a school in the Armenian village of Vardadzor has shocked people across Armenia. A relative of the girl told journalists that she was so frightened by the incident that she had refused to return to school.

The girl’s parents appealed to the Gegharkunik regional administration, demanding that the teacher be dismissed. However, they were told that this would only be possible if complaints were filed by at least seven parents.

Social media users responding to the video called on the Interior Ministry to investigate the incident and launch criminal proceedings.

The Education Ministry said it had contacted the Interior Ministry, the Education Inspectorate and the National Centre for Educational and Psychological Support to ensure a thorough investigation.

“Relevant legal procedures will begin shortly to strip this teacher of the right to teach,” the ministry said.

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, described the violence against the schoolgirl as “unacceptable and deeply concerning”.

The Investigative Committee opened a criminal case over allegations of “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”.

By the time of publication, reports had emerged that the teacher had been detained.

What happened

A relative of the second-grade pupil told Shamshyan.com that the class teacher had first beaten the girl in the classroom. The violence continued in the corridor after the pupil left the classroom. The girl returned home with swollen eyes and marks from the blows on her neck and arms.

“There had been slaps before, but never beatings like this – with hands and a pointer,” the relative said.

The girl has not attended school since the incident. According to family members, she later encountered the teacher by chance in the street and ran home in terror.

The girl’s mother said she did not want the teacher to face criminal prosecution but insisted that she be dismissed.

Armenian media reported that the incident was discussed at the school the following day.

“The teacher admits her guilt. She submitted a written statement acknowledging what she had done and asked not to be punished. As a result, I issued her a written reprimand,” school headteacher Gevorg Nersesyan said.

He also said such incidents were unacceptable and expressed surprise that a teacher with 30 years of experience could have treated a second-grade pupil in this way.

‘Schools must be a safe environment for children’

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, stressed that schools must provide a safe environment for children.

“Any form of violence against a child or any other form of inappropriate treatment is fundamentally incompatible with respect for the child’s dignity, safety and rights,” she said.

According to Manasyan, children must be protected not only through responses to individual incidents, but also through effective measures to prevent and address potential cases of violence.

Manasyan also questioned the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to protect pupils in schools, particularly the work of pupil protection groups.

“The effectiveness of these mechanisms should be assessed primarily on the basis of how they work in practice,” she said.

Pupil protection groups were established in all schools on 1 September 2026 by order of the Minister of Education, Science, Culture and Sport. They were specifically set up to prevent violence, bullying and other high-risk situations. Following the incident at the school in Vardadzor, the pupil protection group held a meeting. However, according to the girl’s relatives, no steps were taken to help her return to school.

The Office of the Human Rights Defender said it had launched an investigation into the incident.

Not the first case of violence since start of school year

Two weeks ago, a maths teacher at a school in the village of Berdavan in Armenia’s Tavush region slapped a 13-year-old boy across the face. He also pushed the pupil, forcibly made him sit at his desk and hit him on the head with a notebook, striking the child’s eye with its edge.

According to the boy’s mother, the teacher’s wife, who is the school’s deputy headteacher, also treated him harshly. She slapped him across the face, pushed him into her office and made him stand in the corner.

Although the boy continues to attend school, his mother told journalists that he had been left psychologically distressed by the incident.

The teacher has also been charged with “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”. He has been released on an undertaking not to leave the country and suspended from his duties.

Social media reactions

“A written reprimand is not enough. A teacher like this should be barred from working in education.”

“If people like this were prosecuted, teachers would think twice before raising a hand against someone else’s child.”

“Someone who displays such aggressive and unacceptable behaviour simply has no right to call themselves a teacher. What can such a person teach children – respect, kindness or compassion for others?“

“If a similar incident had happened in Germany, for example, the teacher could have faced up to five years in prison. Moreover, if the headteacher had seen the footage – had seen a child being beaten – but failed to take appropriate action, questions would also arise about his professional responsibility.“

“If the teacher behaves so brazenly in front of a camera, it is frightening to imagine what she might have done in a classroom without cameras. She should be dismissed, made to apologise to the child and permanently banned from teaching.”

“The situation is much the same in almost every school. In some, there is physical violence; in others, psychological pressure; and in some, children are simply ignored. At parents’ request, cameras should be installed not only in school corridors but also in classrooms.”

“When such incidents become public, headteachers condemn the teacher’s actions and express utter surprise that someone with more than 30 years of teaching experience could behave this way. But before things reach that point, when we ask for cameras to be installed, those same headteachers come up with a thousand excuses to prevent it.”

“They just don’t want teachers to be embarrassed or parents to see how often a teacher talks on the phone during lessons.“

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Everything is in place for Prime Minister Kobakhidze’s resignation’
World.content:
Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili predicts that Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could resign soon. The analyst focuses on Kobakhidze’s remarks at a government meeting on 7 October, where he spoke about projects completed and currently under way during his time as prime minister.

Also on 7 October, Kobakhidze appointed Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili as deputy prime minister. Khukhashvili sees this as a possible signal of upcoming changes in the government. He believes Kvrivishvili could eventually replace Kobakhidze.

On 7 October, the government held its first meeting in a month. Irakli Kobakhidze spoke about projects completed and currently under way in various sectors during his time as prime minister. Kobakhidze spent more than half an hour reviewing the government’s record.

Gia Khukhashvili: “Everything is in place for his [Kobakhidze’s] resignation. In fact, he has been powerless for a long time. No minister in the executive branch feels accountable to him. A purely technical government has been formed.

I would not rule out the possibility that [his lengthy speech at today’s government meeting] means exactly that. I can support this with the fact that Mariam Kvrivishvili has been promoted to deputy prime minister. That also happened today, and it is another sign that the end of his premiership is near.

It is possible that during the transition period, Mariam Kvrivishvili could become acting prime minister to ensure continuity until a new prime minister takes office. However, I would not rule out the possibility that Kvrivishvili herself could become the new prime minister.”

“Anything is possible — these are games at the royal court, after all. I do not see either Kobakhidze or [former prime minister] Garibashvili as real actors in the political process. There have been periods when they were given more room to manoeuvre, but they are not real players.

Anything is possible. The main and most important decisions, the fundamental ones, are made elsewhere. Someone else decides whom to hang and whom to pardon, and we all know his first and last name [Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream — JAMnews].

And this is just some petty squabbling among small-time people.”

Gia Khukhashvili on possible resignation of Kobakhidze

World.title: EU prepares to expand without Georgia: what ‘candidate status on paper’ means
World.content:
The European Union is preparing for a new round of enlargement and drawing up concrete roadmaps for four leading candidates — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

Georgia is no longer part of this process. The European Commission does not mention it at all in its main communication. An accompanying 149-page document explicitly says that Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold.

Against this backdrop, the political conflict between Tbilisi and Brussels has become increasingly clear. So has their different understanding of European integration itself. The European Commission says democratic reforms and alignment with EU foreign policy form part of the conditions for membership. Leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, meanwhile, have increasingly openly portrayed some of Brussels’ demands as pressure that harms the country’s interests.

“A candidate only on paper”

On 6 October, the European Commission published a communication titled “Communication on Pre-Enlargement Policy Reviews – Preparing for a Wider Union” (“Pre-Enlargement Policy Review — Preparing for a Wider Union”).

The document outlines how the EU itself should prepare for future enlargement. One of the main areas involves gradually integrating candidate countries before they achieve full membership.

At the same time, the European Commission is considering stronger safeguards in case a new member violates the EU’s fundamental principles after joining. In the most serious cases, such a mechanism could even suspend the member state’s voting rights in the Council of the EU.

The European Commission will prepare roadmaps for four countries — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

The main 25-page communication does not even mention Georgia.

On 6 October 2026 in Brussels, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos described Georgia’s position in response to a question from a Georgian journalist:

“As you know, Georgia is a candidate country only on paper. I regret that. I would like Georgia, with the huge support of the Georgian people, to be at the same level as Moldova and Ukraine today.

How we continue working with the country will depend to a large extent on how the member states assess its future. But much of what is happening in the country [in Georgia] will appear in the enlargement reports at the end of October. You can imagine which direction things will take.”

The working document accompanying the communication does mention Georgia among the enlargement countries, but it adds an important caveat:

“Georgia’s accession process has been de facto halted in line with the conclusions of the European Council.”

This is an important point: the EU has not revoked Georgia’s candidate status, and it did not take any new decision to do so on 6 October.

However, despite retaining its formal status, Georgia does not rank among the candidates for which the European Commission is now planning the next stage of accession.

A common starting point, different trajectories

Georgia applied to join the European Union in March 2022, at the same time as Ukraine and Moldova.

It received candidate status in December 2023, subject to fulfilling nine steps set out by the European Commission.

The three countries then took sharply different paths.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova in 2024. In Georgia’s case, however, EU documents state that steps taken by the authorities since 2024 have harmed the country’s European path and effectively halted the accession process.

On 28 November 2024, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028 and would reject all EU budget grants.

The new 2026 package makes the difference even clearer: Moldova and Ukraine now rank among the four leading candidates, while Georgia does not.

“Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t”

Statements by Georgian Dream show that relations between Tbilisi and Brussels have become increasingly confrontational.

Georgian authorities respond to criticism from the EU not only by defending their policies, but also by openly rejecting and criticising Brussels’ demands themselves.

Government representatives also frame compliance with some EU demands as a question of protecting Georgia’s national interests.

Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili contrasted Marta Kos’s statement about Moldova’s progress with economic indicators. He said Georgia’s economic growth was higher.

Papuashvili linked this difference to Georgia’s approach to Brussels’ recommendations:

“[Moldova] deserves more and more praise, but our experience tells us that the more Brussels praises you, the more its decisions and imposed directives harm you.”

Papuashvili also compared poverty rates in the two countries and linked the differences to their respective approaches to Brussels’ policies.

*“What is the difference? Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t. […] The conclusion is clear: those who listen to Brussels suffer; those who do not listen to Brussels but listen to their own people come out ahead economically. The only thing Moldova is really ahead of us in is Brussels’ beautiful words.

We certainly do not need such beautiful words if those words only mean that we suffer from policies imposed by Brussels,”* Papuashvili said.

Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirchkhalia gave a similar response.

He said the Georgian authorities were ready to carry out the reforms needed for European integration, but that Georgia had “red lines” and national interests that it could not sacrifice to join the EU.

He compared compliance with Brussels’ political demands to “blind obedience” and said Georgia wanted EU membership “not at any cost”.

“If Brussels now considers a country’s ‘progress’ to depend on how blindly it follows specific political demands, then this is no longer merit-based European integration, but an assessment of blind obedience. […] So when we are told that Georgia is ‘lagging behind’ Ukraine and Moldova, our answer is simple: Georgia chooses dignity and peace!” Kirchkhalia said.

What the European Commission says

The European Commission’s 2026 document sets out very different criteria. Alongside economic development, the central issues in the accession process include the rule of law, democratic standards and alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP).

According to the document, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and North Macedonia fully align with the CFSP, while Moldova and Ukraine demonstrate a high level of alignment. Georgia and Serbia need to make significant progress in this area, while Georgia and Turkey have low levels of alignment.

The European Commission sees this as an indication of a candidate country’s strategic choice and says these issues must be resolved before accession.

The document also gives Russia a separate focus. According to the European Commission, enlargement directly counters Russian influence because the accession process requires countries such as Georgia and Serbia to fully align with EU foreign policy and legislation. This includes sanctions, energy, trade, foreign investment and visa policy.

The document also states:

“At present, the Georgian authorities are not actively pursuing EU and NATO membership, while Ukraine is making changes to achieve full compatibility with NATO.”

This ranks among the strongest formulations in the new document because the assessment concerns not just the implementation of a specific reform, but the authorities’ overall political course.

The opposition on Moldova’s example

Salome Samadashvili, one of the leaders of the opposition Lelo — Strong Georgia alliance, contrasts Moldova’s example with Georgian Dream’s narrative about a so-called “second front”.

She says Moldova did not open a “second front” against Russia. Instead, the EU is helping Moldova strengthen its security and defence capabilities in response to threats from Russia.

Samadashvili also links Moldova’s European progress to its efforts to tackle oligarchic influence, arguing that Georgia has gone in the opposite direction.

“Unfortunately, Georgia has gone in the opposite direction: an oligarch has taken complete control of the government, destroyed all state institutions, and as a result, our EU accession agenda has been cancelled,” Samadashvili says.

Ban on opposition parties

The political context of Georgia’s relations with the EU is also visible in the European Parliament’s current agenda.

On 7 October, the European Parliament is due to hold a debate officially titled “Attempts by the ruling Georgian Dream party to ban opposition parties in Georgia”. A vote on the corresponding resolution will take place on 8 October.

This is a separate procedure from the European Commission’s enlargement package, and it would be incorrect to directly link the two.

However, the two processes also illustrate the different political contexts between Georgia and the other leading candidates. The EU is working on the next stages of integration with four countries, while the European Parliament is discussing the possible banning of opposition parties in Georgia.

The next important assessment of Georgia will come at the end of October, when the European Commission publishes its enlargement reports.

EU enlargement without Georgia

World.title: Ex-German intelligence chief arrested as investigators probe links to Azerbaijani intelligence
World.content:
German intelligence passed information to Azerbaijan

Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has not specified which foreign country is involved. However, according to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer and whether he prepared analytical materials for the officer using classified information.

Hanning has also served for many years on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.

Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was detained on 6 October. His former chief of staff, Manfred D., was also arrested as part of the same investigation.

According to the Federal Prosecutor’s Office, Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage involving treason, obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service. Manfred D. is suspected of attempted treason and aiding and abetting espionage.

The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations have yet to be considered by a court on their merits. No final judicial decision has been made in Hanning’s case.

Around 2,000 BND documents

According to investigators, several years after leaving the BND, Hanning reached an agreement with his former employee to provide him with classified information.

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office believes that around spring 2010, Hanning and Manfred D. struck an agreement under which D. would regularly provide his former boss with important information obtained from the BND in exchange for payment.

Manfred D. worked with Hanning at the BND before following him to Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior. In 2012, he returned to the BND, where he held a senior position in the offices of subsequent heads of the intelligence service until March 2026. In this role, he had access to classified information.

According to preliminary findings by investigators, between 2010 and 2022, Manfred D. provided Hanning with around 2,000 documents. A significant proportion contained classified information and were intended exclusively for internal use within the BND.

Some of the materials contained information intended for the BND leadership, as well as for regular meetings of intelligence service representatives at the German Federal Chancellery. According to an investigation by WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the documents included material on Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military, as well as information obtained from Germany’s partner intelligence services.

Prosecutors say Hanning intended to use the information for commercial purposes as part of his private consultancy work.

How did Azerbaijan connection emerge?

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office does not mention Azerbaijan or any other country in its official statement.

According to the official account, Hanning once used classified information obtained from Manfred D. to prepare an analysis for “an employee of a foreign intelligence service”. Investigators have so far been unable to establish whether the analysis was actually passed to its intended recipient.

The possible Azerbaijan connection emerged in reports by German media citing sources familiar with the investigation.

According to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer. The magazine also reports that the analysis Hanning prepared using classified BND information was intended for this individual. The same information has also been reported by WELT, t-online and other German media.

Hanning sits on board of German-Azerbaijani Forum

Another factor drawing attention to the possible Azerbaijan connection is Hanning’s longstanding public ties with the country.

He has for many years served on the board of the Deutsch-Aserbaidschanisches Forum (German-Azerbaijani Forum).

In an announcement about the election of the forum’s new leadership in August 2025, Hanning was again listed as a board member. The same list also included Elmar Mammadov, a representative of Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR in Germany.

The forum describes itself as an independent platform promoting political, economic, academic and cultural ties between Germany and Azerbaijan. LobbyControl, a German organisation that monitors lobbying in Germany, has previously described the forum as one of the lobbying organisations with close ties to the Azerbaijani authorities.

Hanning has served on the forum’s board for many years. As early as 2017, Tagesspiegel reported that the former BND chief was a member of the organisation’s board. It said that even then, the forum’s structures included former ministers, MPs and senior government officials.

Previous ‘Azerbaijan case’ in Germany

The current espionage investigation is not the first major scandal in Germany involving Azerbaijan.

In recent years, German authorities have investigated a number of criminal cases involving the alleged bribery of politicians in Azerbaijan’s interests.

In July 2025, a Munich court gave former CSU MP Eduard Lintner a nine-month suspended prison sentence for his role in transferring funds originating from Azerbaijan in an effort to influence decisions by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). The court explicitly described this as vote-buying.

In January 2026, former CDU MP Axel Fischer was given a 14-month suspended prison sentence. According to the court, while serving in PACE, Fischer received tens of thousands of euros from Azerbaijan and, in return, made positive statements about the country and passed on confidential documents.

Legally, these cases are unrelated to the current investigation into Hanning. The Lintner and Fischer cases concerned political corruption and lobbying on behalf of the Azerbaijani government’s interests. The Hanning case concerns state secrets and suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Classified documents discovered during unrelated investigation

Suspicions of espionage involving Hanning emerged under unusual circumstances.

In September 2025, German law enforcement officers searched Hanning’s home and offices as part of a separate criminal investigation into the kidnapping of the children of businesswoman Christina Block. Hanning also denied the allegations in that case.

During the searches, investigators reportedly discovered classified BND material. The documents were subsequently handed over to federal authorities, and in May 2026 a covert investigation into Hanning and Manfred D. was launched.

The findings of the investigation could have serious implications for Germany’s intelligence service. BND chief Martin Jäger said an internal review was also under way and that the initial suspicions had been further substantiated. German lawmakers responsible for overseeing the intelligence services have called for a comprehensive investigation into what happened.

If reports of Hanning’s links to Azerbaijani intelligence are confirmed, the case would go beyond previous scandals involving Azerbaijani lobbying in Germany: this time, the issue is not political influence but the possible transfer of classified German intelligence to a foreign intelligence service.

World.title: Uzbekistan, EBRD discuss mining, geology cooperation
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Uzbekistan and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) discussed expanding cooperation in mining and geology, including regulatory development and technical assistance for investment projects, during a meeting in Tashkent on Oct. 8.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology of Uzbekistan, following a meeting between F. Khamidova, first deputy minister of mining and geology of Uzbekistan, and EBRD experts Paul Moffatt, Eric Rasmussen and Matthew Starnes.

The discussions focused on cooperation in the mining and geological sectors, particularly the development of subordinate regulations and legal acts governing the industries.

Additionally, the sides exchanged views on opportunities for EBRD technical assistance in preparing investment projects and attracting investors to Uzbekistan’s mining and geological sectors.

"The sides discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in mining and geology, including regulatory development and technical assistance for investment projects and investor attraction," the Uzbek Ministry of Mining and Geology said.

The meeting forms part of Uzbekistan’s efforts to develop its mining and geological industries, improve the regulatory framework and attract investment into projects involving the exploration and development of mineral resources.

The parties discussed potential areas for further engagement, with a focus on practical support for project preparation and investment mobilization.

World.title: Awaza summit opens the way for Azerbaijan to chair the CIS
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. The CIS summit has begun in Awaza, Turkmenistan. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has arrived at the Caspian resort alongside his fellow leaders from the Commonwealth, and for Baku, the meeting looks well beyond the immediate agenda. The leaders will decide who will chair the CIS in 2027 and, at the same time, map out the organization’s calendar for the coming years. Azerbaijan features prominently in that calendar: in 2027, it will become a co-chair, and in 2028, it will chair the Commonwealth.

The CIS chairmanship changes every year on January 1, with the rotation following the Russian alphabetical order of country names. Turkmenistan, the host of the current summit, currently holds the chairmanship. Alongside it are two co-chairs - Tajikistan, which chaired the organization last year, and Uzbekistan, which will take over the chairmanship in January. Azerbaijan will follow.

There are always two co-chairs in the Commonwealth: the outgoing and incoming chairs. The arrangement is designed to ensure continuity, allowing responsibilities to be transferred smoothly and major events to be prepared jointly by the three countries. The chair sets the agenda for the year and hosts the main events, including meetings of the Council of Heads of State and the Council of Heads of Government. In other words, CIS leaders will travel to Azerbaijan in 2028.

For the same year, the CIS is proposing to declare 2028 the “Year of Social Development and Quality of Life.” The theme is broad enough to encompass almost everything, from pensions and healthcare to labor migration, giving the chair considerable room to shape the agenda. The following year, 2029, is proposed as the “Year of Transport Connectivity.” The theme is particularly relevant for Baku: in recent years, Azerbaijan has been emerging as one of the key transit hubs between Europe and Asia and has invested heavily in this sector.

The agenda also includes an anniversary. On December 8, the CIS will mark its 35th anniversary - the agreement establishing the organization was signed in Minsk in 1991 by Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. The heads of state will adopt a joint statement on the occasion. They will also decide where they will meet next. The answer is not difficult to predict: Uzbekistan, as the chairmanship passes to Tashkent.

Azerbaijan joined the Commonwealth later than its founders. The Council of Heads of State approved its admission on September 24, 1993, during one of the most difficult periods in the country’s history. Over more than three decades, Baku has developed its own approach to working within the CIS, and it is well known in Minsk, where the organization is headquartered. Azerbaijan takes part in areas that serve its interests and firmly maintains its position where it differs from the common line. Baku has attached reservations and special opinions to a number of CIS documents. Azerbaijan does not participate in the CIS Economic Court, one of the organization’s seven statutory bodies. There is plenty to choose from, however: the Commonwealth has 84 bodies in total, including 66 sectoral bodies.

Baku takes the summits themselves seriously. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has attended all the meetings in recent years. In December 2020 and October 2021, at the height of the pandemic, the leaders met by videoconference. They were followed by in-person meetings in Astana, Bishkek, Moscow and Dushanbe. Awaza is the seventh consecutive summit attended by the Azerbaijani president. For post-Soviet leaders, such meetings have long provided a convenient opportunity to hold a whole series of bilateral talks over a day or two, and today is unlikely to be an exception.

The most notable recent changes concern Armenia. For many years, Azerbaijan’s position within the CIS included one consistent provision: Baku would work with all Commonwealth members except Yerevan in cultural, humanitarian, scientific and other areas. Azerbaijan has now lifted its previous restrictions on the transit of goods to Armenia. The two countries are taking their first steps in economic and trade cooperation. Azerbaijani goods and transit cargo from third countries are already moving to Armenia through Azerbaijani territory. Until recently, this would have seemed almost unimaginable. Against this backdrop, the proposed “Year of Transport Connectivity” in 2029 carries considerably more substance than such titles usually suggest.

The CIS Charter is full of the right words about friendship, good-neighborliness, trust and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The history of the Commonwealth has also included wars between its members and the withdrawal of entire countries - something Baku remembers better than most. What Azerbaijan values in the organization are more tangible things: direct dialogue with neighbors, trade and humanitarian ties.

There is more than a year to go before January 2028. Preparations for Azerbaijan’s chairmanship are, in effect, beginning today in Awaza. Under President Ilham Aliyev, Azerbaijan has gained extensive experience in chairing various international organizations. It is enough to recall the country’s chairmanship of the Non-Aligned Movement - the world’s second-largest organization after the UN - which effectively gave the movement a new lease of life and brought it back into the ranks of relevant international organizations.

The CIS, too, may soon receive a new impetus for development - under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev.

World.title: Sadyr Japarov strengthens partnership with Azerbaijan - new chapter in relations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov took part in the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan on October 8. The meeting is being held at the Avaza complex in Turkmenistan. The summit was also attended by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan.

Sadyr Japarov’s speech at the meeting shows that Bishkek sees cooperation with Azerbaijan not only as a political partnership, but also as an opportunity to expand practical ties in trade, industry, transport, the digital economy and tourism. Several of the initiatives are directly linked to strengthening economic ties between Central Asia, and the South Caucasus.

One of the key proposals from the Kyrgyz side was the creation of a unified electronic trading platform for Central Asia and Azerbaijan.

"In this regard, we propose creating a unified electronic trading platform for Central Asia and Azerbaijan. This would provide consumers and businesses with broader access to goods produced in the countries of the region," Sadyr Japarov said.

According to him, the development of e-commerce should go hand in hand with stronger industrial cooperation. Kyrgyzstan proposes that the governments of the countries in the region identify specific mutually beneficial projects in agricultural processing, light industry, construction materials and logistics, including the participants, sources of financing and implementation timelines.

Such an approach could create a basis for moving from growing mutual trade to more sustainable industrial cooperation. If such projects are implemented, Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan could have additional opportunities to promote each other’s products, while Central Asian companies could use Azerbaijani infrastructure to access the South Caucasus and other international markets.

Transport remains one of the most important elements of the emerging regional connection. Sadyr Japarov proposed that the transport authorities of the countries, together with carriers, develop practical solutions for unified freight tariffs, coordinated schedules, shorter waiting times and digital cargo tracking.

"Our focus should be on measurable results: reducing delivery costs and travel time. At the same time, every country should have the opportunity to fully participate in regional transport projects and receive economic benefits from them," the Kyrgyz president said.

In this context, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project is particularly important. Its further integration with routes through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan could create an additional land-sea connection between China, the countries of the region and South Caucasus markets. For Kyrgyzstan, this could provide more options for reaching foreign markets, while for Azerbaijan it could strengthen its role as a transport link between Central Asia and wider international routes.

Trade figures also show that economic ties between the two countries already have a basis for further growth. In 2025, trade turnover between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan amounted to $77.17 million, increasing about 1.9 times compared with 2024. Azerbaijan’s imports from Kyrgyzstan reached $53.75 million, while Azerbaijan’s exports to Kyrgyzstan amounted to $23.42 million.

In January-July 2026, the situation changed. Azerbaijan’s exports to Kyrgyzstan reached $30.03 million, exceeding the full-year 2025 figure by 28.2 percent, while imports from Kyrgyzstan amounted to $4.03 million. As a result, Azerbaijan’s trade surplus with Kyrgyzstan reached about $26 million during the period. This trend creates room for further growth in mutual supplies and a wider range of goods.

The Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund is another important basis for investment cooperation. In July 2026, its capital was increased from $100 million to $200 million. At the same time, three joint projects were opened and eight more initiatives were launched, creating a financial basis for moving toward larger industrial projects.

Tourism is another important area of bilateral relations. In July, the Azerbaijani-built five-star Baku Resort & Spa was opened in the village of Kara-Oy on Lake Issyk-Kul. The project covers more than 17 hectares and includes 111 rooms and 10 cottages. It can accommodate 330 guests and is expected to create 255 jobs at the initial stage. Projects like this not only develop tourism infrastructure but also create additional opportunities for people-to-people and business ties.

Against this background, cooperation between Azerbaijan and Kyrgyzstan is gradually moving beyond individual projects. The political foundation of relations is also becoming stronger. The two countries have previously signed a Treaty on Allied Relations. Kyrgyz Ambassador to Azerbaijan Maksat Mamytkanov said earlier that following Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s state visit to Kyrgyzstan, relations had reached a higher level of interstate cooperation and that ties were expected to become more active in all areas.

Further cooperation could develop in several directions. One could be an increase in mutual trade through a wider range of goods and new industrial projects. Another could involve the gradual creation of a common digital and logistics environment, including e-commerce, digital documents, cargo tracking and coordinated tariffs.

Another possible scenario is closer integration of Kyrgyzstan’s transport projects with routes through the Caspian Sea and Azerbaijan. In this case, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway could become part of a wider regional transport system connecting Central Asia with Azerbaijan and international markets.

Investment and tourism could also support further cooperation. The increased capital of the Azerbaijan-Kyrgyz Development Fund could provide financing for new projects, while joint promotion of tourism routes could strengthen contacts between the people of the two countries. Environmental cooperation also remains a possible area, including the sustainable use of natural resources and the protection of glaciers and mountain ecosystems.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan have jointly nominated US President Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s National Bank discloses re-export figures
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Re-exports from Kyrgyzstan amounted to $195.7 million in 2025, increasing by 14.6% compared with the previous year.

This was reported based on statistical data published by the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic.

The National Bank has already published updated balance of payments data for the first quarter of 2026; however, a separate re-export figure for the period is not provided in the table.

For comparison, re-exports amounted to $170.8 million in 2024, $150.7 million in 2023 and $154.7 million in 2022. Thus, the 2025 figure was the highest recorded over the period under review.

During 2025, the volume of re-exports varied by quarter. Re-exports amounted to $34.3 million in the first quarter, $68.8 million in the second quarter, $42.4 million in the third quarter and $50.2 million in the fourth quarter. The highest quarterly volume was recorded in the second quarter.

Re-export refers to the shipment outside the country of goods previously imported into its territory and is one of the components of foreign trade operations. Its dynamics can reflect changes in regional trade flows and the structure of Kyrgyzstan’s foreign trade.

Trend estimates that, based on the $195.7 million recorded in 2025 and the quarterly pattern of re-exports, the indicator could remain within the $190–220 million range in 2026 if regional trade flows remain broadly comparable with the previous year. This is a Trend estimate and is not an official forecast of the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic.

According to Trend’s calculations, the quarterly distribution in 2025 shows that re-export volumes can vary considerably during the year, with the second quarter accounting for the largest amount at $68.8 million. If quarterly volumes in 2026 remain broadly within the $40–60 million range, the annual figure could approach $200–220 million.

World.title: Sister of 13yo critically injured in alleged arson pleads with other teens
World.content:
The sister of a boy clinging to life after an alleged botched arson is pleading with Victorian children to resist cash offers to commit crimes amid a spate of firebombings wreaking havoc across Melbourne.

Warning: This story contains details that may distress some readers.

The 13-year-old was among a group of people allegedly involved in the firebombing of two cars in Melbourne's north-west in the early hours of Monday morning, which backfired when the boy himself caught fire, leaving him with burns to almost his entire body.

Speaking to the ABC as the schoolboy remains in a critical condition, the boy's sister said falling in with the "wrong crowd" could cost him his life.

"I want the community to know that street violence isn't worth their life and never will be," she said.

"It's not just a crime, but a life on the line.

"He's fighting for his life."

Despite the boy undergoing a 12-hour skin graft surgery at the Royal Children's Hospital, police yesterday told a court it was "very possible" he could die from his injuries.

The 13-year-old boy was left with burns to almost all of his body. (Supplied)

The youths allegedly inadvertently covered themselves in petrol while dousing the vehicles before setting them alight.

They allegedly then tried to flee in a stolen car but crashed it moments later, running away and "leaving the child engulfed in flames, fighting for his life", according to prosecutors

Two 16-year-old boys, including one out on bail at the time, are behind bars after police laid a raft of charges over the incident.

Despite having no prior criminal history, one of the boys failed in his bid for freedom yesterday afternoon in a children's court.

A third 15-year-old boy was arrested and released without charge.

A detective yesterday told the court that the 13-year-old was "screaming for help before collapsing" in the aftermath of the incident.

"It breaks my heart," his sister told the ABC.

"I cannot imagine how scared he would've been burning alive."

Do you know more? Contact Antonia O'Flaherty at Oflaherty.Antonia@abc.net.au or on antoniaoflaherty@protonmail.com

Co-accused apologised to family, offered cash payment

The ABC can reveal new details about how one of the accused teens contacted the 13-year-old boy's family admitting to his involvement, offering them cash and apologising for the injuries the boy suffered.

After her brother was rushed to hospital with burns to 90 per cent of his body, his sister pleaded for information about the blaze, prompting one of the accused teens to contact her, the court heard.

In Snapchat messages obtained by the ABC, the boy admitted his involvement and apologised to the family.

"I am so deeply sorry for everything and please believe me when I say this, I'm not asking for your forgiveness and don't expect you to like me at all but I am so sorry for what happened to [him] and it's my fault this all happened," one message read.

"I've sent $1'000 [sic] to a friend to give to you guys and [the boy] when he recovers hopefully that helps you guys out.

"And I did not mean to leave [him] behind I didn't leave on purpose or any of that the news makes fake shit."

The boy vowed to "change my life around and start going to church and get into boxing".

Two cars were destroyed and a home was damaged during the arson attack. (ABC News)

It was yesterday revealed that the group of youths was tasked with lighting the fire by middlemen on WhatsApp.

The boy's sister said youths such as her brother were at higher risk of being targeted by older offenders with organised crime links through friends already engaging in criminal behaviour.

"Walk away. Speak up. Tell someone. Protect your life," she said.

Police allege the teens were promised a $3000 payment to commit the arson.

The wounded boy's sister described her brother as sweet, insisting he would not want to hurt anyone.

"He was there for others and was a genuine, sweet soul," she said.

"I love that he will fight for the people he loves, even if that meant suffering."

The incident on Monday is among a string of similar arson attacks reported across Melbourne over consecutive nights this week.

World.title: MP Luke Gosling vows to seek Labor preselection despite pending assault case
World.content:
Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling says he will seek preselection again ahead of the next election, despite unresolved assault and breach of bail charges hanging over his head.

The Darwin-based Member for Solomon has been charged with two counts of assaulting Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly at the NT Thai Grand Festival in July.

Mr Gosling was subsequently charged with breaching his bail in August.

He denies all the allegations and his lawyer, Marty Aust SC, told the Darwin Local Court last month he would write to prosecutors requesting the charges be withdrawn due to "insufficient evidence".

David Connolly is the NT administrator, the equivalent of a state governor. (ABC News: Sam Parry)

Speaking at a press conference this morning alongside three Country Liberal Party (CLP) members of the NT parliament, Mr Gosling reaffirmed his view that his arrest had been politicised.

"I'll absolutely be running for preselection to keep representing the people of Solomon through our normal party processes," he said.

"I've been so encouraged by the support from not only my party members here in the Northern Territory, but everyday Territorians who see very clearly what is happening here and are wishing me all the best and all the support they can possibly give me.

" No distractions, no politicisation of processes that may be used against political opponents from time to time will distract me from that important work. "

In September, Mr Aust told the court in relation to the assault charges there was "not a single eyewitness to any event, nor a witness that gives opportunity for an event to occur".

Luke Gosling says future Territorians will "shake their head" when reflecting on the charges against him. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Save except for [Mr Connolly's wife] who puts it at a different place, at a different time and a different description," he said at the time.

"It has all the hallmarks of confusion or collusion."

Mr Gosling said in the future, Territorians would look back on his arrest and prosecution and find it hard to believe.

"This will in the future go down as something that the Territory will look at, shake their head, but ultimately move on from, as I have already, because the job that I have never stopped doing every day is delivering for the people of Darwin and Palmerston," he said.

Renewed scrutiny on administrator's appointment

A former president of the NT Cattlemen's Association, David Connolly was appointed to the role of NT administrator by the CLP government in December.

The NT administrator serves as the Crown's representative in the Territory, in a vice-regal role equivalent to a state governor.

In the lead-up to Mr Connolly's February swearing-in, there were calls for his appointment to be rescinded after past social media posts emerged from his deleted X (formerly Twitter) account.

David Connolly apologised to anyone who had been offended by his past social media activity before he was sworn in in February. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Some of the posts were labelled as "racist" and "denigrating of women".

The night before he was sworn in, Mr Connolly apologised to people who may have been hurt by the posts, saying he deeply regretted them.

Asked today if there should be renewed scrutiny over Mr Connolly's appointment if the charges against him were thrown out, Mr Gosling said the saga had been "a real education [and] eye-opener as to some of the dynamics going on here in the Northern Territory".

"It is obviously an issue for others to reflect on different appointments that have been made at different times," he said.

Luke Gosling says Anthony Albanese's federal Labor government doesn't do "captain's picks". (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"In the federal Labor team, we believe in strong cabinet processes, we believe in Caucus members having a say, and I think that is the way of good government.

" Captain's picks aren't the way of good government, generally. That is true across the board. "

Responding to Mr Gosling's comments at the press conference, the CLP's Youth, Seniors and Equality Minister Jinson Charls said the NT government had already provided responses about Mr Connolly's appointment.

He said if Mr Gosling's charges were dropped, the NT government would provide a further response about the appointment "if that question is still relevant at that point in time".

Territory Labor president Clare Martin said preselections for the next federal election were not yet open either in the NT or nationally.

She said the timing would be determined by Labor's federal executive.

World.title: Families of men killed on Mexico surf trip call for maximum sentences
World.content:
The mother of two Australian surfers who were shot dead in Mexico has called for their accused killers to receive maximum prison sentences, as the court prepares to deliver its verdict.

West Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, as well as their American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, were shot dead after being robbed while on a surfing trip in Mexico in April 2024.

Their bodies were found at the bottom of a well along Mexico's Pacific coast after they were reported missing.

Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús are charged with aggravated homicide, aggravated robbery, violent robbery and grand theft auto.

Ángel Jesús has been in custody in a local jail. (Supplied)

Jesús Gerardo, also known as "El Kekas", faces a possible sentence of 378 years. (Supplied: Mexican police handout)

Irineo Francisco has links to the Sinaloa cartel, according to court documents. (Supplied)

Closing arguments in the trial were heard in an Ensenada courthouse on Thursday, local time.

The defence cast doubt on the credibility of the investigation into the trio's deaths, as well as the testimony prosecutors relied on.

The families of the victims then addressed the court ahead of a verdict due to be delivered on Friday.

"Callum and Jake were our only children," said Debra Robinson, who has attended most of the trial with her husband, Martin.

" Their loss has taken not only the sons we loved, but also the future we had imagined with them. "

Ms Robinson cried as she read her statement and requested the judge hand down "a maximum sentence of imprisonment on those responsible".

"No sentence can bring Callum and Jake back; nothing can undo what has happened, but accountability matters," she said, adding that the protection of other families should also be considered.

"We never want another family to experience the devastation and suffering that has been inflicted on ours."

Jake and Callum Robinson and Carter Rhoad were killed near a remote beach in northern Mexico. (Supplied)

Jake, a 31-year-old doctor from Perth, had travelled to California to meet up with Callum, 32, who had been living in the US for 12 years after moving over to play lacrosse.

They then travelled south with Mr Rhoad to Mexico to go camping and surfing.

"We struggle to understand how three young men who showed kindness and trust, even in their final hours, could have been treated with such cruelty," Ms Robinson said.

"We understand that they gave up their keys and wallets, then begged for their lives and asked not to be killed.

" To know that their pleas were ignored is something we will carry with us for the rest of our lives. "

Ms Robinson previously asked for a timely verdict, as she and her husband are due to leave Mexico on October 9.

Debra and Martin Robinson are in Mexico after their sons Jake (left) and Callum (right) were killed. (Facebook: Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation)

The three accused looked uncomfortable in their seats as they listened to Ms Robinson's statement via a translator.

Mr Rhoad's fiancée, Natalie Weirtz, spoke on behalf of his family.

She described Mr Rhoad as an "incredible person" who dedicated his time to helping youths.

He had previously volunteered on humanitarian trips to South Africa, Guatemala and Mexico.

"I believe the accused are guilty and justice should be served in the highest degree," she said.

All three defendants previously rejected plea deals that would have seen them serve jail terms between 47 and 52 years.

A verdict is expected to be handed down on Friday. (ABC News: Timothy Myers)

Ari Gisell, the ex-girlfriend of Mr Gerardo, was sentenced to 20 years behind bars in November for her role in the robbery.

She was also fined 54,285 Mexican pesos ($4,323).

World.title: Ambulance ramping data casts doubt over LNP promise to reduce wait times
World.content:
Queues of long-wait ambulance patients outside many of Queensland's major hospital emergency departments have barely budged in the last two years.

The latest Queensland Health performance data for August shows statewide ambulance ramping is sitting at 42 per cent across Queensland's 26 top public hospital emergency departments (ED).

That means 42 per cent of patients who arrive at those hospitals by ambulance are waiting longer than 30 minutes to be transferred off a stretcher into an ED.

In July, ambulance ramping across the same hospitals stood at 38.7 per cent — 3.3 percentage points better than the August figures.

Ambulance ramping figures have barely budged in the last two years. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

The numbers are only marginally better than the August before the Crisafulli Government came to power in 2024, when ramping stood at 43.9 per cent.

In 2025 — Queensland's worst flu season on record — August ramping rates were at 45.6 per cent under the LNP Government.

Pressure to reduce ramping

The latest August data comes just ahead of the halfway mark in the Crisafulli Government's first four-year term and on the back of a late flu season.

It puts in serious doubt the Premier's commitment ahead of the 2024 election to get ambulance ramping down to under 30 per cent before the 2028 poll.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls is under pressure to get ramping under 30 per cent before 2028. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The latest figures pile more pressure on Health Minister Tim Nicholls after Premier David Crisafulli tied his cabinet future to cutting ambulance ramping to below 30 per cent before the next election.

Opposition leader Steven Miles predicted ramping figures would continue to worsen.

"You can't fix ramping while not delivering growth funding to our hospitals, not having a workforce plan, and not building the new beds that are needed," he said.

"The government still hasn't delivered a workforce plan to deliver the staffing those hospitals need and of course, they've delayed the build of new beds that would provide some relief to the bed block that is choking our emergency departments."

Opposition leader Steven Miles said ramping figures were likely to worsen. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

August ramping figures show hospitals in the Metro South Health region are particularly struggling.

Logan Hospital, south of Brisbane, recorded ramping levels at 61.8 per cent and at the Princess Alexandra Hospital, more than half of the patients arriving at the emergency department by ambulance were ramped for more than half an hour.

In the regions, Cairns Hospital ramping was 45.6 per cent in August, Bundaberg Hospital was only marginally better at 44.7 per cent, and at Rockhampton Hospital, it was 39.1 per cent.

Gold Coast University Hospital just snuck in under the 30 per cent target, recording 28.9 per cent — a huge improvement on when the Miles Government was in power when ramping was at 48.2 per cent in August 2024 — two months before the Queensland election.

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital has been cut to 34.5 per cent since August 2024. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital, west of Brisbane, has also turned around in the past two years.

In August 2024, a whopping 63.5 per cent of patients arriving by ambulance to the hospital, were ramped for more than the recommended benchmark of 30 minutes.

That has been cut to 34.5 per cent on the back of the Mater Springfield Hospital opening in May.

A spokeswoman for acting Health and Ambulance Services Minister Dale Last said the 2026 August ramping data was the lowest August figures in five years.

In August 2021, ambulance ramping was 38.7 per cent at Queensland’s major public hospitals.

This year’s data comes amid a record high 211,664 presentations to Queensland public hospital emergency departments in August.

World.title: How the card surcharge ban could change our relationship with cash
World.content:
With the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) ban on card surcharges now in effect you might start seeing local businesses offering discounts if you pay in cash.

Cash payments in Australia are much less common than they were a decade ago, but the RBA's latest data showed a slight uptick in cash use in 2025.

How could the ban on card surcharges impact how cash is used in Australia?

How often do people use cash?

This graph from the RBA's 2025 Consumer Payments Survey tracks the percentage of Australians who use cash in a typical week.

As you can see, 2025's figure of 50 per cent is much lower than the 97 per cent in 2007.

But it's slightly higher than 2022's figure of 47 per cent.

Will we move back to cash?

John Hawkins, a senior economic lecturer at the University of Canberra, doesn't expect cash use to skyrocket.

"From January the government has required most grocery stores and petrol stations to accept cash, which may see some modest increase in its use," Dr Hawkins says.

"On the other hand, about 20 per cent of consumers say they used cash to avoid card surcharges.

"As these no longer apply we could see some drop in cash use."

Loading...

Angel Zhong, a finance professor at RMIT, says she would be surprised if the surcharge ban reverses the long-term trend of card payments.

"I expect a modest uptick [in cash use] mostly at the margins: the café, the barber or the tradie offering a few per cent off for cash," Professor Zhong says.

"Australians moved to cards and mobile wallets mainly because of convenience, speed and record keeping, not because of price.

"A small discount at a handful of businesses is unlikely to change entrenched habits for most people."

Government backs down on ATO credit card ban The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warned that losing the payment option would put them under pressure.

Data from the RBA's 2025 survey showed people aged 65 and older were the most likely to use cash.

Cash might also still be preferred by people in regional areas with limited bank access or poor internet signal, people managing tight budgets, and people who have privacy concerns.

Professor Zhong says the goal should be to continue offering people the choice of using cash or paying by card.

Why would cafés offer cash discounts?

Professor Zhong sees cash discounts as a sign of how much pressure small businesses are under.

"The RBA paired the ban with a cut to interchange fees, which was meant to soften the blow by lowering what businesses pay to accept cards," she says.

"But interchange is only one part of the cost.

"Small businesses typically pay their payment service provider a bundled rate, and there's no guarantee that the interchange savings flow through to that rate."

Card payments are much more common than they were in 2007. (AAP: Dan Peled)

While big businesses could leverage their bargaining power to negotiate savings in their contracts, smaller businesses don't have that option.

And that means losing the ability to surcharge while missing out on a drop in costs.

"Against thin margins and rising operating costs, offering a discount for cash is one of the few ways a small business can steer customers toward a cheaper payment method," Professor Zhong says.

Are cash discounts legal?

Yes.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) says businesses can offer discounts to customers paying via particular means such as cash or PayID, but there are a few rules.

In charts: Cash use in Australia has increased Cash use has dropped by more than 50 per cent in almost 20 years. But there has been a slight increase in cash payments since 2022.

Discounts should be clearly disclosed before payment and they have to advertise the non-discounted price.

They're not allowed to display the discounted price more prominently than the full price.

Is it legal to hike prices to cover the surcharge ban?

Yes, but there are rules about how businesses label these price hikes.

"They must not mislead consumers about prices, including about the reasons for any price increases," the ACCC says.

An example of this might be nursery that used to apply a 1 per cent credit card surcharge for its products.

Price hikes are legal, but businesses have to be careful with their labelling. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

To compensate for that cost, they might increase the cost of a $10 pot plant to $10.10.

But let's say the nursery owner decides that, while they're setting new figures, they'll increase the pot plant's price to $12 to cover the rise in their electricity and water bills.

That's totally legal too.

But they aren't allowed to say the price increase from $10 to $12 is because of the ban.

"This will be misleading because the price increase also reflects other business costs, not just the cost of accepting card payments," the ACCC says.

World.title: The fruit and vegetables to look out for this month
World.content:
Asparagus is "absolutely sublime" at the moment, according to green grocer Jo Toscano.

Snow peas are also in season during spring. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Asparagus, snow peas and garden peas are increasingly prominent on shelves as spring sets in.

While no-one doubts the convenience of frozen peas, Effie Ramos from organic market garden Remi's Patch in Naarm/Melbourne says there's something special about the ritual of slowing down and popping the pods open yourself.

University of Newcastle nutrition professor Clare Collins says shopping seasonally can help us to introduce variety into our diets.

"If you eyeball all the veggies and fruit, look at what hasn't visited your trolley for a few weeks," she says.

What can you look for?

Vegetables:

Asparagus

Garden peas

Snow peas

Broad beans, including broad bean tips

Broccoli

Cauliflower

Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli and bok choy

Capsicum

Beetroot

Fresh garlic

Celery

Fruit:

Citrus, such as alfourer mandarins, navel and blood oranges

Mangoes, as availability increases

Asparagus, peas and broad beans

Asparagus is expected to peak in mid-to-late October, Ms Toscano says.

People tend to avoid the thick asparagus spears, but she says they're "juicy and full of flavour".

Four spring asparagus recipes From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these easy recipes will put spring asparagus on your weeknight menu.

White asparagus doesn't offer the "great value" of green asparagus, Ms Toscano says "it is divine". She recommends peeling it as the exterior can be "quite fibrous".

Dr Collins says asparagus works well in an omelette, quiche or with a simple cheese sauce.

Garden peas are also in season.

"Fresh peas sort of stay elevated in price but when they're good they're really good and it's worth it," Ms Toscano says.

When garden peas are fresh and young, she suggests using the pods (after they've been shelled) to flavour homemade vegetable stock or blitzing and sieving that mixture to make an intense pea-flavoured cooking liquid.

Broad beans are also "awesome" right now, Ms Toscano says.

Ms Ramos says the leafy green tip of the broad beans have been popular and are "really good, fresh in a salad".

Effie Ramos says there is nothing as good as peas when they are at their peak. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm )

Brassicas and Asian greens (again)

Broccoli and cauliflower "are pretty good value" and Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli are another good buy, Ms Toscano says.

Dr Collins says brassicas, including cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage, can be divisive because they can taste bitter to "super tasters" — people with a more sensitive sense of taste.

"But the good news, especially for parents, is that [through] repeated exposure you increase your tolerance," she says.

Avoid overcooking the produce and try roasting it or masking the flavour with something like a cheese sauce if someone you are cooking for finds it bitter, she suggests.

Jo Toscano says carrots are available year-round, but they are "unbelievable at the moment as well". (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Seeing red (capsicum and beetroot)

Ms Toscano says lots of red capsicums are coming from Queensland and that there are "bargains to be had" over the next couple of weeks.

Dr Collins says you can use affordable capsicums and Asian greens in stir-fries.

Ms Ramos says it's a good time for beetroot, which can be added to salads, raw or cooked.

"A lot of people sort of underestimate the power of the leaves of the beets. You can have them raw, or I just blanch them with a little bit of olive oil," she says.

Ms Ramos expects an abundance of spring onions, coriander, parsley, which will decrease prices.

October fruit offerings

Grapes have started but they're still very expensive, Ms Toscano says, and the first stone fruit will begin appearing this month.

"With the confluence of WA and Queensland mango seasons in a few weeks, prices are expected to fall," she says.

Cathy Senn from Sensational Berries in Naarm/Melbourne says supplies of Victorian berries will increase as the month continues, adding to those coming from northern Australia.

Lemon delicious pudding A hot pudding doused in cream is always welcome in cooler months.

"Starting with the strawberries and then we'll go on to raspberries and then later on we'll have the blueberries come on and then the strawberries, the blackberries after that," she says.

Citrus varieties are "diminishing", Ms Senn says, pointing to her "about finished" blood oranges, cara cara oranges and ruby grapefruits.

Dr Collins says at this time of year you can often buy bags of great value lemons and oranges. If she's got people coming over, she likes to cook her lemon-and-orange delicious.

"You use the rind, the more rind the better," she says.

Separating the egg white from the egg yolks is "the tricky bit", but it's also a good opportunity to teach kids or grandkids how to do it.

World.title: Man accused of deliberately injuring sheep at Canberra property refused bail
World.content:
An 18-year-old man accused of breaking into a rural property in Canberra's south and injuring several sheep last month has been refused bail.

Warning: This story contains details some readers may find distressing.

Police were called to the property adjacent to the Monaro Highway in Tuggeranong on September 17, after the owner arrived and found multiple injured sheep in a holding pen.

It is alleged several people went to the property the night before and used dogs to round up eight sheep and herd them into the pen.

Police say several of the sheep were deliberately injured with both firearms and edged weapons.

ACT Policing seized a large knife during a search warrant at the Richardson property. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

One sheep died and another had to be euthanased.

The home on the property was also allegedly ransacked.

Police raided a home in Richardson yesterday and arrested Memphis Auld, 18, and seized a number of items including cannabis and a large knife.

A 16-year-old was also arrested but released pending further investigation.

Investigators say a 27-year-old man, who is currently in custody for other matters, is also expected to be charged over the incident.

ACT Policing says it seized cannabis from the Richardson property. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

Firearm used in the incident still missing

Mr Auld faced the ACT Magistrates Court today charged with four counts of joint commission aggravated animal cruelty causing death and one count of joint commission aggravated animal cruelty causing serious injury.

He was also charged with committing aggravated burglary with intent to damage property, possession of a prohibited firearm, trafficking cannabis, and multiple motor vehicle and driving offences.

Mr Auld applied for bail, with the duty lawyer telling the court his partner relied on his Centrelink payments to make ends meet and his family were willing to support him to meet any conditions.

But the prosecutor opposed his release, arguing police held concerns a firearm — believed to have been used in the incident — was yet to be found.

"The offending really speaks for itself," the prosecutor said.

"That kind of injury to animals is quite awful, frankly, and it goes towards the safety and welfare of people."

Police say the incident happened near Tuggeranong Pines in Canberra's south. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

The court also heard officers had uncovered images on a mobile phone of a person pointing a firearm at a sheep while wearing clothing police believe match those found at Mr Auld's home.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt refused bail, saying the likelihood of Mr Auld reoffending, endangering the wellbeing of others or interfering with evidence was "so great that his detention in custody is currently justified".

"There is … an outstanding firearm that was used in the commission of these offences," she said.

"There was, in my view, some attempts to conceal and some attempts to evade detection by the group, with the firearm being concealed on the CCTV footage and number plates on vehicles being replaced.

"There is also possibly a risk that there may be some interference or communication about the firearm."

Mr Auld was remanded in custody to return to court later this month.

Police are urging anyone with information to provide details via the Crime Stoppers ACT website, quoting 8502989.

World.title: Remand centre built for adults to remain open to children over capacity concerns
World.content:
A police watch house designed for adults should continue holding Queensland children due to concerns over capacity at youth detention centres under proposed breach bail, go to jail laws, an independent watchdog says.

Queensland detention services inspector Anthony Reilly made the finding in his report into the Wacol Youth Remand Centre.

The centre, originally built for adults, opened in April last year to hold children aged 10 to 18 as a safer alternative to a police watch house while they wait for a room at one of Queensland's three youth detention centres.

The inspector noted in the report the draft consultation had recommended the "institutionalised" centre cease holding children when the state's fourth youth detention centre at Woodford opens.

The hallway outside children’s accommodation pods at the Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied: Queensland Ombudsman)

However, Mr Reilly said the impact of the proposed laws may mean the state's youth detention centres "do not have sufficient capacity".

"As a consequence, it is possible that children will need to be detained in large numbers and for lengthy periods in watch houses," he said.

Mr Reilly, who is also the state's ombudsman, said in that scenario it would therefore be "beneficial" to continue to accommodate children at the remand centre.

"While we do not consider the centre to be a suitable facility for the detention of children, we consider it to be more suitable than detention in police watch houses," the report states.

David Crisafulli says the government is continuing to invest in more facilities, early intervention and rehabilitation. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

When questioned, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said his government had increased capacity by 20 per cent and would continue to invest in more facilities, early intervention and rehabilitation.

"But faced with the choice of a few extra people in jail and a few less people in your lounge room, I'm on the side of Queensland victims, and I'm choosing the latter," he said.

"We're working across the system, and that's my commitment to people. We're doing what we said we're going to do."

An exercise yard at the Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied: Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support)

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said the need to keep the centre open showed the "government that has refused to plan for the consequences of their own decisions".

Mr Reilly noted while changes to the centre had been made to help accommodate children, its infrastructure is "institutional" and lacks the space, privacy and natural light children need.

The report made 13 recommendations to the department, including making efforts to soften the centre's environment.

In response, the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support said it would continue to explore ways to "soften" the environment and prioritise allowing children to access programs and outdoor facilities at other youth detention centres.

A mural outside one of the accommodation pods at Wacol Youth Remand Centre. (Supplied)

In the 12 months to June 20, the average number of children at the centre each day was 32, however, the report states the number has "significantly increased" to 54 as of August 2026.

The inspection report found the increased capacity to hold children is being "diminished" as the number being detained rises.

The average length of a child's stay was 7.1 days, according to data from the first 11 months of the centre.

However, the inspectors found not all children are "moved quickly".

Concerns over child's 49-day stay

The report also found children identified as being high-risk are being transferred from youth detention centres to the remand centre and, in some cases, staying for more than a month.

Between April 2025 and March this year, 20 children were returned to the centre as a strategy to manage high-risk and complex behaviours, the report states.

Inside a secure admissions holding cell where the centre plans to paint a mural. (Supplied)

This included one child who was held at the centre for a total of 49 days, before being returned to the youth detention centre where they were previously housed.

"We found no records that show the decision-making process or risk assessments that informed the child's continued stay at the centre," the report states.

Similarly, the inspector found no explanation of the decision-making process or risk assessments that informed the child's return to the detention centre.

In response to the inspector's recommendation, the Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support said it had strengthened governance and oversight for "risk-based transfers" to the centre.

Qld bail breach laws carry 12 month sentence Premier David Crisafulli confirmed the legislation, which is set to be introduced into parliament this week, will apply to both youths and adults.

The ombudsman acknowledged children received better support in the centre than they would in a police watch house.

Mr Crisafulli said the government would "keep reducing the amount of time that a child spends in a watch house", and wanted to try "early intervention to stop them going there in the first place".

"But for those that don't learn, that don't understand there are consequences for actions."

World.title: Big Hits: Dalaroo leads with stellar West African gold strike
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Big Hits: Dalaroo leads with stellar West African gold strike Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright October 9, 2026 — 4:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
