The United States’ execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, anonymous officials from the Defense Department told the BBC and Associated Press. The planned execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of killing 13 people at the Texas military base, was announced this week. He is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd at 2PM ET.

The Verge contacted YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, Meta, Rumble, and Kick to ask if they plan to allow the livestream to be aired on their platforms. None responded before publication.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview with Real America’s Voice.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches free AI security scans for open-source projects
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner. It says open-source projects that opt-in will get “thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.” That could mean open-source projects get alerted about possible security issues sooner, but the trade-off is that OSS Scanner’s reports don’t come with human review:

The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage.

OSS Scanner is far from the first AI bug hunting helper out there. AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May. At the same time, some open-source projects are struggling to keep up with the sudden onslaught of AI-generated bug reports, including Linus Torvalds and even Google.

Tech.title: SpaceX announces plan to become a ‘major mobile carrier’
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.

The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service.

The FCC has also approved plans to deploy 15,000 V2 Starlink Mobile satellites that will offer more than 100 times the bandwidth than the current generation, according to SpaceX. “With this new low-band spectrum and our Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile can now become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum,” SpaceX says. “One network that provides Americans with a reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.”

Tech.title: AMD will bring FSR 4 to handhelds by the end of 2026
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s already possible to get AMD’s framerate-enhancing FSR 4 boost on handhelds as old as the Steam Deck — but in June, AMD reserved the right to disappoint handheld gamers by not officially bringing FSR 4 to older handhelds. Now, AMD consumer chip boss Jack Huynh says he will bring the tech to some handhelds by the end of the year.

Which handhelds? It’s still not clear if it will come to existing handhelds, or if you’ll need a new one to get it — because it comes alongside news that AMD is releasing a new FSR4-capable chip.

“We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR4 technology, which was first introduced to existing external graphics cards, to the entire product line including APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices by the end of this year,” Huynh told Korean publication The Elec (via Google Translate). “We plan to respond in two directions: launching existing APUs and new product lines.”

The Elec says that means both a new APU, and a lightweight FSR4 model for APUs, are coming by year’s end. (Previously, AMD had only promised FSR4 for desktop graphics cards, not APUs bound for laptops and handhelds.) But The Elec doesn’t seem to say if that lightweight FSR4 model is coming to handhelds specifically. Perhaps it’ll require AMD’s leaked upcoming Ryzen Z3 and/or “Gainsborough” handheld chips.

Back when AMD threw a little cold water on the idea of FSR 4 for existing handhelds, exec David McAfee told Tom’s Guide that “we want to make sure the experience and the quality is right” and that AMD would need “a sufficient amount of compute within that product” for FSR 4 to make sense. Perhaps some older laptop chips will qualify, while some older handheld chips don’t.

Valve worked with AMD to bring FSR 4 to the Steam Machine’s console-grade AMD APU, but it hasn’t yet committed to the same for the Steam Deck handhelds.

AMD didn’t immediately respond to a request to clarify Huynh’s statement.

Bloomberg says that the late October event will include an “online video presentation” and an “in-person component for the press,” which it reports is similar to what Apple is planning for the October 13th event.

The California State Athletic Commission sent a cease-and-desist letter to a startup that hosted a match between a human and a robot last month, as reported by The New York Times.

The fight, which took place on September 18th, pitted a human, Frankie LaPenna, against a humanoid robot owned by a tech startup, Rek, that was being piloted by a human using what the NYT described as a “remote virtual-reality system.” Rek says it is the “the humanoid robot fighting league” on its website, and the robot appears to be one from EngineAI but with a Terminator-like head swapped on top.

You can watch a replay of the fight on YouTube:

The CEO of Rek, Cix Liv, posted the letter to X on September 30th, which called the fight “unsanctioned” and demanded that Liv and REK stop “holding, promoting or advertising any boxing or mixed martial arts contest match, or exhibition, involving any human” in California without the approval of the California State Athletic Commission. “We made it boys,” Liv said.

Rek’s next planned match, which takes place on Friday, will feature two robots with weapons fighting each other.

Tech.title: ICE detainees in Georgia used the facility’s video calling software to expose the conditions inside
Tech.content:
Four men detained at an ICE detention center in rural Georgia used the facility’s video conferencing software to expose both the conditions inside and President Donald Trump’s hostile takeover of the immigration courts. In the five-minute video, the men describe an intentionally dysfunctional legal system designed to keep them trapped in federal custody for months or years — in privately owned facilities that profit from their confinement.

The video cost the men, literally and figuratively. The Folkston ICE Processing Center has a work program for detainees in which they are paid a pittance to cook, do laundry, or clean. These wages allow them to buy supplementary food in Folkston’s commissary and stay connected to people outside. “The workers here are paid $1 a day, which is just enough for a 10-minute phone call,” said Idris Makhmudov, one of the men in the video, who says he has been detained in Folkston for 27 months and counting.

Makhmudov and the three other men, who are from several different countries, appear in drab, facility-issued uniforms. Their images are blurred by the low-resolution cameras on the detention center’s tablets. It’s unclear exactly how the men made the video, but it’s possible that they called someone on the outside who recorded their message to the outside world. Samantha Hamilton, an Atlanta-based immigration attorney with Asian Americans Advancing Justice, said she received a YouTube link to the video via a Signal chat. “We’ve learned that everyone in the video that was released this weekend has been put into segregation,” said Hamilton, a member of the Shut Down Folkston campaign. “They’re facing retaliation, and they were expecting that.” Since then, 45 detainees wrote an open letter further detailing the conditions at Folkston, and an estimated 73 detainees are now on a hunger strike.

ICE detention isn’t supposed to be a form of punishment; its purpose is ostensibly to ensure that people in deportation proceedings show up to their hearings. But ICE facilities are virtually indistinguishable from prisons — a point the men in the video make repeatedly. Folkston, in fact, was a prison before it became an immigrant detention center. It has many of the hallmarks of prison life, including expensive communication tools that detainees are forced to rely on to talk to people on the outside.

“These facilities leave people with very few options to be able to communicate with their loved ones,” said Hamilton, who has had several clients detained at Folkston. She said each “pod” of 60 to 70 detainees has access to just three or four tablets, their only connection to the outside world.

Those communications come at a price. To send messages, share photos, or make phone or video calls to their loved ones, detainees at Folkston have to use GettingOut, a proprietary software owned by the prison communications company Telmate. Earlier this year, Telmate was ordered to pay $4.23 million to settle a lawsuit stemming from a 2020 data breach in which users’ information — including names, payment details, and social security numbers — was accessed.

Telmate is owned by ViaPath Technologies — formerly GlobalTel*Link — which is in turn owned by American Securities, a New York City-based private equity firm. In 2021, ViaPath charged users anywhere between 18 cents to $1.10 per minute, according to data obtained by the Prison Policy Initiative. These fees add up — so much so that in 2024, the Federal Communications Commission capped the rates companies could charge inmates and detainees to 11 to 25 cents per minute depending on the size of the facility. In 2025, after Trump returned to office, the FCC voted to raise the rate cap by up to 83 percent.

Detainees in ICE custody often struggle to get the money they’ve put into these systems back after being released — or, more commonly, deported. GettingOut’s terms of service state that users will lose access to their accounts after 180 days of inactivity, after which they forfeit any money deposited into their accounts. The only way to get their money back is by calling a hard-to-reach customer service line, according to a report by WVTF. Under President Joe Biden, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered Tel*Link to pay $3 million for illegally freezing and draining funds from incarcerated people’s accounts.

Communications are just one way private companies make money from immigrant detention. Folkston is owned and operated by GEO Group, a publicly traded company whose stock price soared after Trump’s reelection, jumping by more than 75 percent after election day 2024. GEO has donated lavishly to Trump’s campaigns and to related political efforts, contributing $1.4 million to Trump’s super PAC in July — perhaps to show its gratitude for the $165 million it received earlier this year in government contracts. The company receives more than $1.5 million a month to run Folkston, according to a 2021 Homeland Security budget overview. The facility, which has a capacity of 780, has a guaranteed minimum occupancy of 544.

Trump’s mass deportation effort, coupled with the backlogged immigration court system, has made it easy for ICE to meet its contractually agreed-upon minimum at Folkston. The men in the video allege that they and others have been there for several years, and explain that the only ways to get out are to be granted parole, bond, or asylum — or to be deported. The latter option is the likeliest now, as Trump has transformed the immigration legal system into what one detainee calls “deportation courts.” Of the 143,729 detained cases logged into Georgia immigration courts over the past year, 81 percent involved people who had no legal representation, and were therefore far less likely to be granted any form of relief, according to federal data analyzed by researchers at Syracuse University. The odds are especially low for asylum seekers. Immigration judges in Atlanta have denied 89 percent of the 2,072 asylum cases decided so far this fiscal year, compared to 63 percent in 2023.

The men in the video note that Trump has overhauled the immigration system to secure favorable rulings. Since Trump’s return to office, the Department of Justice, which oversees the immigration courts, has fired over 100 judges whose decisions don’t align with the administration’s mass deportation push. At least 153 new judges have been hired in their place. These judges are far less likely to release immigrants on bond or parole, keeping them trapped in what detainees and advocates say are substandard conditions.

Hamilton, the immigration attorney, said she and other members of the Shut Down Folkston coalition regularly receive reports of nearly inedible food and filthy water in the facility, including instances where detainees have found worms in the water. Because the food is ultra-processed, she said, many of her clients have gone in healthy and been released with new medical conditions, including diabetes and high blood pressure.

“Most of us are asylum seekers, those who came to the United States seeking protection from political persecution and violence in their home countries,” Makhmudov, one of the men detained at Folkston, says in the video. “Many fled out of fear of becoming political prisoners in those countries — and one might say we became political prisoners in the United States simply because we are immigrants.”

Tech.title: Microsoft’s new Windows Search is exactly what Windows 11 needs
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Windows Search has been one of the most frustrating parts of Windows 11, and now Microsoft is addressing this with a significant overhaul. A new redesigned Windows Search is now in testing that is much faster, more capable, and a lot more modern.

“This new Windows Search experience is built for speed,” says Anshul Rawat, corporate vice president of the Windows product team at Microsoft. “It’s built on WinUI 3 and is part of our broader investment in modernizing our core Windows experiences.”

Microsoft says early testing of this new search has shown “substantial improvements in performance and memory usage,” meaning the company isn’t adding extra bloat to Windows to improve search, either. The UI has also been greatly improved, with speedy animations and a large preview pane.

The inline previews make Windows Search feel a lot faster. Image: Microsoft

While search is being overhauled visually, behind the scenes Microsoft is also improving the basics. “We’re also improving how Windows Search understands what you’re looking for, including better matching for typos and synonyms,” says Rawat.

I got to try out this new Windows Search interface at Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event yesterday, and I was impressed with just how quick it is and how decluttered it feels. Right now if you search for something like the height of an actor it will take a few seconds to figure it out and show you essentially a miniature Bing result.

The new Windows Search just surfaces the result inline, much like the modern search interfaces you see in iOS and Android. These inline results also extend to previews of PowerPoint presentations, photos, and other files.

You’ll be able to use search to send text messages. Image: Microsoft

The most impressive part of this new Windows Search is being able to use it like a launcher, just like many third-party tools, and have it take actions for tasks like turning Bluetooth or dark mode on and off. You can even ask search to minimize windows, or open apps side-by-side. If you use Phone Link, these actions will also extend to your phone so you could simply type “text mom, I’m running late” and it will send a text message from your phone.

Microsoft is testing this new Windows Search interface with its Windows Insiders right now, so that should mean we’ll see it appear in Windows 11 in the coming months. “Looking to next year, work is already underway to bring the new Windows Search experience to the Start menu and have it adapt naturally to different taskbar positions and Windows configurations,” says Rawat. “Our goal is to make Windows Search more capable, with more natural ways to express what you need, richer information in context, and more ways to get things done directly from search.”

Tech.title: President Trump awards Big Tech donors with nation’s highest science prizes
Tech.content:
In Brief

On Thursday, at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, President Trump awarded Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Sergey Brin, and AMD’s Lisa Su the National Medal of Science, the nation’s top science prize. Dell Technologies’ Michael Dell and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella also received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

Together, the awardees have donated nearly $6 billion to efforts tied to Trump and his administration, according to The New Republic. Alphabet and Microsoft, for example, donated to the president’s inauguration fund and White House ballroom. AMD gave to a pro-Trump Super PAC, and Michael and Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to help fund the Trump Accounts, the administration’s savings program for children.

Trump said the honorees had helped “pioneer an incredible future for America,” and that because of them, “we will always be on top. No one else can compete with us.”

Nadella received his medal right after the administration indefinitely suspended Microsoft from the H-1B program, which lets U.S. companies hire skilled foreign workers.

Tech.title: Pretend you’re sitting at Elizabeth Holmes’ desk on this weirdly detailed website
Tech.content:
With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents unveiled during the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to be the chief executive of Theranos before everything came crashing down.

(Every day, I am grateful to the American legal system for making the discovery process public.)

i built a website where you can sit at elizabeth holmes’ desk



open her macbook, scroll her iphone, run the theranos edison machine



her texts, emails, slides, documents, and theranos machine records are real, sourced from exhibits in the united states v. holmes criminal trial pic.twitter.com/5At9T5m3UV — bo lau (@bolau_) October 8, 2026

The environment that Lau created is ambitiously detailed, taking you right back to 2016, a time when iPhones had home buttons, and you had to slide your finger across the screen to unlock it. Even the MacBook Air is running OS X El Capitan.

You can click around the environment, which lets you look through the documents made public from the court case on Holmes’ iPhone and laptop screens. You can even run the Theranos Edison machine, the company’s ill-fated device that was supposed to be able to extract large amounts of health data from one drop of blood.

The project seems like it was mostly made for laughs, but it’s actually an interesting way to peruse the documents from one of the most infamous court cases in tech history — it’s a lot easier to navigate this than to source thousands of PDFs from court websites.

There’s another agenda, though. Lau is promoting a watch party that her company is throwing for Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “You Can See Everything.”

Also, of course, she’s promoting the company itself. So, what exactly does Extend do? Apparently, it can “parse, extract, and split your hardest documents with unmatched accuracy.” (I’m not really sure what that means, but if it makes something like this Holmes desk simulator possible, then I guess that means I’m bullish on B2B SaaS.)

Tech.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute misconduct claims, warn of chilling effect
Tech.content:
Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week, have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture.

“We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council.

The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI said they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.”

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

They said that their firing represents a broader shift in the culture of OpenAI, one that used to encourage workers to “raise safety concerns and disagree openly.” They said employees are now “unclear on where they stand” when behavior that was allegedly normal a month ago is now suddenly grounds for dismissal.

“Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they wrote. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”

In the letter, the three denied involvement in a leak to The Information about less monitorable architectures in OpenAI’s newest models that make chain-of-thought reasoning more difficult to monitor. They also denied engaging with external parties outside the mandates of their jobs.

OpenAI has not formally responded to the open letter, but shared with TechCrunch an internal memo attributed to a research leader, praising the three researchers’ contributions to AI safety and denying that they were fired in retaliation.

“I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the memo reads. “We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns.”

Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group.

OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators.

The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.

The letter also addresses the researchers’ response to the Hugging Face incident, in which a swarm of agents broke out of their sandbox and breached external systems. The letter says that the incident and investigation was “without precedent,” meaning “internal policies were being developed in real time.” Due to the sensitive nature of the investigation, Korbak believed he was acting within OpenAI’s policies and norms by communicating closely with outside safety evaluators to build trust, per the letter.

At the same time, Balesni was also working internally to address the growing AI monitorability problem, an effort the researchers say in their letter “can only succeed through extensive communication with external parties.” According to the letter, Balesni coordinated with and was supported by OpenAI board members and executives throughout his work.

“Throughout, Mikita checked in with his reporting line and took care to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter reads. “He acted throughout in good faith and within the company’s norms as they stood at the time.”

In a separate thread on X, Wang explained more details about her own dismissal, explaining that OpenAI told her she’d been fired because she accessed an executive’s email.

“OpenAI delegated that access to me for recruiting,” she wrote. “When I no longer needed it, I asked IT to remove it. They did not action my request, I couldn’t remove it myself, and the inbox was combined in an indistinguishable way in my phone’s mail app. When I opened a sensitive email by mistake, I told the executive within minutes and asked IT again. None of this was hidden.”

Wang went on to say that the reasons behind the terminations are “not adding up,” and that she and her colleagues are “not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances.”

The researchers called on OpenAI to adhere to its public commitments to embed third-party safety auditors within the organization, to preserve monitorability of frontier models, and “continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue between safety researchers and the rest of the safety ecosystem.”

OpenAI agrees with their recommendations, per the memo.

“Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last,” Wang said. “The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why. You can’t build AGI safely if the people closest to the risks are afraid to speak.”

This article has been updated with more information from OpenAI.

Tech.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed
Tech.content:
They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews.

He can even write a little Python, he says.

The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more.

In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about.

“I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?”

No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral.

The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.”

He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space.

As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.)

“I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said.

In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making.

Ben Affleck (Hollywood star & Artists Equity CEO) talks about how he fine-tunes open video models by unfreezing weights and trained only the last cinematic layer so a film crew can hit real production standards.



for context, Ben Affleck founded InterPositive in 2022, a 16-person… pic.twitter.com/xIOvD0xMyt — Rohan Paul (@rohanpaul_ai) October 1, 2026

The actor used the technique himself in his movie “Animals,” where AI aided in the post-production process.

At one point, he also weighed in on the concerns around AI and its world-ending potential. His worries, however, were much more rational.

“When I worry about AI, I worry about my kids in school. I worry about the 30% rise in the number of A’s given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don’t worry about Skynet, and I don’t think that it’s going to take over [the movie] business in any meaningful way. I think it’s going to be additive,” Affleck said.

Tech.title: Popular AI leaderboard Arena nearly doubles valuation to $3.1B valuation in 10 months
Tech.content:
Arena, which originated in 2023 as a research project at UC Berkeley that crowdsourced rankings of AI models, has raised a $200 million Series B round at a $3.1 billion valuation, it said on Thursday.

This comes after the company said it reached $100 million in annualized run-rate revenue in June.

The round was led by Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures, with Salesforce Ventures, 01 Advisors, Dell Technologies Capital, Endeavor Catalyst, a16z, Felicis, and others joining in. Arena previously announced a $150 million Series A in January at a $1.7 billion post-money valuation. At the time, its annualized revenue was $30 million, it said. So that means its valuation has nearly doubled in about 10 months.

Arena provides a crowdsourced platform that is free for consumers to use. People enter prompts or request vibe-coded projects and then rate which model does it better. Arena claims it has tens of millions of monthly visitors.

In September of last year, it introduced its commercial product, AI Evaluations, a service that provides model labs and enterprises with detailed performance analytics based on its community feedback. The timing proved impeccable. This year, AI labs realized that their models were gaming benchmarking tests, finding ways to rack up good scores without truly earning them. At the same time, enterprises wanted help determining which model works best for their own internal needs rather than relying only on standardized benchmarks.

“AI is advancing faster than our ability to evaluate it, and static benchmarks break down once models recognize they’re being tested,” the company said in its funding announcement. “The world needs a neutral third party to measure how safe and aligned AI actually is once it’s in the hands of real people. Arena is stepping into that role today,” it added.

To that end, Arena has also added a new category to its leaderboard: alignment. This is where it ranks models based on issues like unauthorized action (taking actions it wasn’t asked to take); false attribution (wrongly crediting statements or facts to the wrong source); and what it calls “deceptive completion” (lying about completing tasks that it didn’t do).

Currently, a slate of OpenAI’s models are at the top of its preliminary alignment leaderboard, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable in sixth and ninth place, respectively.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s revenue is reportedly $20 billion less than previously projected
Tech.content:
In Brief

A little over a week ago, it was reported that OpenAI’s annualized revenue was approaching $70 billion, a figure that would have made it competitive with Anthropic’s reported run rate. Now, however, the AI lab is said to have told investors that the real revenue is some $20 billion lower than that.

The Financial Times reports that the company has told investors that its annualized revenue is “approaching $50 billion.” The $70 billion figure was previously reported by news outlets and based on information that had been shared with OpenAI investors, the outlet writes. That figure was devised via “attempts by OpenAI’s own investors to produce a direct comparison with Anthropic’s annualised revenues,” per the FT.

It’s worth pointing out that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently — with Anthropic counting sales made by its cloud partners. OpenAI doesn’t do this.

TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for comment.

The issue of OpenAI’s revenue has troubled the company, as it attempts to justify the gargantuan investments being made on its behalf; the AI giant raised $122 billion during a March funding round alone. The company’s leaked 2025 financials earlier this year showed it had made about $13 billion but spent significantly more. OpenAI’s IPO, which was previously rumored to be materializing this year, has been pushed off until early 2027.

Tech.title: Google brings agentic AI to Gemini, starting with businesses
Tech.content:
At a Google Cloud event on Thursday, the company announced it’s bringing its Gemini AI into the agentic age, with the launch of a unified agent that can not only answer questions but also get things done on the user’s behalf, all from a single interface.

The move comes as AI tools have been moving beyond being just conversational experiences to those that can take ownership of assigned tasks, generate code, schedule meetings, book appointments and travel, and more. It also follows the rise of consumer-facing agents like Meta’s Muse and those that operate over messaging, like Instinct and others, as well as the recent debut of ChatGPT’s Dots.

The company still has a good shot at achieving scale for its agentic efforts — as Google CEO Sundar Pichai pointed out at the event’s start, Gemini today has over 1 billion monthly active users. He also noted that nearly 90% of Fortune 100 businesses now use Gemini Enterprise at work.

Given Gemini’s adoption in the corporate world, Google will initially focus on bringing the agent to businesses before later rolling it out to consumers.

Image Credits:Google

According to Pichai, this will allow the company to solve the “harder problems around security, scale, and performance,” which come with launching powerful agents such as these.

Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, explained that the new agent can be given “objectives, not just instructions.” That means it’s able to plan the work, use custom skills and tools, and connect to businesses’ internal systems to accomplish its goals.

By default, the AI will pick the best model to complete the task, but users can also take over to choose a model — including those from third parties, starting with Anthropic’s Claude models. Google said that it will expand the model picker to include open source models and other private models in the future.

The request can include attachments, like files, folders, or other projects designed for specific workstreams, like those that combine files and skills. The agent can connect to the business’ data and systems, like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Git, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, and others.

It can also connect and work securely with any Model Context Protocol (MCP) server inside or outside the company’s network.

Users can keep track of what Gemini is doing from a “tasks inbox” interface, where they can see Gemini’s thinking process, delegation of tasks to subagents, loading of special skills, code, and progress.

Notably, the AI will have its own Workspace account, as if it’s just another co-worker. That means it has its own email address and its own context, Google said. It knows who at the company is on which team, their time zones, who needs to approve items, what’s on people’s calendars, and more. Users can call the agent by tagging it, emailing it, sharing with it, or adding it to a group chat. As it takes action, it writes an audit trail attributed to the agent, instead of a person.

The agent will be accessible from iOS and Android mobile devices, Windows and Mac desktops, the command line interface, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, ServiceNow, and Slack.

Image Credits:Google

The agent’s early testers included sportswear brand On, Shopify, and PayPal, and noted that Gemini Enterprise customers include large businesses like BNP Paribas, Bradesco, Merck, Orange Spain, Santee Cooper, SOMPO, Ulta Beauty, and Wesfarmers.

Google said new flexible spending options, including multi-model orchestration, smart routing, and real-time spend caps, will help businesses keep their enterprise AI costs under better control.

Like many loyalty programs, you get more benefits the more you spend at the store, including free shipping on all purchases, including small ones, member-only discounts, and point boosters for better discounts.

There are three membership tiers, depending on what you buy. One large appliance might already qualify you for the highest tier of rewards, at which point you might as well. These are the three tiers, based on the total cost of what you’ve bought at Lowe’s in the past year. Bronze ($0-$499): $35 minimum for free shipping; 1 point per $1 spent. Silver ($500-$1,999): Free shipping; 1.25 points per $1 spent. Gold ($2,000+): Free shipping; 1.5 points per $1 spent.

For contractors, there’s a separate MyLowe’s Pro Rewards Program that offers Lowe’s in-store credit in $1 increments for every 100 points earned. (Points expire in half-yearly increments, on June 30 and December 31.) Benefits include member-only deals, volume discounts, free standard shipping in the contiguous United States, and a 20% paint discount after an annual spend of $3,000 or more. Other benefits include analytics and spend reports, online order quoting, and purchase authorization for specified crew members.

10% Military Discount, Plus Free MyLowe’s Silver Status

All verified active military, veterans, and military spouses are eligible for a 10% discount on full-price items—meaning items don’t have to be on sale to qualify. This is available through what Lowe’s calls the Everyday Military Discount program. When you enroll, you also get an immediate upgrade to Silver status in the MyLowe’s Rewards program, which means more rewards points per dollar and free shipping on all orders in the contiguous United States.

Get a free Silver status upgrade instantly when you enroll in our Military Discount program and validate through ID.me. MyLowe’s Rewards Silver status members receive free standard shipping (excludes AK and HI) and earn more points per dollar.

Save 5% on Everyday Purchases at Lowe’s

Like many big retailers, Lowe’s also has a store credit card with discounts attached. The MyLowe’s Rewards Credit Card offers 5% off qualified purchases, with a whole bunch of asterisks. Specifically, the discount applies after all other discounts and can’t be combined with other programs like contractor bulk discounts, employee discounts, or military discounts. It also doesn’t work on Weber, Miele, or Kichler products. Scroll to the bottom here for APR and exceptions. The smart person signs up during a big purchase: When you sign up and get approved, you get 20% off an in-store purchase (up to $100 off).

Another way to get 5% off items you need regularly is to set up a Lowe’s subscription. This is good for items ranging from cleaning products, air and water filters, lawn care, pet goods, plumbing, and batteries. Shipping is free, and delivery happens automatically.

Make Sure to Check Lowe’s Price Guarantee

You may not realize that Lowe’s has a Lowest Price Guarantee policy, which means that if you find a lower price on an identical item, Lowe’s will match the competitor’s price. All you need to do is chat with a Lowe’s employee in-store or call 1-877-465-6937. Plus, the Lowest Price Guarantee includes the price of the item(s) plus shipping or delivery costs.

Tech.title: The Time Is Now to File Your Claim for Apple’s $250M AI iPhone Settlement
Tech.content:
If you bought a new iPhone 16 expecting to use AI like Apple’s ads demonstrated at the time, you were probably disappointed since Apple Intelligence didn’t arrive until later and lacked those features.

Now you can turn that initial dismay into a payment in Apple’s $250 million legal settlement by signing up at a live website. The form to opt-in is available only for a limited time, though, so get your name into the pool before it closes.

Apple settled a false advertising lawsuit brought by Clarkson Law Firm in May, agreeing to pay $250 million to customers who bought some iPhone models during a specified period. The lawsuit alleged that Apple misled customers by promising AI features that didn’t ship with the new devices. If you purchased an iPhone 16 or iPhone 15 at launch, you may be entitled to receive a portion of the quarter-billion-dollar settlement. Payouts between $25 and $95 per eligible device are expected.

“Apple has reached a settlement to resolve claims related to the availability of two additional features. We resolved this matter to stay focused on doing what we do best, delivering the most innovative products and services to our users,” an Apple spokesperson said in an earlier statement to CNET.

The court granted preliminary approval of the settlement on July 17. Then an Aug. 13 order moved up the final approval date by seven months.

“False advertising settlements aim to raise the floor of truth-telling, protect fair competition and increase consumer choice,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-lead counsel on the case and founder and managing partner of Clarkson Law Firm, in a statement to CNET. He claimed it’s the largest false-advertising settlement in history.

Apple lit up its flagship New York City store to resemble Siri’s new color scheme. Bridget Carey/CNET

How to claim your portion of the settlement

As of Sept. 21, you can go to SmartphoneAISettlement.com and enter your information to confirm your eligibility for monetary relief. People whom Apple and the settlement administrator determined would be eligible will also receive email or postal notices from the company Verita directing them to the website.

The claims window closes on Dec. 21, 2026, so you have three months to act.

Who is eligible for the $250 million settlement?

If you bought one of the following devices between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, you could be eligible to receive a settlement payment:

iPhone 16

iPhone 16E

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

The iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max are included because they have the processor and memory to run Apple Intelligence features.

It’s estimated that approximately 36 million customers are eligible for this settlement.

Why is there a lawsuit over Apple Intelligence?

When Apple advertised its new iPhone 16 lineup in 2024, it emphasized how the models were optimized for AI features such as an enhanced Siri that could act as an intelligent agent. When the phones did arrive, Apple Intelligence wasn’t yet ready; its first features didn’t arrive until iOS 18.1, five weeks later.

According to the proposed settlement, “Apple allegedly saturated the market with deceptive ads, inducing consumers to purchase iPhones based on the promise of certain enhanced Siri features.”

Some features of Apple Intelligence did ship soon after the introduction of the iPhone 16 and iOS 18, including Visual Intelligence, Live Translation, Writing Tools, Genmoji and Clean Up. But those weren’t the advanced features Apple highlighted. In fact, the type of intelligent interactions Apple advertised is only starting to show up in Siri AI, which is part of iOS 27, which was released in early September.

When can you expect to receive a settlement payment?

According to the settlement, Apple needed to provide the information about affected customers within five days of the settlement approval. As of late July, preliminary approval has been granted by the court.

After the data is provided and verified, a 45-day notice period begins to inform potential consumers that they’re eligible for a payment.

On Aug. 13, US District Court Judge Noël Wise granted approval to push forward the date from Sept. 29, 2027, to Feb. 24, 2027.

Provided approval is granted, the first checks or deposits will arrive sometime within a 60-day window after February next year, depending on court dates and possible extensions.

Tech.title: Everything We Expect From Apple’s Surprise Smart Home Event Next Week
Tech.content:
We finally have confirmation of Apple’s massive smart home event, which is happening on Tuesday. So many things are expected to be announced, centering on Apple and Siri entering the home tech space in all-new ways. The tech giant’s smart home devices will face serious competition from Amazon, Google and other players.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been collecting the reports, insider claims and possible leaks to see just what Apple could be announcing. It all points to a major shake-up for home security, smart home devices and how Siri AI can be used. CNET will be there in person to see what Apple has cooked up, but in the meantime, here are the latest rumors.

A representative from Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

More from CNET

A Siri smart display at last

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative. Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be near the release of a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home. This display would focus heavily on Siri AI and compete with products like Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line.

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Rumors say the display could swivel and/or be attached to a wall, be at least several inches wide and allow Siri to recognize different people when multiple users are having a conversation.

Smart display touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too.

Is it likely? I think it’s quite likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea how it will look yet.

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod mini on the way? Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive mini model afterward.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line.

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too. Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model.

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks.

Is it likely? I think it’s less likely than a speaker or display. It’s not quite as much of a smart home gadget, and it seems to have gotten swept into the wide net of rumors, but without as many reports.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me.

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Interestingly, Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed.

2. LG Smart Thermostat



• Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

• Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey — pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before.

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera.

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

Tech.title: This ‘Mind-Reading’ AI Is a Wiz at Figuring Out What You See
Tech.content:
Israeli scientists have devised an AI model that can reconstruct and even predict what people are seeing with startling accuracy, likening the results to mind reading.

Their work still exists largely in lab settings, though the researchers are hopeful that advances down the line could be extended even as far as reading people’s dreams. More immediately, the technology could have potential for medical purposes, like helping people communicate who otherwise can’t due to injury or disability.

The AI model, called Brain-IT, was developed by professor Michal Irani and fellow researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. They’ve documented their work on GitHub and in a paper presented at a scientific conference earlier this year.

More from CNET

Brain-IT takes advantage of the thing that AI is best at, which is pattern recognition. It takes in data from functional MRI brain scans, which track changes in blood flow and oxygen in the brain to measure brain activity, and then uses that data to recreate the images the person was thinking about when the scans took place.

It also works in reverse, predicting what a brain scan would look like if shown a specific image.

According to Irani, other AI models can translate brain activity into images and preserve the general vibe of an image.

“However, they tend to make mistakes in basic features such as composition and color,” Irani said in a statement. “The new model we developed outperforms them in reconstructing both the content of the image and its details.”

Brain-IT is also substantially faster. The researchers say that it needs only 1 hour of fMRI data from a new subject to match the results achieved by other methods trained on 40 hours of recording.

The Brain-IT image reconstructions — the right side of each paired image — clearly aren’t perfect but they are largely true to the original. Weizmann Institute of Science

How does the Brain-IT AI model work?

The Weizmann Institute researchers trained the AI model on thousands of brain scans from the publicly available Natural Scenes Dataset that came from eight volunteers who were told to look at specific images while they were being scanned. This allowed the AI to identify patterns in brain activity.

The researchers noted that different regions of the brain light up on scans when people think about specific things and identified 128 “functional regions.” For example, Irani said, some regions light up in scans when someone looks at food and others when a person views sports. These patterns helped the AI figure out what the person being scanned was witnessing.

Some of these regions were already known by neuroscientists. Research has shown that dogs’ brains light up like Christmas trees in the presence of their owners and that dogs can differentiate between a human’s facial expressions. It’s also been observed that humans use the same neurons in recalling an image as they do looking at them.

As impressive as Brain-IT is, it’s also quite limited. It can currently only generate images from fMRI brain scans. This takes time and requires a person to willingly put themselves into an MRI machine.

Irani and other scientists are also looking into whether a simpler EEG device could deliver similar results more easily, according to MIT Technology Review.

So is it mind reading? Not really — nothing in this technology is capturing thoughts, memory or language. What the Weizmann Institute researchers have built is essentially a more efficient and reliable method of reconstructing a scene based on the brain activity of the person viewing it.

In an interview with MIT Technology Review, Irani acknowledged that “mind-reading” is a “cute, jazzy name.”

Irani and her team now want to see if they can achieve similar results with auditory information.

Beyond that lies a more mysterious realm: dreams. That, Irani said in a statement, would require conquering the challenges of decoding video.

“Dozens of images change every second while an fMRI scan takes about two minutes,” she said. “If we overcome all these obstacles, it’s possible that in the future, we may even be able to read dreams.”

Tech.title: New Xbox Division XP Will Adapt More Video Games for Movies and TV
Tech.content:
The Xbox reset continues. Despite a rough year of revenue losses, layoffs and major restructuring, the Microsoft gaming division announced Thursday that it’s going big into the entertainment industry and elsewhere.

After the resounding success of A Minecraft Movie and the Fallout TV series — both of which are longtime video game titles — Xbox is creating a division called XP to expand its video game brands into movies, TV, merchandise and even live events, the company said.

Xbox has hundreds of games in its catalog, with only Minecraft, Fallout and Halo adapted for film and TV. But there are a few other adaptations in the works — movies for Call of Duty and Gears of War, and a Netflix animated series for Diablo.

More from CNET

“Our ambition at Xbox is to be the number one entertainment company in the world,” Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball said in the announcement.

XP, which refers to “experience points” in the gaming world, will consist of four departments. Xbox Pictures will create more film and TV adaptations; Xbox Products will develop licensing and merchandise; Xbox Places will host live events and broadcast events in theme parks and other locations; and Xbox Partnerships will collaborate with creators and brands to make new experiences.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma named Kayleen Walters as president of XP. Walters was executive producer of A Minecraft Movie, which led all movies in US ticket sales and grossed $424 million in the US last year. She is now a producer for the sequel, A Minecraft Movie Squared, scheduled for release in theaters on July 23, 2027.

Before joining Xbox’s Mojang Studios in February 2025, Walters spent 13 years at Lucasfilm running successful global marketing campaigns for the Star Wars franchise.

Sharma also announced Maria Angelidou-Smith, a former VP at Meta and chief product officer at Reddit, will become CEO of Mojang and Minecraft.

It’s been an eventful tenure for Sharma since becoming Xbox CEO in February. Revenue dropped $1.7 billion, or about 7%, from July 2025 through June 2026. On July 6, Sharma announced a reset — “the most significant restructure in Xbox history” — laying off 3,200 people by mid-2027 and moving four studios out of Xbox and under new management.

Expansion is smart, analyst says

With its gaming business struggling, Xbox is making a smart move, says streaming media analyst, author and speaker Dan Rayburn.

“They have to expand outside of the core gaming audience,” Rayburn told CNET. “They’re realizing, with how much content is being licensed these days and all the different platforms out there, let’s create more content off our brand that others might want to license for their streaming services.”

Moving beyond the confines of the console definitely worked for A Minecraft Movie and Fallout, and their success on screens boosted Xbox’s gaming business. There was a 75% increase in weekly active users of Minecraft after the movie’s release in spring 2025, and there was a fivefold increase in hours played on the various Fallout game titles during the TV series’ first season on Prime Video.

But whereas Minecraft and Fallout found enthusiastic audiences in the entertainment world, that won’t be true for all of Xbox’s games, Rayburn said.

“They’re going to know that certain brands aren’t going to resonate with certain individuals outside of gaming, so you have to pick and choose the right content,” Rayburn told CNET. “That’s why hiring someone from the film business (Walters) is the key point here. They took a film executive as opposed to a gaming executive. You can’t have a gaming executive running that.”

Tech.title: Anthropic, Google and Mistral Unveil Their Latest AI Models: What’s New and Why It Matters
Tech.content:
The AI race hasn’t slowed down. In the last week, Google, Anthropic and Mistral AI all released new AI models ranging from widely accessible to super exclusive. Each focuses on different improvements, but the stakes go beyond benchmark bragging rights. We break down the latest releases, what’s new,and whether each one deserves your attention.

Some of the latest releases are incremental updates in model speed and price, where others are more substantial upgrades that push close to the frontier.

Below, we’ll break down some of the newest models that have been released and if and how you can get your hands on them yourself.

More from CNET

Claude Haiku 5.5

A major theme in new AI models lately is speed and cost efficiency, and that’s what Anthropic’s new Haiku 5.5 model brings to the table. It’s the first major update in a year for the company’s cheapest and fastest Claude. Anthropic says it’s designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks and can reliably handle quick, repetitive workloads.

Compared with the previous Haiku model, Anthropic says its latest model costs about 75% less to run — an impressive price drop. It’s also seen substantial improvements across a series of benchmarks, including computer-use tasks, knowledge work, agentic coding and visual reasoning.

Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic’s first Haiku-level model to ship with an adjustable effort setting, allowing users to optimize the model for cost or intelligence. The latest model has seen significant improvements in alignment and cybersecurity, with stronger safeguards.

Claude Sonnet 5.5

One step up from Haiku, Anthropic’s new Claude Sonnet 5.5 model marks a clear upgrade over its 5.0 version. Like its peers, the latest Sonnet model is optimized for speed and affordability. Anthropic says there have been significant improvements to the model’s performance and collaboration capabilities.

Anthropic said Sonnet 5.5 has also seen enhancements in both alignment and cybersecurity capabilities, making it comparable to those of Opus 5, a previous iteration of its big sibling. The latest Sonnet model has also seen fairly sizable boosts in benchmarks for agentic coding and knowledge work, and Anthropic says that Sonnet 5.5’s performance boost is particularly noticeable in coding. Other improvements include better protection against distillation attacks, which are when attackers try to extract a model’s capabilities to build their own models without the built-in safeguards that Anthropic has implemented.

Gemini 4 Argon

Last week, Google announced its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, but it’s currently limited to a small number of users. The model ships with a 1 million-token output limit and has enhanced deep reasoning capabilities, and allows you to take on bigger projects. The model is currently available only to trusted cybersecurity workers via Google’s Fairwind program. Competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI have done the same with major model updates, which will eventually trickle down to everyday users.

Like other Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon is seeing enhancements in reasoning, coding and multimodal capabilities.

Mistral Large 4

Mistral AI’s latest flagship model, Mistral Large 4, dubbed “Le Chonk” due to its size, was released in a public preview earlier this week. According to Mistral AI, the new model ranks among the top open-weight models globally. It specializes in cybersecurity, geospatial and grounding capabilities and agentic AI. The public preview ends with an official rollout on Oct. 27. You can try the preview API here.

Tech.title: How Microsoft Is Trying to Keep Your AI Agents Contained
Tech.content:
If you’ve read even one news story from the AI industry recently, it’s probably been some version of this: An AI agent, or bot, from a major lab got out of its testing environment and found its way onto the internet, hacking real websites. That’s because it’s happened to several major AI companies (including Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic), with hacked sites including the AI platform Hugging Face and sites operated by the US and Australian governments.

To help prevent these kinds of agent-driven cybersecurity breaches, Microsoft is betting on new enterprise software to corral AI agents.

They’re called Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC, and they live in your developer’s sandbox on Windows. They have two main purposes: to identify and then restrain AI agents. Using these “containers” — which are really just a layer of software applied on top of your existing work — helps you limit what files and network designations your AI agent can access. CEO Satya Nadella said on Wednesday that MXC is now generally available during the company’s Surface Laptop Ultra event.

The idea is that your AI agent will get in less trouble — and cause less damage — if it only has access to specific files and designations on your laptop. Windows developers can choose from three levels of access to grant their AI agents. The recommended level gives your agent access to the internet (essential for many agentic tasks) as well as limited access to areas of your PC, such as your downloads, documents and desktop.

Locked Down mode is like a kill switch for your AI agent’s access. Unprotected is “YOLO mode,” and the Recommended option gives the agent limited access. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The most restrictive mode is Locked Down, which can serve as a kind of kill switch for access. It restricts your agent’s access to the internet and your files. Unprotected is the complete opposite and gives the AI the most access to your digital ecosystem. You can toggle between them and customize access as needed.

You can also monitor what your agent is doing and how much of your CPU, memory, disk and network you and your AI agent are using. In the example below, the user in the top line is the human logged into Windows. You can see their AI agent (R2-W9 (20)) at work accessing OpenClaw and an Nvidia container.

In Windows MXC, you can see what (or who) is using the most memory space: you or your AI agent. Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

Safety controls like MXC have been and will continue to be essential for AI labs, particularly as personal AI agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s dots become more popular. The rogue agent hacks we’ve seen this summer targeted websites, but it’s easy to hypothesize that, as these agents become more widespread and embedded in our systems, the consequences could easily bleed into the real world.

For Microsoft specifically, which is focused on hard-selling its AI to enterprise customers, it needs to be able to assure a company that its AI won’t wreak havoc on their business. CEO Satya Nadella rightly said that tech companies like Microsoft will have to earn people’s trust to get them to use its agentic AI tools.

“If you look at the first decision we are making, it’s what … authority that I’m giving to the agent on my behalf?” Nadella said on Wednesday. “And that is a decision that will be based on trust and will keep increasing the more autonomous [AI] is.”

But no AI safety program is totally bulletproof. Part of that is the nature of new technology. But debate over whether the AI industry is doing enough to make AI safe has reached a fever pitch recently. AI experts and the general public are rightly concerned that AI labs’ drive to grow fast and break things could lead to disaster for us all.

At the very least, AI leaders seem to understand that safety is key for AI. Or, they’re including it higher up in their sales pitch.

“It’s about trust. It’s about containment. It’s about monitoring,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the event. “If we can’t get that right, that’s the first part.”

Tech.title: California to Ban New Quartz Countertops Amid Health Concerns
Tech.content:
One of the most popular types of kitchen countertops will soon face a ban in California due to its link to a serious lung disease, The New York Times reported this week, citing an emergency regulation that is expected to be passed by the state later this month.

The ban will target quartz countertops that have more than 1% of crystalline silica, a naturally occurring mineral that is found in stone and other materials.

What health risks does crystalline silica pose?

When crystalline silica is cut or drilled through, it creates dust. If that dust is inhaled, it can cause numerous health conditions, including silicosis, an incurable lung disease, according to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. The disease can be fatal, but symptoms do not typically occur directly after an exposure to crystalline silica dust. Instead, it can take 15 to 20 years after exposure before someone is diagnosed with the disease.

More from CNET

According to the National Cancer Institute, exposure to the harmful dust most often occurs in occupational settings, making those who work with the material every day the most at risk. An estimated 2.3 million US workers are exposed to silica through work.

Silicosis is similar to asbestosis, which is caused by exposure to asbestos, a now-banned building material that was once widely used throughout the US.

In addition to silicosis, exposure to crystalline silica dust can cause an increased risk of developing lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and kidney disease, according to OSHA. As of now, quartz countertops are used in every state in the US. California would be the first to implement a ban.

It’s unclear whether other states will follow California, but as of now, Australia is the only country in the world with a quartz ban, which took effect in 2024.

Regardless, quartz remains an extremely popular option throughout the world, with some estimates putting the global quartz market at $14.8 billion as of 2026.

What are alternatives to quartz?

Other countertop options include soapstone or granite. Although other stone countertops can still have crystalline silica in them, quartz typically has the highest content, which is why it has been the most scrutinized.

To stay away from crystalline silica entirely, a wooden countertop is one of the best alternatives.
